entries.t: How USAAIO works and how to use this site
entries.x: This lesson covers three things: the stages of the contest, how Round 1 is run and scored, and how this site works. The scoring rule decides when you should guess, so it is worth points on exam day. The path to Team USA USAAIO (USA AI Olympiad) runs the USA-North America AI Olympiad (USA-NA-AIO), the contest you registered for. It has three stages: 1. Round 1 : Friday, February 19, 2027, 12:00 to 3:00 pm Eastern Time. You take it on your own laptop at a proctored site (your school or another approved test site). Everything on this site before February targets Round 1. 2. Round 2 : invitation only, "March or April 2027". It covers the whole syllabus, including transformers and generative models, and some problems use a GPU. In 2026 the organizers invited "nearly 200" students from Round 1. 3. Round 3 : the USAAIO camp in June 2027. Team USA is chosen at camp. The team goes to IOAI (International Olympiad in Artificial Intelligence), which is in Singapore on July 4 to 10, 2027. Round 1 in 2027 The 2027 format is new this year. Round 1 has two parts with a 15-minute gap between them. Part 1 (no coding) Part 2 (coding) --- --- --- Start window 12:00 to 12:15 pm ET 1:30 to 1:45 pm ET Length 60 minutes; closes 1:15 pm 75 minutes; closes 3:00 pm Problems 20; each is 5-choice multiple choice or an integer 000 to 999 coding tasks shown on contest.usaaio.org, solved in Google Colab Resources none (blank scratch paper from the proctor) only two organizer documents (lesson u00-l04 covers both) Scoring 7.5 right, 0 wrong, 1.5 blank; 150 total not published Integer answers are always entered as three digits: 7 is entered as 007. Part 2 runs on CPU only; GPUs are not allowed. The number of Part 2 problems is not published. The official 2027 sample set has five Part 2 problems: a NumPy function with banned functions, a regression class with fit and predict , a pandas data-cleaning task, a small PyTorch network built by hand, and an open-ended model scored on hidden test data. The official Round 1 topic list: Markdown in Google Colab, math foundations for AI (linear algebra, probability, multivariable calculus, optimization), basic coding (Python, NumPy, pandas, matplotlib, scikit-learn), machine learning, PyTorch, deep learning foundations, and basics of CNNs. Transformers, language models and generative models are Round 2 topics. Part 1 scoring: when to guess A blank is worth 1.5 points, so a blank beats a wrong answer. To decide whether to guess, compare the blank's 1.5 with the expected score of answering: the average points per question you would get if you faced the same situation many times. If you are right with probability $p$, the expected score of answering is Answering beats a blank exactly when $7.5p 1.5$, that is, when $p \frac{1}{5}$. Your situation $p$ Expected score of answering Decision --- --- --- --- Pure guess, 5 choices 1/5 1.5 tie: leave it blank Eliminated 1 choice 1/4 1.875 guess Eliminated 2 choices 1/3 2.5 guess Eliminated 3 choices 1/2 3.75 guess Integer item, no idea 1/1000 0.0075 leave it blank The rule in one line: guess on a multiple-choice item once you can rule out at least one choice; never guess blindly on an integer item. You can check the arithmetic here. This box is a try block : edit the code and run it. The value of the last line is shown, the same way a Colab cell shows it. How to use this site - Today picks what to do in a session, sized to the minutes you have: reviews that are due, the next lesson, and one coding task. - Lessons are short. Try blocks run Python in your browser (Pyodide, which downloads on the first run, so that run takes longer). Its NumPy, pandas and scikit-learn versions differ a little from Colab's (Colab: Python 3.13, NumPy 2.4.6, pandas 2.2.3, scikit-learn 1.6.1), and NumPy integers default to int32 there instead of int64, so a few printed results can differ from Colab's. PyTorch does not run in the browser: those try blocks show output recorded with PyTorch 2.14.1 for CPU, and a Copy code button lets you run them in a Colab cell. A try block cannot break anything, so change the numbers and rerun. - Checks are Part 1-style questions inside lessons. After you answer, you see a worked solution and the mistake behind each wrong choice. Questions you miss come back later for review. - Cards ask you to type one line of code from memory, such as "sum each row and keep the result 2D". Your line is run and checked by what it does, so any correct way passes. Part 2 allows no documentation, so this recall is what the cards train. - Coding lab has Part 2-style problems. Run checks the visible examples. Submit runs hidden tests and also checks imports, banned functions, time limits, and that your code did not change its inputs. Those are the same kinds of checks the official grader makes. - Mocks are full Round 1 practice exams under the official timing. Words in a lesson that show as links, like expected score, have a short definition when you hover over them. Part 1 is 20 problems in 60 minutes, so about 3 minutes each. On a first pass, answer what you can and skip what is slow. Then come back and apply the guessing rule to what is left.

Every Part 2 problem is solved in Google Colab, under time pressure and with no documentation. Knowing where things are in Colab and how its memory works saves minutes and prevents one specific disaster: a notebook that works on your screen but not when the grader runs it fresh. Notebooks and cells Google Colab is a website (colab.research.google.com) that runs Python for you on a Google computer. You sign in with a Google account; notebooks are saved in your Google Drive, in a folder named "Colab Notebooks". A notebook is a document made of cells, saved as a .ipynb file. A cell is one box in the notebook. There are two kinds: - A code cell holds Python. When you run it, its output appears right under it. - A text cell holds Markdown: headings, lists and math (lesson u00-l03). Running it shows the formatted text. Double-click a text cell to edit it again. The "+ Code" and "+ Text" buttons near the top of the notebook add cells. To run a code cell, click the run button at its left, or press Shift+Enter (run, then move to the next cell) or Ctrl+Enter (run and stay; on a Mac, Cmd+Enter also works). Tools Keyboard shortcuts lists the rest. If the last line of a code cell is an expression, Colab displays its value without print . Earlier lines need print to show anything. The try blocks on this site follow the same rule: The runtime: where your variables live When you run a cell, the code goes to the runtime , a Python process on a Google machine that stays alive between cells. Variables, imported modules and defined functions live in the runtime's memory, not in the notebook file. So cells share variables, and the order in which you ran cells matters, not the order they appear on the page . The number in brackets beside a cell, like [3] , says it was the third cell run in this session. Suppose a notebook has these cells: Running Cell 2 three times leaves total at 25, even though the page shows one + 5 . If you delete Cell 1, total still exists in memory until you restart. This invisible leftover state is called hidden state , and it is how a notebook can work on your screen and fail for the grader. The Runtime menu has the fixes (the exact wording can change between Colab versions; look for these words): - Restart session (older name: Restart runtime): wipes all variables and imports. Files you wrote to disk stay. - Run all : runs every cell from top to bottom. - Restart session and run all : both. This is the official check in miniature: in Part 2 your notebook, run top to bottom in a fresh session, must reproduce the file you submit. - Disconnect and delete runtime : throws the machine away, including every file on it. Files: the Files panel, upload and download The runtime has its own disk. Your notebook starts in the folder /content . Click the folder icon in the left sidebar to open the Files panel; a fresh runtime shows a sample data folder there. - Upload : use the upload icon at the top of the Files panel, or drag files from your computer into the panel. - Download : open the menu next to a file in the panel (three dots or a right-click) and choose Download. - Files on the runtime are temporary. They disappear when the runtime is deleted, which Colab also does on its own after a period of inactivity. Download anything you need to keep. - The notebook itself is saved to Drive automatically. File Download Download .ipynb gives you the notebook file to upload as part of a Part 2 submission. File Download Download .py turns the whole notebook into one script, test cells included. It is not the module a problem asks for. You write that file from a cell with %%writefile (lesson u00-l04), then download it from the Files panel. A line in a code cell that starts with ! runs a terminal command on the runtime instead of Python. Useful ones: Colab also has a Python helper for files, used only inside notebooks (it is not part of your submitted file): CPU or GPU, and checking versions Runtime Change runtime type chooses the hardware: CPU, or a GPU such as a T4. Round 1 is CPU only, so leave it on CPU. Changing the type restarts the runtime and loses your variables and files. This cell prints the versions of everything the contest uses. Colab updates its packages from time to time, so run it in Colab once a month and compare with the versions this site uses (listed in lesson u00-l01). On a CPU runtime the last line prints False . Two settings to fix before exam day - AI features. Colab has built-in AI tools (Gemini, and gray AI code suggestions that appear as you type). The 2026 rules banned them explicitly, including using the gray suggestions as hints. The 2027 rules list only the two organizer documents as allowed resources, so treat all AI features as banned. Look in Tools Settings for a section about AI assistance and turn off AI completions and generative AI features. The labels change between versions, so check it again a week before the contest. - help(). In 2026, Colab's autocompletion and help() were explicitly allowed. The 2027 page does not mention them. If they are allowed, help(sorted) prints the documentation of sorted inside the notebook. Confirm this when the final 2027 instructions come out. In short, the Part 2 setup is: a CPU runtime, AI features off, only the two organizer documents open, and one monitor (multiple monitors are prohibited; lesson u00-l05 has the full exam-day rules).

entries.t: Markdown and LaTeX in text cells
entries.x:
"Markdown in Google Colab" is the first topic on the official Round 1 list. In past contests, derivations were typed into notebook text cells, and photos of handwritten math were not accepted (2026 rule). The 2027 open-ended sample problem asks for a Markdown write-up of your approach. This lesson gives you the Markdown and the LaTeX math you need, as templates you can paste into a Colab text cell. Markdown: formatting in a text cell Markdown is a plain-text way to write formatted text: you type symbols, and the text cell shows the formatted result when you leave it. Type this into a Colab text cell: What each piece does: - , , at the start of a line make headings, from largest to smallest. - bold and italic . - Backticks make inline code: fit . Three backticks on their own lines start and end a code block, as in lesson code. - Lines starting with - make a bullet list; 1. makes a numbered list. Indent by two spaces to nest. - Pipes and a line of dashes make a table. - A single line break inside a paragraph is ignored: the two lines are joined. Leave a blank line to start a new paragraph. LaTeX: math in a text cell LaTeX is the standard way to type math as text. In a text cell, math goes between dollar signs: - $...$ puts math inline, inside a sentence. - puts math on its own centered line (display math). Use it for anything with a fraction or a sum. This renders as: the mean is $\mu =  rac{1}{n}\sum {i=1}^{n} x i$, and the variance is Inside math, commands start with a backslash, and braces { } group things . Most LaTeX mistakes are missing braces. What you want Type Result --- --- --- subscript, one character x i $x i$ subscript, several characters x {ij} , x {10} , x {i,j} $x {ij}$, $x {10}$, $x {i,j}$ superscript x^2 , e^{-x^2} , w^{(t+1)} $x^2$, $e^{-x^2}$, $w^{(t+1)}$ both x i^2 $x i^2$ fraction  rac{a+b}{2n} $ rac{a+b}{2n}$ sum, product \sum {i=1}^{n} x i , \prod {k=1}^{K} p k $\sum {i=1}^{n} x i$, $\prod {k=1}^{K} p k$ square root \sqrt{x} , \sqrt[3]{x} $\sqrt{x}$, $\sqrt[3]{x}$ partial derivative  rac{\partial L}{\partial w j} $ rac{\partial L}{\partial w j}$ gradient 
abla L(w) $
abla L(w)$ transpose X^	op $X^	op$ hat, bar, tilde \hat{y} ,  ar{x} , 	ilde{y} $\hat{y}$, $ ar{x}$, $	ilde{y}$ bold vector \mathbf{w} $\mathbf{w}$ real numbers (here: all $n 	imes d$ real matrices) \mathbb{R}^{n 	imes d} $\mathbb{R}^{n 	imes d}$ relations \le , \ge , 
e , \approx , \in $\le$, $\ge$, $
e$, $\approx$, $\in$ products a \cdot b , n 	imes d $a \cdot b$, $n 	imes d$ arrows, infinity 	o , \infty $	o$, $\infty$ log, exp \log p , \exp(z) $\log p$, $\exp(z)$ arg min (the $w$ that makes $L(w)$ smallest) \arg\min {w} L(w) $\arg\min {w} L(w)$ words inside math 	ext{if } x 0 $	ext{if } x 0$ space a \quad b $a \quad b$ Greek letters are their names with a backslash: \alpha  eta \gamma \delta \epsilon \eta 	heta \lambda \mu \pi \sigma \phi . A capital first letter gives the capital form: \Sigma , \Delta . You get $\alpha,  eta, \gamma, \delta, \epsilon, \eta, 	heta, \lambda, \mu, \pi, \sigma, \phi, \Sigma, \Delta$. Two more you will use often. A norm is written \ x\ 2 and renders as $\ x\ 2$. Tall brackets that grow to fit what is inside are \left( and ight) , always as a pair: \left(  rac{a}{b} ight)^2 gives $\left(  rac{a}{b} ight)^2$. Matrices Rows are separated by \ and entries within a row by & . The environment name picks the brackets: bmatrix gives square brackets, pmatrix round ones, vmatrix vertical bars (a determinant), and plain matrix no brackets at all. Multi-line derivations and cases For a derivation, use aligned inside . Put & just before the symbol you want lined up (usually = ), and end each line except the last with \ : (Here $w^	op x i$ is the dot product of the vectors $w$ and $x i$, and $x {ij}$ is the $j$-th entry of $x i$. The $	op$ means transpose; lesson u03-l01 explains why the dot product is written this way.) For a function defined piece by piece, use cases . The & lines up the conditions. The example is ReLU, a function used inside neural networks; the formula is its whole definition: A complete answer cell to copy \, adds a thin space, which makes products easier to read. - A subscript or superscript longer than one character without braces: x 10 shows $x 10$, and e^-x puts only the minus sign up high. - Two superscripts in a row, like x^2^3 : that is an error. Write {x^2}^3 or x^{6} . - A \left( without its ight) , or a missing closing brace: the whole formula fails, and you see red error text or the raw source. - A missing \ between matrix rows puts every entry in one row. - Spaces inside math are ignored. Use \quad , \, or 	ext{ } when you want space. This site draws math with a renderer called KaTeX; Colab may use a different one. Every command in this lesson is standard and should look the same in both, but paste the answer template into a Colab text cell once before the contest to confirm. A place to test formulas This try block draws formulas with matplotlib, a plotting library you will meet later; the drawing code is only a renderer here. It handles inline-style math (fractions, sums, Greek, hats) but not aligned , cases or matrices, and its fractions come out small. Edit the strings in the list and run it. A broken formula, such as one with a missing brace, makes it stop with an error that names the problem. The r before each string keeps Python from treating backslashes as special characters.

Part 2 is graded by a program, not a person. It imports the .py file you submit and calls your function or class on hidden inputs. Correct numbers printed in your notebook earn nothing unless the file works on its own. This lesson is the exact workflow from a Colab cell to a graded file, plus what is in the two documents you are allowed during Part 2. Modules and import A module is a .py file that other code can import. import problem1 submission as sub does three things: 1. finds the file problem1 submission.py (Colab looks in the current folder, /content , among other places), 2. runs the whole file once, top to bottom, which defines its functions and classes, 3. gives you the result as sub , so the function f in the file is sub.f . A grader works the same way: it imports your file, looks up the function or class by the exact name the problem gave, and calls it. %%writefile: from a cell to a file In Colab, a code cell whose first line is %%writefile name.py saves the rest of the cell into that file instead of running it. Colab prints Writing name.py the first time and Overwriting name.py after that. %%writefile is a Colab (Jupyter) command, not Python, so it works only in a notebook cell. The try blocks on this site are plain Python, so they write the file with open(...) instead. The effect is the same. The pycache folder is Python's saved compiled copy of the module. Ignore it. A comment or any code above %%writefile breaks it. In standard Jupyter the cell fails with UsageError: Line magic function %%writefile not found (tested). The official cheat sheet shows a comment line above %%writefile ; do not copy that layout. Put comments below the first line. The file is all the grader sees A module has its own set of names. Variables and imports from your notebook cells do not exist inside it. If you ran import math in an earlier cell but the file itself does not import math , the function fails as soon as the grader calls it: The habit that prevents this: test by importing the file, never by running a copy of the function in an ordinary cell. Then you see exactly what the grader sees. Importing again does nothing Python imports each module once per session. After you change the file and rerun the %%writefile cell, a second import hands back the old version that is already in memory. importlib.reload reads the file again. Restarting the session also works. What the grader checks The official grader's code is not published. The 2027 sample problems say it checks results, banned functions, imports, time and file limits, and that "correct numbers alone do not guarantee acceptance". The SP1 and SP2 samples also require that your code does not modify its inputs. This site's grader makes the same kinds of checks, and a small version of it fits in one try block. Note that it finds the banned name mean in a function that is never called: it reads your source text before running anything. The rules that follow from this: - Use the exact file name, function or class name, argument order and return order the problem states. - Put every import the file needs at the top of the file, and import nothing the problem does not allow, even if it is unused. - Keep banned names out of the whole file, including helper functions you no longer call. - Do not change the inputs (lesson u01-l08 shows how mutation happens by accident). - Leave test code, print calls and reading of your own data files out of the file. They would run when the grader imports it, which wastes time or crashes on a machine without your files. - Time limits are measured on Colab's CPU. Code under if name == " main ": at the bottom of a module runs only when the file is run as a script ( !python problem1 submission.py in Colab), not when it is imported. You can keep a quick self-test there. A separate test cell in the notebook is simpler. The workflow, cell by cell 1. Cell A (one per file): %%writefile problem1 submission.py , then the imports and your solution. 2. Cell B (testing): import the module, reload it, and run it on the example from the statement: 3. Fix Cell A, run A, run B. Repeat. 4. Before uploading: Runtime Restart session and run all. The rules say the notebook, run top to bottom in a fresh session, must reproduce the submitted .py . This catches hidden state and cells run out of order. 5. Download the .py from the Files panel and the notebook with File Download Download .ipynb, then upload both on contest.usaaio.org. Limits from the 2027 samples: the .py at most 100 KB, the notebook at most 10 MB, and up to 5 uploads per file. Upload a working version early and replace it later if you improve it. The two documents allowed in Part 2 1. "Guideline: Submitting Trained Models for Open-Ended Problems" (October 4, 2026) This covers open-ended problems, where you train any model you like and it is scored on hidden test data (sample SP5 is one). The provided materials are four notebooks: - Training notebook : train and validate the model, then save every file inference needs (preprocessing parameters, model architecture, learned weights). - Inference notebook : load those files, write submission.py (the function the grader will call), and package submission.py together with all the training outputs into one ZIP file. - Self-check notebook : run it on your ZIP to see whether the grader will accept it. Never edit it. - Write md notebook : produces the required Markdown explanation of your approach, when the problem asks for one. You then upload the training notebook, the inference notebook, the ZIP and the .md file. The guideline says the grader works much like the self-check notebook: it extracts the ZIP, imports submission.py , calls the prediction function with the path to a hidden test file, and scores the output. In SP5 the function is predict(test path) , it must return a Python list, each call may take at most 30 seconds on CPU, the inference notebook must not retrain, and any error counts as the worst score. The whole round trip in one try block. json.dump writes Python dicts and lists to a JSON file and json.load reads them back (lesson u01-l06 covers JSON fully). file is the path of the module's own file, so HERE is the folder submission.py was unpacked into. Change os.path.join(HERE, "weights.json") to plain "weights.json" and run again: you get FileNotFoundError , because the grader runs from a different folder. It is not documented which folder the official grader runs from. Building paths from HERE works either way; if the starter code shows its own way of finding files, follow the starter. 2. "AI Save & Load Cheat Sheet" (June 20, 2026) A Colab notebook showing how to save and load each common kind of object. Its quick guide: What you have Format Save Load --- --- --- --- table (pandas DataFrame) .csv df.to csv("scores.csv", index=False) pd.read csv("scores.csv") dict or list .json json.dump(obj, f, indent=2) json.load(f) one NumPy array .npy np.save("X.npy", X) np.load("X.npy") several NumPy arrays .npz np.savez("dataset.npz", X=X, y=y) data = np.load("dataset.npz") , then data["X"] scikit-learn model or scaler .joblib joblib.dump(model, "model.joblib") joblib.load("model.joblib") PyTorch model .pt torch.save(checkpoint, "model.pt") torch.load("model.pt", map location="cpu") For JSON it opens files as with open("config.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f: to save and with "r" to load. For PyTorch it shows one pattern twice (a small CNN, then a BERT text classifier): 1. Write the model class to its own file with %%writefile cnn model.py , so the inference side can from cnn model import SmallCNN . 2. Save a checkpoint : a dict holding "model config" (the arguments used to build the model), "training hyperparameters" , "model state dict" (from model.state dict() , the learned numbers) and "optimizer state dict" . 3. To load: ckpt = torch.load(path, map location="cpu") , rebuild with SmallCNN( ckpt["model config"]) (the passes a dict as keyword arguments, lesson u01-l03), then model.load state dict(ckpt["model state dict"]) , model.eval() , and predict inside with torch.no grad(): . You will learn the PyTorch pieces in the PyTorch unit. Three traps the sheet does not warn about: - df.to csv(...) without index=False adds an extra unnamed column of row numbers to the file. - JSON keys are always strings. Save {0: "cat"} and you load back {"0": "cat"} , so loaded[0] raises KeyError . Tuples come back as lists. - The comment line above %%writefile in its PyTorch cells (see the warning above).

entries.t: Exam day: proctor, OBS, Lateran AI, timing
entries.x: Round 1 has strict setup rules, and a missed one can lock you out of a part or void your score. Most of the work happens weeks before the contest: finding a proctor and testing your recording. Facts here come from the official 2027 contest page and the proctor page, read on 2026-11-18. Anything from the 2026 rules is marked as 2026. Weeks before: proctor and laptop Proctor. Every round must be taken onsite with a proctor; an unproctored score is not certified and cannot advance. Allowed sites: K-12 schools (not homeschools), colleges, libraries, testing centers, and any site that has hosted AMC, F=ma, USNCO or USABO. Parents and relatives cannot proctor. 1. Check the official proctor list (a Google Sheet linked from usaaio.org/proctors). 2. If your school is not on it, email contact@usaaio.org to add it. 3. The proctor's account on contest.usaaio.org is activated near the contest date and shows the site ID and the test-day site code. You enter the proctor information only during the contest. Laptop. You use your own computer. - OBS Studio (free recording software): record the whole screen and your face, camera on, for the entire exam. Capture the full display, not one window. Make a test recording well before the day and watch it back. - Lateran AI : the official page says to keep it running until the competition ends and not to turn it off early. Its purpose is not stated on the page; install it when the organizers say how. - One monitor only. Multiple monitors are strictly prohibited. - Colab settings from lesson u00-l02: AI features off, runtime on CPU. The day: timeline (Eastern Time) Time (ET) What happens --- --- 12:00 to 12:15 pm Part 1 start window. Start inside it. before 12:30 pm You may not leave. 1:15 pm Part 1 closes, sharp. 1:30 to 1:45 pm Part 2 start window. before 2:00 pm You may not leave. 3:00 pm Part 2 closes, sharp. by Sat Feb 20, 11:59 pm Submit your recording URL (YouTube, Google Drive or Vimeo) and any other supplementary documents. In Central Time, subtract one hour from every time in the table. Each part's window closes at a fixed time (1:15 and 3:00), so starting late in a start window can only cost you minutes. Start at the beginning of each window. Leaving the room during a part ends that part. There are no restroom breaks. Rules during each part Part 1 is closed book. App lockdown is on: do not switch to any other app or website. Phones, smartwatches, smart glasses, earbuds and other devices are not allowed, and neither are rulers, compasses or your own paper. The proctor gives you blank scratch paper and collects it after each part. Part 2 : lockdown is turned off so you can use Google Colab. The only allowed resources are the two organizer documents (lesson u00-l04). Treat everything else as banned: search engines, other websites, your notes, and every AI tool, including Colab's own AI features. Locks. A rule violation can cause a temporary or a permanent lock. Only the proctor can remove a temporary lock. If you get locked, stop, raise your hand, and tell the proctor. Do not try to work around it. Honesty. One cheating incident means a permanent ban from all future USAAIO contests. In 2026, the organizers also listed suspicious patterns: leaving the computer for a long time and then solving many problems very quickly, pausing the recording, blocking the camera, or stopping the recording before submitting. Time plan Part 1 (60 min, 20 problems). Pass 1, about 35 minutes: answer everything you can do in about 2 minutes and skip the rest. Pass 2, about 20 minutes: the skipped ones, hardest last. Final 5 minutes: apply the guessing rule from lesson u00-l01 (guess on multiple choice only after ruling out a choice; leave an integer item blank unless you computed it) and confirm every integer answer has three digits. Part 2 (75 min). For each problem: 1. Read the restrictions first: allowed imports, banned functions, time limit, file name, function or class name, return format. 2. Write the simplest correct version, test it on the statement's example, and upload it early. You have up to 5 uploads per file. 3. Improve only after something is safely uploaded. 4. Keep the last 10 minutes for Restart session and run all, downloading, and the final uploads. Checklist A month before: proctor confirmed and on the list; OBS installed and a test recording watched back; Colab settings checked (AI off, CPU); a full timed mock done on this site. The day before: laptop charged and charger packed; OBS and Lateran AI start correctly; signed in to contest.usaaio.org and to the Google account you use for Colab; second monitor unplugged; notifications off. At the site: phone, watch and earbuds away; start the OBS recording before opening any problem; get the site code from the proctor; start inside the 12:00 to 12:15 window. After: upload the recording and submit its URL by Saturday, February 20, 11:59 pm ET. In 2026 the rules also banned discussing the problems online for about ten days after the contest; expect a similar rule.

Part 1 has "what does this code print?" questions. In the official 2027 sample, the last step of one such question is int(100 ...) , so the answer depends on exactly how Python divides, rounds and truncates. Part 2 answers are often rounded with Python's round and compared with a tolerance. This lesson covers the number rules that decide those digits. Four basic types Every value in Python has a type . The four simplest: - int : whole numbers, any size, always exact. 2 100 is computed exactly. - float : numbers with a fractional part, like 3.5 , 1e-9 (which means $1 \times 10^{-9}$) or 2.0 . Stored in binary with about 16 significant digits, so usually not exact. - bool : True or False . In arithmetic they act as 1 and 0. - None : a single special value meaning "nothing here", such as "not fitted yet" or "no value". type(x) tells you the type; isinstance(x, float) asks whether x is a float. Division, floor division and remainder Expression Value Rule --- --- --- 7 / 2 3.5 / always gives a float 6 / 2 3.0 still a float, even when exact 7 // 2 3 // is floor division : divide, then round down -7 // 2 -4 down means toward minus infinity, so $-3.5$ becomes $-4$ 7 % 2 1 % is the remainder -7 % 2 1 the remainder takes the sign of the divisor, so that (a // b) b + a % b == a 2 -1 0.5 is power Mixing an int and a float gives a float: 3 + 0.0 is 3.0 . Turning floats into ints Three different rules, and they disagree on negative numbers and halves: - int(x) truncates : it drops the fractional part, moving toward zero. int(2.7) is 2 and int(-2.7) is -2 . - math.floor(x) rounds down, toward minus infinity: math.floor(-2.7) is -3 . math.ceil(x) rounds up. - round(x) rounds to the nearest integer, and a value exactly halfway goes to the even neighbor ("round half to even", also called banker's rounding). So round(2.5) is 2 , round(3.5) is 4 , and round(0.5) is 0 . round(x, 4) rounds to 4 decimal places and returns a float. The 2027 pandas sample problem asks for answers rounded exactly this way. Floating point: why 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 A float stores the closest binary fraction to your number. Most decimals, such as 0.1, have no exact binary form, just as $\frac{1}{3}$ has no exact decimal form. The tiny errors show up in sums and comparisons: The lesson for code: never test floats with == . Compare with a tolerance (an allowed error): Graders do the same: the 2027 samples accept answers within 1e-6 or 1e-4, depending on the problem. The trap in the try block, int(0.29 100) giving 28, is exactly the kind of thing a "what does this print?" question tests. When the true value is a whole number but the computed float can land just below it, round is safe and int is not. Printing numbers f-strings format numbers inside text. The part after the colon is the format: f"{x:.4f}" makes text; round(x, 4) makes a number. Use the one the problem asks for. Truth values and None The condition after if (or after if inside a comprehension, or after while ) does not have to be True or False . Python accepts any value and decides whether it counts as true. This is called truthiness . - Falsy (counts as false): False , None , the number zero in any form ( 0 , 0.0 ), and every empty string or container ( "" , [] , () , {} , set() ). - Truthy (counts as true): everything else. That includes every nonzero number, negative ones too ( -3 , 0.5 ), and every nonempty string or container, even "0" , " " and [0] . bool(x) shows which one a value is. The most common use in contest code is a remainder as a condition. x % 2 is 1 for odd x and 0 for even x , so if x % 2: means "if x is odd", and if not x % 2: means "if x is even". Likewise if x % 3: means "if x is not divisible by 3". To test for None , write x is None , not if not x . Otherwise a value of 0 is treated like "missing": Classes often start with self.weights = None and set real values in fit . Check with if self.weights is None: . With if not self.weights: , a fitted value of 0.0 would look unfitted, and a NumPy array raises an error there.

entries.t: Lists, tuples, dicts, sets and slicing
entries.x: Lists, tuples, dicts and sets are the containers every contest solution uses: a list of predictions, a tuple returned by a function, a dict of label ids, a set of distinct customer IDs. Slicing rules carry over directly to NumPy arrays and PyTorch tensors, so time spent here pays off twice. Lists A list is an ordered, changeable sequence: a = [3, 1, 4] . Indexes start at 0, and negative indexes count from the end: a[-1] is the last element. a.sort() sorts the list in place and returns None . sorted(a) returns a new sorted list and leaves a alone. Both take reverse=True to sort from largest to smallest. Lesson u01-l08 explains why that difference matters for grading. Slicing a[start:stop:step] takes elements from index start up to, but not including , stop , moving step at a time. Any part can be left out: start defaults to the beginning, stop to the end, step to 1. Two facts worth memorizing: a[i:j] has j - i elements (when both are in range), and a[:k] plus a[k:] is the whole list. A slice is a new list, so changing the slice does not change a . Strings slice the same way: "problem5.zip"[:-4] is "problem5" . Tuples A tuple is like a list that cannot be changed after it is made: t = (3, 4) . You meet tuples constantly: - Functions return several values as one tuple: return Z, means, stds, C returns a 4-tuple in the official SP1 sample, and Z, means, stds, C = f(X) unpacks it into four names. - NumPy and PyTorch shapes are tuples: (n, d) . - A one-element tuple needs a comma: (5,) . Plain (5) is just the number 5. Dicts A dict maps keys to values: d = {"cat": 0, "dog": 1} . Look up with d[key] ; a missing key raises KeyError . d.get(key, default) returns the default instead. key in d checks the keys. Dicts remember the order in which keys were inserted. Keys must be unchangeable values: numbers, strings and tuples work, lists do not. Sets A set holds distinct values with no order: s = {1, 2, 3} . Adding a value already there does nothing, and in is fast. len(set(xs)) counts the distinct values in xs , which comes up often (for example, distinct customer IDs in the official pandas sample). An empty set is set() ; {} is an empty dict. Comprehensions A comprehension builds a list, dict or set in one expression: It means: for each item , if condition holds, put expression in the result. The if part is optional. The condition follows the truthiness rules from lesson u01-l01: it can be any value, and it counts as true when it is nonzero or nonempty. So [x for x in xs if x % 2] keeps the odd values (remainder 1 is truthy), and [s for s in names if s] drops empty strings. The dict inversion line is copied from the official cheat sheet. Read a nested comprehension from the outside in: for each row r , build the inner list over c . When a loop variable is not used at all, the convention is to name it , as in [0 for in range(3)] .

Every Part 2 problem states an exact function signature, and the grader calls it in a fixed way. Signatures use default values and keyword arguments (the official SP2 class is built as WeightedLinearRegression(learning rate, steps, regularization) ), the official cheat sheet builds a model with SmallCNN( model config) , and tie-breaking rules like "ties alphabetical" are one sorted(..., key=...) call. This lesson covers all of it. Defining and returning A function without a return statement returns None . return a, b returns one tuple, which the caller can unpack. Positional, keyword and default arguments A parameter is a name in the def line; an argument is the value passed in a call. Arguments can be passed by position or by name (a keyword argument ). A parameter with a default value may be left out of the call. The rules Python enforces: - In a def , parameters with defaults come after those without. - In a call, positional arguments come before keyword arguments. - Every parameter without a default must get a value, exactly once. - Parameters after a lone in the def line are keyword-only : they can only be passed by name. These TypeError messages are exactly what a grader shows when your signature does not match the problem's. A default value is created once, when the def runs, and then shared by every call. A list or dict default therefore remembers changes between calls: Use None as the default and make a new list inside: if bucket is None: bucket = [] . Lesson u01-l08 explains why this happens. args, kwargs, and unpacking in calls In a def , args collects any extra positional arguments into a tuple, and kwargs collects any extra keyword arguments into a dict. The names args and kwargs are only a convention; the stars do the work. In a call, the stars do the reverse: f( seq) passes the items of seq as separate positional arguments, and f( d) passes the entries of a dict as keyword arguments. The cheat sheet uses the second form to rebuild a model from a saved config. Functions are values; lambda A function is an object like any other: you can store it in a variable or pass it to another function. A lambda is a one-expression function written inline: lambda x: x x is the same as a def that returns x x . The most common use is the key= argument of sorted , min and max . The key function is applied to each element, and the elements are ordered by the results. How the third line works: Python compares tuples element by element, so (-90, "ana") comes before (-90, "cy") comes before (-85, "ben") . Negating the score sorts it from high to low while the name still sorts from A to Z. With reverse=True instead, equal scores keep their original order (Python's sort is stable : it never reorders ties), which is not alphabetical here. zip and enumerate zip(a, b) pairs up elements of two sequences and stops at the shorter one. enumerate(seq) pairs each element with its index; start=1 counts from 1. Local variables Names assigned inside a function are local : they exist only during that call and do not change variables of the same name outside. A function can read an outside (global) variable, but assigning to that name inside the function makes a new local one. Contest functions should get everything through their arguments and give results back with return . A function created inside a loop, a comprehension or another function can use names from the place where it was created. Such a function is a closure . Python looks those names up when the function runs , not when it is created. This is called late binding , and it surprises people in one common spot: every lambda made in a loop sees the loop variable's final value. The fix is a default value. Defaults are evaluated once, when the function is created (the same fact behind the shared list default above), so i=i freezes the current i inside each lambda. A generator is a function whose body contains yield . Calling it runs none of the body: it returns a generator object. Each next(g) runs the body until the next yield , hands out that value, and pauses there. A for loop, list(g) or sum(g) keeps calling next until the body ends. A generator expression, (x x for x in nums) , works the same way. Objects like these, which hand out values one at a time, are called iterators . zip , map , filter and enumerate also return iterators. Three facts decide what such code prints: - An iterator is used up after one pass. A second list(g) gives [] and a second sum(g) gives 0, with no error. A list can be read any number of times, so call list(...) once if you need the values twice. - The body runs late. Anything it reads, such as len(data) , is read when the body reaches that line during a next call, not when you called the generator function. - x in g takes values out of g until it finds x , so those values are gone afterwards.

Many Part 2 problems ask for a class. The official SP2 sample is a class WeightedLinearRegression whose fit method must return self , with exact attribute names and a rule about repeated calls. Every scikit-learn model is a class with fit and predict , and every PyTorch model is a class. This lesson builds classes from nothing, then the exact fit / predict pattern graders check. A class and its objects A class is a blueprint for a kind of object. An object made from a class is an instance of it. Here is a complete class: Line by line: - class Counter: starts the definition. Class names use CapitalizedWords by convention. - A function defined inside a class is a method . Counter has two. - init (two underscores on each side) is the constructor . You never call it by name: writing Counter(5) makes a new empty object and then runs init on it with start=5 . - self is the object the method is working on. Python fills it in automatically. - self.count = start creates an attribute : a variable stored on the object. It lives as long as the object does, so other methods can use it later. What self really is a.add(3) is shorthand for Counter.add(a, 3) : Python looks up add in the class and passes the object itself as the first argument. That is why every method lists self first, and why self never appears in the call. Inside a method, every attribute and every other method is reached through self : self.count , self.add(2) . A bare count is a different, local name. Reading it raises NameError ; assigning to it creates a local variable that disappears when the method ends. Errors you will meet Error Usual cause --- --- TypeError: Counter.add() takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given self is missing from the def add(...) line, so Python's automatic argument plus yours is one too many. NameError: name 'count' is not defined wrote count where you meant self.count . TypeError: Counter() takes no arguments the constructor is misspelled ( init , int ), so Python never finds it. TypeError: Counter. init () missing 1 required positional argument: 'start' the object was created without an argument the constructor needs. AttributeError: 'Counter' object has no attribute 'cnt' a typo, or the attribute is only created in a method that has not run yet. The fit/predict pattern Some vocabulary first. A model is an object that makes predictions from data. Training a model means computing numbers from example data; those numbers are its learned parameters . A hyperparameter is a setting you choose before training, such as the learning rate (the step size of a training method). By convention: - init stores the hyperparameters and nothing else happens yet. - fit(data) trains: it computes the learned parameters and stores them as attributes. - predict(data) (or transform(data) ) uses the learned parameters on new data. Here is a small, complete example. To standardize a list of numbers means to subtract their mean and divide by their standard deviation, so the result has mean 0 and standard deviation 1. The class learns the mean and standard deviation from training data in fit , then applies them to any data in transform . It uses the population standard deviation, $\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum i (v i - \mu)^2}$, as the official SP1 sample does, and like SP1 it outputs 0 when $\sigma$ is at or below a tolerance. The rules graders check, taken from the wording of the official SP2 sample: 1. Store each constructor argument under exactly the given name. SP2 says to store learning rate , steps and regularization "under those names"; the grader reads model.learning rate . 2. Create the learned attributes in init with the stated starting values (SP2: self.weights = None , self.bias = 0.0 ). 3. fit returns self . That makes Model(...).fit(X, y).predict(X2) work, and a grader may check model.fit(X, y) is model . 4. Every fit starts from scratch. SP2: "every fit resets weights to float zeros and bias 0.0". Nothing from an earlier fit may leak into the next one. The grader "also checks repeated method calls". 5. No method changes its inputs. Lesson u01-l08 shows how that happens by accident. Forgetting return self gives a confusing error, because a method with no return returns None : Reading a class someone else wrote Problem statements and starter code often hand you a class. Read it in this order: 1. The init arguments: what you must pass to create one. 2. Every self.something = ... line in init : the object's state. 3. For each method: which attributes it changes, and what it returns. Try it on this class, then check yourself by running it: Reading it: creating one needs lr ; factor and every have defaults. The state is lr , factor , every and a step counter. step adds 1 to the counter, halves lr (with the default factor) on every every -th call, and returns the current lr . So with every=2 , the rate halves on calls 2 and 4: 0.8, 0.4, 0.4, 0.2, 0.2. A variable assigned directly in the class body (not through self ) is a class attribute , shared by every instance. That is fine for constants, but a list or dict there is shared too, so one instance's changes show up in all the others. Keep per-object state in self. attributes created in init . Printing an object shows something like . Defining a method def repr (self): return f"Counter({self.count})" controls what print and the notebook display show. PyTorch models define repr , which is why printing a model shows its layers.

Every PyTorch model is a class that inherits from nn.Module , and its constructor must start with super(). init () . The official SP4 sample asks for SegmentCenterModel(nn.Module) , and the 2026 paper asked for modules built from scratch. This lesson explains inheritance and super() from zero, then shows the exact pattern nn.Module uses, including why you write forward but call model(x) . Subclasses Inheritance lets a new class start from an existing one. In class Child(Parent): , Child is a subclass of Parent , and Parent is its parent class (also called the base class). The subclass gets every method of the parent without rewriting them, and it can add new ones or override existing ones by defining a method with the same name. When you call m.predict(...) , Python looks for predict in the object's own class first, then in its parent, then in the parent's parent, and uses the first one it finds. ConstantModel has its own predict , so Model.predict is never reached. describe is only in Model , so that one is used. An instance of a subclass also counts as an instance of the parent for isinstance . raise NotImplementedError(...) is the usual way for a parent class to say "subclasses must define this method". super(): calling the parent's version super() gives you the parent class's version of a method, from inside the subclass. Two uses: 1. Extending a method instead of replacing it: super().describe() runs the parent's describe , and you add to its result. 2. Running the parent's constructor. If a subclass defines its own init , the parent's init no longer runs on its own. Whatever the parent sets up is then missing, unless you call super(). init (...) , normally as the first line. Now delete the super(). init (name) line and run it again. self.history was never created, so predict fails with AttributeError: 'ScaledModel' object has no attribute 'history' . That is the whole reason super(). init () exists. You may see older code write super(ScaledModel, self). init (name) . It means the same thing. The nn.Module pattern Here is a tiny imitation of PyTorch's nn.Module , in plain Python, so every line is visible. It uses one new idea: a method named call runs when you use an object as if it were a function. layer(x) means layer. call (x) . (Names with double underscores on both sides, like init and call , are methods Python calls for you in response to ordinary syntax.) The real nn.Module works the same way. Its call does bookkeeping (it runs "hooks", small functions other code can attach) and then calls your forward . So: - you define forward(self, x) , - you call model(x) , never model.forward(x) , - and the constructor starts with super(). init () , because nn.Module. init creates the internal records where PyTorch keeps track of layers and parameters. Here is a real PyTorch model. nn.Linear(4, 2) is a layer object, explained in the PyTorch unit; here only the class structure matters. cannot assign module before Module. init () call is the message to recognize: the fix is always to add super(). init () as the first line of the constructor. Every class has a method resolution order (MRO): the list of classes Python searches, in order, when it looks up a method or attribute. For a chain where C inherits from B and B from A , it is C, B, A, object ( object is the class every class ends with). C. mro shows it. A class with no init of its own uses the first init along this list. super() does not mean "my parent class". Inside a method of class K , super().m() means: take the MRO of the object's own class, type(self) , find K in it, and call m from the next class after K that defines it. In a single chain this is always the parent. With two parent classes it is not: The MRO keeps the parents in the order written ( Left before Right ), lists every class exactly once, and puts a shared parent after all of its subclasses. So for a Both object, Base.hello runs once, last. One more rule follows from "the parent's init runs when you call it": if a subclass sets self.x and only then calls super(). init () , a parent that also assigns self.x replaces the subclass's value. Calling super(). init () on the first line avoids that.

Every Part 2 problem begins with an import rule, such as "Only import numpy as np " (SP1) or "Only numpy and pandas, no standard library imports" (SP3), and breaking it can score zero. Open-ended problems also read and write files: JSON for settings and data, CSV for tables. Lesson u00-l04 showed how a grader imports your file; this lesson covers the import statements themselves and reading and writing files. Four ways to import A package is a folder of modules; torch is a package, and torch.nn is a module inside it (a submodule ). The four forms: Statement What you then write Notes --- --- --- import math math.sqrt(2) the module's name becomes available import numpy as np np.zeros(3) an alias : a shorter name for the same module from math import sqrt sqrt(2) brings in one name directly from math import sqrt as root root(2) one name, renamed The aliases the contest uses everywhere: import numpy as np , import pandas as pd , import torch.nn as nn , import torch.nn.functional as F , import matplotlib.pyplot as plt . import torch.nn as nn and from torch import nn give the same object. Avoid from math import . It dumps every name of the module into yours, so you can no longer tell where a name came from, and it can silently replace your own names. What counts as an import under contest rules - Every import and from ... import line in your file counts, including standard-library modules such as math , os , json or collections . SP3 bans all of them. - An unused import still counts. - from numpy import linalg is an import of numpy, but it still uses linalg , which SP1 bans by name. Bans apply to names, however you reach them. Names that hide other names Two classic bugs, both from reusing a name: 1. A file named like a library. If your folder contains json.py or numpy.py , then import json may load your file instead of the real module. Never name your files after libraries. 2. A variable named like a built-in function. list , sum , max , min , len , input , id and type are ordinary names that you can overwrite by accident: In Colab the overwritten name stays broken until you delete it ( del sum ) or restart the session. Pick names like total , values list , best . Reading and writing text files open(path, mode) opens a file. The modes you need: "r" read (the default), "w" write (creates the file, or erases an existing one), "a" append (adds to the end). Always open files in a with block: it closes the file when the block ends, even after an error, and a written file is only complete on disk once it is closed. Pass encoding="utf-8" as the cheat sheet does, so text means the same on every machine. repr shows a string with its quotes and with \n for newlines, which makes invisible characters visible. .strip() removes spaces and newlines from both ends. Paths. A relative path like "notes.txt" is looked up in the current folder (in Colab, /content ). os.path.join("data", "train.json") builds data/train.json with the right separator. os.path.exists(p) checks for a file and os.listdir(".") lists the current folder. JSON JSON is a text format for nested data, and the json module converts between it and Python: Python JSON --- --- dict object {...} , keys always strings list, tuple array [...] (comes back as a list) str string, double quotes only int, float number True / False / None true / false / null Four functions: json.dump(obj, f) writes to an open file and json.load(f) reads one; json.dumps(obj) and json.loads(text) do the same with a string (the s stands for string). CSV with the csv module A CSV file is a table as text: one row per line, values separated by commas, usually with a header row of column names. The csv module reads it. Every value comes back as a string , so convert numbers yourself. The pandas unit covers pd.read csv , which does far more; the official SP3 sample even loads every column as text on purpose. row["score"] + row["score"] joins two strings ( "9090" ); only int(...) or float(...) makes a number. newline="" is what the csv module documentation asks for when opening CSV files; without it, rows can come out with extra blank lines on some systems.

In Part 2 you debug alone, against the clock, with no search engine. The fastest debugger reads the error message properly and checks one assumption at a time. This lesson covers reading a traceback, the exceptions you will meet most, raise and assert , and a short routine for when the grader says your answer is wrong. Reading a traceback When code fails, Python raises an exception (an error object with a type and a message) and prints a traceback : the chain of function calls that led to the failure, oldest call first. Read it in this order: 1. The last line : the exception type and message. ZeroDivisionError: division by zero . 2. The last frame (the File ... line ... entry just above it): where it happened. Line 4, in mean , which is return sum(values) / len(values) . 3. Walk up until you reach a line that explains why. Line 11, in prepare , passed data["train"] , an empty list, so len(values) was 0. The crash is in mean , but the cause is the data. This sandbox prints only line numbers. Colab also prints each line of code under its frame, with ~~~^~~~ marks under the failing operation, and it includes frames inside libraries such as NumPy or PyTorch. Skip past library frames to the last frame in your own code. The exceptions you will meet Exception Example message Usual cause --- --- --- SyntaxError , IndentationError invalid syntax , unexpected indent typo, missing colon or bracket, mixed indentation; nothing in the cell ran NameError name 'np' is not defined missing import, a typo, or a cell that has not been run TypeError can only concatenate str (not "int") to str wrong type, or wrong number of arguments to a function ValueError invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc' right type, bad value IndexError list index out of range index past the end KeyError 'b' dict key not present (the message is just the key) AttributeError 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'shape' usually a variable is None because some function returned nothing ZeroDivisionError division by zero empty input, or a zero count or standard deviation ModuleNotFoundError No module named 'sklearnx' misspelled or uninstalled module NumPy reports shape mismatches as ValueError , and you will see these constantly in later units: The message names both shapes, (3, 2) and (3,), which is the clue to the fix. raise: signaling an error yourself raise ValueError("message") stops the function and reports the problem. Raise an exception when a problem statement says to (for example "raise a ValueError for an unseen label"), or when continuing would only produce garbage. Choose the type that fits: ValueError for bad values, TypeError for bad types, RuntimeError for calling things in the wrong order ( predict before fit ), NotImplementedError for a method a subclass must supply. try / except catches an exception so that code can continue: A bare except: (or except Exception: ) also swallows the bugs you need to see, such as a misspelled name inside the try . Your function then quietly returns wrong results, which the grader marks wrong with no hint why. Catch only the exception you expect, around only the line that can raise it. assert: checking your own work assert condition, "message" does nothing when the condition is true and raises AssertionError with your message when it is false. Use asserts in a test cell to check your function against the example from the problem statement before uploading: For floats, assert with a tolerance: assert abs(got - want) < 1e-6 . Printing to debug The quickest debugging tool is a well-labeled print. f"{x=}" prints the expression together with its value, which saves typing labels: For arrays and tensors, print the shape and type before the values; most bugs in the later units are shape bugs. Remove debugging prints from the submitted file. When the grader says "wrong" 1. Rerun the statement's example and compare every number, not only the first one. 2. Reread the restrictions and the output spec: names, return order, return types (Python list or NumPy array?), shapes. 3. Try the edge cases the statement allows: the smallest sizes (n = 2, d = 1), a constant column, an empty list, ties. 4. Check that your function does not modify its inputs, and that calling it twice gives the same result. 5. Restart session and run all, in case hidden state (lesson u00-l02) made a test pass.

"Do not modify X" appears in the official SP1 sample, and SP2 says "No method may modify inputs". Graders check it by saving a copy of each input, calling your code, and comparing. A solution that prints all the right numbers but changes its input in place fails. This lesson explains how Python variables really work, so you can see when code changes something it should not. Names point at objects A Python variable is a name attached to an object; it is not a box holding a value. b = a does not copy anything: it attaches a second name to the same object. Two names for one object are called aliases . == asks whether two objects have equal values; is asks whether they are the very same object. Mutable and immutable objects To mutate an object is to change it in place. Mutable objects can be changed in place: lists, dicts, sets, NumPy arrays, pandas DataFrames and PyTorch tensors. Immutable objects cannot: ints, floats, bools, strings, tuples and None . With immutable objects, aliasing never causes surprises, because nothing can change them. "Changing" an int really makes a new int and moves the name to it: The difference between M += [3] and M = M + [3] is the difference between mutating an object and rebinding a name (pointing it at a different object). For lists, NumPy arrays and tensors, += , -= , = mutate in place. Function arguments are shared, not copied When you call f(z) , the parameter inside f becomes another name for the same object z refers to. So a function that mutates its parameter changes the caller's object. A function that only rebinds its parameter does not. This is exactly how the "modified input" bug happens in contest code. The official SP1 sample needs column means subtracted from X . One -= mutates the caller's array: Here X.sum(axis=0) sums each column and X.copy() makes an independent copy; the NumPy unit covers both. The rule: inside a function, never use += , -= , = , /= , item assignment ( X[i] = ... ) or a mutating method on an input. Build new objects instead, or start the function with X = X.copy() and then do anything you like to the copy. Methods that mutate and return None Python's convention: a method that changes an object in place returns None . A function that leaves its input alone returns a new object. Mutates in place, returns None Returns a new object, input unchanged --- --- a.sort() sorted(a) a.reverse() a[::-1] , list(reversed(a)) a.append(x) , a.extend(b) , a += b a + [x] , a + b d.update(e) , d[k] = v { d, e} (a new merged dict) a.pop() , a.remove(x) , del a[i] a[:-1] , [v for v in a if v != x] So a = a.sort() loses your list: a becomes None . Shallow and deep copies list(a) , a[:] , a.copy() and dict(d) make a shallow copy : a new outer container whose elements are the same objects as before. For a list of numbers that is all you need. For a list of lists, the inner lists are still shared. copy.deepcopy(x) makes a deep copy : it copies everything, all the way down. [[0] 3] 2 is a classic trap: repeats the reference to the inner list, so both "rows" are the same object. The comprehension runs [0] 3 once per row, making separate lists. Storing inputs inside an object A class that keeps training data, such as a nearest-neighbor model whose fit stores the examples, must store a copy. If fit does self.X = X , the model and the caller share one list; when the caller later changes their data, the model silently changes too. Write self.X = [list(row) for row in X] (or X.copy() for an array). How a grader checks "do not modify" The site's grader does this. The official grader's code is not published, but any check for modified inputs needs a snapshot like this one: It costs the grader a few lines, and it costs you a failed test (or the whole problem) if your code changes an input. Two habits make it a non-issue: build new objects instead of changing inputs, and check it yourself in your test cell, as in the try block above. Slicing a Python list makes a copy. Slicing a NumPy array does not: row = X[0] is a view , a window onto the same memory, so row[0] = 100 changes X . The NumPy unit covers views in detail. Until then, call .copy() whenever you plan to change part of an array you were given.

entries.t: Arrays: making them, shape and dtype
entries.x: Every Part 2 task hands you NumPy arrays and wants arrays back with exact shapes. The official 2027 sample SP1 says "return shapes (n, d) , (d,) , (d,) , (d, d) ", and the grader checks each one. This lesson covers how to make arrays and how to read the three facts that describe one: its shape, its number of axes, and its dtype. What an array is A NumPy array is a grid of numbers that all have the same type. You make one from a Python list with np.array . Arithmetic on an array acts on every entry, which a list does not do. Run this, then change the numbers and run it again: np is the standard short name. Every contest starter cell begins with import numpy as np . Shape, ndim, size The shape of an array is a tuple giving its length in each direction. Each direction is an axis , numbered from 0. Here is a table with 2 rows and 3 columns, drawn with its axes labeled: Its shape is (2, 3) . The first number is the length along axis 0 (how many rows), the second the length along axis 1 (how many columns). Moving along axis 0 means moving down, from row to row; moving along axis 1 means moving right, from column to column. - a.shape is the tuple of lengths. - a.ndim is the number of axes, the same as len(a.shape) . - a.size is the total number of entries, the product of the shape. In ML code a data table X of shape (n, d) almost always holds n samples (rows) and d features (columns). A sample is one example, such as one patient; a feature is one measured quantity, such as age. So row i is everything known about sample i. Three shapes look alike on paper but are different arrays. Mixing them up is the most common shape bug in the contest: (3,) is a 1D array with 3 entries; the comma is how Python writes a tuple with one element. A 1D array is neither a row nor a column. Lesson 5 shows why that matters. dtype The dtype (data type) is the type shared by every entry. The two you will see most are int64 (64-bit integers) and float64 (64-bit floating point, the same as Python's float ). NumPy picks the dtype from the data: all integers gives int64 , and one float makes the whole array float64 . .astype(t) returns a new array converted to dtype t . The original is unchanged. An array never changes its dtype when you assign into it. If a holds integers, a[0] = 12.75 stores 12 , with no warning. Make arrays that will hold results as floats from the start: np.zeros(n) is float by default. One display detail. NumPy 2 shows a single number taken out of an array together with its type, like np.float64(2.5) or np.int64(3) . It is still an ordinary number; print shows just 2.5 . These lesson boxes show the last line's value that way, like a Colab cell does: Making arrays without typing them Call Result --- --- np.zeros((2, 3)) 2 by 3 array of 0.0 np.ones(4) [1. 1. 1. 1.] np.full((2, 2), 7.0) 2 by 2 array of 7.0 np.arange(start, stop, step) start, start+step, ... , stopping before stop np.linspace(a, b, num) num evenly spaced points from a to b , both ends included np.eye(3) the 3 by 3 identity matrix np.zeros like(X) , np.ones like(X) same shape and dtype as X The shape goes in as one tuple: np.zeros((2, 3)) . Writing np.zeros(2, 3) fails, because the second argument is the dtype. arange with a float step can gain or lose an end point through rounding. Use linspace when you know how many points you want. reshape and -1 reshape puts the same entries into a new shape. Entries are read and filled in row-major order : row by row, with the last axis changing fastest. The total size must stay the same. One length may be -1 , which means "work this one out from the others". Three more shape tools. X.ravel() and X.flatten() make a 1D array, like X.reshape(-1) . X.squeeze() (or np.squeeze(X) ) removes every axis of length 1. Exam habits - Write the shape of every array in a comment when you make it: Z = np.zeros((n, d)) (n, d) . - When something fails, print x.shape and x.dtype first. - Return floats when the task asks for floats. np.zeros(n) is float; np.zeros like(int array) is not.

Part 2 tasks keep asking for pieces of arrays: the first column, the last k entries, a block of rows. Graders also check that your function did not change its inputs, and the usual way people break that rule is through a view , an array that shares memory with another array. This lesson covers indexing and slicing, then views and copies. 1D: the same as Python lists A slice is start:stop:step , and any part can be left out. The rules match list slicing (u01-l02). 2D: one index per axis For a 2D array, X[i, j] is row i , column j . Any position can hold a slice instead. One rule decides the shape of the result: - An integer index removes that axis. X[:, 2] has shape (3,) . - A slice keeps that axis, even when it has length 1. X[:, 2:3] has shape (3, 1) . So X[1] and X[1:2] hold the same numbers but have shapes (4,) and (1, 4) . Predict each shape below before you run it: ... (Ellipsis) stands for as many : as needed. X[..., 0] takes index 0 on the last axis whatever the number of axes. It is common with images stored as (height, width, channels) . X[i][j] also works, but it first builds the row X[i] and then indexes that. Prefer X[i, j] . With slices the two spellings differ: X[:][2] is row 2, because X[:] is all of X . Assigning into slices You can write into a slice. A single number is copied into every position it covers. Views and copies Basic slicing does not copy data. It returns a view: a new array object that looks at the same memory. Writing through the view changes the original. This is the opposite of Python lists, where lst[1:4] is a copy. reshape , ravel and the transpose .T (lesson 7) usually return views too. Indexing with arrays of integers or booleans (lesson 6) returns copies. When in doubt, np.shares memory(a, b) tells you. An array is one block of memory plus a description of how to read it: the dtype, the shape, and the strides . The strides say, for each axis, how many bytes to move to reach the next entry along that axis. np.arange(12).reshape(3, 4) holds 8-byte integers in row-major order, so its strides are (32, 8) : the next column is 8 bytes on, the next row is 32 bytes on (4 entries). Entry [i, j] sits at byte $32i + 8j$ from the start. A basic slice only writes a new description. a[:, 1::2] starts 8 bytes in, has shape (3, 2) and strides (32, 16) . The transpose swaps the strides: a.T has strides (8, 32) . No data moves, which is why these are views and why they cost almost nothing. A view must be describable by one starting point and one stride per axis . Indexing with an integer array or a mask can pick entries that no stride pattern reaches, so NumPy copies. reshape returns a view only when the new shape can be read from the same memory with fixed strides. a.reshape(-1) can (stride 8). a.T.reshape(-1) would have to visit bytes 0, 32, 64, 8, 40, ..., which no single stride does, so it copies. An array whose entries sit in memory in row-major order with no gaps is called contiguous ; a is, a.T and a[:, 1::2] are not. Not modifying inputs A function receives the caller's array itself, not a copy (u01-l08). Anything that writes into it changes the caller's data. That includes assigning into a slice and the in-place operators -= , += , = , /= . An in-place operation overwrites an existing array instead of making a new one. Graders check this. One of the deliberately wrong solutions to the official SP1 writes X -= means and fails for exactly this reason. X = X - m is safe. The right side builds a new array, and the name X inside the function now points at it, leaving the caller's array alone. X -= m writes into the existing array. If you want to work step by step in place, start with X = X.copy() . Before you submit, look for -= , += , = , /= , and any assignment into a slice of an input. For each one, either add .copy() at the start or rewrite it out of place.

Most formulas in ML apply one function to every entry of an array: a sigmoid on every score, a square on every error, a log on every probability. NumPy does this in one call with no loop. This lesson covers elementwise arithmetic, the common math functions, the special values nan and inf , and comparisons, which produce arrays of True and False. Elementwise arithmetic Elementwise means entry by entry. For two arrays of the same shape, a + b adds matching entries. All of + - / // % work this way. A single number is combined with every entry. Combining a number with an array is the simplest case of broadcasting, the general rule for mixing shapes (lesson 5). For two matrices, A B multiplies matching entries. The matrix product $AB$ is A @ B (lesson 7). When the shapes match, NumPy gives no error for A B ; the answer is just wrong. Universal functions A ufunc (universal function) is a NumPy function that acts on every entry of an array. The ones the contest uses: Function Meaning --- --- np.exp(x) $e^x$ np.log(x) natural log $\ln x$ ( np.log2 , np.log10 for other bases) np.sqrt(x) square root np.abs(x) absolute value np.square(x) $x^2$ np.sin , np.cos , np.tanh sine, cosine, hyperbolic tangent np.maximum(a, b) , np.minimum(a, b) the larger or smaller of two arrays, entry by entry np.round(x, k) , np.floor(x) round to k decimals, round down Two common ML functions take one line each. ReLU is $\max(0, x)$ applied to every entry; neural networks use it between layers (unit 11). The sigmoid $\sigma(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z})$ squashes any real number into the interval $(0, 1)$; logistic regression uses it to turn a score into a probability (unit 7). The 2025 Round 1 asked for exactly my sigmoid(z) with no loop. np.maximum(a, b) compares two arrays entry by entry and keeps the shape. np.max(a) returns the single largest entry (a reduction, lesson 4). np.max(x, 0) does not mean "max with 0": the 0 is read as axis=0 . nan and inf Some inputs have no finite answer. NumPy does not stop. It returns a special float value and prints a RuntimeWarning . inf is infinity. nan ("not a number") marks an undefined result, and it spreads: any arithmetic with nan gives nan. exp(1000) turning into inf is the reason for the stable softmax trick in lesson 8. Comparisons make boolean arrays , = , == , != are elementwise too. The result has dtype bool . Combine conditions with & (and), (or) and ~ (not), and put each comparison in parentheses, because & binds tighter than < . The words and , or , not do not work on arrays: they need a single True or False, so they raise ValueError . Booleans count as numbers: True is 1 and False is 0. So (x 0).sum() counts the positive entries. ( .sum() adds all the entries of an array; lesson 4 covers sums along one axis.) Comparing floats Floats carry rounding error, so 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is False (u01-l01). To compare float arrays, use np.isclose(a, b) (entry by entry) or np.allclose(a, b) (one True or False for the whole array). Graders compare your output this way, with a small tolerance.

A reduction turns many numbers into fewer: a sum, a mean, a maximum. Almost every Part 2 task needs a reduction along one axis (one result per feature, or one per sample), and many tasks ban the shortcuts. The official SP1 bans np.mean , np.std and np.var , so you build them from sum . The skill is choosing the right axis and keeping the right shape with keepdims . The whole array Along one axis Take a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3) and draw it with its axes labeled (lesson 1): a.sum(axis=0) adds along axis 0 , which means down the rows. Each column is squashed into one number: 0 + 3 = 3, 1 + 4 = 5, 2 + 5 = 7. Axis 0 (the length 2, the rows) is gone. Axis 1 (the length 3, the columns) is left. a.sum(axis=1) adds along axis 1 , which means across the columns. Each row is squashed into one number: 0 + 1 + 2 = 3 and 3 + 4 + 5 = 12. Axis 1 is gone and axis 0 is left. The rule to remember: the axis you name is the one that disappears. To find the result's shape, write the shape and cross out the named position. (2, 3) with position 0 crossed out leaves (3,) ; with position 1 crossed out it leaves (2,) . Every reduction follows this rule: sum , max , min , mean , prod , argmax . For a data table of shape (n, d) , n samples by d features, axis=0 gives one number per feature, shape (d,) , and axis=1 gives one number per sample, shape (n,) . Predict each line before you run it: The rule is the same in any number of dimensions: cross the named axis out of the shape. A tuple of axes crosses out all of them. argmax and argmin Three ML terms from u06-l01, used from here on. In classification each sample belongs to one of k classes (categories), numbered 0 to k-1, and its true class is its label . A classifier is a model that predicts the class; it usually gives each sample one score per class and predicts the class with the highest score. argmax returns the index of the largest entry, not its value. Along an axis it gives one index per row or per column. On a tie it returns the first one. With no axis, it returns a position in the flattened array (the entries read in row-major order). any and all reduce boolean arrays. (X 0).all(axis=1) is True for each row whose entries are all positive; (X 0).any() is True if any entry is. keepdims keepdims=True keeps the reduced axis with length 1 instead of removing it. A row sum of an (n, d) array then has shape (n, 1) instead of (n,) . This matters as soon as you combine the result with the original array, for example to make every row sum to 1: Why the second line is wrong: a (2,) array lines up with the last axis of the (2, 2) array, the columns, so column 0 is divided by 4 and column 1 by 2. The matrix is square, so nothing complains. The (2, 1) version lines up with the rows. Lesson 5 gives the full rule, broadcasting. Until then, one habit covers it: when you reduce and then combine the result with the original array, pass keepdims=True . Mean, variance and standard deviation by hand The mean of numbers $x 0, \dots, x {n-1}$ is $\mu = \frac{1}{n}\sum i x i$. The variance is the mean squared distance from the mean, $\frac{1}{n}\sum i (x i - \mu)^2$. The standard deviation is the square root of the variance; it measures spread in the data's own units. Dividing by $n$ gives the population variance, which is what np.var and np.std compute by default. The sample variance divides by $n - 1$ instead ( np.var(x, ddof=1) ). A task always says which one it wants. SP1 asks for the population standard deviation (divide by $n$) to standardize, but its last output, the covariance matrix $Z^\top Z / (n - 1)$, divides by $n - 1$; mixing these up is one of its planted wrong solutions. When mean , var and std are banned, build them from sum . Per-column statistics of a table X of shape (n, d) : X - mu works because a (d,) array lines up with the columns, which is what we want here. For statistics along axis 1 (one per row), the mean must keep its axis. The safe pattern for any axis a :

Broadcasting is NumPy's rule for combining arrays of different shapes: axes of length 1 are stretched to match, without copying data. It is how you subtract a mean from every row, compare every point with every center, or build a whole table of distances in one line. It is also behind most silent bugs in contest code. Learn the rule exactly and you can predict any shape on paper, which Part 1 asks you to do. The rule, step by step To combine two arrays elementwise ( + , - , , / , comparisons), NumPy works out the result's shape in three steps: 1. Write both shapes and line them up from the right. If one shape is shorter, pad it on the left with 1s until both have the same length. 2. Compare position by position. In each position the two lengths must be equal, or one of them must be 1. 3. Stretch the 1s. A length-1 axis is repeated to match the other length. The result takes the larger length in each position. If some position has two different lengths and neither is 1, NumPy raises ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together . Worked example 1: np.ones((4, 1)) + np.ones(3) Step 1.
