The fix: do every comparison on validation data (or with cross-validation, lesson 8), freeze the final choice, then evaluate that one model once on a separate test set that played no part in any decision. Renaming sets, adding the test examples to training, or re-running the same evaluation does not undo the selection. Making the splits in code train test split from scikit-learn shuffles the examples and cuts them in two. For three sets, call it twice. Line by line: test size=0.2 is the fraction that goes to the second pair of outputs. The outputs come in the order X first, X second, y first, y second . random state=0 fixes the shuffle so the split is the same every run. For classification, adding stratify=y keeps the class proportions equal in both parts, which matters when one class is rare. Data leakage Data leakage is any way information that will not be available at prediction time gets into training or into the features. Leakage makes validation and test scores look better than the model will really do. Common forms: 1. A feature that is a consequence of the label. Predicting whether a customer will cancel next month, using the feature "cancellation confirmation email sent". The model scores perfectly and is useless. 2. Features computed with future data. Predicting tomorrow's sales using the average over the whole dataset, which includes the test days. Each feature must use only data up to the moment of prediction. 3. Random splits of time-ordered data. If tomorrow's examples sit in the training set, the model has seen the future. Split by time instead: train on earlier dates, test on later ones. 4. The same object on both sides. If one patient has 10 scans and some land in training and some in test, the test set measures how well the model recognizes patients it has already seen, which is the wrong question. Split by patient (a group split ), so each patient is entirely in one set. 5. Preprocessing fitted on all the data , such as rescaling a feature using a mean computed over train and test together. Lesson 9 shows the fix. Before trusting a score, ask: when the model is used for real, will it have this feature, and will the new cases be new people, new objects, or later dates? Make the test set look like that.

2026 Round 1 asked how bias and variance change as a model gets more complex. More generally, reading "training error vs validation error" and saying what is wrong and what to do is one of the most common ML exam questions. This lesson builds both from one small experiment. Capacity The capacity of a model family is how flexible it is: how many different shapes of function it can fit. A polynomial of degree 9 has more capacity than a line. More parameters usually means more capacity. One experiment, three models The true pattern is $y = \sin(2\pi x)$, but every label also has random noise added, like real measurements. We get 10 training points and fit polynomials of degree 1, 3 and 9 by least squares (the coefficients with the smallest training MSE). Then we measure MSE on 200 fresh test points. degree train MSE test MSE diagnosis --- --- --- --- 1 0.212 0.284 underfitting 3 0.041 0.070 about right 9 0.000 0.406 overfitting The 200 fresh points play the role of a validation set here. The noise alone has MSE about $0.2^2 = 0.04$ (even the true curve misses each label by its noise), so no model can get test MSE much below 0.04. Degree 3 comes closest. - Underfitting : the model is too simple to capture the pattern. Training error is high, and validation error is about as high. - Overfitting : the model fits the noise in its training examples. Training error is very low, validation error is much higher. Degree 9 has 10 coefficients for 10 points, so it passes through every training point exactly and swings wildly between them. Training error almost always falls as capacity grows. Validation error falls, bottoms out, then rises: a U shape. Pick the capacity at the bottom of the U, using the validation set. Bias and variance Imagine collecting a brand-new training set (same 10 inputs, new noise) many times, refitting the model each time, and looking at its prediction at one input $x 0$. - Bias : how far the average of those predictions is from the truth. It is error from the model being too simple, and it would remain even with no noise. - Variance : how much the predictions spread out from their own average across training sets. It is error from the model reacting to the particular noise in its training set. (Numerically: the average squared distance of each prediction from the average prediction.) As the degree goes 1, 3, 9, the squared bias falls (0.446, 0.002, 0.00005) and the variance rises (0.006, 0.012, 0.039). That is the bias-variance trade-off : as capacity grows, bias goes down and variance goes up. For squared error, the test MSE averaged over many training sets splits exactly as (proved once probability is covered). The noise term cannot be reduced by any model, and the best capacity minimizes the sum of the other two. Fix one input $x 0$ and write $f = f(x 0)$ for the true value there. A test label is $y = f + \varepsilon$, where the noise $\varepsilon$ averages 0, has variance $\sigma^2$ (the average of $\varepsilon^2$), and is independent of the training set. The prediction $\hat{y}$ depends only on the training set. Write $E[\cdot]$ for the average over many training sets and test noises, and $m = E[\hat{y}]$ for the average prediction. First split off the noise: Because $\varepsilon$ is independent of $\hat{y}$, the middle term is $2\,E[f - \hat{y}]\,E[\varepsilon] = 0$, and the last term is $\sigma^2$. Now add and subtract $m$ inside the first term: The middle term is 0 because $E[\hat{y}] = m$. What remains is $\text{bias}^2 = (f - m)^2$ plus $\text{variance} = E[(\hat{y} - m)^2]$, so the average test MSE at $x 0$ is $\text{bias}^2 + \text{variance} + \sigma^2$. The same trick works both times: split off a piece whose average is 0, and its cross term vanishes. Averaging over test inputs gives the version for a whole test set. The split is exact only for squared error; for 0-1 loss (1 for each wrong classification, 0 for each right one) there is no clean decomposition. Learning curves A learning curve plots training and validation error against the number of training examples (or against training time). Two patterns to recognize: - Both curves high and close together : high bias, underfitting. More data will not help much; a model with more capacity or better features will. - Low training error, a large gap up to validation error : high variance, overfitting. More data shrinks the gap; so do regularization (lesson 4) and a simpler model. symptom (in error or loss) name things that help --- --- --- train error high, validation error high underfitting (high bias) more capacity, better features, less regularization, train longer train error low, validation error much higher overfitting (high variance) more data, regularization, simpler model, early stopping (lesson 4) Exams and training logs often report accuracy , where higher is better, so the gaps point the other way. For a classifier: training accuracy validation accuracy diagnosis --- --- --- 99% 70% overfitting: a 29-point gap; it has memorized its training examples 74% 72% underfitting (if the task allows better): both low and close together 93% 91% healthy: both high, small gap The rule of thumb: compare the two numbers first (a big gap means overfitting), then compare the validation number with what is achievable (both low means underfitting). A training accuracy of 99% is not good news by itself; it only says the model fits the examples it was trained on. Diagnose with training and validation numbers. Looking at the test set to decide what to change turns it into a second validation set (lesson 2).

2026 Round 1 asked which of two models, one with an L1 penalty and one with an L2 penalty, ends up with fewer non-zero weights. This lesson shows why the answer is L1, with a one-line calculation you can redo in the exam. Regularization is also the main tool against the overfitting from lesson 3. The idea Regularization is any change to training that stops a model from fitting its training data too closely, so that it generalizes better. The most common form adds a penalty on the size of the weights to the loss: The regularization strength $\lambda \ge 0$ is a hyperparameter. With $\lambda = 0$ there is no regularization. As $\lambda$ grows, training accepts a worse fit to the data in exchange for smaller weights, so the model gets simpler: too large a $\lambda$ underfits. The bias $b$ is usually not penalized, since shifting all predictions up or down does not make the model more wiggly. The two standard penalties, for a model with $d$ features and weights $w 1, \dots, w d$: - L2 penalty : $\sum j w j^2$. Linear regression with it is called ridge regression . In neural networks the same idea is called weight decay . - L1 penalty : $\sum j w j $. Linear regression with it is called lasso . (Some books write $\frac{\lambda}{2}\sum j w j^2$; the factor only rescales $\lambda$.) Why L1 makes weights exactly zero Take the simplest case, which already shows the whole effect: linear regression whose features are uncorrelated and scaled to the same size. Then the data loss, up to a constant factor (which only rescales $\lambda$) and a constant term, is a sum of one squared term per weight, so the regularized loss splits into a separate one-variable problem for each weight: where $a$ is the weight you would get with no penalty. Solve it for both penalties. L2 , using the $\frac{\lambda}{2}w^2$ version because it makes the algebra cleaner: $f'(w) = (w - a) + \lambda w = 0$ gives Every weight shrinks by the same factor, and none becomes zero unless $a$ was already zero. L1 , penalty $\lambda w $. The absolute value has a corner at 0, so take the two sides separately. - If $w 0$: $f'(w) = w - a + \lambda = 0$ gives $w = a - \lambda$. That is positive only when $a \lambda$. - If $w < 0$: $f'(w) = w - a - \lambda = 0$ gives $w = a + \lambda$. That is negative only when $a < -\lambda$. - If $ a \le \lambda$: $f$ is decreasing for all $w 0$, so the minimum is exactly $w = 0$. Together this is soft thresholding : where $\operatorname{sign}(a)$ is $1$ for positive $a$ and $-1$ for negative $a$. Unpenalized weights $a = (3,\ 0.5,\ -0.2,\ -2)$. L2: divide by $1 + \lambda = 2$, giving $(1.5,\ 0.25,\ -0.1,\ -1)$. Four non-zero weights. L1: move each toward 0 by 1 and stop at 0, giving $(2,\ 0,\ 0,\ -1)$. Two non-zero weights. The reason in one sentence: the L1 penalty pushes toward zero with the same force $\lambda$ however small the weight is, while the L2 push is $\lambda w$, which fades away as $w$ approaches 0. A model with many exactly-zero weights is called sparse ; L1 therefore also does feature selection, switching off features that do not help enough. An equivalent view: minimize the data loss subject to $ w 1 + w 2 \le t$ (L1) or $w 1^2 + w 2^2 \le t$ (L2). The L1 region is a diamond with corners on the axes, the L2 region is a disk. The contours of the data loss usually first touch the diamond at a corner, where one weight is 0; a disk has no corners, so the touching point almost never lies on an axis. In scikit-learn Ridge shrinks every weight a little and keeps all 10 non-zero. Lasso keeps the 3 real features and sets the other 7 to exactly zero (a printed -0. is a zero). scikit-learn calls $\lambda$ alpha , and each class scales its loss its own way, so the same alpha means different strengths in Ridge and Lasso . Using both penalties at once is called elastic net . What regularization looks like in numbers Go back to lesson 3's overfitting experiment: 10 noisy points from $\sin(2\pi x)$, and a degree-9 polynomial. Give it the features $x, x^2, \dots, x^9$, fit it with ridge regression at several strengths, and watch three numbers: training MSE, validation MSE, and the largest weight. $\lambda$ train MSE validation MSE largest $\lvert w \rvert$ reading --- --- --- --- --- 0 0.000 0.407 about 512,000 overfitting: perfect on training, huge weights $10^{-4}$ 0.031 0.064 8.7 about right: lowest validation MSE 100 0.354 0.533 0.0 underfitting: weights crushed to zero As $\lambda$ grows, training MSE only goes up, the weights only shrink, and validation MSE first falls and then rises. You choose $\lambda$ at the bottom of the validation curve, exactly like choosing the polynomial degree in lesson 3. Huge weights that nearly cancel each other are the typical fingerprint of an overfit model, and the penalty removes them. The penalty treats all weights alike. If one feature is in grams and another in kilograms, their weights differ by a factor of 1000 for the same effect, and the penalty punishes them very differently. Standardize features first (lesson 9). Early stopping Many models (neural networks especially) are trained by repeating a small update step thousands of times, each step lowering the training loss a little. Plot the losses against the step number: training loss keeps falling, while validation loss falls, reaches a lowest point, and then rises as the model starts fitting noise. Early stopping means keeping the parameters from the step with the lowest validation loss (in practice: save a copy whenever validation loss improves, and stop after it has not improved for a while). It counts as regularization because the weights start small and move further from that start the longer training runs; fewer steps means a simpler model. The number of steps becomes a hyperparameter, chosen on validation data. Other regularizers you will meet later: dropout and data augmentation (for neural networks), and simply choosing a smaller model.

Official 2027 sample Problem 1 gives four counts and asks for the recall. 2026 Round 1 asked when F1 beats accuracy, and its Problem 9 was graded by macro-F1. These are free points once the definitions are automatic, and the main trap is mixing up precision and recall. Learn the table below until you can draw it without thinking. The confusion matrix In binary classification (exactly two classes) one class is called the positive class (label 1): the thing being detected, such as spam, fraud, or "bird present". The other is the negative class (label 0). Every prediction lands in one of four cells: predicted positive predicted negative --- --- --- actually positive TP (true positive) FN (false negative, a miss) actually negative FP (false positive, a false alarm) TN (true negative) This table of counts is the confusion matrix . The second word says what the model predicted; the first says whether that prediction was right. A false negative is a predicted negative that was wrong, so it is an actual positive. scikit-learn and most exam problems put actual classes on the rows and predicted classes on the columns, as above. Some sources flip it. Read the labels before you read the numbers. The four metrics Running example: a spam filter sees 200 emails, 40 of them spam. It flags 48 emails, of which 32 are spam. So TP = 32, FP = 16, FN = 40 − 32 = 8, TN = 200 − 32 − 16 − 8 = 144. - Accuracy : the fraction of all predictions that are right. With $n = TP + FP + FN + TN$ examples, $\frac{TP + TN}{n} = \frac{176}{200} = 0.88$. - Precision : of the examples the model called positive, the fraction that really are. $\frac{TP}{TP + FP} = \frac{32}{48} \approx 0.667$. "When it says spam, how often is it right?" - Recall : of the examples that really are positive, the fraction the model found. $\frac{TP}{TP + FN} = \frac{32}{40} = 0.8$. "Of all the spam, how much did it catch?" Recall is also called sensitivity or the true positive rate . - F1 score : the harmonic mean of precision $P$ and recall $R$ (the harmonic mean of two numbers is $\frac{2}{1/P + 1/R}$), The second form of $F 1$ needs no fractions and is faster in an exam. A harmonic mean stays close to the smaller of the two numbers, so F1 is high only when precision and recall are both high. Precision and recall both ignore TN. One more you will see: specificity (true negative rate) $= \frac{TN}{TN + FP} = \frac{144}{160} = 0.9$, the recall of the negative class. Precision divides by a column total (everything predicted positive). Recall divides by a row total (everything actually positive). If a question gives "the system predicts present" counts, those are columns. Try making the false positives large and watch precision fall while recall does not move; then do the same with false negatives. Class imbalance: when accuracy lies Class imbalance means one class is much rarer than the other. Take 1000 card transactions, 10 of them fraud, and a "model" that always answers "not fraud". Its accuracy is $990/1000 = 99\%$, and it catches nothing: recall is $0/10 = 0$. Its precision is $0/0$, which scikit-learn reports as 0 (with a warning). Its F1 is 0. So when the positive class is rare, accuracy is dominated by the easy negatives and says little. F1 (or precision and recall separately) focuses on the positive class and exposes the useless model. That is the 2026 answer: F1 is preferred over accuracy when the classes are highly imbalanced. 1000 people are screened and 1% (10 people) have a disease. The test flags 90% of the sick and 10% of the healthy. Gut feeling says "a flagged person is sick about 90% of the time" or "about 10%". Count instead: flagged not flagged total --- --- --- --- sick TP = 9 FN = 1 10 healthy FP = 99 TN = 891 990 Precision $= \frac{9}{9 + 99} = \frac{9}{108} \approx 8.3\%$. Recall is 90% and accuracy is $\frac{9 + 891}{1000} = 90\%$, yet only 1 in 12 flags is a real case, because 10% of a large healthy group (99 people) swamps 90% of a tiny sick group (9 people). Whenever a question gives a rate of positives and two rates of flagging, build this table with a round total like 1000; estimating in your head is how "about 10%" happens. Which of precision and recall matters more depends on the costs. Missing a cancer (FN) is far worse than an extra follow-up scan (FP), so a screening test wants high recall. Sending a real email to the junk folder (FP) annoys users more than one spam getting through (FN), so a spam filter wants high precision. Computing them in code Every scikit-learn metric takes (y true, y pred) in that order. Swapping them swaps FP with FN, which swaps precision with recall. In Part 2 these functions may be banned, so know the mask version: y pred == 1 is an array of True/False, & is elementwise "and" on two such arrays (the parentheses are required), and np.sum counts the True entries. More than two classes With $K$ classes the confusion matrix is $K \times K$: entry (row $t$, column $p$) counts examples of true class $t$ predicted as class $p$. The diagonal holds the correct predictions. For each class $c$, treat $c$ as positive and every other class as negative ( one-vs-rest ): $TP c$ is the diagonal entry, $FP c$ is the rest of column $c$, $FN c$ is the rest of row $c$. That gives a precision, recall and F1 for each class. To get one number, average them: - Macro average : compute the metric for each class, then take the plain mean. Every class counts equally, so a rare class that is handled badly pulls the score down hard. - Micro average : add up TP, FP and FN over all classes first, then apply the formula once. When each example has exactly one true and one predicted class, every mistake is one FP (for the predicted class) and one FN (for the true class), so micro precision = micro recall = micro F1 = accuracy. - Weighted average : the per-class metrics averaged with weights equal to each class's support (its number of true examples). Rows are actual, columns predicted, in the order cat, dog, fox: Fox: $TP = 6$, $FP = 2 + 5 = 7$ (column), $FN = 0 + 4 = 4$ (row), so $F 1 = \frac{12}{12 + 11} \approx 0.522$. In the same way cat has $F 1 = \frac{80}{95} \approx 0.842$ and dog $\frac{60}{82} \approx 0.732$. Macro-F1 $= (0.842 + 0.732 + 0.522)/3 \approx 0.699$. Micro-F1 $=$ accuracy $= 76/100 = 0.76$. Macro is lower because the rare fox class is handled worst. In the from-scratch line, np.bincount counts how many times each code 0, 1, ..., $K^2 - 1$ appears, and reshape(K, K) puts code $Kt + p$ at row $t$, column $p$. average=None returns one score per class.

Most classifiers output a score, and a threshold turns the score into a label. Questions about "what happens when the threshold is lowered", about ROC curves and about AUC follow directly from the confusion matrix of lesson 5. AUC also has a counting definition that turns an area question into a quick integer answer. Scores and thresholds A typical classifier outputs a score for each example: a number where higher means "more likely positive" (often an estimated probability between 0 and 1). The predicted label is for a threshold $t$ that you choose (0.5 is the usual default for probabilities). The threshold is not learned by training. Changing it does not change the model or its scores, only which examples are called positive. Eight examples, sorted by score: score 0.95 0.85 0.70 0.60 0.45 0.40 0.30 0.10 --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- actual 1 1 0 1 0 1 0 0 threshold predicted positive TP FP precision recall --- --- --- --- --- --- 0.80 2 2 0 1.00 0.50 0.50 4 3 1 0.75 0.75 0.35 6 4 2 0.67 1.00 Lowering the threshold can only add predicted positives. So TP and FP can only go up, recall can only go up, and precision usually goes down (not always: if the newly added examples are mostly true positives, precision can rise). Raising the threshold does the reverse. Picking a threshold means picking a trade-off between misses and false alarms; choose it on validation data, using the costs of each kind of mistake. Suppose the scores are calibrated probabilities: among examples given score $p$, a fraction $p$ really are positive. A false positive costs $c {FP}$ and a missed positive (false negative) costs $c {FN}$. For one example with score $p$, predicting positive costs $c {FP}(1 - p)$ on average, and predicting negative costs $c {FN}\,p$. Predict positive when the first is smaller: Equal costs give the usual 0.5. If a miss costs 9 times a false alarm, the threshold drops to $1/10$. If the scores are not calibrated (many models' scores are not), the formula does not apply directly; choose the threshold by computing the total cost on validation data instead. The ROC curve Two rates, one per row of the confusion matrix: - True positive rate $TPR = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}$, the recall: the fraction of actual positives above the threshold. - False positive rate $FPR = \frac{FP}{FP + TN}$: the fraction of actual negatives above the threshold. (It equals $1 -$ specificity.) The ROC curve (receiver operating characteristic) plots TPR against FPR for every possible threshold. With the threshold above every score nothing is positive, which is the point $(0, 0)$; with the threshold below every score everything is positive, which is $(1, 1)$. To draw it by hand, sort by score from high to low and walk down the list: each actual positive moves you up by $1/P$, each actual negative moves you right by $1/N$, where $P$ and $N$ are the numbers of actual positives and negatives. For the table above ($P = N = 4$) the labels in order are 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0: up, up, right, up, right, up, right, right. A perfect scorer puts all positives first and goes straight up to $(0, 1)$, then right. Random scores give, on average, the diagonal from $(0,0)$ to $(1,1)$. AUC The AUC is the area under the ROC curve, between 0 and 1. The diagonal has area 0.5 (no better than random) and a perfect scorer has area 1. There is an equivalent definition that is much faster in an exam: with tied pairs counted as one half. In the table, the positive at 0.95 beats all 4 negatives, 0.85 beats 4, 0.60 beats 3 (all but 0.70), and 0.40 beats 2 (0.30 and 0.10). So AUC $= \frac{4 + 4 + 3 + 2}{16} = \frac{13}{16} = 0.8125$. (Check against the walk: the right-steps happen at heights 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1, each of width 0.25, total area $0.25 \times 3.25 = 0.8125$.) Two consequences of the pair definition: - AUC depends only on the order of the scores. Any change that keeps the order (squaring scores that are all above 0, taking logs, multiplying by 10) leaves AUC unchanged, even though precision at a fixed threshold may change. - AUC does not depend on any threshold. It measures how well the scores rank positives above negatives. Take the walk down the sorted list, with no tied scores first. Each negative is a step right of width $1/N$, taken at the current height, and the current height is (number of positives already passed)$/P$, which is (number of positives scoring above this negative)$/P$. The area is the sum of these strips: With ties, a group of $a$ positives and $b$ negatives at one score is a single threshold, so the curve moves diagonally by $(b/N,\ a/P)$. The trapezoid under that diagonal is the rectangle at the old height plus a triangle of area $\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{b}{N} \cdot \frac{a}{P}$: exactly half credit for the $ab$ tied pairs. As a probability, AUC is the chance that a randomly chosen positive scores higher than a randomly chosen negative, with ties settled by a coin flip. (Statisticians call the pair count the Mann-Whitney $U$ statistic.) Both functions take the true labels first and the scores second (not predicted labels). scores[y true == 1] keeps only the scores whose label is 1. diff uses broadcasting (unit u02 teaches it) to subtract every negative score from every positive score at once, and np.mean(diff 0) is the fraction of pairs where the positive is higher. Precision-recall curves The precision-recall curve plots precision against recall over all thresholds. It is the better picture when positives are rare. Say there are 10 positives and 10,000 negatives, and at some threshold TP = 8 and FP = 100. Then $FPR = 100/10000 = 0.01$, which looks excellent on an ROC plot, but precision is $8/108 \approx 0.074$: more than 92% of the alarms are false. ROC hides this because FPR divides by the huge number of negatives; precision does not. A one-number summary of the PR curve is average precision ( average precision score in scikit-learn), roughly the area under it. Threshold-dependent metrics (precision, recall, F1, accuracy) describe one choice of threshold. ROC AUC and average precision describe the scores across all thresholds. With heavy class imbalance, prefer precision-recall to ROC.

When the label is a number, the model is scored with a regression metric. Exams ask you to compute these, to say which one a big outlier affects most, and to read an $R^2$ value. Open-ended Part 2 problems are often scored by MSE or RMSE on hidden data, so you should know exactly what is being measured. The four metrics For labels $y 1, \dots, y n$ and predictions $\hat{y} 1, \dots, \hat{y} n$, the residual of example $i$ is $y i - \hat{y} i$, the part of the label the model missed. - MSE (mean squared error): $\frac{1}{n}\sum i (y i - \hat{y} i)^2$. Units are the label's units squared. - RMSE (root mean squared error): $\sqrt{\text{MSE}}$, back in the label's units. - MAE (mean absolute error): $\frac{1}{n}\sum i y i - \hat{y} i $, also in the label's units. - $R^2$ (coefficient of determination): $R^2 = 1 - \frac{SS {res}}{SS {tot}}$, where $SS {res} = \sum i (y i - \hat{y} i)^2$ and $SS {tot} = \sum i (y i - \bar{y})^2$, with $\bar{y}$ the mean of the labels. $y = (3, 5, 2, 8, 7)$, $\hat{y} = (2.5, 5, 3, 6, 8.5)$. Residuals $0.5, 0, -1, 2, -1.5$. MSE $= (0.25 + 0 + 1 + 4 + 2.25)/5 = 1.5$. RMSE $= \sqrt{1.5} \approx 1.225$. MAE $= (0.5 + 0 + 1 + 2 + 1.5)/5 = 1$. $\bar{y} = 5$, so $SS {tot} = 4 + 0 + 9 + 9 + 4 = 26$, $SS {res} = 7.5$, and $R^2 = 1 - 7.5/26 \approx 0.712$. Reading $R^2$ $SS {tot}$ is the squared error of the laziest model, one that always predicts the mean $\bar{y}$. So $R^2$ compares your model with that baseline: - $R^2 = 1$: perfect predictions. - $R^2 = 0$: no better than always predicting the mean. - $R^2 < 0$: worse than predicting the mean. This cannot happen for a linear model fit by least squares (with a bias term) on its own training data, but it happens on test data with a bad model. $R^2$ has no lower limit. Because it is a ratio, $R^2$ has no units, so it can compare models across datasets with different scales. MSE, RMSE and MAE cannot. Squares vs absolute values Squaring makes big errors count much more. One error of 8 adds 64 to the sum of squares, while eight errors of 1 add only 8. So MSE and RMSE are sensitive to outliers (a few examples with huge errors), and MAE is less so. The same difference shows up in the best constant prediction. For data $1, 2, 3, 4, 20$: - The constant $c$ minimizing $\sum (y i - c)^2$ has derivative $-2\sum(y i - c) = 0$, so $c$ is the mean , here 6. - The constant minimizing $\sum y i - c $ has derivative (number of $y i$ below $c$) minus (number above $c$), which is zero when half lie on each side: $c$ is the median (the middle value after sorting), here 3. The single outlier 20 drags the mean from 2.5 (the mean of the first four) to 6, while the median barely moves. metric use it when --- --- MSE the training loss for regression (smooth, easy to differentiate); large errors are especially bad RMSE you want MSE's behavior but a number in the label's units MAE outliers should not dominate; you want "average miss" in plain units $R^2$ you want a unitless "fraction of variation explained" to compare across problems Each line prints the scikit-learn value next to the NumPy formula. As with classification metrics, the true values go first. Colab has scikit-learn 1.6, where mean squared error(y, y hat, squared=False) raises a TypeError (that argument was removed). Use root mean squared error(y, y hat) or np.sqrt(mean squared error(y, y hat)) .

Lesson 2 said "choose hyperparameters on validation data". This lesson shows the standard way to do that when data is limited, k-fold cross-validation, and how to search over many hyperparameter settings. Exam questions ask what each example is used for, how many models get trained, and which scheme avoids leakage. The problem with one validation split A single validation set has two costs. Its examples are not used for training. And its score is noisy: with a few dozen validation examples, a lucky or unlucky split can move accuracy by several points, enough to pick the wrong hyperparameter. k-fold cross-validation Cross-validation (CV) reuses the training data for validation in turns. In k-fold CV : 1. Shuffle the training data and cut it into $k$ equal parts called folds . 2. For each $i = 1, \dots, k$: train a fresh model on the other $k - 1$ folds and score it on fold $i$. 3. Report the average of the $k$ scores (and look at their spread). Every example is used for validation exactly once and for training $k - 1$ times. The price is $k$ trainings instead of one. Common choices are $k = 5$ or $k = 10$. With $k = n$ (each fold is one example) it is called leave-one-out CV. Each row index appears in exactly one validation fold. To get the data for a fold you would index with these arrays: X[train idx] , X[val idx] . Variants you should know by name: - Stratified k-fold : each fold keeps the same class proportions as the whole set. Important when a class is rare. scikit-learn uses it automatically when you pass an integer cv=5 with a classifier. - Group k-fold : all examples from one group (one patient, one user) stay in the same fold, for the reason in lesson 2. - Time-series split : always train on earlier data and validate on later data (for example: train on months 1-6, validate on 7; train on 1-7, validate on 8; ...). A shuffled k-fold would let the model train on the future. After CV has chosen the hyperparameters, retrain one model with them on all the training data, and evaluate that model once on the test set. Searching over hyperparameters - Grid search : list candidate values for each hyperparameter and try every combination. Three values of $\lambda$ and four polynomial degrees make $3 \times 4 = 12$ combinations; with 5-fold CV that is $12 \times 5 = 60$ trainings, plus one final refit with the winner on all the training data. - Random search : sample a fixed number of random combinations instead. When only a few hyperparameters really matter, it tries more distinct values of the important ones for the same budget. A $3 \times 3$ grid over two hyperparameters tests only 3 values of each; 9 random points test 9 values of each. - Strengths and learning rates are usually searched on a log scale, such as $0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1$. Look at the five fold scores: they range from about 0.86 to 1.0 for one and the same setting, which is why a single small validation split is unreliable. GridSearchCV takes the model, a dictionary from hyperparameter name to candidate values, and cv . After fit , best params is the winner, best score its mean CV score, and the object itself predicts with the refit model. best score is the maximum over many settings, so it has the same selection effect as lesson 2's test-set reuse (smaller, since the settings are few). Report the test score, not best score . Nested cross-validation Sometimes there is too little data for a separate test set, but you still want an honest score for "tune with grid search, then train". Nested CV puts the whole tuning procedure inside an outer CV loop: for each outer fold, run grid search with an inner CV on the outer training part only, refit, then score on the outer validation fold. With 5 outer folds, 3 inner folds and 8 combinations, that is $5 \times (3 \times 8 + 1) = 125$ trainings. The outer score estimates the procedure; it never saw the outer fold during tuning.

Real data arrives with columns on wildly different scales, text categories, and blanks. Turning it into a clean numeric matrix is called preprocessing, and doing it wrong is the most common source of leakage. Round 1 Part 2 problems (the 2027 pandas sample, the 2026 kNN problem) are mostly preprocessing, and Part 1 asks which procedure is correct. Scaling numeric features Some models compare features directly, so a feature measured in large units drowns out the others: - kNN and k-means (a clustering method, in a later unit) use distances. If income is in dollars (tens of thousands) and age in years (tens), the distance is almost entirely income. - L1 and L2 penalties treat all weights alike (lesson 4). - Gradient-based training (later units) converges much faster when features have similar scales. Decision trees split one feature at a time and do not care about scale. Standardization (z-scoring) rescales each feature to mean 0 and standard deviation 1: where $\mu$ is the feature's mean and $\sigma$ its standard deviation , the square root of the average squared distance from the mean: $\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum i (x i - \mu)^2}$. (This is the "population" version that divides by $n$; probability lessons explain the $n - 1$ version.) The result $z$ says how many standard deviations $x$ is above the mean. Min-max scaling maps each feature to $[0, 1]$ with $\frac{x - \min}{\max - \min}$. It is simple but one extreme value squashes everything else. Fit on the training set only The mean and standard deviation are numbers learned from data, just like parameters. Compute them from the training set only, then apply those same numbers to the validation and test sets. Computing them over all the data lets test examples influence the training pipeline: that is leakage (lesson 2, item 5), and it makes scores optimistic. Training values $2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9$: $\mu = 5$, squared distances $9, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 4, 16$ with average $4$, so $\sigma = 2$. A test value $8$ becomes $(8 - 5)/2 = 1.5$, and a test value $1$ becomes $-2$. The test values are never used to compute $\mu$ or $\sigma$. The pattern is the same for every scikit-learn preprocessing step: fit on training data, transform on everything. fit transform(X train) does both in one call, for the training data only. Never call fit or fit transform on test data. With cross-validation the scaler must be refit inside every fold, on that fold's training part. A pipeline does this automatically: make pipeline(StandardScaler(), model) chains the steps into one model whose fit fits the scaler and then the model. Scaling raises kNN's CV accuracy from about 0.69 to about 0.95 on this dataset. Categorical features: one-hot encoding A categorical feature takes values from a set of names, such as city $\in$ {Austin, Boston, Chicago}. Coding them as 0, 1, 2 tells a model that Chicago (2) is twice Boston (1) and that Boston sits exactly halfway between Austin and Chicago, which means nothing. One-hot encoding instead makes one 0/1 column per category, with a single 1 marking the example's category: city city=Austin city=Boston city=Chicago --- --- --- --- Boston 0 1 0 Chicago 0 0 1 A feature with $m$ categories becomes $m$ columns. When the categories do have a real order with roughly even steps (small < medium < large), ordinal encoding as 0, 1, 2 is reasonable. A category seen only at test time has no column; the usual choice is to encode it as all zeros. Missing values: imputation Real datasets have blanks, stored as NaN ("not a number") in NumPy. Options: - Drop rows with blanks. Simple, but it throws data away, and if the blanks are not random (say, older patients skip a question) it biases the data. - Impute : fill each blank with an estimate. Imputation for a numeric column usually uses the column's mean or median, computed on the training set only; the median is safer when there are outliers. For a categorical column, use the most frequent category, or a new category "missing". - Add a missing indicator : a 0/1 column saying "this value was blank". Whether a value is missing often carries information (a blank income field may mean something). The 2027 pandas sample asks for exactly such a flag ( price imputed ). sparse output=False makes OneHotEncoder return an ordinary array (the default is a compressed "sparse" format that prints badly). In NumPy, np.isnan gives a boolean mask of the blanks and np.where(mask, a, b) takes a where the mask is true and b elsewhere. Feature engineering Feature engineering means building new features from existing ones, so that a simple model can use information that was only implicit. Common moves: - ratios and differences: price per square meter, income minus debt; - parts of a date: day of week, month, hour; - the log of a heavily skewed positive amount (incomes, prices), so a few huge values do not dominate; - polynomial and interaction features ($x^2$, $x 1 x 2$), which let a linear model fit curves; - binning : turning a number into ranges, like the sample's quantity bands Small 1-5, Medium 6-20, Large over 20. Every engineered feature must be computable at prediction time from the information available then (lesson 2, leakage).

entries.t: Linear regression and the normal equations
entries.x: Linear models are the most common Round 1 coding task. The official 2027 sample SP2 is a linear regression trained from scratch, and 2025 Problem 3 (100 points) was logistic regression derived by hand and then coded under bans. Every one of these starts the same way: write the model, write the loss, take its gradient with the transpose in the right place. This lesson does that for linear regression and solves it exactly. The model Linear regression predicts a number as a weighted sum of the features plus a constant. For one example with feature vector $x = (x 1, \dots, x d)$: The $w j$ are the weights, one per feature, and $b$ is the bias term, also called the intercept (it is the prediction when every feature is 0). The hat on $\hat{y}$ marks a prediction; plain $y$ is the true target. For all $n$ examples at once, stack the feature vectors as the rows of a matrix $X$ of shape $(n, d)$, called the design matrix . Row $i$ is example $i$, column $j$ is feature $j$. Then $Xw$ has shape $(n,)$, and "$+\, b$" adds the number $b$ to every entry, which is exactly what NumPy broadcasting does with X @ w + b . "Linear" means linear in the parameters $w$ and $b$. The features can be anything computed from the raw input: with features $x, x^2, x^3$ the model fits a cubic curve and is still linear regression (the ML unit's polynomial fits were exactly this). The loss The usual loss is the mean squared error: Write $r i = \hat{y} i - y i$ for the residual of example $i$, so $L = \frac{1}{n}\sum i r i^2 = \frac{1}{n}\lVert r \rVert^2$. Some books define the residual the other way, $y i - \hat{y} i$. The square does not care, but the sign of every gradient below flips, so write down which one you use. Contest statements fix the constant in front: $\frac{1}{n}$, $\frac{1}{2n}$ (SP2 uses this form), or a plain sum. The minimizing $w$ is the same for all of them, but the gradient is scaled differently, and a grader that checks your weights after 50 gradient steps will notice. Folding the bias into the weights Derivations are shorter without a separate $b$. Append a column of ones to $X$ and the bias to $w$: The last "feature" is always 1, so its weight acts as the intercept. From here until the code, $X$ means the matrix that already has the ones column, $w$ includes $b$, and $d$ counts all the columns, the ones column included. The normal equations, by calculus Minimize $L(w) = \frac{1}{n}\sum i r i^2$ with $r i = \sum j X {ij} w j - y i$. Take the partial derivative with respect to one weight $w k$. Only the term $j = k$ of $r i$ contains $w k$, so $\partial r i / \partial w k = X {ik}$, and the chain rule gives The sum $\sum i X {ik} r i$ walks down column $k$ of $X$: it is (column $k$) $\cdot\ r$. The columns of $X$ are the rows of its transpose $X^\top$, so all $d$ of these dot products at once are the vector $X^\top r$. The gradient (the vector of all partial derivatives) is Shape check: $X^\top$ is $(d, n)$ and $Xw - y$ is $(n,)$, so the product is $(d,)$, the shape of $w$. A gradient always has the shape of the variable. $X(Xw - y)$ would be $(n, d)$ times $(n,)$, which does not multiply. This is how the transpose earns its place: it comes from summing over the examples $i$. Set the gradient to zero and drop the factor $\frac{2}{n}$: These are the normal equations from the linear algebra unit. When $X^\top X$ is invertible (no column of $X$ is a combination of the others), $w = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top y$. A formula that gives the answer directly, with no iterating, is called a closed-form solution . Why is the zero-gradient point the minimum and not a maximum or a saddle? The second partial derivatives are $\frac{\partial^2 L}{\partial w k \partial w l} = \frac{2}{n}\sum i X {ik} X {il}$, which together form the matrix $\frac{2}{n} X^\top X$. For any vector $v$, $v^\top X^\top X v = \lVert Xv \rVert^2 \ge 0$, so this matrix is positive semidefinite. A function whose matrix of second derivatives is positive semidefinite everywhere is convex: shaped like a bowl, with no hills. For a convex function, every point where the gradient is zero is a global minimum. Fit $\hat{y} = wx + b$ to $x = (1, 2, 3, 4)$, $y = (2, 3, 5, 6)$, keeping $b$ separate. $\partial L / \partial b = \frac{2}{n}\sum i (w x i + b - y i) = 0$ gives $b = \bar{y} - w\bar{x}$, where the bar means the average. So the best line passes through the point $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$. $\partial L / \partial w = \frac{2}{n}\sum i (w x i + b - y i)\, x i = 0$. Substitute $b$: $\sum i \big(w(x i - \bar{x}) - (y i - \bar{y})\big)\, x i = 0$. The bracket sums to zero over $i$, so $x i$ may be replaced by $x i - \bar{x}$ without changing the sum, which gives Numbers: $\bar{x} = 2.5$, $\bar{y} = 4$. Numerator $(-1.5)(-2) + (-0.5)(-1) + (0.5)(1) + (1.5)(2) = 7$. Denominator $2.25 + 0.25 + 0.25 + 2.25 = 5$. So $w = 1.4$ and $b = 4 - 1.4 \cdot 2.5 = 0.5$. The geometry, in one paragraph As $w$ varies, $Xw$ runs over the column space of $X$. The closest such point to $y$ is the projection of $y$ onto that space, and the leftover residual is orthogonal to every column: $X^\top r = 0$, which is the normal equations again. With a ones column, "orthogonal to the ones column" says $\sum i r i = 0$: the residuals of a fitted model with an intercept always sum to zero, and the average prediction equals the average target. In code np.linalg.solve(A, c) returns the $w$ with $A w = c$. Use it on the normal equations instead of np.linalg.inv(A) @ c : computing the whole inverse does more work and adds more rounding error, and Part 2 problems sometimes ban inv . scikit-learn's LinearRegression does the same fit and adds the intercept itself. LinearRegression() has fit intercept=True by default. If you also append a ones column yourself, sklearn gives that column weight 0 and puts the intercept in intercept anyway. When $X^\top X$ is not invertible $X^\top X$ is singular when some feature is a combination of others (a length in centimeters next to the same length in inches) or when there are fewer examples than features. Then infinitely many $w$ fit equally well. np.linalg.solve raises LinAlgError only when the matrix is exactly singular; with rounding it often returns one of the many answers without complaint. Fixes: drop the duplicate feature, add a ridge penalty (lesson 3), or take the minimum-norm solution with np.linalg.lstsq or the pseudo-inverse (linear algebra unit, lesson 6). Forming $X^\top X$ squares the condition number (for $X$: the ratio of its largest to its smallest singular value): if $X = U\Sigma V^\top$ then $X^\top X = V\Sigma^2 V^\top$, so a condition number of $10^6$ becomes $10^{12}$, and solving $X^\top X w = X^\top y$ in double precision (about 16 digits) can lose about 12 of them. QR avoids this. Gram-Schmidt on the columns of $X$ gives $X = QR$ with $Q$ ($n \times d$) having orthonormal columns and $R$ ($d \times d$) upper triangular. Substitute into the normal equations: $R^\top Q^\top Q R w = R^\top Q^\top y$, and since $Q^\top Q = I$ and $R$ is invertible, this is a triangular system solved from the last entry up (back substitution). Only $X$'s own condition number enters. np.linalg.lstsq goes further and uses the SVD, which also handles dependent columns. For $L = \frac{1}{n}\lVert Xw - y\rVert^2$ the gradient is $\frac{2}{n}X^\top(Xw - y)$. Graders and Part 1 distractors are built from these slips: no transpose ($X(Xw - y)$, wrong shape), no $\frac{1}{n}$ (the step is $n$ times too big), the sign flipped by mixing $y - \hat{y}$ with $\hat{y} - y$, and a factor 2 dropped or added when the loss had a $\frac{1}{2}$. Check the shape and recompute the constant from the loss as written.

The official 2027 sample SP2 bans np.linalg , so the closed form from lesson 1 is off the table: you must train by gradient descent, with exactly the number of steps given, and the grader compares your weights to its own to six digits. Getting those digits right takes four details: the sign of the step, the constant in the gradient, updating all parameters from the same point, and (for mini-batches) the exact order of the random shuffles. Gradient descent, restated Gradient descent starts from some parameters (often all zeros) and repeats $\eta$ (the Greek letter eta) is the learning rate, a small positive number you choose. The gradient $
abla L$ points in the direction in which $L$ increases fastest, so stepping against it lowers the loss. Moving along $+
abla L$ is gradient ascent, which climbs toward a maximum. Numbers: $L(w) = (w - 3)^2$ has its minimum at $w = 3$ and derivative $L'(w) = 2(w - 3)$. At $w = 1$, $L'(1) = -4$: the loss goes down as $w$ grows. With $\eta = 0.1$, the descent step gives $1 - 0.1 \cdot (-4) = 1.4$, closer to 3. The wrong sign gives $1 + 0.1 \cdot (-4) = 0.6$, further away. Why a small step always helps: to first order, $L(w - \eta g) \approx L(w) - \eta\, g \cdot g = L(w) - \eta \lVert g Vert^2$, which is smaller than $L(w)$ whenever the gradient $g$ is not zero. The gradients, with a separate bias Take SP2's form of the loss, with residuals $r = Xw + b - y$ (shape $(n,)$): Exactly as in lesson 1, $\partial r i / \partial w k = X {ik}$, and the $ rac{1}{2}$ cancels the 2 from the square. Each $r i$ has slope 1 in $b$. So The constant depends on how the loss is written. Read it off the statement every time: loss $
abla w L$ $\partial L / \partial b$ --- --- --- $\sum i r i^2$ $2X^	op r$ $2\sum i r i$ $ rac{1}{n}\sum i r i^2$ $ rac{2}{n}X^	op r$ $ rac{2}{n}\sum i r i$ $ rac{1}{2n}\sum i r i^2$ $ rac{1}{n}X^	op r$ $ rac{1}{n}\sum i r i$ Full-batch gradient descent in code Using all $n$ examples for every gradient is called full-batch gradient descent. Compute both gradients from the current $w$ and $b$, then update both. w = w - lr gw followed by recomputing the residuals and then updating b computes the bias gradient at the new w . That is a different algorithm with different numbers, and SP2's statement forbids it ("compute both gradients from the same current weights and bias"). Compute every gradient first, then update. Choosing the learning rate Too small a learning rate wastes steps. Too large a one overshoots the bottom of the bowl by more than it gained, and the loss grows every step until it becomes inf or nan . Same data as above: The loss after 100 steps is about 1.14 at 0.01 (still falling), 0.1229 at 0.1 and at 1.0 (converged), and about $3 	imes 10^{13}$ at 2.0 (diverged). The working habit: print the loss every few steps, and if it ever goes up, lower the learning rate. Features on very different scales make this worse: the weight of a feature measured in large numbers needs a tiny step, while the others need a big one, and a single learning rate cannot serve both. Standardizing the features first fixes it. Let $w^ $ be the minimizer (bias folded into $w$, with the ones column in $X$) and $H =  rac{1}{n}X^	op X$. The gradient is $ rac{1}{n}X^	op(Xw - y) = Hw -  rac{1}{n}X^	op y = H(w - w^ )$, because the normal equations say $ rac{1}{n}X^	op y = Hw^ $. So one step gives $w - w^ \leftarrow (I - \eta H)(w - w^ )$. Along each eigenvector of $H$ with eigenvalue $\lambda$ the error is multiplied by $1 - \eta\lambda$ per step. It shrinks exactly when $ 1 - \eta\lambda < 1$ for every eigenvalue, that is when $\eta < 2/\lambda {\max}$. For this data the eigenvalues of $H$ are about 0.87, 1.03 and 1.09, so the limit is $2/1.09 \approx 1.84$. Mini-batches and stochastic gradient descent With millions of examples one full gradient is expensive. A mini-batch is a small subset of the examples (say 32), and its gradient is the same formula with the mean taken over the batch only. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is gradient descent using these noisy mini-batch gradients ("stochastic" means random). An epoch is one pass over the whole training set, so with $n$ examples and batch size $B$ an epoch has $\lceil n/B ceil$ updates ($\lceil\cdotceil$ rounds up), and the last batch may be smaller than $B$. Contest problems that use SGD spell out the order, because the grader replays it. The usual specification looks like this: The slips a grader catches: creating the generator inside the epoch loop (every epoch then gets the same shuffle), shuffling X and y with two different permutations, dividing by B on a short last batch, and drawing extra random numbers that shift every later shuffle. Weighted losses (2027 sample SP2) Sometimes examples matter unequally. Give example $i$ a sample weight $s i \ge 0$, write $S = \sum i s i$, and use the weighted mean of the squared residuals: With every $s i = 1$ this is the $ rac{1}{2n}$ loss again. A weight of 2 counts like having that example twice, and a weight of 0 removes it. The derivative picks up the weight inside the sum: Here $s \odot r$ is the elementwise product, s r in NumPy. So the weighted gradient is the ordinary one with the residuals scaled by their weights first, and divided by $S$ instead of $n$. $X =  egin{pmatrix} 1 \ 0 \end{pmatrix}$, $y = (1, -1)$, $s = (1, 3)$, $\eta = 0.1$, starting at $w = 0$, $b = 0$. Residuals $r = (0 - 1,\ 0 + 1) = (-1, 1)$, so $s \odot r = (-1, 3)$ and $S = 4$. $
abla w L =  rac{1}{4}(1 \cdot (-1) + 0 \cdot 3) = -0.25$ and $\partial L/\partial b =  rac{1}{4}(-1 + 3) = 0.5$. New $w = 0 - 0.1 \cdot (-0.25) = 0.025$ and new $b = 0 - 0.1 \cdot 0.5 = -0.05$, the numbers in the statement. (SP2 also has a penalty term; at $w = 0$ its gradient is 0, so this first step does not see it. Lesson 3 adds it.) Practice: u07-p02 Mini-batch SGD with a fixed shuffle order (15 minutes). The weighted loss with its penalty is SP2, at the end of lesson 3.

entries.t: Ridge, lasso and weighted least squares
entries.x:
SP2's loss ends with $+ rac{\lambda}{2}\sum j w j^2$ and the sentence "the regularization term applies to $w$ but not to $b$". One of the official wrong demo solutions penalizes the bias anyway. This lesson puts the penalty into the gradient and into the closed form, shows why the bias stays out, and ends with SP2 itself as the capstone. Ridge: the penalty in the gradient Recall from the ML unit: regularization adds a penalty on the size of the weights to the loss, and with the L2 penalty linear regression is called ridge regression. With regularization strength $\lambda \ge 0$: The penalty's partial derivative with respect to $w k$ is $ rac{\lambda}{2} \cdot 2w k = \lambda w k$, and it does not contain $b$. So The gradient descent step for $w$ then rearranges to Every step first shrinks the weights by the factor $1 - \eta\lambda$, then takes the ordinary data step. That shrinking is why L2 regularization is also called weight decay. Ridge in closed form Setting the gradients to zero gives two equations. The bias equation is $ rac{1}{n}\sum i (x i \cdot w + b - y i) = 0$, so $b =  ar{y} -  ar{x} \cdot w$ as in lesson 1, where $ ar{x}$ is the vector of column means of $X$. Substitute it into the residual: $r = Xw +  ar{y} -  ar{x}\cdot w - y = X c w - y c$, where $X c = X -  ar{x}$ (every column minus its mean) and $y c = y -  ar{y}$ are the centered data. In the weight equation, $X^	op r = X c^	op r$, because $X = X c + \mathbf{1} ar{x}^	op$ and the bias equation says $\mathbf{1}^	op r = \sum i r i = 0$. So the weight equation $ rac{1}{n}X^	op r + \lambda w = 0$ becomes For $\lambda 0$ this matrix is positive definite: $v^	op ig( rac{1}{n}X c^	op X c + \lambda I ig)v =  rac{1}{n}\lVert X c vVert^2 + \lambda\lVert vVert^2 0$ for every $v 
e 0$. So it is invertible, and ridge has exactly one solution even when features are duplicated, which plain least squares did not (lesson 1). An equivalent way keeps the ones column (last) in $	ilde{X}$ and penalizes every entry of $	ilde{w}$ except the last: $ ig( rac{1}{n}	ilde{X}^	op	ilde{X} + \lambda D ig)	ilde{w} =  rac{1}{n}	ilde{X}^	op y$ with $D = \operatorname{diag}(1, \dots, 1, 0)$, the identity matrix with its last 1 replaced by 0. scikit-learn's Ridge(alpha=...) minimizes $\sum i r i^2 + \alpha\lVert w Vert^2$: a plain sum, no $ rac{1}{2}$, intercept not penalized. Multiplying our loss by $2n$ gives $\sum i r i^2 + n\lambda \lVert wVert^2$, so our $\lambda$ is sklearn's alpha = n lam . Every library scales its loss its own way; check before comparing numbers. Why the bias is not penalized The penalty exists to keep the model from being wiggly. The bias only shifts every prediction up or down, which makes nothing wigglier. Penalizing it pulls predictions toward 0, so the fit would depend on where the zero of $y$ happens to be (degrees Celsius or Fahrenheit, say). With the bias left out, adding a constant to every target adds the same constant to $b$ and leaves $w$ alone. With the bias free, shifting the targets by 1000 changes only the last entry (5.159 becomes 1005.159). With the bias penalized, the weights jump from about $(1.39, -0.01, -1.00)$ to $(19.76, -8.51, -76.37)$: the model distorts its slopes to avoid paying for a large intercept. Lasso, briefly The L1 penalty $\lambda\sum j w j $ gives lasso, which sets small weights exactly to zero (the ML unit's soft thresholding). Its derivative is $\lambda\operatorname{sign}(w j)$ away from 0, but $ w $ has a corner at 0 where no derivative exists. Plain gradient descent with $\operatorname{sign}(w)$ (and np.sign(0) = 0 ) therefore never lands on 0; it hops back and forth across it by about $\eta\lambda$. Libraries use a different algorithm (coordinate descent, which applies soft thresholding one weight at a time) and get exact zeros. sklearn's Lasso(alpha=...) minimizes $ rac{1}{2n}\sum i r i^2 + \alpha\sum j w j $, so here alpha is $\lambda$ directly. Split the lasso loss into a smooth part $g(w) =  rac{1}{2n}\lVert Xw - yVert^2$ and the corner part $\lambda\lVert wVert 1$. A gradient step on $g$ alone from $w$ lands at $v = w - \eta
abla g(w)$. That $v$ is the minimizer over $u$ of the model $g(w) + 
abla g(w)^	op(u - w) +  rac{1}{2\eta}\lVert u - wVert^2$, which (complete the square) equals $ rac{1}{2\eta}\lVert u - vVert^2$ plus a constant. Proximal gradient descent (ISTA) keeps the corner part exact instead of linearizing it: This splits into one-variable problems $ rac{1}{2\eta}(u j - v j)^2 + \lambda u j $. Multiply by $\eta$: it is the ML unit's $ rac12(u - a)^2 + \lambda' u $ with $a = v j$ and $\lambda' = \eta\lambda$, solved by soft thresholding. So With $\eta \le 1/\lambda {\max}( rac{1}{n}X^	op X)$ the quadratic model lies above $g$, so each step cannot increase the loss, and weights that should be 0 land exactly on 0 instead of jittering around it. Weighted least squares in closed form Lesson 2 trained the weighted loss by gradient descent. It also has a closed form. With the bias folded into $w$, set the gradient of $\sum i s i (x i \cdot w - y i)^2$ to zero: where $\operatorname{diag}(s)$ is the $n 	imes n$ matrix with $s$ on its diagonal. Never build it: X.T @ (s[:, None] X) scales row $i$ of $X$ by $s i$ first (an $(n, d)$ array) and gives the same $(d, d)$ matrix without ever storing $n^2$ numbers. The constant $ rac{1}{2S}$ does not change where the minimum is. SP2's loss adds the bias-free penalty, and then the stationary point solves $ ig( rac{1}{S}	ilde{X}^	op\operatorname{diag}(s)	ilde{X} + \lambda D ig)	ilde{w} =  rac{1}{S}	ilde{X}^	op(s \odot y)$. SP2 bans np.linalg , but outside the exam this is how you check that your gradient descent is heading to the right place. Practice: u07-p01 Ridge regression in closed form (12 minutes) asks for exactly this solution with np.linalg.solve , inv banned. Capstone: SP2 Now do the official 2027 sample SP2 (weighted linear regression) under exam conditions (20 minutes). The organizers post the 2027 sample problems on contest.usaaio.org, linked from the 2027 contest page. Everything it needs is in lessons 2 and 3: - $
abla w L =  rac{1}{S}X^	op(s \odot r) + \lambda w$ and $ rac{\partial L}{\partial b} =  rac{1}{S}\sum i s i r i$, with $r = Xw + b - y$ and $S = \sum i s i$. - init stores learning rate , steps , regularization , sets self.weights = None and self.bias = 0.0 . - Every fit resets to np.zeros(d) and 0.0 , makes exactly steps updates from the same point, and returns self . - predict returns shape (m,) . No method changes its inputs; no np.linalg . The grader's wrong demo solutions divide by $n$ instead of $S$, penalize the bias, update $b$ after $w$ has moved, and skip the reset on a second fit . Each one fails a hidden test.

2025 Round 1 Problem 3 (100 points) asked, in order: the logistic regression loss, the sigmoid's derivative written with $\sigma$ only, the gradient as a sum and as a matrix product, the Hessian, a convexity proof, and then a from-scratch class. This lesson covers the model, the loss and the gradient; lesson 5 does the Hessian and the training code. Logistic regression is also the model behind most "predict a probability" questions in Part 1. From a score to a probability In binary classification the label is $y \in \{0, 1\}$, with 1 for the positive class. We want the probability that $y = 1$ given the features $x$. A linear score $z = w \cdot x + b$ can be any real number, so squash it into $(0, 1)$ with the sigmoid: This model is logistic regression (a classifier, despite the name). Four facts about $\sigma$ get used constantly: - $\sigma(0) = \frac{1}{2}$; $\sigma(z) \to 1$ as $z \to \infty$ and $\to 0$ as $z \to -\infty$. - $\sigma(-z) = 1 - \sigma(z)$, because $1 - \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}} = \frac{e^{-z}}{1 + e^{-z}} = \frac{1}{e^{z} + 1}$. - $\sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)\big(1 - \sigma(z)\big)$. From $\sigma = (1 + e^{-z})^{-1}$: $\sigma'(z) = \frac{e^{-z}}{(1 + e^{-z})^2} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}} \cdot \frac{e^{-z}}{1 + e^{-z}} = \sigma(z)\big(1 - \sigma(z)\big)$. Its largest value is $\frac{1}{4}$, at $z = 0$. - Solving $p = \sigma(z)$ for $z$ gives $z = \ln\frac{p}{1 - p}$. The ratio $\frac{p}{1 - p}$ is the odds (odds of 3 mean "3 to 1": $p = 0.75$), and $z$ is the log-odds . So logistic regression is linear regression on the log-odds: raising feature $x j$ by 1 adds $w j$ to the log-odds, which multiplies the odds by $e^{w j}$. Probabilities versus labels The model outputs a probability $p i$ for each example. To output a label, compare with a threshold, usually $\frac{1}{2}$: The decision boundary is the set of points where the model is exactly undecided, $w \cdot x + b = 0$: a line in 2D, a plane in 3D, a hyperplane in general. A classifier whose boundary is a hyperplane is a linear classifier . A different threshold $t$ moves the boundary parallel to itself, to $w \cdot x + b = \ln\frac{t}{1 - t}$. $w = (2, -1)$, $b = -1$. The boundary is $2x 1 - x 2 - 1 = 0$, the line $x 2 = 2x 1 - 1$. For $x = (1, 0)$: $z = 2 - 0 - 1 = 1$ and $p = \sigma(1) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-1}} \approx 0.731$, so the label is 1. For $x = (0, 0)$: $z = -1$, $p \approx 0.269$, label 0. The loss: log-loss The standard loss for one example is the log-loss (also called binary cross-entropy): Only one term is alive at a time: $\ell = -\ln p$ when $y = 1$ and $\ell = -\ln(1 - p)$ when $y = 0$. So the loss is the minus log of the probability the model gave to the true label. Confident and right costs almost nothing ($-\ln 0.9 \approx 0.105$); confident and wrong costs a lot ($-\ln 0.1 \approx 2.303$, $-\ln 0.001 \approx 6.91$). The training loss is the mean $L = \frac{1}{n}\sum i \ell i$; 2025 Problem 3 used the plain sum, which has the same minimizer and a gradient $n$ times larger. Why this loss and not MSE: it is what "make the observed labels as probable as possible" gives. The model says $P(y i = 1) = p i$, so the probability it assigns to the label actually seen is $p i^{y i}(1 - p i)^{1 - y i}$ (this is $p i$ if $y i = 1$ and $1 - p i$ if $y i = 0$). Treating the examples as independent, the probability of all $n$ labels is the product of these. That product, viewed as a function of the parameters, is the likelihood (u05-l07). Maximizing it is the same as maximizing its log, $\sum i \big[y i \ln p i + (1 - y i)\ln(1 - p i)\big]$, which is the same as minimizing the log-loss. (MSE on $p$ would also train, but it is not convex in $w$, and its gradient almost vanishes on examples that are confidently wrong.) The gradient First the derivative of one example's loss with respect to its score $z$. Using $\sigma' = \sigma(1 - \sigma)$: Prediction minus label, the same as the residual of linear regression. Then the chain rule with $z i = x i \cdot w + b$, so $\partial z i / \partial w = x i$ and $\partial z i / \partial b = 1$: where $p = \sigma(Xw + b)$ is applied entry by entry. Shape check: $(d, n)(n,) = (d,)$. With the 2025 sum loss and a ones column for the bias, this is $X^\top(p - y)$, the posted answer. Unlike linear regression, setting this to zero gives no formula for $w$: $p$ depends on $w$ through the sigmoid, so the equations are not linear. Logistic regression is always trained by iterating (lesson 5). At the minimum the bias gradient is zero: $\frac{1}{n}\sum i (p i - y i) = 0$. So for logistic regression with an intercept (and no penalty on it), the average predicted probability on the training set equals the fraction of positive labels, whatever the features are. With 12 positives out of 40, the fitted $p i$ average exactly $0.3$. The weight gradients say more: $\sum i (p i - y i)\,x {ij} = 0$ for each feature $j$, so the model reproduces the label-weighted averages of every feature. Linear regression with an intercept has the same property: its residuals sum to zero. Computing it stably 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z)) returns exactly 1.0 for every $z \ge 37$ in float64, because $1 + e^{-37}$ rounds to 1. Then $\ln(1 - p) = \ln 0 = -\infty$, and for an example with $y = 1$ the code computes $0 \cdot (-\infty) =$ nan . Very negative $z$ also overflows np.exp(-z) . The fix is to write the loss in terms of $z$, never forming $1 - p$. Since $-\ln\sigma(z) = \ln(1 + e^{-z})$ and $-\ln(1 - \sigma(z)) = \ln(1 + e^{z})$, (Check: for $y = 1$, $\ln(1 + e^z) - z = \ln(e^{-z} + 1)$.) The function $\ln(1 + e^z)$ is the softplus, and np.logaddexp(0, z) , which computes $\ln(e^0 + e^z)$ without overflow, gives it stably. For the sigmoid itself, use $e^{- z }$, which is always at most 1: In scikit-learn Three things to remember. predict proba returns one column per class, so the probability of class 1 is [:, 1] . coef is 2D, shape (1, d) , even for two classes. And the default LogisticRegression() is regularized: it minimizes $\frac{1}{2}\lVert w\rVert^2 + C\sum i \ell i$ with C=1.0 , where C is the inverse of the regularization strength. Pass penalty=None when a task asks for plain logistic regression. In Colab's current versions the default solver also prints OptimizeWarning: Unknown solver options: iprint . It is harmless (SciPy is newer than this scikit-learn expects) and the fit is unaffected; the warnings line above only hides it.

entries.t: Logistic regression by GD and Newton
entries.x: 2025 Problem 3 ended with 45 points of logistic regression: the Hessian in matrix form, a convexity proof, the gradient descent and Newton updates, and a class My Log Reg(solver, lr, num iter) that trains by either one. The posted official solution got the Hessian wrong and called the loss "concave". This lesson derives both correctly and codes both solvers. Notation: the ones column is folded into $X$ (shape $(n, d)$, last column all ones), so $w$ includes the bias. $p = \sigma(Xw)$ entrywise, and the loss is the mean log-loss from lesson 4, with Gradient descent The update is $w \leftarrow w - \eta\,\frac{1}{n}X^\top(p - y)$, recomputing $p$ at every step. Use the stable sigmoid and the stable loss from lesson 4, and print the loss now and then to see it fall. The Hessian The Hessian is the matrix of second partial derivatives, $H {kl} = \partial^2 L / \partial w k \partial w l$. Differentiate entry $k$ of the gradient, $\frac{1}{n}\sum i (p i - y i)X {ik}$, with respect to $w l$. Only $p i$ depends on $w$, and by the chain rule $\partial p i / \partial w l = \sigma'(z i)\, X {il} = p i(1 - p i)X {il}$. So $\operatorname{diag}(\dots)$ is the $n \times n$ matrix with those numbers on its diagonal and zeros elsewhere, so $(X^\top S X) {kl} = \sum i X {ik} S {ii} X {il}$, matching the sum. Shape: $(d, n)(n, n)(n, d) = (d, d)$. For the 2025 summed loss drop the $\frac{1}{n}$. The 2025 statement called the vector of probabilities $z$ and wrote $Z = \operatorname{diag}(z i)$; in that notation $S = Z(I - Z)$ and It gave the Hessian as $X^\top Z X$, missing the factor $(I - Z)$ that comes from $\sigma' = \sigma(1 - \sigma)$. And after showing the Hessian is positive semidefinite, it concluded the loss is "(weakly) concave". A positive semidefinite Hessian means convex . Students pointed out both errors in the forum replies. Convexity proof. For any vector $v$, because each $p i(1 - p i) 0$ and each square is $\ge 0$. So $H$ is positive semidefinite at every $w$, and the log-loss is a convex function: any point where the gradient is zero is a global minimum, and gradient descent with a small enough step cannot get stuck anywhere else. If the columns of $X$ are independent, $x i \cdot v = 0$ for all $i$ only when $v = 0$, so $H$ is even positive definite. Newton's method Newton's method uses the Hessian to choose the step. Near the current $w$, the second-order Taylor approximation is Its gradient with respect to $\Delta$ is $g + H\Delta$, which is zero at $\Delta = -H^{-1}g$. So the update jumps to the bottom of the local quadratic bowl: In code, solve $H\Delta = g$ with np.linalg.solve(H, g) instead of forming the inverse. And never build the $n \times n$ matrix $S$: $X^\top S X$ equals X.T @ (X s[:, None]) with s = p (1 - p) , which scales row $i$ of $X$ by $s i$. (With $n = 100{,}000$, np.diag(s) alone would be 80 GB.) 2025 Problem 3 also gave Newton a learning rate, $w \leftarrow w - \eta H^{-1}\nabla L$; this is called damped Newton, and with $\eta = 1$ it is the plain method. Newton reaches the minimum loss $0.40142381\ldots$ to 12 digits in 6 steps. Gradient descent with learning rate 1 took about 1000 steps for the same accuracy. The price is per step: one step costs steps needed good when --- --- --- --- gradient descent $X^\top(p - y)$: about $nd$ hundreds to thousands $d$ is large (images, text) Newton $X^\top S X$ and a solve: about $nd^2 + d^3$ about 5 to 10 $d$ is small (tabular data, a few dozen features) If some $w$ classifies every training example correctly (the data are linearly separable), scaling that $w$ up drives the loss toward 0 forever, so no minimum exists: $p i(1 - p i) \to 0$, $H$ becomes nearly singular, and the weights blow up. A feature that duplicates another also makes $H$ singular. The standard fix is a small L2 penalty: add $\lambda w$ to the gradient and $\lambda I$ to the Hessian. The 2025-style class Part 2 of the exam wraps this in a class. The shape of a solution (the full task is problem u07-p04 ; u07-p03 is gradient descent alone with a stable loss):

Most classification tasks have more than two classes: ten digits, five land-cover types, a thousand image categories. Softmax regression is logistic regression for $K$ classes, and it is also exactly the last layer of nearly every classifier network, so its gradient $P - Y$ comes back in every neural network unit. The 2027 sample Part 1 Problem 4 used the same loss with soft targets. The NumPy unit coded softmax and log-softmax stably; here they become a model you train. The model Labels are $y i \in \{0, 1, \dots, K - 1\}$. The model gives each class its own linear score, $z k = w k \cdot x + b k$. Put the $K$ weight vectors side by side as the columns of a matrix $W$ of shape $(d, K)$ and the biases in $b$ of shape $(K,)$. For all examples at once, Row $i$ of $Z$ holds the $K$ logits of example $i$ ("$+\, b$" broadcasts over the rows), and row $i$ of $P$ is their softmax: $K$ positive numbers that sum to 1, the model's probability for each class. The predicted class is the largest entry of the row, P.argmax(axis=1) , which is also Z.argmax(axis=1) because softmax keeps the order of the scores. This model is softmax regression (also called multinomial logistic regression). It has $dK + K$ parameters. PyTorch's nn.Linear(d, K) and scikit-learn's coef store the weights the other way round, shape $(K, d)$, and compute $XW^\top + b$. It is the same model; read which shape a statement gives before writing the gradient. One-hot targets and cross-entropy Write the labels as a one-hot encoding $Y$ of shape $(n, K)$: $Y {ik} = 1$ if $y i = k$ and 0 otherwise. In NumPy, np.eye(K)[y] picks row $y i$ of the identity matrix for each example. The loss is the cross-entropy loss: With one-hot rows only the true class's term survives, so this is again minus the log of the probability given to the true label, exactly like the log-loss of lesson 4. If the rows of $Y$ are any probability vectors ("soft targets", as in the 2027 sample P4), the first form still applies unchanged. The gradient Take one example with logits $z$ and target row $Y$ (dropping the index $i$). By the log-softmax identity from the NumPy unit, $\ln P k = z k - \operatorname{LSE}(z)$, where $\operatorname{LSE}(z) = \ln\sum j e^{z j}$ is the log-sum-exp. Because $\sum k Y k = 1$, The derivative of $\operatorname{LSE}$ is the softmax: $\frac{\partial}{\partial z j}\ln\sum m e^{z m} = \frac{e^{z j}}{\sum m e^{z m}} = P j$. So Probabilities minus targets, the multiclass version of logistic regression's $p - y$. Now the chain rule through $Z = XW + b$. $Z {ik} = \sum j X {ij}W {jk} + b k$, so $\partial Z {ik}/\partial W {jk} = X {ij}$ and Shape check: $(d, n)(n, K) = (d, K)$, the shape of $W$. The bias gradient is the column means of $P - Y$, shape $(K,)$: (P - Y).sum(axis=0) / n . Two classes: logistic regression again With $K = 2$, the probability of class 1 is which is logistic regression with weights $w 1 - w 0$ and bias $b 1 - b 0$. This also shows that adding the same vector to every column of $W$ (and the same number to every $b k$) changes no probability, so the best $W$ is not unique. That does not hurt gradient descent, and an L2 penalty makes it unique. Training it Full-batch gradient descent, with the loss computed from the stable log-softmax: The loss starts at $\ln 3 \approx 1.0986$ (all zeros gives every class probability $\frac{1}{3}$) and falls to about 0.275, with training accuracy about 0.90; the blobs overlap, so no linear model gets them all. In scikit-learn, LogisticRegression handles several classes with this same softmax model by default: predict proba returns shape $(n, K)$ and coef has shape $(K, d)$. Use penalty=None for the plain loss, as in lesson 4. Practice: u07-p05 Softmax regression trained by gradient descent (20 minutes).

The perceptron is the oldest learning rule in ML and the unit that neural networks are built from. Part 1 likes to ask you to run it by hand for a few steps, and to recognize data that no linear model can classify, with XOR as the standard example (a USA-J-AIO sample problem asks exactly this). Both take a few minutes once you have seen them. The model and the update rule The perceptron is a linear classifier with labels $y \in \{-1, +1\}$ instead of $\{0, 1\}$. It predicts $+1$ when $w \cdot x + b 0$ and $-1$ when $w \cdot x + b < 0$. The $\pm 1$ labels make "correct" a single inequality: example $i$ is classified correctly exactly when The perceptron rule visits the examples one at a time in a fixed order. Whenever $y i(w \cdot x i + b) \le 0$ (a mistake, counting a point exactly on the boundary as a mistake), it updates and otherwise it changes nothing. Training starts at $w = 0$, $b = 0$ and repeats passes over the data (epochs) until one full pass makes no mistake. Why the update helps: after it, the same example's score times its label becomes using $y i^2 = 1$. The quantity that has to be positive grows by $\lVert x i\rVert^2 + 1$. One update may not fix the example, and it can break others, but it always moves the right way on the one it saw. Points in this order: $x 1 = (1, 2)$, $y 1 = +1$; $x 2 = (2, 0)$, $y 2 = -1$; $x 3 = (0, 0)$, $y 3 = -1$; $x 4 = (3, 1)$, $y 4 = +1$. Epoch 1. $x 1$: score $0$, mistake, so $w = (1, 2)$, $b = 1$. $x 2$: score $2 + 0 + 1 = 3$, times $y = -1$ is $-3$, mistake: $w = (1, 2) - (2, 0) = (-1, 2)$, $b = 0$. $x 3$: score 0, mistake: $w$ unchanged (since $x 3 = 0$), $b = -1$. $x 4$: score $-3 + 2 - 1 = -2$, mistake: $w = (2, 3)$, $b = 0$. Epoch 2. $x 1$: score $8$, correct. $x 2$: score $4$ with $y = -1$, mistake: $w = (0, 3)$, $b = -1$. $x 3$: score $-1$, correct. $x 4$: score $2$, correct. Epoch 3. Scores $5, -1, -1, 2$, all with the right sign. Done: $w = (0, 3)$, $b = -1$ after 5 updates. The boundary is the line $x 2 = \frac{1}{3}$. Linear separability and convergence A dataset is linearly separable when some $w, b$ classify every example correctly, that is, some hyperplane has all the $+1$ points strictly on one side and all the $-1$ points strictly on the other. The perceptron convergence theorem: if the data are linearly separable, the perceptron makes only finitely many updates and then stops with a separating hyperplane. The final line depends on the order of the examples, and it is just some separating line, not the best one (the support vector machine of u04-l08 picks the one with the largest margin). Fold $b$ into $w$ by appending a 1 to each $x i$. Suppose a unit vector $u$ separates with room to spare: $y i(u \cdot x i) \ge \gamma 0$ for all $i$, and let $R = \max i \lVert x i \rVert$. Each update adds $y i x i$ to $w$, so $u \cdot w$ grows by $y i(u \cdot x i) \ge \gamma$, and after $k$ updates $u \cdot w \ge k\gamma$. Also $\lVert w + y i x i \rVert^2 = \lVert w\rVert^2 + 2y i(w \cdot x i) + \lVert x i\rVert^2 \le \lVert w\rVert^2 + R^2$, because updates happen only when $y i(w \cdot x i) \le 0$; so $\lVert w\rVert^2 \le kR^2$. By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, $k\gamma \le u \cdot w \le \lVert w\rVert \le \sqrt{k}R$, hence $k \le R^2/\gamma^2$. XOR: data no line can separate The four points of XOR ("exclusive or") are $(0, 0)$ and $(1, 1)$ with label $-1$, and $(0, 1)$ and $(1, 0)$ with label $+1$. Suppose $w 1, w 2, b$ separated them. The four conditions are Adding the last two gives $w 1 + w 2 + 2b 0$, so $w 1 + w 2 + b -b 0$, which contradicts the second. So XOR is not linearly separable, and the perceptron never finishes an epoch without a mistake: it cycles forever. Every linear classifier, logistic regression included, fails on XOR the same way. Stacking several linear layers does not help either, because a linear function of a linear function is still linear. The fix is a nonlinear feature. Add $x 3 = x 1 x 2$. Then $w = (1, 1, -2)$, $b = -0.5$ separates: the scores are $-0.5, -0.5, 0.5, 0.5$ for $(0,0), (1,1), (0,1), (1,0)$. In the new 3D feature space the data are separable. A neural network's hidden layer learns such features by itself (neural networks unit). Practice: u07-p06 The perceptron, in exact order (10 minutes).

The 2026 Round 1 paper ended with a 50-point open-ended problem: classify breast tumors as malignant or benign from 30 numeric features, using only k-nearest neighbors, graded by macro-averaged F1 on a hidden test set. Every point came from preparing the data and tuning one simple model. This lesson covers the model and its settings; lesson 9 gives the scikit-learn template for the whole task, and problem u08-p03 is a timed version of it. The algorithm You met k-nearest neighbors (kNN) in the NumPy unit (u02-l10) as array code. As a model it works like this: - Training : store the training examples. That is all. A model that postpones all its work to prediction time is called a lazy learner . - Prediction for a query point $q$: compute the distance from $q$ to every training example, take the $k$ closest ones (the neighbors ), and predict the most common label among them, a majority vote . The number $k$ is a hyperparameter. The distance is usually the Euclidean distance. Six training points and the query $q = (3, 3)$, sorted by distance to $q$: point $x 1$ $x 2$ label squared distance to $q$ --- --- --- --- --- A 2 3 1 $1 + 0 = 1$ B 1 4 0 $4 + 1 = 5$ C 5 1 0 $4 + 4 = 8$ D 3 0 1 $0 + 9 = 9$ E 6 2 1 $9 + 1 = 10$ F 6 1 0 $9 + 4 = 13$ - $k = 1$: only A votes. Predict 1. - $k = 3$: A, B, C vote 1, 0, 0. Predict 0. - $k = 5$: A to E vote 1, 0, 0, 1, 1. Three votes for 1: predict 1. You can rank by squared distance and skip the square root: $\sqrt{\ }$ is increasing, so it does not change the order. The prediction changes with $k$, and this one query cannot tell you which $k$ is best on new data. Only a validation score can. A classifier can also report class probabilities.
