For kNN, predict proba gives the fraction of the $k$ neighbors in each class: at $k = 5$ that is $(0.4, 0.6)$ for classes 0 and 1. fit returns the model, so KNeighborsClassifier(...).fit(X, y) can be written on one line. kneighbors returns two arrays of shape (n queries, k) : the distances (not squared) and the row indices of the neighbors, nearest first. model.kneighbors(q, n neighbors=3) asks for 3 neighbors instead of the model's own $k$. Choosing k - $k = 1$: every training point is its own nearest neighbor, so training accuracy is 100% (unless two identical points have different labels). The boundary bends around every noisy point. This is overfitting: high variance. - Large $k$: the vote averages over a wide area, so the boundary gets smoother. At $k = n$ (all $n$ training points) every query gets the same $n$ neighbors and the model predicts the majority class everywhere: underfitting. - Choose $k$ by cross-validation (u06-l08). With two classes, an odd $k$ avoids tied votes. The picture shows the regions each model assigns to the two classes on noisy two-moon data, for $k = 1$, $15$ and $150$ (all 150 training points). The line between the colored regions is the decision boundary. model.score(X, y) returns the accuracy of the model's predictions on X . $k = 1$ scores 1.00 on training data but 0.89 on test data; $k = 15$ scores 0.93 on both. $k = 150$ colors the whole plane with the training set's majority class and scores 0.57 and 0.43. Scale the features first kNN compares raw coordinate differences, so a feature measured in large units dominates the distance. In u06-l09, standardizing the wine data raised kNN's cross-validated accuracy from 0.69 to 0.95. Always put a StandardScaler before kNN, inside a pipeline so the scaler is fit on training data only. Every feature also counts equally in the distance. A feature that has nothing to do with the label still adds noise to every distance, so removing useless features ( feature selection ) can help kNN a lot, while most other models just learn to ignore them. Other distances The Manhattan distance is $\sum j a j - b j $, the L1 norm of $a - b$ (the distance walking along a city grid). In scikit-learn, metric="manhattan" . The default is metric="minkowski" with p=2 . The Minkowski distance is $\left(\sum j a j - b j ^p\right)^{1/p}$, so p=2 is the Euclidean distance and p=1 is Manhattan. For long vectors such as word counts, metric="cosine" uses $1 -$ cosine similarity. Distance-weighted votes With weights="distance" , each neighbor votes with weight $1/d$, where $d$ is its distance (not squared) to the query. Close neighbors count more. For $k = 3$: class 1 gets $1/\sqrt1 = 1$ from A. Class 0 gets $1/\sqrt5 + 1/\sqrt8 \approx 0.447 + 0.354 = 0.801$ from B and C. Weighted prediction: 1, although the plain vote said 0. predict proba divides by the total weight: $(0.801, 1)/1.801 \approx (0.445, 0.555)$. If the query lands exactly on a training point ($d = 0$), $1/d$ is infinite; scikit-learn then lets only the zero-distance neighbors vote. Weighted votes rarely tie, and they make a large $k$ less harmful, since far neighbors count little. Problem u08-p02 asks you to code this weighted rule in NumPy, zero distances included. For a numeric label, KNeighborsRegressor predicts the mean of the neighbors' labels (or the weighted mean with weights="distance" ). Cost and the curse of dimensionality Training costs nothing, but every prediction computes $n$ distances in $d$ dimensions, about $nd$ operations per query. For a few thousand rows that is instant. (scikit-learn may use a tree data structure to find neighbors faster; the answers are the same.) kNN assumes that nearby points have similar labels. In many dimensions, "nearby" loses its meaning: the distances from a query to the nearest and to the farthest training point become almost equal. This is one form of the curse of dimensionality . The ratio climbs from near 0 in 2D toward 1 in 1000D. Real data usually lies near a lower-dimensional shape, so kNN still works on 30 features, but fewer and better features help, and so does dimensionality reduction such as PCA (lesson 7). Standardize, then kNN, in one pipeline. Tune n neighbors (odd values 1 to 31), weights ( "uniform" or "distance" ) and p (1 or 2) by cross-validation scored with macro F1, not accuracy, because that is the metric graded. Try dropping weak features. Lesson 9 writes this as code.

Decision trees are the building block of random forests and gradient boosting (lesson 3), which are usually the strongest models on tables of numbers. Round 1 Part 1 can ask you to compute a Gini impurity, an entropy or an information gain by hand, or to pick the best split from a small table. The arithmetic is quick once you know the definitions. What a tree is A decision tree is a flowchart of yes/no questions. Each question has the form "is feature $j$ at most $t$?" for one feature $j$ and a number $t$ (the threshold). - A node is one box of the flowchart. The first one is the root . - An internal node asks a question and sends each example left (yes) or right (no). This is a split . - A leaf is a node with no question. It stores a prediction: the majority class of the training examples that reached it. - The depth of a tree is the number of questions on its longest path from the root to a leaf. To predict, start at the root, answer the questions for your example, and output the label of the leaf you reach. predict proba outputs the class fractions of the training examples in that leaf. Here is a tiny dataset: did a student pass (1) or fail (0), given hours studied and hours slept? student a b c d e f g h i j --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- studied 1 2 3 4 5 5 6 7 8 9 slept 6 8 5 7 4 9 7 8 5 6 pass 0 1 0 0 0 1 1 1 1 1 A depth-2 tree classifies all ten correctly: The rest of the lesson is how a computer finds those questions. Impurity: how mixed is a node? A good split produces children that are each mostly one class. An impurity measure scores how mixed a node is: 0 for a node with one class, largest for an even mix. Let $p c$ be the fraction of the node's examples in class $c$. - Gini impurity : $G = 1 - \sum c p c^2$. It is the chance that two examples drawn at random (with replacement) from the node have different classes. - Entropy (from u05-l08): $H = -\sum c p c \log 2 p c$ bits, with $0 \log 0 = 0$. class fractions Gini entropy (bits) --- --- --- $(1, 0)$, pure $1 - 1 = 0$ 0 $(0.5, 0.5)$ $1 - 0.25 - 0.25 = 0.5$ 1 $(0.6, 0.4)$, the root above $1 - 0.36 - 0.16 = 0.48$ 0.971 For two classes Gini is at most 0.5 and entropy at most 1 bit. With $K$ classes the maximums are $1 - 1/K$ and $\log 2 K$, both at the even mix. Scoring a split A split sends $n L$ of the node's $n$ examples left and $n R$ right. Its quality is the weighted impurity of the children, each weighted by its share of the examples: where $I$ is Gini or entropy. Lower is better. The drop from the parent's impurity is the improvement. It is never negative: Gini and entropy are concave functions of the class fractions, so the weighted average of the children's impurities is at most the parent's. With entropy, that drop has a name, the information gain : The root has 6 passes and 4 fails: Gini 0.48, entropy 0.971. Split A: studied $\le 5.5$. Left: a to f, 2 passes and 4 fails. Right: g to j, 4 passes. - Gini: left $1 - (2/6)^2 - (4/6)^2 = 4/9 \approx 0.444$, right 0. Weighted: $\frac{6}{10}(0.444) + \frac{4}{10}(0) = 0.267$. - Entropy: left $H(1/3, 2/3) = 0.918$, right 0. Weighted $0.6 \times 0.918 = 0.551$. Gain $0.971 - 0.551 = 0.420$ bits. Split B: slept $\le 6.5$. Left: a, c, e, i, j, with 2 passes and 3 fails. Right: b, d, f, g, h, with 4 passes and 1 fail. - Gini: left $1 - 0.16 - 0.36 = 0.48$, right $1 - 0.64 - 0.04 = 0.32$. Weighted $0.5(0.48) + 0.5(0.32) = 0.40$. - Entropy: left 0.971, right $H(0.8, 0.2) = 0.722$. Weighted 0.846. Gain $0.125$ bits. Split A wins under both criteria: weighted Gini 0.267 against 0.40, gain 0.420 against 0.125. Gini and entropy almost always pick the same split. Gini is the scikit-learn default because it needs no logarithm. Growing the tree The algorithm for one node: 1. For every feature, sort the distinct values that reach the node. The candidate thresholds are the midpoints between consecutive values (studied has values 1, 2, ..., 9, so candidates 1.5, 2.5, ..., 8.5). Any threshold between two neighboring values gives the same split, and the midpoint is the convention. 2. Score every (feature, threshold) pair by weighted impurity, and keep the best. 3. Split, and repeat steps 1 and 2 on each child. Stop when a node is pure or a limit is reached. Each split is chosen as the best one right now, with no look-ahead to later splits; such an algorithm is called greedy . Greedy trees are not always the smallest possible, but they are fast to build. On the student data the root search tries 8 thresholds for studied and 5 for slept (slept has 6 distinct values). Split A is the best of all 13. In the left child (a to f), slept $\le 7.5$ separates the fails a, c, d, e from the passes b and f, so both grandchildren are pure and the tree stops. Problem u08-p01 asks you to code the threshold search for one feature. export text prints the learned questions. feature importances adds up, for each feature, the impurity decrease of every split on it (weighted by the share of examples at that node), scaled to sum to 1. Here slept gets 0.56 and studied 0.44. The root split on studied lowers the weighted Gini by $0.48 - 0.267 = 0.213$; the split on slept turns 6 of the 10 examples from Gini $4/9$ into pure leaves, a decrease of $\frac{6}{10} \cdot \frac49 = 0.267$. Importance measures how much a feature was used, not whether it was asked first. Depth and overfitting Without limits, a tree keeps splitting until every leaf is pure. Then training accuracy is 100%, and the last splits often isolate single noisy examples: overfitting. The usual limits, all hyperparameters of DecisionTreeClassifier : - max depth : at most this many questions on any path. - min samples leaf : every leaf must keep at least this many training examples. - min samples split : a node with fewer examples than this is not split. - max leaf nodes : at most this many leaves. Cutting back a fully grown tree afterwards is called pruning ; scikit-learn does it with ccp alpha (larger values remove more branches). Tune these by cross-validation. The boundaries are made of horizontal and vertical segments, because every question looks at one feature. The depth-2 and depth-4 trees both score 0.89 on training and test data. The unlimited tree grows to depth 10, scores 1.00 on training data and drops to 0.85 on test data: its extra boxes chase single noisy points. What trees are good and bad at - No scaling needed. A question "$x j \le t$" gives the same split if feature $j$ is multiplied by 1000 (the threshold moves with it). Standardizing does nothing for a tree. - Readable. A shallow tree is a set of rules a person can check. - Mixed features. Numbers, 0/1 flags and ordinal codes all work directly. - Axis-aligned boundaries. A diagonal boundary like $x 1 x 2$ needs a staircase of many splits. - Unstable. Change a few training examples and the root split can change, and with it the whole tree: high variance. Lesson 3 fixes this by averaging many trees. Regression trees For a numeric label, a leaf predicts the mean label of its training examples, and the impurity of a node is the mean squared error of predicting that mean, which is the variance of its labels. Splits are chosen to make the weighted MSE of the children as small as possible. DecisionTreeRegressor has the same depth and leaf-size settings. Its predictions are a step function: constant on each leaf's region.

One decision tree is unstable: small changes in the data change the whole tree. Combining many trees fixes this, and the results, random forests and gradient boosting, are the first models to try on any table of numbers. For Round 1 you need the ideas (what bagging and boosting each reduce, what the randomness is for), a few small computations, and the scikit-learn classes. Why combining models helps An ensemble is a model made of many models whose predictions are combined: a majority vote for classes, an average for numbers. Five classifiers are each right 70% of the time, and their mistakes are independent. The majority is right when at least 3 of the 5 are right: With 25 such voters the majority is right 98.3% of the time. The catch is independence. For averages: if each of $B$ models has prediction variance $\sigma^2$ and every pair has correlation $\rho$, the average has variance (Expand $\mathrm{Var}\big(\frac1B \sum b f b\big)$ as in u05: $B$ variance terms $\sigma^2$ and $B(B - 1)$ covariance terms $\rho\sigma^2$, all divided by $B^2$.) More models shrink the second term toward 0, but the first term stays. Models trained on the same data make the same mistakes ($\rho$ near 1), and then averaging gains little. So an ensemble needs models that are each good and as different from each other as possible. Bagging and random forests create the differences with randomness. Bagging A bootstrap sample of a training set of size $n$ is $n$ examples drawn from it at random with replacement : some examples appear twice or more, others not at all. (u05-l09 used resamples like this to estimate a standard error.) Bagging (short for bootstrap aggregating) trains one model on each of $B$ bootstrap samples and combines their predictions by vote or average. How much of the data does one bootstrap sample miss? A given example is skipped by one draw with probability $1 - 1/n$, so by all $n$ draws with probability For $n = 10$ it is $0.9^{10} \approx 0.349$. So each bootstrap sample contains about 63.2% of the distinct examples. The other 36.8% are that model's out-of-bag (OOB) examples. Predicting each training example with only the models that did not train on it gives a free validation score, the OOB score , with no separate validation set. Bagging works best with models that have low bias and high variance, such as deep trees: each tree overfits in its own way, and the average cancels much of it. Random forests Bagged trees are still similar: if one feature is very strong, nearly every tree asks about it at the root. A random forest adds a second source of randomness. At every split, the tree may only choose among a random subset of the features, drawn fresh at that node. In scikit-learn, max features="sqrt" (the default for classifiers) allows $\sqrt d$ of the $d$ features per split. This lowers the correlation $\rho$ between trees, which lowers the variance of the average. Settings of RandomForestClassifier : - n estimators : the number of trees. More trees never hurt accuracy on average; they only cost time. A few hundred is typical. - max features : features considered per split. Smaller means more different trees, each a bit weaker. - max depth , min samples leaf : as for a single tree. Forests usually grow deep trees. - oob score=True : compute the OOB score, available as oob score after fit . predict proba averages the class fractions of the leaves each tree reaches, and feature importances averages the trees' importances. Boosting Boosting builds the ensemble in sequence: each new model is trained to fix the mistakes of the ensemble so far. The models are deliberately small, such as trees of depth 1 to 3, so each one alone underfits. A tree of depth 1, a single question, is called a decision stump . Boosting reduces bias. Gradient boosting for a numeric label, with squared error: 1. Start with a constant prediction $F 0(x) = \bar y$, the mean label. 2. For $m = 1, 2, \dots, M$: compute the residuals $r i = y i - F {m-1}(x i)$, fit a small regression tree $h m$ to the pairs $(x i, r i)$, and update $F m(x) = F {m-1}(x) + \eta\, h m(x)$. The step size $\eta$ is the learning rate (also called shrinkage), usually 0.05 to 0.3. Data $x = 1, \dots, 6$ with $y = 3, 5, 4, 10, 12, 14$. Mean 8, so $F 0 = 8$ and the MSE is $106/6 \approx 17.7$. - Residuals $-5, -3, -4, 2, 4, 6$. The best stump splits at $x \le 3.5$ and predicts the mean residual on each side, $-4$ and $4$. Now $F 1 = 4, 4, 4, 12, 12, 12$, MSE $10/6 \approx 1.67$. - Residuals $-1, 1, 0, -2, 0, 2$. The best stump now splits at $x \le 5.5$ and predicts $-0.4$ (the mean of the first five) and $2$. Now $F 2 = 3.6, 3.6, 3.6, 11.6, 11.6, 14$, MSE $5.2/6 \approx 0.87$. Why "gradient": for the loss $\frac12(y i - F i)^2$, the derivative with respect to the prediction $F i$ is $-(y i - F i)$. So the residual is the negative gradient, and each round takes a gradient descent step in the space of predictions, with a tree approximating the step. For classification, gradient boosting models the log-odds and fits trees to $y i - p i$, the negative gradient of the log-loss, the same quantity as in the logistic regression gradient (u07). Settings of GradientBoostingClassifier and GradientBoostingRegressor : n estimators (rounds, default 100), learning rate (default 0.1), max depth (default 3), subsample (below 1.0, each round uses a random fraction of the rows). A smaller learning rate needs more rounds. Unlike a random forest, boosting can overfit if it runs too many rounds, so the number of rounds is tuned on validation data, or set automatically with n iter no change (stop when a held-out score stops improving, which is early stopping). HistGradientBoostingClassifier is a much faster version for large datasets that also accepts missing values. XGBoost and LightGBM are popular libraries built on the same idea. Bagging and boosting side by side bagging, random forest boosting --- --- --- models trained independently (in parallel) in sequence, each fixing the last typical trees deep (low bias, high variance) shallow (high bias, low variance) mainly reduces variance bias more trees never hurts, only slower can overfit; tune the number All four reach 1.000 on the training data. On the test data the single tree scores 0.906, bagging and boosting 0.936, and the forest 0.953; its OOB score (0.970) was computed from the training data alone. On one split of 171 test examples, differences of one or two percent are within noise; use cross-validation to compare models properly. The picture shows the regions of one deep tree, a random forest and gradient boosting on the noisy moons from lessons 1 and 2. The forest's average of 200 staircase boundaries is smoother than any single tree. The shading is predict proba for class 1: a single tree is all or nothing in each box, while the ensembles give graded probabilities.

Support vector machines are on both the theory and the practice lists of the international syllabus. Round 1 questions can ask you to compute a hinge loss, say what the setting C does, evaluate a kernel, or say which training points matter. This lesson extends the hard-margin SVM from the calculus unit (u04-l08) to overlapping classes and curved boundaries. Recap: the widest gap Labels are $y \in \{-1, +1\}$, and the support vector machine (SVM) predicts the sign of $f(x) = w \cdot x + b$. When a line (a hyperplane, in more dimensions) separates the classes, there are many such lines, and the SVM picks the one with the widest margin. Scaling $w, b$ so that the closest points have $ f(x) = 1$, the margin is $1/\lVert w\rVert$, and the problem is The product $y i f(x i)$ is positive when example $i$ is on its correct side, and at least 1 when it is also outside the margin. The support vectors are the points with $y i f(x i) = 1$, on the margin. In u04-l08 the KKT conditions gave $w = \sum i \alpha i y i x i$ with $\alpha i 0$ only for support vectors, so the other points could move (without crossing the margin) and nothing would change. Class $-1$: $(0, 0), (1, 1), (0, 2)$. Class $+1$: $(3, 0), (3, 2), (4, 1)$. The widest gap is between the lines $x 1 = 1$ and $x 1 = 3$, so the boundary is $x 1 = 2$. With $w = (1, 0)$, $b = -2$: $f = x 1 - 2$ equals $-1$ at $(1, 1)$ and $+1$ at $(3, 0)$ and $(3, 2)$. Those three are the support vectors, and the margin is $1/\lVert w\rVert = 1$. decision function returns $f(x)$, the signed score before taking the sign. coef (the vector $w$) exists only for kernel="linear" . Soft margin and the hinge loss Real classes overlap, and then no line satisfies every constraint. The soft-margin SVM lets example $i$ fall short of the margin by a slack $\xi i \ge 0$, at a price: At the optimum each slack is as small as allowed: $\xi i = \max(0,\, 1 - y i f(x i))$. Substituting removes the constraints: The term $\max(0, 1 - yf)$ is the hinge loss . Its graph is flat at 0 for $yf \ge 1$ and a straight line of slope $-1$ below that (the shape of a hinge): $y f(x)$ 2 1 0.5 0 $-1$ --- --- --- --- --- --- hinge loss 0 0 0.5 1 2 meaning outside margin on margin inside margin, correct on boundary wrong side Logistic regression (u07) uses the log-loss, which in $\pm 1$ labels is $\ln(1 + e^{-yf})$: it is never exactly 0, so every point pulls a little. The hinge loss is exactly 0 for every point outside the margin, so only the points on or inside the margin, or misclassified, affect the solution. All of those are the support vectors of a soft-margin SVM. The setting C $C$ is the price of each unit of slack. - Large $C$ : violations are expensive. The SVM fits the training data closely with a narrow margin: lower bias, higher variance, risk of overfitting. - Small $C$ : a wide margin that tolerates many violations: more regularization. Dividing the objective by $C$ gives $\sum i \text{hinge} i + \frac{1}{2C}\lVert w\rVert^2$: an L2 penalty with strength $1/(2C)$. So $C$ works like the inverse of the regularization strength $\lambda$ in ridge regression (u06-l04). The default is $C = 1$; tune it on a log scale (0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100) by cross-validation. Kernels: curved boundaries Points of class $+1$ at $x = -1, 0, 1$ and class $-1$ at $x = -3, -2, 2, 3$ cannot be split by one threshold on the line. Map each $x$ to $\varphi(x) = (x, x^2)$: now the line $x^2 = 2.5$ separates them. A linear SVM on mapped features $\varphi(x)$ draws a curved boundary in the original space. Mapping to many features is expensive, but an SVM never needs the mapped vectors themselves. Since $w = \sum i \alpha i y i x i$, and training can also be written using only dot products $x i \cdot x j$. So replace every dot product with a kernel $K(x, z) = \varphi(x) \cdot \varphi(z)$, a function that computes the mapped dot product directly. This substitution is the kernel trick . - Polynomial kernel $K(x, z) = (x \cdot z + c)^p$. For example, in 2D, $(x \cdot z)^2 = \varphi(x) \cdot \varphi(z)$ with $\varphi(x) = (x 1^2, \sqrt2\, x 1 x 2, x 2^2)$: expand $(x 1 z 1 + x 2 z 2)^2$ to check. - RBF kernel (radial basis function, or Gaussian kernel, after the bell shape of the normal distribution) $K(x, z) = e^{-\gamma\lVert x - z\rVert^2}$: 1 when $x = z$, near 0 when they are far apart. Its $\varphi$ has infinitely many features, yet $K$ is one line of code. With the RBF kernel, $f(x) = \sum i \alpha i y i\, e^{-\gamma\lVert x i - x\rVert^2} + b$ is a sum of bumps centered at the support vectors. $\gamma$ sets the bump width: a large $\gamma$ gives narrow bumps and a wiggly boundary that can wrap single points (overfitting); a small $\gamma$ gives a smooth boundary. $\gamma = 0.1$ gives a nearly straight boundary (training accuracy 0.80, test 0.87). $\gamma = 1$ follows the moons (0.93 and 0.95). $\gamma = 50$ draws islands around single training points: training accuracy rises to 0.98 while test accuracy drops to 0.85, and 134 of the 150 training points become support vectors. SVMs in scikit-learn - SVC(kernel="rbf", C=1.0, gamma="scale") are the defaults. gamma="scale" means $1/(d \cdot \text{variance of all entries of } X)$. Other kernels: "linear" , "poly" ( degree is the $p$ above, default 3; coef0 is the $c$). - After fit : support vectors , support (their row indices), n support (count per class), decision function(X) . - predict proba works only with SVC(probability=True) , which fits extra models by internal cross-validation: slower, and its probabilities can disagree slightly with predict . - More than two classes: SVC trains one SVM per pair of classes and takes a vote. - Scale the features. The RBF kernel uses distances and the linear kernel uses dot products, so the same warning as for kNN applies: make pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC()) . - Training time grows faster than $n^2$, so kernel SVMs suit up to roughly tens of thousands of rows. For large data with a linear boundary, LinearSVC is much faster.

k-means is the clustering method you are expected to know in depth: by hand for Part 1 (assign points, move centers, compute the objective, reason about initialization) and as code for Part 2. You already wrote its two steps in NumPy (u02-l10, problem u02-p07). This lesson adds what the algorithm optimizes, why it stops, why it can stop in the wrong place, and how to choose $k$. The objective Clustering groups examples that have no labels. k-means describes each of $k$ clusters by a center $\mu j$, also called a centroid , and assigns each example $x i$ to one cluster $c(i)$. It tries to make the inertia , the total squared distance from each point to its own center, as small as possible: Inertia is also called the within-cluster sum of squares. The algorithm (Lloyd's algorithm) alternates two steps until the assignments stop changing: 1. Assign : each point goes to its nearest center. 2. Update : each center moves to the mean of its points. Why it stops Each step can only lower $J$ or leave it the same: - With the centers fixed, sending each point to its nearest center makes every term of $J$ as small as it can be. - With the assignments fixed, the point $\mu$ that minimizes $\sum {i \in \text{cluster}} \lVert x i - \mu\rVert^2$ is the mean of the cluster. (Set the gradient $-2\sum i (x i - \mu)$ to zero; this is the vector version of "the mean minimizes squared error" from u06-l07.) There are finitely many ways to assign $n$ points to $k$ clusters and $J$ never goes up, so the algorithm stops after finitely many steps. Points $0, 2, 3, 9, 11, 12$ with starting centers $0$ and $3$. step centers assignment $J$ --- --- --- --- assign 0, 3 $\{0\}$, $\{2, 3, 9, 11, 12\}$ $0 + 1 + 0 + 36 + 64 + 81 = 182$ update 0, 7.4 same 85.2 assign 0, 7.4 $\{0, 2, 3\}$, $\{9, 11, 12\}$ 49.68 update 1.667, 10.667 same 9.333 assign 1.667, 10.667 no change: stop 9.333 $J$ drops at every step. The final centers are $5/3$ and $32/3$. Local minima and initialization The algorithm stops at a local minimum of $J$: no single step improves $J$, but a different clustering may be much better. Four points $(0, 0), (0, 1), (4, 0), (4, 1)$, $k = 2$. Splitting left from right gives centers $(0, 0.5)$ and $(4, 0.5)$ and $J = 4 \times 0.25 = 1$. But start the centers at $(2, 0)$ and $(2, 1)$: the bottom two points go to $(2, 0)$ (squared distance 4, against 5 to the other center), the top two to $(2, 1)$, the means are the same centers again, and the algorithm stops at $J = 16$. Two fixes, both used by scikit-learn: - k-means++ initialization. Pick the first center uniformly at random from the data points. Then repeat until there are $k$ centers: compute $D(x)^2$, the squared distance from each point to its nearest chosen center, and pick the next center at random with probability $D(x)^2 / \sum {x'} D(x')^2$. Far-away points are likely picks, so the centers start spread out. Problem u08-p05 asks you to code it. - Several restarts. Run the whole algorithm n init times from different starting centers and keep the run with the lowest inertia. In scikit-learn 1.6, KMeans() uses init="k-means++" and n init="auto" , which means a single run for k-means++ (10 runs for init="random" ). Passing n init=10 costs little and is safer. (scikit-learn's k-means++ is a greedy variant: at each step it samples a few candidates and keeps the one that lowers inertia most.) Choosing k Inertia always goes down as $k$ grows: with $k = n$ every point is its own center and $J = 0$. So minimizing inertia cannot choose $k$. Two common tools: - Elbow method : plot inertia against $k$ and pick the $k$ where the curve bends, after which extra clusters buy little. - Silhouette score : for each point, let $a$ be its mean distance to the other points of its own cluster and $b$ its mean distance to the points of the nearest other cluster. Its silhouette is $s = \frac{b - a}{\max(a, b)}$, between $-1$ and $1$: near 1 when the point is much closer to its own cluster, near 0 on a border, negative when it probably belongs elsewhere. The silhouette score is the mean of $s$ over all points; pick the $k$ with the highest score. Clusters $\{0, 2, 4\}$ and $\{10, 12\}$ on a line. For the point 4: $a = (4 + 2)/2 = 3$ and $b = (6 + 8)/2 = 7$, so $s = (7 - 3)/7 \approx 0.571$. What k-means assumes Each point goes to its nearest center, so the boundary between two clusters is the perpendicular bisector of their centers, and every cluster is a convex region (it contains the straight segment between any two of its points). k-means works well for compact, roughly round clusters of similar size, and badly for long, curved or nested shapes. Like kNN, it uses distances, so standardize features first. Means are pulled by outliers, and every point, outliers included, is assigned to some cluster. The cluster numbers are arbitrary: rerunning with another seed can call the same group 2 instead of 0. To compare a clustering with known classes, use a score that ignores the numbering, such as adjusted rand score(y, labels) from sklearn.metrics (1 for identical groupings, about 0 for random ones). The figure lets you step through the algorithm. Watch the inertia fall at each step, and try different starts. On the blobs, the inertia curve bends at $k = 4$. The silhouette score is highest at $k = 2$ (0.724), with $k = 4$ second (0.697): one blob sits far from the other three, so "far blob against the rest" also scores well. The two tools can disagree, and neither is a proof; plot the data when you can. On the moons, k-means splits the plane with a straight line, because its clusters must be convex. Lesson 6 covers methods that follow the shapes. In scikit-learn KMeans(n clusters=4, n init=10, random state=0) . After fit(X) : labels (cluster of each training point, shape (n,) ), cluster centers (shape (k, d) ), inertia , n iter . predict(X new) assigns new points to the nearest center, fit predict(X) fits and returns labels , and transform(X) returns the distance from each point to each center, shape (n, k) .

The syllabus lists hierarchical clustering, DBSCAN and spectral clustering at practice level: know what each does, what its settings mean, and when to choose it over k-means. A Round 1 question might give six points and ask which are noise for DBSCAN, or ask which method fits a described dataset. Hierarchical (agglomerative) clustering Hierarchical clustering builds a whole tree of clusterings. The usual bottom-up version, agglomerative clustering , works like this: start with every point as its own cluster. Repeatedly merge the two closest clusters, until one cluster holds everything. The record of merges is a tree called a dendrogram : the height at which two branches join is the distance at which they merged. Cutting the tree at some height (or asking for a number of clusters) gives a clustering, so you can look at the tree before choosing $k$. "Closest clusters" needs a rule, the linkage : - single : the distance between the two closest points, one from each cluster; - complete : the distance between the two farthest points; - average : the mean of all pairwise distances; - Ward (scikit-learn's default): merge the pair whose merge increases the inertia the least. Single linkage can follow long chains of points, so it finds curved shapes, but one stray point between two groups can join them. Complete and Ward linkage prefer compact, round clusters. Points $0, 1, 4, 6, 12$. - Single linkage. Merge $\{0, 1\}$ at distance 1, then $\{4, 6\}$ at 2. The closest points of those two clusters are 1 and 4, so they merge at 3. Last, 12 joins at $12 - 6 = 6$. - Complete linkage. Merge $\{0, 1\}$ at 1, then $\{4, 6\}$ at 2. Now $\{0, 1\}$ to $\{4, 6\}$ is $6 - 0 = 6$ (farthest pair), and $\{4, 6\}$ to $\{12\}$ is $12 - 4 = 8$, so $\{0, 1\}$ and $\{4, 6\}$ merge at 6. Last, everything joins at $12 - 0 = 12$. Cut into 3 clusters, both give $\{0, 1\}, \{4, 6\}, \{12\}$; the merge heights differ. DBSCAN DBSCAN (density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise) grows clusters through dense regions. It has two settings, a radius eps and a count min samples . - A core point has at least min samples points within distance eps , counting itself. - Core points within eps of each other belong to the same cluster, and so do chains of them. - A border point is not core but lies within eps of a core point; it joins that core point's cluster. - Any other point is noise and gets the label $-1$. Points $0, 1, 2, 3, 10, 11, 20$ with eps = 1.5 , min samples = 3 . Within 1.5 of 1 are $\{0, 1, 2\}$, three points, so 1 is core; likewise 2 ($\{1, 2, 3\}$). Point 0 has only $\{0, 1\}$, so it is not core, but it is within 1.5 of the core point 1: a border point. Point 3 is a border point of 2. Points 10 and 11 have only each other (2 points), and no core point is near: noise. 20 is noise. Result: one cluster $\{0, 1, 2, 3\}$ and three noise points. DBSCAN does not need $k$, finds clusters of any shape, and labels outliers instead of forcing them into a cluster. It struggles when clusters have very different densities (one eps cannot fit them all), and the result is sensitive to eps . As always with distances, standardize the features first. Spectral clustering Spectral clustering turns the data into a graph and clusters the graph: 1. Build a similarity matrix $W$: $W {ij}$ is large when points $i$ and $j$ are close, for example 1 if one is among the other's nearest neighbors, else 0. 2. Form the graph Laplacian $L = D - W$, where $D$ is the diagonal matrix of row sums of $W$. 3. Take the eigenvectors of $L$ for its $k$ smallest eigenvalues (u03-l07), and use their entries as $k$ new coordinates for each point. 4. Run k-means on those new coordinates. Why it works: if the graph falls into $k$ separate pieces, $L$ has eigenvalue 0 exactly $k$ times, and its eigenvectors are constant on each piece. So in the new coordinates each piece collapses to one point, and k-means separates them easily. Points joined by a chain of close neighbors end up together even when the chain is curved. Spectral clustering needs $k$, and computing eigenvectors of an $n \times n$ matrix limits it to moderate $n$. Points 0, 1, 2 are linked to each other, and points 3, 4 to each other, with no links between the groups. For any vector $v$, $v^\top L v = \frac12\sum {i,j} W {ij}(v i - v j)^2$ (expand both sides to check). This is 0 exactly when $v$ is constant on each connected piece. So the vectors $(1, 1, 1, 0, 0)$ and $(0, 0, 0, 1, 1)$ give 0, and in fact $Lv = 0$: entry $i$ of $Lv$ is $D {ii}v i - \sum j W {ij}v j = \sum j W {ij}(v i - v j)$, and every linked pair has $v i = v j$. Eigenvalue 0, twice. Choosing a method method needs $k$? cluster shapes outliers settings to tune --- --- --- --- --- k-means yes compact, round, convex assigned to a cluster $k$, n init agglomerative yes, or cut the tree Ward: compact; single: chains assigned $k$, linkage DBSCAN no any shape labeled $-1$ eps , min samples spectral yes any connected shape assigned $k$, the similarity graph All four need scaled features. None of the last three has a predict for new points in scikit-learn: call fit predict(X) on the data you want labeled. ARI is the adjusted Rand score from lesson 5 (1 means the clustering matches the true moons exactly). k-means and Ward split the data into compact pieces that mix the two moons (0.23 and 0.30). Single linkage and DBSCAN follow the chains of nearby points and recover both moons (1.00), and spectral clustering nearly does (0.99). On data with noise points between the moons, single linkage would chain the moons together, while DBSCAN would label those points $-1$.

Principal component analysis (PCA) is the standard way to squeeze many features into a few. It is linear algebra you already have (eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix, u03-l08; the SVD, u03-l09; the first principal component as a Lagrange problem, u04-l08) put to work on data. Part 1 asks for explained variance from given eigenvalues or how many components to keep; Part 2 can ask for PCA from scratch with scikit-learn banned (problem u08-p04). The goal You have $n$ examples with $d$ features, a matrix $X$ of shape $(n, d)$. You want $k < d$ new features, each a linear combination of the old ones, that keep as much of the data's spread as possible. Picture a cloud of 2D points stretched along a diagonal: one number per point, its position along the diagonal, describes the cloud almost completely. That diagonal is the first principal component. Building it Step 1: center. Subtract each column's mean: $X c = X - \bar x$, where $\bar x$ is the row of $d$ column means, subtracted from every row (centered data). PCA is about spread around the mean, so the mean is removed first and added back when reconstructing. Step 2: covariance. The sample covariance matrix of the features is Entry $S {jj}$ is the variance of feature $j$ and $S {jl}$ the covariance of features $j$ and $l$ (u05-l06). $S$ is symmetric and positive semidefinite. Step 3: the best direction. Project every point onto a unit vector $w$: the scores are $z = X c w$, one number per point. Their mean is 0 and their variance is Over unit vectors $w$, $w^\top S w$ is largest at the eigenvector of $S$ with the largest eigenvalue $\lambda 1$, and the maximum is $\lambda 1$ (u03-l08 and u04-l08 proved this two ways). So the first principal component is the top eigenvector of $S$, and the variance along it is $\lambda 1$. Step 4: the rest. The second component is the best unit direction perpendicular to the first; it is the eigenvector for the second-largest eigenvalue $\lambda 2$, and so on. By the spectral theorem the eigenvectors are orthonormal. Sorting eigenvalues $\lambda 1 \ge \lambda 2 \ge \dots \ge \lambda d \ge 0$, the principal components are the matching eigenvectors $v 1, \dots, v d$. Step 5: project. Put the top $k$ eigenvectors in the columns of $W k$, shape $(d, k)$. The new features are the scores To go back, $\hat X = Z W k^\top + \bar x$ is the reconstruction : each point replaced by its projection onto the $k$-dimensional subspace. $X$ has rows $(4, 6), (5, 5), (2, 2), (1, 3)$. The mean is $(3, 4)$, so $X c$ has rows $(1, 2), (2, 1), (-1, -2), (-2, -1)$. $X c^\top X c = \begin{pmatrix} 10 & 8 \\ 8 & 10 \end{pmatrix}$, so $S = \frac13 \begin{pmatrix} 10 & 8 \\ 8 & 10\end{pmatrix}$. Its eigenvalues are $\frac{18}{3} = 6$ for $v 1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, 1)$ and $\frac23$ for $v 2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt 2}(1, -1)$. Scores on $v 1$: $\frac{3}{\sqrt2}, \frac{3}{\sqrt2}, -\frac{3}{\sqrt2}, -\frac{3}{\sqrt2}$ (about $\pm 2.12$). Reconstructing from $v 1$ alone sends $(4, 6)$ and $(5, 5)$ both to $(4.5, 5.5)$, and $(2, 2)$ and $(1, 3)$ both to $(1.5, 2.5)$. Explained variance The total variance, the sum of the feature variances, is the trace of $S$, and the trace equals the sum of the eigenvalues: So component $j$ carries the fraction $\lambda j / \sum l \lambda l$ of the total, its explained variance ratio . In the example, $6/(6 + \frac23) = 0.9$: the first component keeps 90% of the variance. To choose $k$: add the ratios until the running total passes a target such as 90% or 95%, or plot the eigenvalues in decreasing order (a scree plot ) and look for the elbow, as with k-means inertia. The total is 10, so the ratios are 0.6, 0.3, 0.06, 0.04, and the running totals 0.6, 0.9, 0.96, 1. Two components keep 90%; reaching 95% takes three. Reconstruction error How much is lost? The squared length of what projection removes, summed over all points, is the dropped eigenvalues times $n - 1$. Why: the eigenvectors are an orthonormal basis, so each centered point is $\sum j (x {c,i} \cdot v j) v j$, and the reconstruction keeps only the terms $j \le k$. What is removed has squared length $\sum {j k} (x {c,i} \cdot v j)^2$, and summing over the points gives $\sum {j k} \lVert X c v j\rVert^2 = (n - 1)\sum {j k} \lambda j$ by step 3. In the example, keeping $k = 1$ loses $3 \times \frac23 = 2$: each of the four points moves by $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$, and $4 \times \frac12 = 2$. Keeping the top $k$ components therefore does two things at once: it keeps the most variance and it makes the reconstruction error as small as any $k$-dimensional subspace can. This is the Eckart-Young theorem of u03-l09 in statistical clothing. The SVD view Take the thin singular value decomposition of the centered data, $X c = U\Sigma V^\top$. Then which is the eigendecomposition of $S$. So: - the principal components are the right singular vectors, the rows of NumPy's Vh ; - the eigenvalues are $\lambda j = \sigma j^2/(n - 1)$; - the scores are $X c V k = U k \Sigma k$. scikit-learn computes PCA this way. The SVD never forms $X c^\top X c$ (squaring the numbers loses precision when some eigenvalues are tiny), and np.linalg.svd already sorts the singular values largest first ( eigh sorts ascending). The three methods agree on the eigenvalues ($6$ and $\frac23$) and on the directions, but not on their signs. An eigenvector times $-1$ is still an eigenvector, so each library picks a sign by its own rule. (scikit-learn 1.6 flips each component so that its entry of largest absolute value is positive.) Never compare components or scores across methods without allowing for a sign flip. Scaling and other cautions - Units matter. PCA chases variance, so a feature measured in large units (income in dollars) dominates the first component simply because its numbers are big. When features have different units, standardize them first; PCA on standardized data is PCA on the correlation matrix. - Linear only. Each component is a straight direction. Curved structure needs a nonlinear method (lesson 8). - Ignores labels. The direction of most variance need not be the one that separates your classes. PCA in scikit-learn PCA(n components=k) , then fit(X) : - components : shape (k, d) , one component per row ; - explained variance : the eigenvalues $\lambda j$ (dividing by $n - 1$); explained variance ratio : the fractions; - mean : the column means it subtracts; - transform(X) : the scores, shape (n, k) ; inverse transform(Z) : the reconstruction; - PCA(n components=0.95) : a number between 0 and 1 asks for the smallest $k$ whose ratios add up to at least 0.95; n components then holds that $k$. As with scalers, fit PCA on training data only and transform everything else; inside a pipeline this is automatic. Two components keep only 28.5% of the variance of the 64 pixels, yet some digits already form their own groups (0 at the bottom, 4 and 6 on the right). 21 components keep 90% and 29 keep 95%.

2026 Round 1 asked, as a 10-point multiple-choice question, what UMAP preserves. t-SNE and UMAP pictures appear in almost every paper that looks at data or at a network's internal features, and the skill being tested is reading them correctly: what a gap, a size or a position in the picture does and does not mean. What these maps do t-SNE and UMAP are nonlinear dimensionality reduction methods built for visualization. Each places every data point at a spot in 2D, chosen so that points that are close neighbors in the original high-dimensional space are also close in the picture. The 2D coordinates are called an embedding . Unlike PCA (lesson 7), the map from the data to the picture is not a projection, so it can unroll curved shapes, but it also bends distances. t-SNE t-SNE (t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding) works in three steps. 1. Neighbor probabilities in the original space. For each point $i$, give every other point $j$ a probability $p {j i} \propto e^{-\lVert x i - x j\rVert^2 / (2\sigma i^2)}$, a Gaussian bump centered at $x i$. ($\propto$ means "proportional to": the values are divided by their sum over $j$, so they add up to 1.) The width $\sigma i$ is set separately for each point so that the bump covers about the same number of effective neighbors everywhere. That number is the perplexity , typically 5 to 50 (scikit-learn's default is 30). Symmetrizing, $p {ij} = (p {j i} + p {i j})/(2n)$, gives one number per pair, and all the $p {ij}$ add up to 1. 2. Neighbor probabilities in the picture. For 2D points $y i$, use $q {ij} \propto (1 + \lVert y i - y j\rVert^2)^{-1}$, a Student t curve, which has much heavier tails than a Gaussian. Here the sum that makes them add to 1 runs over all pairs. 3. Match them. Move the 2D points by gradient descent to minimize the KL divergence $D {\mathrm{KL}}(P \,\ \, Q) = \sum {i \ne j} p {ij}\log\frac{p {ij}}{q {ij}}$ (u05-l08). Why the picture keeps neighborhoods but not large distances: a pair with large $p {ij}$ (true neighbors) placed far apart has tiny $q {ij}$, and $p\log(p/q)$ is then large, so t-SNE pays heavily. A pair with tiny $p {ij}$ (far apart in the data) contributes almost nothing whatever $q {ij}$ is, so t-SNE barely cares where far-apart groups end up. The heavy tails of the t curve let moderately distant points drift far apart in 2D, which opens clear gaps between groups. UMAP UMAP (uniform manifold approximation and projection) builds a graph that links each point to its n neighbors nearest neighbors (default 15), with weights that fall off with distance. It then searches for a 2D layout whose own neighbor graph has nearly the same weights, minimizing a cross-entropy between the two sets of weights. min dist sets how tightly points may pack in the picture. Compared with t-SNE, UMAP is faster on large datasets, usually keeps a bit more of the global arrangement, and can place new points into an existing map ( transform ). The main property is the same: it favors local neighborhood structure over global distances. UMAP is not part of scikit-learn; it comes from the umap-learn package: Reading the picture you can read you cannot read --- --- which points are neighbors distances between clusters (the size of a gap) that a group of points forms a cluster the size or spread of a cluster: t-SNE tends to make clusters look alike that a point sits inside another class's cluster densities: tight and loose clusters can look the same what the axes mean: they have no units and no direction in feature space positions and orientation, which change with the random seed Results also change with perplexity (t-SNE) or n neighbors (UMAP). Small values show fine local detail and can break one real cluster into pieces; large values show more of the global shape. A finding worth believing should survive a few settings and seeds. In the data, B is about 6 times as spread out as A (9.4 against 1.5), and C is about 8 times as far from A as B is (60 against 7.7). PCA, a projection, keeps both gaps exactly here and keeps B much wider than A. t-SNE shows three clean clusters, but B looks only about 1.6 times the size of A (3.9 against 2.5), and C sits only 5 times as far from A as B does (41.4 against 8.3). ( method="exact" is fast for a small dataset like this one; the default "barnes hut" is the fast choice for thousands of points.) Using them well - Use t-SNE and UMAP to look at data, not as input features for a model. scikit-learn's TSNE has only fit transform , no transform for new points. - For data with hundreds of features, reduce to about 50 dimensions with PCA first: faster, and less noise. - Scale features first, as for any distance-based method. - Check what you see in the picture against numbers computed in the original space. PCA t-SNE UMAP --- --- --- --- map linear projection nonlinear nonlinear preserves large-scale variance and distances local neighborhoods local neighborhoods, some global shape new points transform no transform same result every run yes (up to sign) no, depends on seed no, depends on seed speed on large $n$ fast slow faster than t-SNE

When a Part 2 problem allows scikit-learn, the calls have to come from memory: no documentation, 75 minutes. The 2026 open-ended problem (kNN only, macro F1 on a hidden test set) was mostly about using the library fluently. u06 covered splitting, metrics, cross-validation and the preprocessing classes. This lesson covers what every model has in common, pipelines and hyperparameter search, and ends with the template for a P9-style problem. One interface for every model An estimator is any scikit-learn object that learns from data with fit . All of them follow the same rules. 1. Hyperparameters go in the constructor : KNeighborsClassifier(n neighbors=7) . Making the object does not touch any data. 2. fit learns and returns the estimator itself. X is 2D with shape (n, d) , y is 1D with shape (n,) . Unsupervised estimators take fit(X) . 3. Learned values end in an underscore : classes , coef , feature importances , cluster centers , components . Reading one before fit raises NotFittedError . 4. Then, by kind of estimator: - Classifiers and regressors have predict(X) and score(X, y) , which is accuracy for a classifier and $R^2$ for a regressor. Most classifiers also have predict proba(X) , shape (n, n classes) ; some have decision function(X) . - Transformers (scalers, encoders, PCA ) have transform(X) , fit transform(X) and often inverse transform . - Clusterers store labels after fit and have fit predict(X) ; KMeans also has predict . The columns of predict proba follow classes , which holds the labels sorted , not in the order they first appear in y . The probability of class "dog" is column list(model.classes ).index("dog") . get params() returns the hyperparameters as a dict, and set params(n neighbors=9) changes them. clone(model) (from sklearn.base ) makes an unfitted copy with the same hyperparameters; cross-validation does this for every fold. reshape(-1, 1) makes one column (many examples, one feature); reshape(1, -1) makes one row (one example, many features). Pipelines u06-l09 used make pipeline to keep scaling inside cross-validation. The details you need: - make pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier()) names each step after its class in lower case: "standardscaler" , "kneighborsclassifier" . - Pipeline([("scale", StandardScaler()), ("knn", KNeighborsClassifier())]) uses names you choose. - pipe.fit(X, y) runs fit transform on each step in turn, then fit on the last step. pipe.predict(X) runs transform on each step (nothing is refit), then predict . - pipe.named steps["knn"] (or pipe[-1] ) returns one fitted step. - A step's hyperparameter is addressed as the step name, two underscores, then the parameter: pipe.set params(knn n neighbors=9) . When columns need different preprocessing, ColumnTransformer (from sklearn.compose ) applies one transformer per group of columns and joins the results side by side. It works on a pandas DataFrame, selecting columns by name: Grid search: GridSearchCV GridSearchCV (from sklearn.model selection ) runs the grid search of u06-l08 with cross-validation: - It runs 5-fold CV for each of the $3 \times 2 = 6$ combinations (30 fits), then, because refit=True by default, fits the best combination once more on all of X train (31 fits in total). - gs.best params : the best combination, as a dict. gs.best score : its mean CV score. gs.best estimator : the refit pipeline. gs.predict(X) uses best estimator . - gs.cv results : every result; pd.DataFrame(gs.cv results ) shows columns such as params , mean test score , rank test score . - scoring names: "accuracy" (the default for classifiers), "f1 macro" , "roc auc" , "r2" , "neg mean squared error" . Error scores are negated because the search always maximizes. - param grid may be a list of dicts to search several separate grids. RandomizedSearchCV(pipe, param distributions, n iter=20, random state=0) tries 20 random combinations instead of all; param distributions is a dict like param grid , and each value is a list to sample from (or a scipy.stats distribution). - best score is optimistic: it is the best of many noisy scores (u06-l08). Report a final score on test data that the search never saw. The P9 template The whole open-ended routine, on scikit-learn's copy of the breast cancer data (the 2026 P9 dataset had the same 30 features): Scaling plus a small search lifts test macro F1 from 0.910 (unscaled, default $k = 5$) to 0.954. The best setting's CV score, 0.975, is higher than its test score: the optimism of best score described above. The grid has $6 \times 2 \times 2 = 24$ combinations, so the search ran $24 \times 5 + 1 = 121$ fits; kNN fits are just storing data, so it takes a moment. In the real problem, fit the final model on all the training data you have (here gs already refit on X train ), and write the summary cell the problem asks for. Which class for which model model class (module) main hyperparameters scale features? --- --- --- --- kNN KNeighborsClassifier , KNeighborsRegressor ( sklearn.neighbors ) n neighbors , weights , p yes decision tree DecisionTreeClassifier , DecisionTreeRegressor ( sklearn.tree ) max depth , min samples leaf , criterion no random forest RandomForestClassifier , RandomForestRegressor ( sklearn.ensemble ) n estimators , max features , max depth no gradient boosting GradientBoostingClassifier , HistGradientBoostingClassifier ( sklearn.ensemble ) n estimators , learning rate , max depth no SVM SVC , LinearSVC ( sklearn.svm ) C , kernel , gamma yes logistic regression LogisticRegression ( sklearn.linear model ) C (inverse penalty strength), max iter yes k-means KMeans ( sklearn.cluster ) n clusters , n init , random state yes DBSCAN DBSCAN ( sklearn.cluster ) eps , min samples yes PCA PCA ( sklearn.decomposition ) n components if units differ t-SNE TSNE ( sklearn.manifold ) perplexity , random state yes For a new table of numbers, a random forest or gradient boosting with default settings is a strong first baseline that needs no scaling. Distance-based models (kNN, SVM, k-means, DBSCAN) need a scaler in front. 1. Fitting a scaler or PCA on all the data before splitting: leakage. Put it inside the pipeline. 2. Passing a 1D X : reshape to (n, 1) . 3. Reading predict proba columns in the wrong order: check classes . 4. One underscore in a grid key ( knn n neighbors ): GridSearchCV raises "Invalid parameter". 5. Passing the test set to GridSearchCV , or choosing settings by test score: the test score stops being an honest estimate.

pandas is the Python library for tables. Part 2 of Round 1 can hand you CSV files and ask for counts, a cleaned table and a summary table, all to an exact specification (the official 2027 sample SP3 is exactly this). You write it from memory, with no documentation, so this unit drills every method that kind of problem needs. This first lesson is about what a table is in pandas and how to look at one. DataFrames and Series A DataFrame is a table: rows, and columns that each have a name. A Series is one column: a sequence of values plus a label for each value. The labels are called the index . Unless you say otherwise, the index is 0, 1, 2, and so on, like row numbers. The standard import is import pandas as pd . The easiest way to build a small DataFrame is from a dict that maps each column name to a list of values: The left column of the printout (0 to 3) is the index, not data. Pick one column with square brackets and a name. The result is a Series, and it keeps the same index: Shape, columns and dtypes These attributes describe a DataFrame. They have no parentheses because they are not method calls. - df.shape is the tuple (rows, columns). len(df) is the number of rows. - df.columns holds the column names; list(df.columns) turns them into a plain list. - df.dtypes gives each column's dtype, the type shared by every value in that column. You will meet four dtypes in this unit: dtype holds example --- --- --- int64 whole numbers [2, 1, 1, 4] float64 decimals, and nan for missing numbers [12.5, 3.0] object Python strings (and other Python objects) ["ana", "ben"] bool True and False [True, False] A column of strings has object dtype : pandas stores Python objects, so df["customer"].dtype prints object , not str . One missing value in an integer column turns the whole column into float64 , because NaN is a float: Looking at a table df.head(n) shows the first n rows (5 by default) and df.tail(n) the last n . df.info() prints the row count, and for each column its non-missing count and dtype. df.describe() gives summary statistics of the numeric columns: count, mean, standard deviation, minimum, the 25%, 50% and 75% points (a quarter, half and three quarters of the values lie below them; lesson u09-l09 makes this exact), and maximum. s.std() in pandas is the sample standard deviation (divide by $n-1$). np.std(x) divides by $n$. For [1, 2, 3, 4] , pandas gives 1.290994 and NumPy gives 1.118034. Use s.std(ddof=0) when a problem asks for the population version. Quick looks at one column Three Series methods answer most "how many" questions: - s.unique() returns the distinct values, in order of first appearance. - s.nunique() counts the distinct values. It skips missing values. - s.value counts() counts each value, most common first. Reading a CSV file pd.read csv(path) reads a CSV file into a DataFrame. The first line becomes the column names. By default pandas guesses each column's dtype, and the guess can destroy information: an ID like 007 becomes the integer 7. The examples here use io.StringIO(text) from the standard library: it wraps a string so that read csv reads it as if it were a file. In Colab you would pass a file name such as "transactions.csv" instead. With dtype=str , every column has object dtype and every value is exactly the text in the file: "007" , "3" , "2.50" . That is how the official sample SP3 loads its data, so that nothing is changed behind your back. You then convert the columns you need to numbers yourself (lesson u09-l04). SP3 also passes keep default na=False , which stops pandas from turning empty cells and words like NA into NaN; lesson u09-l04 covers it. On the exam, run df.shape , df.dtypes and df.head() right after loading. Most wrong answers in data problems come from a column having a different dtype than you assumed.

Almost every step of a data problem is "keep the rows where something holds" or "count the rows where something holds". In pandas both are one line once you can build a condition and index with it. This lesson covers picking columns, picking rows by position and by label, and filtering with conditions. Columns df["amount"] gives one column as a Series. A list of names inside the brackets gives a DataFrame with those columns, in the order you list them. That is also how you put columns in an exact required order. You usually write the list straight inside the brackets, which puts two opening brackets in a row: the outer pair indexes, the inner pair is the Python list. df["amount", "customer"] (one pair, no list) raises KeyError , because pandas looks for a single column named by the tuple ("amount", "customer") . Rows by position: iloc df.iloc[i] is the row at position i , counting from 0 as in a list. df.iloc[a:b] is a slice of rows, and df.iloc[i, j] is one value (row position i , column position j ). The "i" in iloc stands for integer position. Rows by label: loc df.loc[label] looks up a row by its index label, and df.loc[rows, cols] picks rows and columns by label. Here rows can be one label, a list of labels, or a condition (next section), and cols can be one name or a list of names. While the index is 0, 1, 2, ..., labels and positions agree, so loc and iloc look the same. They stop agreeing as soon as you filter, because filtering keeps the original labels : big.loc[1] would raise KeyError : no row is labeled 1 any more. reset index(drop=True) renumbers the rows from 0. Without drop=True , pandas also keeps the old labels as a new column named index , which you rarely want. Filtering with conditions A comparison on a column gives a Series of True and False, one per row. Indexing with it keeps the rows where it is True. This is the boolean mask idea from NumPy, and it works the same way: mask.sum() counts the True values, because True counts as 1 and False as 0. mask.mean() is the fraction of rows where the condition holds, and 100 mask.mean() is a percentage. Combine conditions with & (and), (or) and ~ (not), and put every comparison in parentheses : & binds tighter than , so df["a"] 1 & df["b"] (1 & df["b"]) < 5 , which raises ValueError: The truth value of a Series is ambiguous . The words and and or raise the same error, because they ask a whole Series for a single True or False. Always write (cond1) & (cond2) . s.isin(values) is True where the value is in the list values , and it is the clean way to say "country is uk or de". df.query("amount 6 and country == 'uk'") does the same filtering with a string, where and and or are allowed. It is handy for exploring, but loc with masks covers every case, so this unit uses masks. Changing values, and working on a copy df.loc[mask, "col"] = value changes col only in the rows where mask is True. df["new"] = ... adds a column (or replaces one). Two rules keep you out of trouble: 1. Start a function with out = df.copy() . Graders check that your function does not mutate its input DataFrame, and df.loc[...] = ... or df["new"] = ... on the input changes the caller's table. 2. Never assign through two sets of brackets. In out[out["amount"] < 0]["amount"] = 0.0 , the first brackets build a new temporary table, and the assignment changes that temporary table, not out . This is called chained assignment . pandas prints a SettingWithCopyWarning and out is unchanged. Use one .loc[rows, col] instead. Exam pattern for a count: build the mask, then .sum() . For "percent of rows": 100 mask.mean() . For "keep these rows": out = out.loc[mask] (or out[mask] ).

Real data files are typed by people and exported by different systems. The same country appears as UK , uk and Uk , and an ID can carry a trailing space that makes "536365 " and "536365" different values. Step 1 of the official SP3 cleaning is exactly this kind of repair: strip spaces from four columns, then lowercase and relabel the country names. This lesson covers the string tools for it. The .str accessor A Python string has methods such as " uk ".strip() and "UK".lower() . A Series of strings does not have them directly: s.strip() raises AttributeError . Instead, s.str gives access to string methods that run on every value of the Series and return a new Series. This .str is called the str accessor . Whitespace means spaces, tabs and newlines. strip() removes it from both ends of each string, never from the middle: "u k" stays "u k" . lstrip() and rstrip() remove it from the left or right end only. Each .str method returns a Series of strings, so you can chain them, writing .str again before each method: Title case capitalizes the first letter of every word and lowercases the rest: "united kingdom" becomes "United Kingdom" . It does this mechanically, so "usa" becomes "Usa" . If a specification says "apply str.title() ", that odd result is the required answer. ( str.capitalize() is different: it capitalizes only the first letter of the whole string, giving "United kingdom" .) Replacing whole values s.replace({old: new, ...}) replaces values that are exactly equal to a key of the dict. Everything else is left alone. This is the right tool for relabeling categories, including turning the empty string "" into a word. s.str.replace(old, new) is a different method: it replaces every substring old inside each value. That is almost never what you want for relabeling: Order matters A relabeling only matches values that are already clean. In SP3 the order is: strip, lowercase, relabel, then title case. Doing the relabel before the strip misses " uk" , because " uk" is not equal to "uk" : "u k" survives as "U K" in both. The rule maps only the exact value "uk" , and following the rule exactly is what the grader checks. Do not add fixes the specification did not ask for. Tests on strings: startswith and contains These return a Series of True and False, ready to use as a boolean mask: - s.str.startswith("C") is True where the value begins with "C" . It is case-sensitive and has no case argument, so to ignore case, change the case first: s.str.strip().str.upper().str.startswith("C") . - s.str.contains("mug", case=False, regex=False) is True where "mug" appears anywhere, ignoring case. contains treats its pattern as a regular expression by default: a small pattern language in which some characters are special. The dot . matches any character, so contains("1.5") also matches "105" . Pass regex=False to search for the literal text. On a NaN or None value, .str methods return NaN instead of True or False, and the result is no longer a clean mask. Pass na=False ( s.str.startswith("C", na=False) ) to count missing values as False. When a file is loaded with keep default na=False (lesson u09-l04), missing cells are empty strings "" instead, so this does not come up. Cleaning several columns To apply the same cleaning to several columns, loop over their names and assign each column back, on a copy: description is left alone because it was not in the list. On the exam, clean exactly the columns named, no more and no fewer.

Half of the official SP3 exploration questions are about what is missing or broken: rows whose quantity is non-empty but not numeric, rows with a nonpositive price, the percentage of rows with no customer ID. To answer them you must know exactly when pandas treats a value as missing, and how to turn text into numbers without crashing. This lesson covers both. Missing values: NaN pandas marks a missing value in a numeric column with NaN, and in an object column with NaN or None . Never test for it with == : np.nan == np.nan is False. Use the methods instead: - s.isna() is True where the value is missing; s.notna() is the opposite. - df.isna().sum() counts the missing values in each column. - Reductions skip missing values: s.sum() , s.mean() , s.median() use only the present values, and s.count() counts them. If every value is missing, s.sum() is 0.0 (the sum of nothing) while s.mean() is NaN. What read csv calls missing By default, read csv turns empty cells and a list of special words into NaN: NA , N/A , NaN , nan , null , NULL , None , and a few more. Often that is convenient. In a data-cleaning problem it destroys information: you can no longer tell an empty cell from a cell that said N/A , and a question like "rows whose quantity is non-empty but not numeric" becomes impossible to answer. keep default na=False turns this off. Combined with dtype=str , every cell is exactly the text in the file, and an empty cell is the empty string "" . This is how the official SP3 loads its files: After loading this way there is no NaN in the table, so isna() finds nothing. "Missing" now means "the empty string", usually after stripping whitespace: (s.str.strip() == "") . Text to numbers: pd.to numeric pd.to numeric(s) parses a Series of strings into numbers. If any value cannot be parsed, it raises ValueError . With errors="coerce" , every value that cannot be parsed becomes NaN instead: Four facts to remember: 1. The result is float64 whenever any NaN appears, even if the good values are whole numbers. 2. Surrounding spaces are allowed: " 4 " parses as 4. 3. Scientific notation parses: "1e1" is 10.0. 4. The empty string becomes NaN, the same as "abc" . So to count values that are present but not numeric, combine two masks: s.astype(float) also converts, but it raises ValueError on "abc" and has no coerce option. Use to numeric(..., errors="coerce") for messy data. NaN in comparisons Every comparison with NaN is False: np.nan 0 , np.nan <= 0 and np.nan == np.nan are all False. This decides whether rows with a missing value survive a filter. SP3 says: drop rows whose unit price is present and nonpositive, but keep rows whose price is missing (they are filled in later). Compare two filters: price 0 and ~(price <= 0) look equivalent but differ exactly on the missing values. When a rule mentions missing values, write the isna() part out explicitly so the intent is visible. Filling, dropping and converting - s.fillna(value) replaces missing values with value . value can also be a Series: each missing entry is filled from the entry with the same index label. Lesson u09-l06 uses this for filling each product's missing price with that product's median. - df.dropna(subset=["price"]) drops the rows where price is missing. Plain df.dropna() drops rows with a missing value in any column, which is usually too much. - s.astype(int) converts to integers. It fails with IntCastingNaNError if any value is NaN, so drop or fill the missing values first. A quantity of "3.0" parses as 3.0, which is a whole number, while "2.5" is not. q % 1 == 0 tests "is a whole number" for floats. On NaN it is False, because NaN % 1 is NaN. Exam pattern for numeric columns loaded as text: out["quantity"] = pd.to numeric(out["quantity"], errors="coerce") , then filter, then astype(int) once no NaN is left. Converting to int is what makes 3 print as 3 instead of 3.0 in an output file.

Three steps of the official SP3 problem come from this lesson: "keep the first occurrence of each record id", "sort by invoice id, product code, record id as strings", and a spending rank where ties share a rank (1, 1, 3). Each is one method call, and each has an argument that, if wrong, quietly changes the answer. Finding duplicates s.duplicated() is True for every value that already appeared earlier in the Series. The first occurrence is False, and each later copy is True. So s.duplicated().sum() counts the extra copies: an ID that appears $k$ times contributes $k - 1$. That equals len(s) - s.nunique() when nothing is missing. The keep argument says which copy is not marked: keep="first" (the default) leaves the first occurrence unmarked, keep="last" the last one, and keep=False marks every copy. On a DataFrame, df.duplicated(subset=["record id"]) looks only at the listed columns. Without subset , it compares whole rows, so two rows with the same ID but a different quantity do not count as duplicates. Dropping duplicates df.drop duplicates(subset="record id", keep="first") keeps the first row for each ID and drops the rest. It is the same as df[~df["record id"].duplicated()] , and it keeps the original index labels. The order of steps changes the result. SP3 removes duplicates (step 3) before it drops invalid rows (step 4). If the first copy of a record is invalid, the whole record disappears, even though a later copy was valid. Doing the steps in the other order keeps that later copy: Sorting by several keys df.sort values(by) sorts the rows. by is one column name or a list of names. With a list, rows are ordered by the first column, ties are broken by the second, and so on. ascending is one bool for all keys, or a list with one bool per key: Sorting keeps the original index labels, so the printout shows them in a new order. Add .reset index(drop=True) if you need labels 0, 1, 2, ... again. Strings sort in lexicographic order : character by character, like a dictionary, using character codes. Two consequences matter on exams: - Digit strings do not sort like numbers: "10" < "100" < "9" , because "1" comes before "9" . - Every uppercase letter comes before every lowercase letter: "B" < "a" . key= takes a function that is applied to the column before comparing (here a lambda that converts to integers). When a specification says "sort as strings", leave the column as strings and do not pass a key. When the keys can tie completely, add one more key that breaks the tie, or pass kind="stable" to keep tied rows in their current order (a stable sort). Ranking with ties s.rank() gives each value its position in sorted order, starting at 1. The method argument decides what tied values get: method ranks for [80, 80, 50, 20] (descending) rule --- --- --- "average" (default) 1.5, 1.5, 3, 4 ties get the mean of the positions they occupy "min" 1, 1, 3, 4 ties get the smallest position; the next rank skips "dense" 1, 1, 2, 3 ties get the smallest; no gap after a tie "first" 1, 2, 3, 4 ties are broken by order of appearance ascending=False gives rank 1 to the largest value, which is what "rank by spending, highest first" means. "Ties share a rank, 1, 1, 3" is method="min" . The result is always float64 , so finish with .astype(int) : Two totals tie only if they are exactly equal as floats. 0.1 + 0.2 and 0.3 differ in the last bit, so they get different ranks. Rank the values exactly as the statement defines them, and do not round them first unless the statement says so.

"Total sales per country", "the mean invoice total", "for each customer: invoices, products, spending" and "fill each product's missing price with that product's median" are all the same move: split the rows into groups, compute something per group, and combine the results. pandas does this with groupby . df.groupby("customer")["amount"].sum() from the placement quiz is one of these lines. groupby is the core of SP3 Parts C and D, so this lesson is the longest in the unit. Split, apply, combine df.groupby("customer") splits the rows into one group per distinct customer. Picking a column and calling a reduction applies it to each group and combines the answers into a Series indexed by customer. This pattern is called split-apply-combine . Look at the groups first, then at the one-line version: Read df.groupby("customer")["amount"].sum() left to right: group the rows by customer, take the amount column within each group, sum it. The result has one entry per customer, and the group keys are sorted (here alphabetically), whatever order they had in df . The common reductions Every Series reduction works per group: sum , mean , median , min , max , count , nunique , std . Two more count rows: - df.groupby("customer").size() counts the rows in each group, missing values included. - df.groupby("customer")["amount"].count() counts the non-missing amounts in each group. The last line is two steps: first the total of each invoice, then the mean of those totals. That is different from df["amount"].mean() , the mean over rows, whenever invoices have different numbers of rows. Several statistics at once: agg agg with named aggregation builds a whole summary table in one call. Each keyword argument is new column=(source column, function) : After groupby , the keys are the index of the result. reset index() turns them back into an ordinary column, which you need before writing a table with a required column order. ( groupby("customer", as index=False) does the same in one step.) Grouping by a list of columns makes one group per combination. The result has a MultiIndex , an index with one level per key, and reset index() again turns the levels into columns: One value per row: transform A reduction gives one value per group . transform gives the group's value back on every row of that group, so the result has the same length and index as df and can become a new column. The SP3 price fill is the standard use: each missing price gets the median of the present prices of the same product. The median is the middle value after sorting; with an even count, it is the mean of the two middle values. Three details from SP3 are visible here: 1. The medians are computed from the present prices before any filling, because med is computed from the original column. ( median skips NaN.) 2. Product z has no present price, so its median is NaN and its price stays missing. SP3 then drops such rows. 3. fillna(med) works because med has the same index as df . Filling with df.groupby("product")["price"].median() instead would fill nothing: that Series is indexed by product name, and fillna matches index labels, not product names. This kind of filling is called imputation. Missing keys are dropped. Rows whose group key is missing (NaN or None ) belong to no group by default, so they vanish from sum , size and every other result. df.groupby("k", dropna=False) keeps them as one extra group, listed last. This is separate from missing values inside a group: sum , mean , count , nunique and first skip those, while size counts every row. Running values per group. Some groupby methods return one value per row, computed from that row and the rows above it in the same group, in the table's current row order (sort first if the order matters): - g.shift(1) : the value from the previous row of the same group, even if that value is missing; NaN on each group's first row. - g.cumsum() : the running total. A missing value stays NaN on its own row and is skipped by later totals. - g.transform(lambda s: s.rolling(3, min periods=2).mean()) : the mean of the current row and up to 2 rows above it, counting only present values; NaN unless at least 2 of them are present. Such a window (the current row plus a fixed number of rows just above it) is a rolling window. rolling(3) alone means min periods=3 . - expanding() in place of rolling(3) uses every row of the group so far. transform calls the lambda (a one-line function, u01-l03) once per group, with that group's values as a Series. Read row 5 (group a ): prev is NaN because the previous a row holds NaN; run is $1 + 2 + 4 = 7$; roll2 averages the window NaN, 4 and gets 4.0; avg so far is $7 / 3$. Which group is largest: idxmax s.idxmax() returns the index label of the largest value ( s.max() returns the value itself). On a groupby result, the label is the group key, so "the country with the greatest sales" is one line. When several values tie for the maximum, idxmax returns the first label. Group keys are sorted, so the first label is the alphabetically first key, which is exactly the usual tie rule "ties: alphabetical": The same works for any per-group number, such as the spread of a product's prices: compute g.max() - g.min() per group, then idxmax() . Best item per group, with ties "Each customer's favorite category is the one with the greatest total quantity; ties go to the alphabetically first category" needs a winner inside each group. The reliable pattern: total per (customer, category), sort so that the winner comes first within each customer, then keep the first row per customer. The sort puts each customer's rows together, the largest quantity first, and among equal quantities the alphabetically first category. drop duplicates then keeps that row. Test the tie rule on a small case like this one before trusting it. Most per-group answers in SP3 are one of three shapes: df.groupby(key)[col].func() (one number per group), .agg(name=(col, func), ...) then .reset index() (a summary table), or .transform(func) (a group value on every row).

Data often comes in more than one file: transactions in one, the category of each product in another. Step 6 of SP3 attaches each product's category with a left join and labels products that are not in the category file as "Unclassified" . A join is also the easiest place to lose or duplicate rows without noticing, so this lesson keeps counting rows. merge A join combines two tables by matching the values of a join key , a column that both tables have. In pandas, left.merge(right, on="code", how=...) returns a new table with the columns of both. For each pair of rows, one from each table, whose keys are equal, the result has one row.
