Work from the loss back to the input, keeping the upstream gradient at each stage. 1. Output: $\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial \hat y} = \hat y - y = -3$. 2. Output layer: $\hat y = w 2 \cdot h + b 2$, so $\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial w 2} = -3\,h = (-3, 0, -3)$ and $\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial b 2} = -3$. 3. Into the hidden layer: $\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial h} = -3\,w 2 = (-6, -3, 3)$. 4. Through ReLU: its derivative is 1 where $z 1 0$ and 0 elsewhere, so multiply entry by entry by $(1, 0, 1)$: $\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial z 1} = (-6, 0, 3)$. 5. First layer: $z 1 = W 1x + b 1$, so entry $(i, j)$ of $\partial L/\partial W 1$ is $\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial z {1,i}}\,x j$, an outer product: Unit 2, which is off for this input, gets zero gradient in its whole row: a ReLU that is off passes nothing back. Autograd agrees: The same thing for a batch, in matrix form Now use a batch of $n$ examples, stored as the rows of $X$ (shape $(n, d)$), PyTorch's weight layout, $k$ outputs, and any loss that is a mean over the batch: with shapes $W 1: (h, d)$, $Z 1, H: (n, h)$, $W 2: (k, h)$, $Z 2: (n, k)$. From here on $h$ is the hidden width (the number of hidden units); the hidden values of the whole batch are the matrix $H$. Write $G 2 = \partial L/\partial Z 2$ for the upstream gradient at the output, a matrix of shape $(n, k)$ (one entry per entry of $Z 2$). The three rules for a linear layer. For $Z = AW^\top + b$, where $A$ is the layer's input ($X$ for the first layer, $H$ for the second), with upstream gradient $G = \partial L/\partial Z$: Why: entry by entry, $Z {ij} = \sum m A {im}W {jm} + b j$. $W {jm}$ appears in $Z {ij}$ for every example $i$, with coefficient $A {im}$, so $\partial L/\partial W {jm} = \sum i G {ij}A {im} = (G^\top A) {jm}$. $b j$ appears in every $Z {ij}$ with coefficient 1, so its gradient sums column $j$ of $G$ over the examples. $A {im}$ appears in $Z {ij}$ for every output $j$, with coefficient $W {jm}$, so $\partial L/\partial A {im} = \sum j G {ij}W {jm} = (GW) {im}$. Check the shapes: $G^\top A$ is $(k, n)(n, h) = (k, h)$, the shape of $W$; $GW$ is $(n, k)(k, h) = (n, h)$, the shape of $A$. If a formula gives the wrong shape, it is wrong. The rule for an activation. For $H = \phi(Z)$ applied entry by entry, each $H {ij}$ depends only on $Z {ij}$, so where $\odot$ means entrywise product. For ReLU, $\phi'(Z)$ is the 0/1 mask of where $Z 0$ (PyTorch uses 0 at exactly 0). The whole backward pass. Apply the rules from the output back: For the mean softmax cross-entropy, $G 2 = (P - Y)/n$, where $P$ is the softmax of each row of $Z 2$ and $Y$ the one-hot labels (u04-l09). For the mean of $\frac12\lVert z {2,i} - y i\rVert^2$, $G 2 = (Z 2 - Y)/n$. The $1/n$ appears once, in $G 2$; the later sums over rows do not divide again. Why backpropagation and not numerical gradients A gradient check with central differences needs two forward passes per parameter. For the 109,386-parameter MLP of lesson 1 that is 218,772 forward passes for one gradient. Backpropagation gets every entry from one forward pass and one backward pass, and the backward pass costs about twice the forward pass (two matrix products per layer, $G^\top A$ and $GW$, against one going forward). That is why every framework uses it, and why the forward pass stores $Z 1$ and $H$: the backward pass needs them. Use central differences only to test a backward pass you wrote, on a tiny network in float64. 1. Transposes. $X^\top G 1$ has shape $(d, h)$, the transpose of $W 1$'s shape. With PyTorch's layout it is $G 1^\top X$. 2. The $1/n$. Forgetting it, or dividing again when summing the bias gradient. 3. The mask. Using $\mathbb{1}[H 0]$ is fine (same as $Z 1 0$ for ReLU), but forgetting the mask, or using it on $G 2$, is not. 4. Bias over the wrong axis. $\partial L/\partial b$ sums over examples (rows), giving one number per unit. Each layer is a map with a Jacobian. The chain rule says the gradient of the scalar loss with respect to the input is the row vector $\frac{\partial L}{\partial Z 2} J {2} J {1}$. Multiplying from the left keeps every intermediate result a vector the size of one layer, never a matrix of size (layer) $\times$ (layer); multiplying from the right would build full Jacobians. That choice of order is called reverse mode, and it is why one backward pass gives all the gradients at once. By hand: write the forward values in a column (with ReLU on/off marked), then walk back one layer at a time: upstream gradient, times the local rule. A ReLU that is off for the input zeroes a whole row of $\partial L/\partial W 1$ (for that example). In code: check each gradient's shape against its parameter, and compare against autograd before submitting if torch is allowed in your notebook.

The activation function is the only nonlinear part of an MLP, and its derivative is a factor in every gradient that passes through it. Round 1 asks for these derivatives directly (2026 Problem 4.1 asked for the derivative of tanh), and asks why deep sigmoid networks train badly. Part 2 problems list the allowed layers by name (SP4 allows nn.ReLU , nn.LeakyReLU , nn.Sigmoid , nn.Tanh , nn.GELU , nn.Softplus ), so you should know what each one computes. The six you need u04-l01 derived the first four derivatives. $\sigma$ is the sigmoid and $\Phi$ is the CDF of the standard normal distribution. name $\phi(z)$ range $\phi'(z)$ $\phi'(0)$ PyTorch --- --- --- --- --- --- sigmoid $\dfrac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$ $(0, 1)$ $\sigma(z)(1 - \sigma(z))$ $0.25$ nn.Sigmoid() tanh $\dfrac{e^z - e^{-z}}{e^z + e^{-z}}$ $(-1, 1)$ $1 - \tanh^2 z$ $1$ nn.Tanh() ReLU $\max(0, z)$ $[0, \infty)$ $1$ if $z 0$, else $0$ $0$ (by convention) nn.ReLU() softplus $\ln(1 + e^z)$ $(0, \infty)$ $\sigma(z)$ $0.5$ nn.Softplus() LeakyReLU $z$ if $z 0$, else $\alpha z$ all reals $1$ if $z 0$, else $\alpha$ $\alpha$ nn.LeakyReLU(0.01) GELU $z\,\Phi(z)$ about $[-0.17, \infty)$ $\Phi(z) + z\,\Phi'(z)$ $0.5$ nn.GELU() - LeakyReLU keeps a small slope $\alpha$ (default negative slope=0.01 ) for negative inputs, so its gradient is never exactly 0. - GELU (Gaussian error linear unit) multiplies $z$ by the probability $\Phi(z)$ that a standard normal is below $z$. For large positive $z$ that is about 1 (so GELU $\approx z$), for large negative $z$ about 0. In between it is smooth and dips slightly below 0, to about $-0.17$ at $z \approx -0.75$. Transformers (u16) use it. nn.GELU(approximate="tanh") uses a faster tanh formula that differs from the exact one by less than 0.0005. - tanh is a rescaled sigmoid: $\tanh z = 2\sigma(2z) - 1$. Its output is centered on 0, which sigmoid's is not. Each also exists as a function: torch.sigmoid , torch.tanh , torch.relu , F.softplus , F.leaky relu , F.gelu (with import torch.nn.functional as F ). The right panel is the one that matters for training: sigmoid's derivative never exceeds 0.25, and both sigmoid and tanh have derivatives near 0 once $ z $ is more than about 3. That flat region is saturation. At $z = 5$, $\sigma'(5) \approx 0.0066$. Vanishing gradients In a deep network the gradient reaching layer 1 is a product of one factor per layer above it: each layer contributes its weights times $\phi'(z)$ (lesson 3: $G 1 = (G 2W 2) \odot \phi'(Z 1)$, repeated). With sigmoid, $\phi' \le 0.25$, so ten sigmoid layers can shrink the gradient by up to $0.25^{10} \approx 10^{-6}$, unless the weights are large enough to make up for it, and large weights push the units into saturation, which shrinks $\phi'$ further. This is the vanishing gradient problem : the early layers get gradients so small that they barely train. The opposite, factors above 1 multiplying up to huge gradients, is the exploding gradient problem (lesson 11 shows the fix, gradient clipping). Measure it. Ten hidden layers of width 64, each activation with the weight initialization that lesson 6 recommends for it; the code compares the gradient size at the first and the last hidden layer: .norm() is the L2 norm of all the entries. With sigmoid, the first layer's gradient is about $3 \times 10^{-7}$ of the last layer's: a learning rate that suits the last layer leaves the first one frozen. With tanh and ReLU the ratio stays within a factor of about 5 (ReLU's derivative is exactly 1 for every active unit). This is why ReLU replaced sigmoid in hidden layers, and one reason early deep networks were so hard to train. Dead ReLUs ReLU has its own failure. A unit whose pre-activation is negative for every training input outputs 0 and has gradient 0 for every input, so no update ever changes its weights: a dead ReLU . It happens after a large update pushes a bias far negative (a learning rate that is too high is the usual cause). LeakyReLU and GELU have nonzero gradient for negative inputs, so their units can recover. In a network that trains normally, a few dead units do no harm. Which activation where - Hidden layers: ReLU is the default. GELU in transformers. LeakyReLU if many units die. Sigmoid and tanh mostly inside gates of recurrent networks (u15), not as hidden activations of deep MLPs. - Output layer: usually none. Regression outputs any real number, so a ReLU at the end would make negative predictions impossible. Classifiers output logits, and the loss applies sigmoid or softmax itself ( BCEWithLogitsLoss , CrossEntropyLoss , lesson 5). Use torch.sigmoid or torch.softmax only when you need the probabilities at prediction time. Softplus at the output gives a positive quantity (a variance, a rate); tanh gives one in $(-1, 1)$. Memorize $\sigma'(0) = 0.25$, $\tanh'(0) = 1$ and $\sigma' = \sigma(1 - \sigma)$, $\tanh' = 1 - \tanh^2$; a by-hand gradient through a sigmoid layer multiplies by $a(1 - a)$, where $a$ is the layer's output. For "why does this deep network not learn", look for sigmoid hidden layers or a large learning rate.

The loss function decides what "good" means, and the wrong one quietly trains the wrong model. Round 1 tests the formulas (the 2027 sample P4 is one gradient step of cross-entropy with a soft target), which loss fits which task, and what PyTorch's loss classes expect as input. You have met every piece before: mean squared error and MAE in u06-l07, cross-entropy and KL divergence in u05-l08, the gradient $p - y$ in u04-l09, and the PyTorch classes in u10-l05. This lesson puts them side by side and adds soft targets and label smoothing. Regression: MSE, MAE and Huber For predictions $\hat y i$ and targets $y i$: Their gradients with respect to one prediction differ in a way that matters: $\frac{2}{n}(\hat y i - y i)$ for MSE, which grows with the error, and $\frac1n\operatorname{sign}(\hat y i - y i)$ for MAE, which has the same size for every wrong prediction. So under MSE one example with a huge error (an outlier , a value far from the rest) can dominate every update; under MAE it counts like any other mistake. The cleanest way to see it: the best constant prediction $c$ for MSE is the mean of the targets, and for MAE it is the median. For targets $1, 2, 3, 4, 100$, MSE picks $c = 22$, which fits none of them, and MAE picks $c = 3$. The Huber loss is quadratic for small errors and linear for large ones, so it is smooth near 0 like MSE but treats outliers like MAE. With threshold $\delta$ and error $e = \hat y - y$, it is $\frac12 e^2$ if $ e \le \delta$ and $\delta( e - \frac12\delta)$ otherwise. PyTorch: nn.MSELoss() , nn.L1Loss() (MAE), nn.HuberLoss(delta=1.0) . Classification: cross-entropy from logits Binary: one logit $z$ per example, $q = \sigma(z)$ is the predicted probability of class 1, and with target $t$ the binary cross-entropy is the log-loss $-[t\ln q + (1 - t)\ln(1 - q)]$. Its gradient with respect to the logit is $q - t$. nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss() takes $z$, not $q$, and computes the same value in the stable form $\operatorname{softplus}(z) - tz$ (substitute $\ln\sigma(z) = z - \operatorname{softplus}(z)$ and $\ln(1 - \sigma(z)) = -\operatorname{softplus}(z)$, both from $1 - \sigma(z) = 1/(1 + e^z)$). Multiclass: one logit per class, $p = \operatorname{softmax}(z)$, and the cross-entropy against a one-hot $y$ is $-\ln p c$ for the true class $c$, with gradient $p - y$. nn.CrossEntropyLoss() takes the logits of shape (N, C) and integer labels of shape (N,) . Both are negative log-likelihoods (u05-l07): minimizing them is maximum likelihood for a model that outputs probabilities. Soft targets A soft target is a probability vector $t$ instead of a one-hot label: $t = (0.7, 0.2, 0.1)$ says "probably class 0, but maybe not". Soft targets come from averaging several annotators, from correcting noisy labels with Bayes' rule (the 2027 sample P4), or from a trained teacher network's probabilities. The loss keeps the same formula, because the derivation of $p - y$ in u04-l09 only used $\sum j y j = 1$. Two facts that matter in practice: 1. The minimum is not 0. Since $H(t, p) = H(t) + D {\mathrm{KL}}(t \,\ \, p)$ (entropy plus KL, u05-l08) and KL is never negative, the smallest possible loss is the entropy $H(t)$, reached at $p = t$. For $t = (0.7, 0.2, 0.1)$ that is about $0.802$. A loss stuck at 0.80 with these targets means the model is perfect, not broken. 2. Minimizing cross-entropy = minimizing KL , because $H(t)$ does not depend on the model. nn.CrossEntropyLoss() accepts soft targets directly: pass a float tensor of shape (N, C) whose rows are probability vectors instead of integer labels. Label smoothing Label smoothing replaces each one-hot target by a soft one: with $K$ classes and smoothing $\varepsilon$, With $K = 4$ and $\varepsilon = 0.1$, the true class gets $0.9 + 0.025 = 0.925$ and each other class $0.025$. Why bother: with a one-hot target the loss $-\ln p c$ only reaches 0 as $p c \to 1$, which needs the gap between logits to grow without limit, so training keeps inflating the logits and the model becomes overconfident. With a smoothed target the best logits are finite. It is one line in PyTorch, nn.CrossEntropyLoss(label smoothing=0.1) , which builds exactly this $t$: Which loss for which task task last layer outputs loss target --- --- --- --- regression real numbers, no activation nn.MSELoss() , or nn.L1Loss() / nn.HuberLoss() with outliers float, same shape as the output binary classification one logit nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss() float 0/1 (or soft), same shape multiclass $C$ logits nn.CrossEntropyLoss() long labels (N,) , or float probabilities (N, C) multi-label (several yes/no per example) $C$ logits nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss() float 0/1 of shape (N, C) In knowledge distillation , a large trained "teacher" network's softmax outputs are soft targets that carry more information than labels (which wrong classes look similar). A small "student" is trained with cross-entropy against them, often after dividing both networks' logits by a temperature $T 1$, which flattens the distributions so the small probabilities matter. PyTorch's nn.KLDivLoss(reduction="batchmean") is the usual tool: it takes the student's log -probabilities ( F.log softmax ) as input and the teacher's probabilities as target. Since KL and cross-entropy differ by the constant $H(t)$, both give the same gradients. Gradient with respect to the logits is always "prediction minus target" ($q - t$ or $p - t$), soft targets included. The minimum of cross-entropy with a soft target is $H(t)$, not 0. PyTorch's classification losses take logits; never apply sigmoid or softmax before them.

Training starts from random weights, and the scale of those random numbers decides whether a deep network trains at all. The 2026 paper asked for the right scale (Problem 7.2, the variance-preserving initialization you derived in u10-l03) and then had you build a layer with it (7.3). Part 2 code often calls nn.init functions, and Part 1 can ask for the standard deviation that Xavier or He initialization gives a layer. This lesson explains the two failure modes, then the formulas. Failure 1: all weights equal Set every weight of a layer to the same number (zero is the common case). Then every hidden unit computes the same function of the input, receives the same gradient, gets the same update, and stays identical to the others forever. The layer behaves like one unit, however wide it is. Random initialization exists to break this symmetry . The weights changed, but all four rows changed the same way. Biases are different: they can start at zero, because random weights already make the units differ. Failure 2: the wrong scale u10-l03 showed that one output $y = \sum {c=1}^{C} w c x c$ of a layer with $C$ inputs has variance when the weights and inputs are independent with mean 0, $\operatorname{Var}(w c) = \sigma w^2$ and $\operatorname{Var}(x c) = \sigma^2$. A layer multiplies the variance by $C\sigma w^2$, and a deep network repeats this. If the factor is 2, ten layers multiply the variance by $2^{10} = 1024$; if it is $\frac12$, they divide it by 1024. Outputs and gradients then explode or vanish (lesson 4), before any training happens. Here is a 10-layer ReLU network of width 256, printing the root mean square of the activations, $\sqrt{E[h^2]}$, after layers 1, 5 and 10: With standard deviation 1 the activations reach about $2.6 \times 10^{10}$. With $1/\sqrt{C}$ they shrink by about $1/\sqrt2$ per layer, to about 0.02. Only $\sqrt{2/C}$ keeps them near 1, and the next section shows why the ReLU needs the extra factor 2. LeCun, He and Xavier The number of inputs of a layer is its fan-in ; the number of outputs is its fan-out . For nn.Linear(in, out) , fan-in is in . For a convolution, fan-in is in channels k k , because each output sums over that many inputs. - LeCun (variance-preserving): $\sigma w^2 = 1/\text{fan-in}$. It makes $C\sigma w^2 = 1$. Right for activations that are close to the identity near 0, such as tanh. - He (also called Kaiming): $\sigma w^2 = 2/\text{fan-in}$. The inputs to a hidden layer are ReLU outputs, $a = \operatorname{ReLU}(z)$. If $z$ is symmetric around 0, ReLU zeroes half of it, so $E[a^2] = \frac12 E[z^2]$. The product formula uses $E[a^2]$ in place of $\sigma^2$ (u05-l04 has the details), so the layer multiplies by $C\sigma w^2 \cdot \frac12$, and $\sigma w^2 = 2/C$ makes that 1. This is He initialization, the right choice for ReLU networks. - Xavier (also called Glorot): $\sigma w^2 = 2/(\text{fan-in} + \text{fan-out})$. The backward pass runs the same argument with fan-out: gradients flowing back through $W^\top$ are multiplied by $\text{fan-out}\cdot\sigma w^2$. Xavier compromises between the two. It is used with tanh and sigmoid. Each has a normal and a uniform version with the same variance. A uniform distribution on $[-a, a]$ has variance $a^2/3$ (uniform distribution, u05-l03), so variance $v$ needs $a = \sqrt{3v}$. For Xavier, $a = \sqrt{6/(\text{fan-in} + \text{fan-out})}$. In PyTorch The functions in torch.nn.init overwrite a tensor in place (the trailing underscore means in place, as in u10) and do not record gradients: To initialize a whole model, write a function for one module and pass it to model.apply , which calls it on every submodule: PyTorch's default for nn.Linear and nn.Conv2d draws weights (and biases) uniformly from $[-1/\sqrt{\text{fan-in}}, 1/\sqrt{\text{fan-in}}]$, which has variance $1/(3\,\text{fan-in})$: smaller than He by a factor of 6. Shallow networks do not care; for deep plain ReLU networks it is one reason to call kaiming normal yourself. Networks with normalization layers (lesson 9) or residual connections (u12) are much less sensitive to the initialization. nn.Linear(400, 300) has fan-in 400 (its input size), so He gives std $\sqrt{2/400}$, not $\sqrt{2/300}$. The weight tensor's shape is (300, 400) : fan-in is the second dimension. Know the three variances: LeCun $1/n {\text{in}}$, He $2/n {\text{in}}$, Xavier $2/(n {\text{in}} + n {\text{out}})$, and the uniform bound $a = \sqrt{3 \cdot \text{variance}}$. The derivation every one of them comes from is $\operatorname{Var}(y) = C\sigma w^2\sigma^2$, which the 2026 paper asked for in full, reasoning included.

The optimizer turns gradients into updates, and the learning rate is the hyperparameter most likely to make or break a training run. Round 1 asks you to run an update rule by hand for a step or two (Adam's first step has a famous shortcut) and what a schedule does to the learning rate; Part 2 needs AdamW , a scheduler and sensible defaults from memory. u10-l06 gave you the constructors and the training step; this lesson shows what the optimizers compute. Notation: $\theta$ is one parameter, weight or bias (the usual letter in optimizer papers and in the 2025 and 2026 problems; earlier lessons wrote weights as $w$). Everything below acts on each entry separately. $g t$ is its gradient at step $t$, and $\eta$ is the learning rate. SGD and the learning rate Plain stochastic gradient descent is $\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\,g t$. On a long, narrow valley the learning rate is capped by the steep direction and the flat direction then crawls. Take whose gradient is $(x, 100y)$. One step multiplies $y$ by $1 - 100\eta$, so $\eta$ must stay below $0.02$ or $y$ grows (u04-l06 showed this limit, $2/\lambda {\max}$). At $\eta = 0.019$, $x$ shrinks by only $1 - 0.019$ per step: after 100 steps it has gone from $-4$ to about $-0.59$. Momentum Momentum keeps a running velocity $v$ and steps along it: with $\mu$ around 0.9 ( torch.optim.SGD(params, lr, momentum=0.9) uses exactly this form, starting from $v = 0$). In a direction where the gradient keeps the same sign, $v$ builds up toward $g/(1 - \mu)$, so the step becomes 10 times larger at $\mu = 0.9$. In a direction where it flips sign every step (bouncing across the narrow valley), the terms cancel. So momentum speeds up the flat direction and damps the steep one. RMSProp and Adam: a step size per parameter RMSProp keeps a running average of squared gradients and divides by its square root: $\sqrt{s}$ is the typical size of this parameter's gradient, so every parameter moves about $\eta$ per step whether its gradients are large or small. The small $\epsilon$ ( 1e-8 ) avoids division by zero. PyTorch: torch.optim.RMSprop(params, lr=0.01, alpha=0.99) . Adam combines both: a running average $m$ of gradients (momentum) and a running average $v$ of squared gradients (RMSProp). With $\beta 1 = 0.9$, $\beta 2 = 0.999$, $m = v = 0$ at the start, and step counter $t = 1, 2, \dots$: The divisions by $1 - \beta^t$ are the bias correction . Because $m$ and $v$ start at 0, after one step $m = 0.1\,g 1$, ten times too small; dividing by $1 - 0.9^1 = 0.1$ fixes that. The correction fades as $t$ grows ($0.9^{50} \approx 0.005$). Adam's first step. At $t = 1$, $\hat m = g 1$ and $\hat v = g 1^2$, so the update is $-\eta\,g 1/( g 1 + \epsilon) \approx -\eta\,\operatorname{sign}(g 1)$. Every parameter with a nonzero gradient moves by almost exactly $\eta$, whatever the size of its gradient. With $\eta = 0.05$, gradients $50$ and $-0.002$ both give a step of size $0.05$. Seeing the difference Four runs on $f(x, y) = \frac12(x^2 + 100y^2)$ from $(-4, 1)$, 100 steps each: - SGD at 0.019 zigzags across the valley and is still at loss 0.18; at 0.021 it diverges (loss near $10^{10}$). - Momentum, with a learning rate four times smaller, reaches about $2 \times 10^{-4}$. - Adam heads almost diagonally at first (its first steps have the same size in $x$ and $y$), then settles, reaching about $5 \times 10^{-4}$. On real networks the picture is similar: Adam with lr=1e-3 is a strong default that needs little tuning, and SGD with momentum 0.9 and a tuned learning rate (often 0.01 to 0.1) with a schedule can match or beat it. Weight decay, and why AdamW exists Weight decay (u06-l04) adds $\frac{\lambda}{2}\lVert\theta\rVert^2$ to the loss, so the gradient gains $\lambda\theta$. For SGD the update becomes each step shrinks the weights by the factor $1 - \eta\lambda$, hence "decay". torch.optim.Adam(params, weight decay=λ) does the same thing, adding $\lambda\theta$ to the gradient, but Adam then divides by $\sqrt{\hat v}$, so parameters with large gradients get almost no decay. AdamW decouples the two: it shrinks the weights directly, $\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\lambda\theta$, and then takes the Adam step using the gradient of the loss alone. Every weight then decays at the same rate. AdamW usually generalizes better, and it is the standard optimizer for transformers. Practice: u11-p03 Adam and AdamW by hand (20 minutes) has you write both and match torch.optim exactly. Learning rate schedules and warmup A learning rate schedule changes $\eta$ during training: large steps early to make progress, small steps late to settle into a minimum. PyTorch's schedulers wrap an optimizer, and you call scheduler.step() once per epoch, after the epoch's optimizer.step() calls: - StepLR(opt, step size=10, gamma=0.1) : multiply the learning rate by gamma every step size epochs, so $\eta t = \eta 0\,\gamma^{\lfloor t/10 \rfloor}$. - CosineAnnealingLR(opt, T max=50) : follow half a cosine from $\eta 0$ down to 0 over T max epochs, $\eta t = \frac{\eta 0}{2}\left(1 + \cos\frac{\pi t}{T {\max}}\right)$. - Warmup : start with a small learning rate and raise it over the first few epochs or steps, for example LinearLR(opt, start factor=0.1, total iters=5) . Early on the weights are random and Adam's averages rest on very few gradients, so full-size steps can throw training somewhere bad; transformers almost always warm up. SequentialLR chains a warmup and a decay. Adam's first step moves each parameter by about the learning rate, in the direction opposite to its gradient's sign. Momentum's velocity after $k$ equal gradients $g$ is $g(1 + \mu + \dots + \mu^{k-1})$. StepLR after $t$ epochs gives $\eta 0\gamma^{\lfloor t/s\rfloor}$ with $s$ = step size . When in doubt in Part 2: AdamW(lr=1e-3) and train longer before tuning anything else.

A network with a hundred thousand parameters can fit almost any training set, noise included, so overfitting is the normal state of affairs, not a rare accident. The IOAI syllabus lists the three standard remedies by name (dropout, early stopping, weight decay), Round 1 asks what each one does numerically (dropout's scaling at train and eval time is a favorite), and in Part 2's open-ended problem they are what turns a model that memorizes into one that scores. u06-l04 introduced regularization for linear models; this lesson covers the versions used for neural networks. Weight decay Weight decay adds $\frac{\lambda}{2}\lVert\theta\rVert^2$ to the loss. With SGD the update becomes $\theta \leftarrow (1 - \eta\lambda)\theta - \eta g$ (lesson 7): every step shrinks every weight a little, and only weights that the data keeps pushing stay large. In PyTorch it is an optimizer argument, not a term you add to the loss: Typical values are $10^{-4}$ to $10^{-2}$. As with ridge regression (u07-l03), biases are usually left undecayed, and so are the scale and shift parameters of normalization layers (lesson 9). An optimizer accepts parameter groups , a list of dicts that each set their own options: Dropout dropout (u10-l08 showed the layer) is a regularizer that randomly switches off units during training. In training mode, nn.Dropout(p) sets each entry of its input to 0 independently with probability $p$ and multiplies the survivors by $\frac{1}{1-p}$: The scaling keeps the expected value unchanged: $E[y i] = \frac{1 - p}{1 - p}x i = x i$. In eval mode the layer does nothing, $y = x$. Because the rescaling happens during training, nothing has to change at test time; this version is called inverted dropout , and it is what PyTorch implements. Example: $p = 0.5$ and $x = (1, 2, 3, 4)$ with mask $m = (1, 0, 1, 1)$ gives $y = (2, 0, 6, 8)$ in training and $y = (1, 2, 3, 4)$ in eval mode. Why it helps. No hidden unit can rely on one particular other unit being present, so the network has to spread what it learns over many units, which makes it less sensitive to the quirks of individual training examples. Another view: each training step trains a different random sub-network (a layer of $m$ units can be thinned in $2^m$ ways), and the full network at test time behaves roughly like an average of all of them, an ensemble. Where it goes. After the activation of hidden layers, for example nn.Linear(256, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Dropout(0.3) . Never after the output layer. Rates of 0.1 to 0.5 are usual. Forgetting model.eval() before predicting leaves dropout on, so predictions are random and worse (u10-l08). Early stopping early stopping (u06-l04) watches the loss on a validation set every epoch and keeps the parameters from the best epoch. A network's training loss keeps falling, but its validation loss usually falls, flattens, then rises as the network starts fitting noise. Patience is the number of epochs without a new best validation loss that you wait before stopping. Save a copy of the best state dict (u10-l08): copy.deepcopy is needed because state dict() returns references to the live tensors, which keep changing. Here a 64-unit network fits 20 noisy points of $\sin 2x$ (noise variance 0.09, so no model can get validation MSE much below 0.09): The validation loss bottoms out at epoch 52 (MSE 0.111) and then creeps up while the training loss keeps falling: the classic overfitting picture. Patience 200 stops the run at epoch 252 and restores the epoch-52 weights. Left to run all 800 epochs, the same network reaches training MSE 0.007 and validation MSE 0.167: it has learned the noise. Data augmentation Data augmentation makes new training examples by transforming existing ones in ways that do not change the label: for images, flips, crops, small rotations and added noise; for audio, noise and time shifts; for tabular data, small Gaussian noise on numeric features. Apply it to the training set only, freshly at random each epoch, so the network rarely sees exactly the same input twice. It is often the single most effective regularizer for images (u12-l08 shows torchvision.transforms ). What else reduces overfitting More data beats every trick. Otherwise: a smaller network (less capacity), label smoothing (lesson 5), and batch norm (lesson 9), which has a mild regularizing effect of its own. In Part 2 the usual recipe is a validation split, AdamW with weight decay, dropout 0.1 to 0.3 if the network is large, and early stopping on the validation loss. Dropout at train time: zero with probability $p$, survivors times $\frac{1}{1-p}$; at eval time: identity. Weight decay with SGD: multiply by $1 - \eta\lambda$, then take the gradient step. Early stopping returns the best validation epoch, not the last one, and stops patience epochs after it.

Normalization layers rescale the values flowing through a network so each layer sees inputs of a steady size. Almost every modern network has them: batch norm in CNNs such as ResNet (2026 Problem 8), layer norm in every transformer (u16). Round 1 asks what they compute on a small batch, how many parameters and buffers they have (u10-l04), and how they behave in training versus eval mode, which is also the classic Part 2 bug. The IOAI syllabus lists batch normalization by name. Batch norm Batch normalization ( nn.BatchNorm1d(C) for input of shape (N, C) ) normalizes each feature, that is each column, using the mean and variance of that column over the batch . For one feature with batch values $x 1, \dots, x N$: - $\sigma^2$ is the biased (divide by $N$) variance, and $\epsilon = 10^{-5}$ guards against dividing by 0. - After the $\hat x$ step each feature has mean 0 and variance about 1 in the batch. That is standardization (u06-l09), done inside the network with the batch's own statistics. - $\gamma$ ( weight , starts at 1) and $\beta$ ( bias , starts at 0) are learned, one per feature, so the network can undo the normalization if that helps. They are the layer's $2C$ parameters. Example, one feature, batch $x = (2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9)$: $\mu = 5$ and $\sigma^2 = \frac{9 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 4 + 16}{8} = 4$, so with $\gamma = 1$, $\beta = 0$ the output is $\hat x = (x - 5)/2 = (-1.5, -0.5, -0.5, -0.5, 0, 0, 1, 2)$ (up to the tiny $\epsilon$). For images, nn.BatchNorm2d(C) takes (N, C, H, W) and computes one mean and variance per channel over the batch and all positions ($N \cdot H \cdot W$ values each). nn.BatchNorm1d(C) also accepts (N, C, L) and averages over $N$ and $L$. Train mode versus eval mode At prediction time there may be a single example, and a prediction should not depend on which other examples happen to share its batch. So batch norm keeps two buffers (u10-l03), running mean and running var , starting at 0 and 1. In training mode each forward pass normalizes with the batch statistics and also updates the buffers: This is an exponential moving average (each update keeps 90% of the old value and mixes in 10% of the new one, so old batches fade out geometrically), and momentum here is not the optimizer's momentum: it is the weight of the new value. One detail: running var is updated with the unbiased batch variance (divide by $N - 1$), even though the normalization itself uses the biased one. In eval mode ( model.eval() , u10-l08) the layer normalizes with the stored running mean and running var and changes nothing. Continuing the example: after that one training batch, running mean $= 0.9 \cdot 0 + 0.1 \cdot 5 = 0.5$ and running var $= 0.9 \cdot 1 + 0.1 \cdot \frac{32}{7} \approx 1.3571$. So in eval mode, the input $x = 5$, which the batch mapped to 0, comes out as $\frac{5 - 0.5}{\sqrt{1.3571}} \approx 3.86$. After many training batches the running statistics settle near the data's true mean and variance and the two modes agree closely, but early in training, or if you forget eval() , they do not. The buffers change during any training-mode forward pass, even inside torch.no grad() : they are not updated by the optimizer. The third buffer, num batches tracked , counts the batches. A batch of one in training mode is an error for BatchNorm1d (a variance of one number is 0); in eval mode it is fine. Why it helps, and where it goes Batch norm keeps every layer's pre-activations near mean 0 and variance 1 however the earlier weights change, which keeps ReLU and tanh units out of their dead and saturated regions. In practice it lets you use larger learning rates, makes training much less sensitive to the initialization (lesson 6), and adds a little regularization, because each example's output depends on the random batch it lands in. The usual placement is nn.Linear(d, h, bias=False), nn.BatchNorm1d(h), nn.ReLU() : the linear layer's bias would be subtracted away with the mean, and $\beta$ replaces it (that is why ResNet's convolutions have no bias, u10-l04). It has two weak points: very small batches give noisy statistics, and the train/eval switch is easy to get wrong. Layer norm Layer normalization ( nn.LayerNorm(D) ) normalizes each example over its own features instead of each feature over the batch. For input of shape (N, D) it computes one mean and one (biased) variance per row , then applies learned $\gamma$ and $\beta$ of shape (D,) : Each example is normalized on its own, so layer norm has no running statistics and no buffers, behaves the same in training and eval mode, and works with batch size 1. For input (N, T, D) (a batch of sequences of $T$ tokens, u15), nn.LayerNorm(D) normalizes each token's $D$ features. That is why transformers use it. If the row is $(2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9)$, layer norm gives the same $(-1.5, -0.5, \dots, 2)$ that batch norm gave for that column. batch norm layer norm --- --- --- statistics over the batch (and positions), per feature the features, per example input (N, D) $D$ means, one per column $N$ means, one per row learned $\gamma, \beta$ of shape (D,) $\gamma, \beta$ of shape (D,) buffers running mean , running var , num batches tracked none train vs eval different identical used in CNNs (ResNet) transformers, RNNs Practice: u11-p04 Batch norm and dropout from scratch (25 minutes) builds MyBatchNorm1d and MyDropout from nn.Parameter and register buffer and checks them against PyTorch in both modes. Batch norm on a tiny batch: subtract the column mean, divide by the square root of the biased variance, then $\gamma\hat x + \beta$. Running statistics move a tenth of the way toward each batch's statistics, with the unbiased variance. Eval mode uses the running values. Layer norm: same formula along each row, no running statistics.

Networks need numbers, but much of the world comes as categories: words, user IDs, product codes, zip codes. An embedding gives each category its own learned vector. Embeddings are the first layer of every language model, and a network's internal vectors for images, sentences or audio clips are also called embeddings and get compared by cosine similarity. 2026 Round 1 Problem 5 (90 points, the largest problem on the paper) was entirely about word embeddings: normalize them, build the similarity matrix, find each word's nearest neighbor, all without loops or np.linalg . The IOAI syllabus lists "data embeddings (text, image, audio)". From one-hot to an embedding table A categorical feature with $n$ possible values (in this lesson $n$ counts categories, not examples) can be fed to a network as a one-hot vector of length $n$ (u06-l09). Two problems: with $n = 50{,}000$ words the vectors are huge and almost all zeros, and every pair of categories is equally far apart, so "cat" is no closer to "kitten" than to "truck". An embedding layer stores a matrix $E$ of shape $(n, d)$, one learned row of length $d$ per category, and maps category $i$ to row $i$. That is exactly a linear layer without bias applied to the one-hot vector, because the product just picks out row $i$. The embedding layer does the lookup directly, without building the one-hot vector or multiplying. The rows start random and are trained by backpropagation like any other weights, so categories that play similar roles in the data end up with similar vectors. The length $d$ (often 16 to 1024) is the embedding dimension , a hyperparameter. In PyTorch, nn.Embedding(num embeddings, embedding dim) has one parameter, weight , of shape (n, d) (so $nd$ parameters, initialized from $N(0, 1)$). Its input is a tensor of integer indices ( torch.long ) of any shape, and the output adds a last axis of length $d$: Only the rows that were looked up receive gradient, and a row used twice gets the sum of both contributions (the "value used in two places" rule from u04-l03). nn.Embedding(n, d, padding idx=0) keeps row 0 at zero and never updates it, for the padding token that fills short sentences up to a common length (u15). Similar things, nearby vectors Trained word embeddings (word2vec and GloVe are the classic ones; 2026 P5 used 100-dimensional GloVe vectors) are fitted so that words appearing in similar contexts get similar vectors. Similarity is measured by cosine similarity (u03-l01), the cosine of the angle between two vectors, which ignores their lengths: For many vectors at once, the 2026 recipe is: divide each row by its L2 norm to get unit rows $W$, then the similarity matrix $S = WW^\top$ holds every pairwise cosine similarity, $S {ij} = \hat v i \cdot \hat v j$, with 1 on the diagonal (every word is identical to itself). To find each word's nearest other word, take the largest entry of each row after blocking the diagonal. Without blocking the diagonal, S.argmax(axis=1) returns every word itself, since $S {ii} = 1$ is the largest possible cosine. The 2026 problem then asked about the SVD of $W$ and low-rank approximations of $S$; that is linear algebra, covered in u03-l09. Embeddings of anything Any network's internal vector for an input is an embedding of that input. Take a trained image classifier, drop its head, and the output of the last hidden layer is a vector that places similar images near each other; the same works for sentence encoders and audio models such as HuBERT (u17). These vectors are used for: - search and retrieval : embed the query and every item, return the items with the highest cosine similarity; - features : train a small classifier, or run k-nearest neighbors or k-means, on the embeddings instead of raw pixels or text; - visualization : t-SNE or UMAP maps of embeddings (u08-l08, where embedding meant the 2D coordinates; same word, same idea of "a vector that represents the item"). To get one vector for a whole sequence of tokens, the simplest method is mean pooling : average the token embeddings, emb(idx).mean(dim=1) for idx of shape (N, T) , leaving out padding tokens if there are any. Because an embedding is a linear layer on a one-hot input, everything you know about linear layers applies: its gradient for row $i$ is the sum of the upstream gradients of the positions where category $i$ appeared, and weight decay shrinks rarely seen rows toward 0. It also explains a classic trick: the output layer of a language model is a linear map from a $d$-vector to $n$ word logits, a matrix of shape $(n, d)$, the same shape as the input embedding table, and many models use one matrix for both ("tied" embeddings), which halves those parameters. nn.Embedding(n, d) : $nd$ parameters, input indices of any shape S , output shape S + (d,) . Cosine similarity: normalize rows, then one matrix product; mask the diagonal before an argmax. Under "no @ " use .dot , np.einsum or broadcasting with .sum .

In Part 2 nobody tells you why your model scores badly; the loss curve and a few quick checks are how you find out, and with 75 minutes for everything you cannot afford to guess. Part 1 also shows loss curves and asks what is wrong. This lesson is a field guide: what each curve shape means, the checks that catch most bugs in a minute, and gradient clipping for the one problem the earlier lessons left open. Reading loss curves Plot the training loss every step or epoch, and the validation loss every epoch (a learning curve against training time, u06-l03). The shapes to recognize: what you see likely cause what to try --- --- --- both losses high and flat, close together underfitting: model too small, learning rate too low, or a bug bigger model, higher learning rate, check the data and the loop training loss falls very slowly, in a straight line learning rate too low multiply it by 3 to 10 training loss jumps around or rises, never settles learning rate too high divide it by 3 to 10; add warmup loss becomes nan or inf learning rate far too high, exploding gradients, or log(0) lower the rate, clip gradients, use logits with the built-in losses training falls, validation falls then rises overfitting early stopping, weight decay, dropout, augmentation, more data (lesson 8) loss stuck at $\ln K$ ($K$ balanced classes), or at the entropy of the class frequencies model outputs the same probabilities for every input: not learning, or all units dead check optimizer.step() , frozen parameters, labels; lower the learning rate The learning rate is behind more of these than anything else. Here is the same network on the three-rings data from u10-l06, trained with SGD (momentum 0.9) at four learning rates: At 0.003 the loss has only crept from 1.09 to 0.80 after 300 steps. At 0.3 it reaches 0.013. At 2.0 it drops, then bounces back up to 1.085: a large step killed every unit of the second hidden layer (dead ReLUs, lesson 4), so the network now outputs the same probabilities for every input, the class frequencies $(0.41, 0.31, 0.28)$, and the loss is stuck at their entropy. At 30 it is nan within 50 steps ( nan points are not drawn). The good range covers about two factors of 10, so trying rates a factor of 10 apart ( 1e-4, 1e-3, 1e-2, ... ) finds it quickly. Checks that catch most bugs 1. Loss at the start. A freshly initialized $K$-class classifier outputs small logits, so its cross-entropy should be close to $\ln K$ (2.30 for 10 classes, u10-l05). Much larger means the logits start huge (bad initialization or unscaled inputs); much smaller means the labels may have leaked into the inputs. 2. Overfit one small batch. Train on 10 to 20 examples for a few hundred steps. Any working model and loop drives that loss close to 0. If it does not, the bug is in the code, not in the model size: check zero grad , backward , step , and that the parameters you train are the ones given to the optimizer. 3. Shapes and dtypes. Print the shape of the model output and of the targets. MSELoss on (N, 1) against (N,) broadcasts to (N, N) with only a warning (u10). CrossEntropyLoss wants logits (N, C) and long labels (N,) , or float probabilities (N, C) . 4. The data. Look at a few inputs and labels. Are the labels in 0..K-1 ? Is the data shuffled, so that a batch is not all one class? Are the features on similar scales? A feature in the thousands next to features near 1 makes the first layer's pre-activations huge and training slow or unstable: standardize with the training set's mean and standard deviation, and apply the same numbers at prediction time (store them with the model, for example as buffers). 5. Modes. model.train() while training, model.eval() and torch.no grad() for validation and prediction (dropout and batch norm, lessons 8 and 9), and back to train() afterwards. 6. The loss input. Raw logits into CrossEntropyLoss and BCEWithLogitsLoss , never probabilities (lesson 5). For regression, no activation on the output (lesson 4). 7. Seeds. torch.manual seed(0) at the start makes runs repeatable, so a change in the result comes from your change and not from luck. Gradient clipping When a few large gradients would throw the parameters far away (exploding gradients, lesson 4; common in recurrent networks and early in training), gradient clipping rescales them first. torch.nn.utils.clip grad norm (model.parameters(), max norm) computes the total norm of all gradients together, as if they were one long vector, and if it exceeds $c$ = max norm , multiplies every gradient by $c/\lVert g\rVert$. The direction is kept; only the length is capped. It goes between backward() and step() , and it returns the norm before clipping, which is worth printing when a run misbehaves: Example: two parameters with gradients $(3, 0)$ and $(0, 4)$ have total norm 5. With max norm=0.5 both are multiplied by $0.1$, to $(0.3, 0)$ and $(0, 0.4)$. (PyTorch actually divides by $\lVert g\rVert + 10^{-6}$, so the clipped values are a hair smaller than the exact ones.) A short debugging order for Part 2 1. Get a baseline end to end first: tiny model, a few epochs, a validation score, a saved file that loads. 2. Overfit a small batch to prove the loop works. 3. Tune the learning rate by factors of 10, watching the validation loss. 4. Only then make the model bigger, and add regularization when validation stops improving while training keeps improving. Practice: u11-p05 Training on badly scaled data (20 minutes) has a dataset that a plain loop trains badly until you find the reason. Loss curve questions are about two quantities, the learning rate and the train/validation gap. Stuck at $\ln K$: not learning. nan : rate too high or log(0) . Gap growing: overfitting. Clipping keeps the direction and caps the total norm at max norm .

The 2027 Round 1 topic list names "basics of CNNs", and the 2026 paper spent 35 of its 300 points on them: P6 asked which layer of an image network produced each of five pictures, and P8 asked for shapes and parameter counts inside ResNet-50. A convolutional neural network (CNN) is a network built mainly from convolution layers, the standard model for images. This lesson computes a convolution by hand, checks it with PyTorch, and adds channels. Lessons 2 to 4 handle shapes, counts and pooling. Images as tensors A grayscale image is a grid of numbers, one per pixel, shape (H, W) for height H and width W. A color image has three grids, one each for red, green and blue. Each grid is a channel , and PyTorch stores the image as (C, H, W) , channels first. A batch of N images is a tensor of shape (N, C, H, W) . PyTorch's image layers are built for this 4D layout (they also accept one unbatched (C, H, W) image, but always keeping the batch axis avoids surprises). Lesson 8 covers converting real images into it. One dimension first A kernel (also called a filter ) is a short list of weights that slides along the input. At each position you multiply the kernel entrywise with the piece of input under it and add the products. With input $x$ of length $L$ and kernel $w$ of length $k$: The kernel fits in $L - k + 1$ positions, so that is the output length. For $x = (1, 3, 2, 0, 4)$ and $w = (1, 0, -1)$: Each $y i$ is the dot product of $w$ with one window of $x$, so the output is large where the window looks like the kernel. In mathematics, convolution flips the kernel first: $\sum j w j x {i-j}$. Deep learning libraries do not flip. What they compute, $\sum j w j x {i+j}$, is called cross-correlation , but everyone still calls it convolution. Since the kernel is learned, flipping would make no difference to what a network can do. For a hand calculation on the exam, slide the kernel as written, without flipping. Two dimensions In 2D the kernel is a small grid, $k$ by $k$, and it slides over every position where it fits completely: The scalar $b$ is the layer's bias, added at every position. An $H \times W$ input and a $k \times k$ kernel give an $(H-k+1) \times (W-k+1)$ output. The output is $(4-3+1) \times (4-3+1) = 2 \times 2$. This $K$ adds the window's left column and subtracts its right column. - $Y[0,0]$: the window is rows 0-2, columns 0-2. Left column $1 + 0 + 2 = 3$, right column $0 + 3 + 0 = 3$, so $Y[0,0] = 0$. - $Y[0,1]$: rows 0-2, columns 1-3. Left column $2 + 1 + 1 = 4$, right column $1 + 1 + 0 = 2$, so $2$. - $Y[1,0]$: rows 1-3, columns 0-2. $(0 + 2 + 1) - (3 + 0 + 1) = -1$. - $Y[1,1]$: rows 1-3, columns 1-3. $(1 + 1 + 0) - (1 + 0 + 2) = -1$. So $Y = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ -1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$. F.conv2d (from import torch.nn.functional as F ) is the convolution as a plain function. It takes an input (N, C in, H, W) and a 4D weight (C out, C in, k, k) , so add the missing axes with [None, None] (each None inserts an axis of length 1): What a kernel detects The output of one kernel over the whole image is a feature map : a grid saying how strongly the kernel's pattern appears at each position. Here is an image that is dark (0) on the left and bright (1) on the right: The output is 0 over flat regions and $-3$ where the window straddles the edge (left column dark, right column bright). This kernel is a vertical edge detector. A trained CNN learns its kernels, and the first layer's kernels usually end up as edge, color and texture detectors like this one. Channels in and channels out A layer has $C {\text{in}}$ input channels and makes $C {\text{out}}$ output channels. Each output channel $o$ has its own kernel of shape $(C {\text{in}}, k, k)$, one $k \times k$ slice per input channel. It slides over all input channels at once and adds everything up, plus one bias $b o$: So the full weight has shape (C out, C in, k, k) , the bias (C out,) , and the output (N, C out, H-k+1, W-k+1) . Every output channel reads every input channel. This is exactly nn.Conv2d(C in, C out, k) , the convolution layer from u10, which stores weight and bias and calls F.conv2d . The loops below compute the formula directly: Why not a linear layer? You could flatten a 28 by 28 image to 784 numbers and use nn.Linear . A convolution differs in three ways: - Local connectivity : each output looks only at a $k \times k$ window, not at all 784 pixels. - Weight sharing : the same kernel is used at every position, so the number of weights does not depend on the image size. - Translation equivariance : shift the input and the feature map shifts the same way (away from the borders). An edge detector finds an edge wherever it is. The savings are large. nn.Conv2d(1, 8, 3) on a 28 by 28 image gives 8 feature maps of 26 by 26 with $8 \cdot 9 + 8 = 80$ parameters. A linear layer from 784 inputs to the same $8 \cdot 26 \cdot 26 = 5408$ outputs needs $784 \cdot 5408 + 5408 = 4{,}245{,}280$. Without loops in NumPy Part 2 problems often ban Python loops. NumPy's sliding window view returns every $k \times k$ window as a view (it changes only the strides, so nothing is copied), and einsum then multiplies and sums: In the einsum string, c , u , v appear in the inputs but not after - , so they are summed: input channel and the two kernel offsets. o (output channel) and h , w (position) stay. Lesson 2 adds padding, stride and dilation to this, and u12-p01 asks for the full version.

Nearly every CNN question starts with a shape. The 2026 P8.2 asked for the output shape of a ResNet-50 stage, and Part 1 likes chains: "an input goes through these four layers; what comes out?" u10-l04 gave the output-size formula without proof. This lesson derives it, adds the third knob (dilation), and builds the habits that make shape questions fast and safe. Padding Padding adds $p$ rows of zeros above and below the input, and $p$ columns of zeros left and right, before the kernel slides. An $H \times W$ input becomes $(H + 2p) \times (W + 2p)$, so a $k \times k$ kernel gives an output of height $H + 2p - k + 1$. Two reasons to pad. Without padding, each layer shrinks the image by $k - 1$, and border pixels sit in fewer windows than central ones. With $p = (k - 1)/2$ (for odd $k$) the output has the same size as the input: $H + (k - 1) - k + 1 = H$. This is same padding : $p = 1$ for $k = 3$, $p = 2$ for $k = 5$, $p = 3$ for $k = 7$. No padding is called valid convolution. PyTorch accepts the strings too: padding="same" works out the padding for you (stride 1 only; for an even $k$ it puts the extra zero row and column on the bottom and right), and padding="valid" means 0. Stride The stride $s$ is how far the window moves each step. The window starts at positions $0, s, 2s, \dots$ of the padded input, and a start $t$ is allowed only if the window fits: $t + k \le H + 2p$. So the allowed starts are $t = ms$ for integers $m$ with and there are $\left\lfloor \frac{H + 2p - k}{s} \right\rfloor + 1$ of them. That is the output height. The floor matters: when $s$ does not divide $H + 2p - k$, the last few rows never start a full window and are ignored. The widget below starts at input length $n = 8$ (the widget's letter for the length), $k = 3$, $p = 0$, $s = 2$. Step through the windows with Next: the last input cell is never used. Then change the numbers and predict the output length before you look. Dilation Dilation $d$ spreads the kernel's entries $d$ apart: the taps sit at offsets $0, d, 2d, \dots, (k-1)d$. A dilated kernel covers $d(k - 1) + 1$ input positions while keeping its $k^2$ weights. For $k = 3$, $d = 2$ the taps are at offsets 0, 2, 4, so the kernel spans 5 positions. Dilation lets a layer see a wider area without more parameters (lesson 5 measures this). Replacing $k$ by the span $d(k-1)+1$ in the stride count gives the general formula, the one in PyTorch's documentation: With $d = 1$ it is the u10 formula. Same padding with dilation needs $p = d(k-1)/2$. Here are the three knobs in 1D, using NumPy's sliding window view from lesson 1. np.pad(x, 1) adds one zero at each end. Stride keeps every $s$-th window ( [::s] ). Dilation takes windows of the full span and keeps every $d$-th entry inside each ( [:, ::d] ): In 2D, np.pad(x, ((0, 0), (p, p), (p, p))) pads only the last two axes of a (C, H, W) array; the pair for each axis says how many zeros go before and after. Worked shapes Height and width are handled separately, each with its own kernel size, padding, stride and dilation if they differ ( kernel size=(3, 5) is 3 tall and 5 wide). The channel axis becomes out channels ; the batch axis never changes. Input Layer Arithmetic Output --- --- --- --- 28 k 3 $(28 - 3)/1 + 1$ 26 28 k 3, p 1 $(28 + 2 - 3)/1 + 1$ 28 28 k 5, p 2 $(28 + 4 - 5)/1 + 1$ 28 32 k 3, p 1, s 2 $\lfloor 31/2 \rfloor + 1$ 16 7 k 3, s 2 $\lfloor 4/2 \rfloor + 1$ 3 8 k 3, s 2 $\lfloor 5/2 \rfloor + 1$ 3 224 k 7, p 3, s 2 (ResNet's first layer) $\lfloor 223/2 \rfloor + 1$ 112 56 k 1, s 2 $\lfloor 55/2 \rfloor + 1$ 28 15 k 3, p 2, d 2 $(15 + 4 - 4 - 1)/1 + 1$ 15 13 k 5, d 2, s 2 $\lfloor (13 - 8 - 1)/2 \rfloor + 1$ 3 Patterns worth knowing by heart: - $k = 3, p = 1, s = 1$ keeps the size. Any odd $k$ with $p = (k-1)/2$ does. - $k = 3, p = 1, s = 2$ gives $\lceil H/2 \rceil$: 32 to 16, 7 to 4. - $k = 1$ (a 1x1 convolution ) never mixes neighboring pixels; it only mixes channels. With $s = 1$ it keeps the size. - $k = 7, p = 3, s = 2$ takes 224 to 112, and then a 3 by 3 max pool with stride 2 and padding 1 takes 112 to 56 (pooling windows follow the same formula; lesson 4). That is the start of every ResNet. Here is a chain checked in code. Read each line, predict the shape, then compare: Exam habits 1. Write the numerator first, $H + 2p - d(k-1) - 1$, then divide by $s$, floor, and add 1. Most wrong answers skip the $+1$ or the floor. 2. Check padding="same" and pooling defaults before using the formula (lesson 4: MaxPool2d(k) has stride $k$, not 1). 3. For "which padding keeps the size?", solve $H + 2p - d(k-1) - 1 + 1 = H$: $p = d(k - 1)/2$. 4. For a long chain, keep a column of numbers: height after each layer. Channels only change at convolutions (to out channels ) and are untouched by pooling and activations. 5. In Part 2, run one dummy input through and print shapes, or use a forward hook (u10-l09). nn.Conv2d(3, 8, 3, stride=2, padding="same") raises an error: PyTorch only allows "same" with stride 1. For a stride-2 layer that halves the size, write padding=1 (for $k = 3$). Practice problem: u12-p01 Conv2d forward in NumPy, no loops (padding, stride, dilation and channels, checked against F.conv2d ).

Counting parameters by hand is a sure Round 1 question. The 2027 sample P3 asks how many parameters still train after a head swap, and the 2026 P8.3 asked for the parameter count of the convolutions in one ResNet-50 block with numel banned, so you had to know the formula. This lesson gives the rule for every kind of convolution, shows where the parameters of a CNN actually sit, and counts the work a layer does. The rule nn.Conv2d(C in, C out, k) stores a weight of shape (C out, C in, k, k) and a bias of shape (C out,) : For a rectangular kernel kernel size=(kh, kw) , replace $k^2$ by $k h k w$. With bias=False drop the $+ C {\text{out}}$. The count does not depend on the image size, the stride, the padding or the dilation. A dilated 3 by 3 kernel still has 9 weights per input channel. Only the four numbers $C {\text{in}}, C {\text{out}}, k$ and the bias flag matter. Layer Count --- --- Conv2d(1, 8, 3) $1 \cdot 8 \cdot 9 + 8 = 80$ Conv2d(3, 16, 3) $3 \cdot 16 \cdot 9 + 16 = 448$ Conv2d(64, 128, 3) $64 \cdot 128 \cdot 9 + 128 = 73{,}856$ Conv2d(64, 128, 3, bias=False) $73{,}728$ Conv2d(8, 16, kernel size=(1, 5)) $8 \cdot 16 \cdot 5 + 16 = 656$ Conv2d(3, 64, 7, stride=2, padding=3, bias=False) (ResNet's first layer) $3 \cdot 64 \cdot 49 = 9{,}408$ BatchNorm2d(64) $2 \cdot 64 = 128$ Large CNNs use bias=False on every convolution that feeds a batch norm. Batch norm subtracts each channel's mean (u10-l04 counted its two parameters per channel, a scale and a shift), so a constant added by the convolution's bias would be removed again; batch norm's own shift does that job. Grouped and depthwise convolutions groups=g splits the input channels into $g$ equal groups and the output channels into $g$ equal groups; output group $i$ reads only input group $i$. This is a grouped convolution . Each kernel now covers $C {\text{in}}/g$ channels, so the weight has shape (C out, C in / g, k, k) and Both $C {\text{in}}$ and $C {\text{out}}$ must be divisible by $g$, or PyTorch raises an error. The bias is not divided: there is still one per output channel. The extreme case $g = C {\text{in}}$ is a depthwise convolution : each channel gets its own $k \times k$ kernel and channels never mix. nn.Conv2d(64, 64, 3, groups=64) has weight (64, 1, 3, 3) and $64 \cdot 9 + 64 = 640$ parameters. A depthwise separable convolution is a depthwise convolution (mixing neighboring pixels within each channel) followed by a 1x1 convolution (mixing channels at each pixel). It replaces one ordinary convolution with far fewer parameters. From 64 to 128 channels with 3 by 3 kernels, no biases: about 8.4 times fewer. Mobile networks (MobileNet) are built from these. Where the parameters sit Convolutions are cheap; the linear layer after a flatten is not. The placement-quiz layer Conv2d(1, 8, 3) on a 28 by 28 image has 80 parameters, but flattening its (8, 26, 26) output into Linear(5408, 10) adds $5408 \cdot 10 + 10 = 54{,}090$. Replacing the flatten with global average pooling (one number per channel, lesson 4) leaves Linear(8, 10) , 90 parameters, and the network then accepts any image size. Modern CNNs do this. For the 2026 P8.3 the block model.layer3[2] of ResNet-50 has three convolutions, all bias=False : The question asked only about convolutional modules. The block's three batch norms add $2(256 + 256 + 1024) = 3{,}072$ more, so the whole block has 1,117,184. Read which modules a question counts. In code, model.modules() walks every submodule, so isinstance picks out one kind: Counting the work: MACs and FLOPs Parameters measure memory; compute measures time. One output value of a convolution needs $(C {\text{in}}/g) \cdot k^2$ multiplications, each added to a running sum. One multiply plus one add is a multiply-accumulate (MAC). Over the whole output: FLOPs (floating-point operations) count multiplications and additions separately, so FLOPs $\approx 2 \times$ MACs. Papers are not consistent (many write "FLOPs" for MACs, some add the bias), so on the exam use the definition the problem gives. Unlike the parameter count, compute grows with the output size: Conv2d(64, 128, 3, padding=1) on a 56 by 56 input does $56 \cdot 56 \cdot 128 \cdot 64 \cdot 9 = 231{,}211{,}008$ MACs per image, about 0.46 billion FLOPs, while having only 73,856 parameters. Practice problem: u12-p02 A CNN from a spec sheet (build it, then count its parameters by formula with numel banned, as in P8.3).

Pooling layers sit in almost every printed CNN, and their defaults differ from Conv2d 's in a way that costs points on shape questions. ResNet's stem uses a max pool, and its head uses global average pooling (u10-l09 met both at the code level). This lesson covers what each pooling layer computes, its output size, its gradient, and the adaptive versions. Max and average pooling A pooling layer slides a window over each channel, like a convolution, but applies a fixed function instead of learned weights. Max pooling takes the largest value in each window; average pooling takes the mean. Each channel is pooled separately, so the channel count never changes, and pooling has no parameters. The output size follows the convolution formula from lesson 2, $\lfloor (H + 2p - d(k-1) - 1)/s \rfloor + 1$. nn.MaxPool2d(3) means kernel 3 and stride 3 : on 10 by 10 it gives $\lfloor 7/3 \rfloor + 1 = 3$. nn.Conv2d(..., 3) has stride 1. For overlapping windows write the stride: nn.MaxPool2d(3, stride=2) or stride=1 . The last line shows ceil mode=True , which replaces the floor by a ceiling (7 becomes 4 instead of 3). The default is the floor. Two details on padding. Max pooling pads with $-\infty$, so padded cells never win. Average pooling pads with zeros and, by default ( count include pad=True ), still divides by $k^2$, so averages near the border are pulled toward 0. Why pool at all: - It shrinks the feature maps, so later layers do less work. A 2 by 2 pool with stride 2 cuts the number of positions by 4. - It makes the output tolerant of small shifts: if the largest value moves within its window, the max is unchanged. - It widens how much of the image each later unit depends on (lesson 5). Adaptive pooling and global average pooling nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(output size) fixes the output size and chooses the windows for you. For input length $L$ and output length $o$, output $i$ averages input positions $\lfloor i L/o \rfloor$ up to (not including) $\lceil (i+1) L / o \rceil$. When $o$ divides $L$ this is ordinary pooling with kernel and stride $L/o$; otherwise neighboring windows overlap a little. For $L = 5$, $o = 3$ the windows are $[0, 2), [1, 4), [3, 5)$. Adaptive pooling matters because it lets one network accept images of any size: whatever $H$ and $W$ arrive, AdaptiveAvgPool2d((7, 7)) returns 7 by 7. The common case is nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1) , global average pooling: each channel becomes its mean over all positions, (N, C, H, W) to (N, C, 1, 1) . nn.Flatten() then gives (N, C) for a linear head. nn.AdaptiveMaxPool2d is the max version. nn.Flatten() keeps axis 0 (its default is start dim=1 ). nn.Flatten(0) would also merge the batch axis, which is almost never what you want. Gradients: routing Backpropagation through pooling is simple and shows up in Part 2 problems that ban autograd: - Max pooling passes each output's gradient back to the one input that was the maximum of its window; every other input in that window gets 0. This is called gradient routing . If two inputs tie for the max, PyTorch sends the gradient to the first one in row-major order. When windows overlap, an input that wins several windows receives the sum of their gradients. - Average pooling spreads each output's gradient equally over its window: each of the $k^2$ inputs gets $1/k^2$ of it. The code below calls out.backward(up) . When out is not a single number, backward needs the gradient of the loss with respect to out , the upstream gradient, passed as up (same shape as out ); backpropagation continues from there to X.grad . Practice problem: u12-p03 Max pooling forward and backward in NumPy .

The 2026 P6 (10 points) showed five feature maps from a pretrained CNN and asked which layer each came from, with reasoning. The concept behind the answer is the receptive field: how much of the image one unit can see, and how that grows with depth. This lesson computes receptive fields layer by layer, then uses them to explain what early and deep layers detect and how to read P6. The receptive field The receptive field of a unit (one entry of a feature map) is the patch of input pixels that can affect its value. Its size is the number of pixels along one side. One 3 by 3 convolution: each output sees 3 by 3 pixels, receptive field 3. Stack a second 3 by 3 convolution (stride 1) on top: a unit of layer 2 sees 3 neighboring units of layer 1 along each axis, and those see input columns $\{0,1,2\}$, $\{1,2,3\}$ and $\{2,3,4\}$ together, so 5 pixels. A third layer gives 7. Each stride-1 layer with kernel $k$ adds $k - 1$. Stride changes the bookkeeping. After a stride-2 layer, neighboring units are 2 input pixels apart, so the next layer's kernel steps over the input twice as fast. Track two numbers after each layer $l$: - $r l$: the receptive field size, in input pixels; - $j l$: the jump , the distance in input pixels between neighboring units of layer $l$'s output (the product of all strides so far). Start from the input itself with $r 0 = 1$, $j 0 = 1$. A layer with kernel $k l$, stride $s l$ and dilation $d l$ spans $k^{\text{eff}} l = d l(k l - 1) + 1$ of its input units, so The first formula says: the window covers $k^{\text{eff}} l$ units of the previous layer, consecutive ones $j {l-1}$ pixels apart, each seeing $r {l-1}$ pixels. Pooling layers count exactly like convolutions. Padding does not change the size (only where the field sits), and 1x1 convolutions and activations add nothing. Layer $k^{\text{eff}}$ $s$ $r$ $j$ --- --- --- --- --- input 1 1 conv 3 by 3, stride 1 3 1 $1 + 2 \cdot 1 = 3$ 1 max pool 2, stride 2 2 2 $3 + 1 \cdot 1 = 4$ 2 conv 3 by 3 3 1 $4 + 2 \cdot 2 = 8$ 2 max pool 2 2 2 $8 + 1 \cdot 2 = 10$ 4 conv 3 by 3 3 1 $10 + 2 \cdot 4 = 18$ 4 Each unit at the end sees an 18 by 18 patch. Note the order inside each row: use the jump from the row above, then update it. You can measure a receptive field directly. Backpropagate from one output unit and see which input pixels get a nonzero gradient (the code uses all-ones weights and average pooling so that no gradient is zero by accident; with max pooling, only the window maxima would receive gradient): The second stack uses dilations 1, 2, 4: $r = 3$, then $3 + 4 = 7$, then $7 + 8 = 15$. Doubling the dilation each layer makes the receptive field grow exponentially with depth while the parameter count grows linearly, which is why dilated stacks are used for audio and for pixel-by-pixel image labeling. Two design consequences Small kernels, stacked. Three 3 by 3 convolutions have receptive field 7, like one 7 by 7, but with $C$ channels throughout they use $3 \cdot 9 C^2 = 27C^2$ weights instead of $49C^2$, and they put three nonlinearities in between. The VGG networks (lesson 6) are built on this. Downsampling grows the field fast. Every stride-2 layer doubles the jump, so every later layer adds twice as much. ResNet-18 along its main path reaches 11 pixels after its stem (7 by 7 stride-2 convolution plus max pool), then 43, 99, 211 and 435 after its four stages. The last number is bigger than the 224 by 224 input: each final unit can see the whole image. The center of output unit $i$ of layer $l$ is at input coordinate $c l + i\, j l$, where $c 0 = 0$ and $c l = c {l-1} + \left(\frac{k^{\text{eff}} l - 1}{2} - p l\right) j {l-1}$ with padding $p l$. With same padding the term in brackets is 0, so the fields stay centered on their pixels. Equivalently, the field of unit 0 begins at input row $a l = a {l-1} - p l\, j {l-1}$ (with $a 0 = 0$; negative rows are padding) and ends at $a l + r l - 1$. Also, pixels near the center of the field affect a unit much more than pixels near its edge (more paths lead from them), so the field that matters in practice, the effective receptive field, is smaller than $r l$. Feature hierarchies What a layer can detect is limited by what it can see. This gives a feature hierarchy : Early layers Middle layers Deep layers --- --- --- --- Receptive field a few pixels tens of pixels most of the image Resolution (H, W) high: 112, 56 28, 14 low: 7 Channels few: 64 128 to 512 many: 512 to 2048 Detects edges, colors, simple textures textures, repeated patterns, object parts whole objects and large parts Feature map looks like the image, edge-filtered busy blobs and texture a few smooth blobs over the object In a ResNet the spatial size halves at each stage while the channel count doubles, so a deep feature map has few, large cells. When it is displayed at the same size as the image, each cell is stretched over many pixels, and the map looks blurry and blob-shaped. Reading 2026 P6 In 2026 Round 1 Problem 6, a photo went through a pretrained CNN, and the problem showed one feature map from each of five layers, numbered 0 to 4, in a shuffled order. You had to say which layer produced each map and why. The figures are in the 2026 Round 1 paper on usaaio.org. Here is a practice version of the same task. The input is a drawn street scene with a robot in the road. Maps (A) to (E) are an illustration made for this site, not the output of a real network: each one imitates what a pretrained ResNet's map looks like at one depth for a 224 by 224 input, at that stage's real resolution (112, 56, 28, 14 or 7 cells on a side), enlarged to the image size for display. Darker means a stronger response. Match each map to its layer before you read on; the answer is in the box after the cues. A drawn street scene with a robot, and five feature maps (A) to (E) in shuffled order Three cues, applied together: 1. Size of the smallest detail. Fine, pixel-level detail means high resolution, so an early layer. Large smooth blobs mean low resolution, so a deep layer. 2. Resemblance to the input. Early maps still show the scene's outlines; deep maps do not. 3. Sparsity and focus. Deep maps respond in a few places, often on the main object. Map (C) is one smooth blob centered on the robot: the deepest, layer 4. Map (A) has a few separate blobs (on the robot's head, the window and the tree) on an empty background and no texture: layer 3. Map (E) is a dense field of small blobs, coarser than (B) and (D) but finer than (A): layer 2. Maps (B) and (D) both keep pixel-level detail. Map (D) still shows the scene itself (the sky, the house, the robot) like a dimmed photo, which is what the first layer's color and brightness filters produce, so layer 0; map (B) is an edge and texture map with the road's perspective lines, layer 1. Answer: (D) layer 0, (B) layer 1, (E) layer 2, (A) layer 3, (C) layer 4. On the exam, the reasoning earns the points: name the cues above and apply them to each map. Practice problem: u12-p04 A receptive-field calculator .

The 2026 P8 (25 points) was entirely about ResNet-50: its parameter count, the output shape of layer2 , the parameters of the convolutions in layer3[2] , and a classifier on a truncated copy. If you know how a ResNet is laid out, all of these take a minute of arithmetic. This lesson walks from the first CNNs to ResNet's blocks and ends with a stage-by-stage table for ResNet-18 and ResNet-50. LeNet-5 and VGG LeNet-5 (1998, handwritten digits) is the pattern every CNN since has followed: convolutions and pooling shrink the image while adding channels, then linear layers classify. On a 32 by 32 grayscale input: Layer Output Parameters --- --- --- Conv2d(1, 6, 5) , tanh (6, 28, 28) $1 \cdot 6 \cdot 25 + 6 = 156$ AvgPool2d(2) (6, 14, 14) 0 Conv2d(6, 16, 5) , tanh (16, 10, 10) $6 \cdot 16 \cdot 25 + 16 = 2{,}416$ AvgPool2d(2) , Flatten (16, 5, 5) = 400 0 Linear(400, 120) , Linear(120, 84) , Linear(84, 10) 10 $48{,}120 + 10{,}164 + 850$ Total 61,706, of which 59,134 are in the linear layers. VGG (2014) made the network deep with one repeated unit: a few 3 by 3 convolutions with padding 1 (size kept), then a 2 by 2 max pool (size halved), with channels 64, 128, 256, 512, 512 across five such blocks. VGG-16 has 13 convolutions and 3 linear layers, and 138,357,544 parameters. 123,642,856 of them are in the three linear layers, and the first one alone, Linear(512 7 7, 4096) , has $25{,}088 \cdot 4{,}096 + 4{,}096 = 102{,}764{,}544$. That flatten-then-linear head is what global average pooling later replaced. Residual connections Stacking more plain layers stops helping after about 20: deeper plain networks reach a higher training error than shallower ones, even though a deeper network could copy the shallow one and set its extra layers to the identity. Training simply fails to find that. ResNet (2015) fixed this with a residual connection (also called a skip connection ): a block computes some layers $F(x)$ and adds its own input back, To act like the identity, the block now only needs $F(x) = 0$, which is easy (weights near zero). And in backpropagation, where a long chain of layers tends to shrink the gradient (the vanishing gradient problem), the derivative of $F(x) + x$ with respect to $x$ is $\frac{\partial F}{\partial x} + I$ (with $I$ the identity matrix): the $I$ carries the gradient straight through every block, so early layers keep receiving a useful signal. A block of this form is a residual block . The addition needs $F(x)$ and $x$ to have the same shape. When a block halves the size or changes the channel count, the shortcut becomes a projection shortcut : a 1x1 convolution with the same stride, followed by batch norm, applied to $x$ before the addition. torchvision calls it downsample . The basic block (ResNet-18 and ResNet-34) A basic block is two 3 by 3 convolutions, each followed by batch norm, with a ReLU between them and another after the addition: These are exactly torchvision's layer1[0] and layer2[0] of ResNet-18 (same counts, 73,984 and 230,144). The bottleneck block (ResNet-50 and deeper) A bottleneck block squeezes the channels before the expensive 3 by 3 convolution and expands them after: 1. 1 by 1 convolution from $4w$ channels down to $w$, batch norm, ReLU; 2. 3 by 3 convolution at width $w$, batch norm, ReLU; 3. 1 by 1 convolution from $w$ back up to $4w$, batch norm; 4. add the shortcut, ReLU. In layer3 of ResNet-50, $w = 256$ and blocks map 1024 channels to 1024. The convolutions cost $1024 \cdot 256 + 256 \cdot 256 \cdot 9 + 256 \cdot 1024 = 1{,}114{,}112$ (the P8.3 answer), plus $2(256 + 256 + 1024) = 3{,}072$ for the batch norms. A basic block working at 1024 channels would need $2 \cdot 1024^2 \cdot 9 \approx 18.9$ million. The bottleneck is how ResNet-50 is deep and wide at once. The first block of each stage takes the previous stage's channels (64 for layer1 , then 256, 512, 1024), has a projection shortcut, and in torchvision puts the stage's stride 2 on its 3 by 3 convolution. The ResNet layout and the stage table Every torchvision ResNet has the same top-level children: conv1 (7 by 7, 64 channels, stride 2, padding 3, no bias), bn1 , relu , maxpool (3 by 3, stride 2, padding 1), then four stages layer1 to layer4 , each an nn.Sequential of blocks, then avgpool ( AdaptiveAvgPool2d((1, 1)) ), a flatten inside forward , and fc ( Linear to 1000 classes). The stride-2 block opens layer2 , layer3 and layer4 , so each of those halves the size; the channel count doubles at each stage. ResNet-18 has 2, 2, 2, 2 basic blocks; ResNet-50 has 3, 4, 6, 3 bottleneck blocks. For a (B, 3, 224, 224) input: Module Output size ResNet-18 channels ResNet-18 params ResNet-50 channels ResNet-50 params --- --- --- --- --- --- conv1 + bn1 112 64 9,408 + 128 64 9,408 + 128 maxpool 56 64 0 64 0 layer1 56 64 147,968 256 215,808 layer2 28 128 525,568 512 1,219,584 layer3 14 256 2,099,712 1024 7,098,368 layer4 7 512 8,393,728 2048 14,964,736 avgpool 1 512 0 2048 0 fc (1000 logits) 513,000 2,049,000 total 11,689,512 25,557,032 So the 2026 P8.2 answer is (B, 512, 28, 28) : $224 \to 112 \to 56 \to 56 \to 28$, with $4 \cdot 128 = 512$ channels. Note where the parameters are: layer4 alone holds more than half of ResNet-50's. The code below rebuilds ResNet-50's column (torchvision is the PyTorch image library; weights=None builds the network with random weights, which is all that shapes and counts need, and lesson 7 covers pretrained weights): (The hook takes n=n as a default argument so each lambda keeps its own name, and it calls shapes. setitem (n, ...) , the method that shapes[n] = ... runs, because a lambda cannot contain an assignment. u10-l09 wrote the same thing with a make hook function.)
