Round 1 gives you 75 minutes on a CPU, which is not enough to train an image network from scratch. A model already trained on ImageNet, with only a new last layer trained, often does far better in a few minutes. The 2026 P8 started with model = resnet50(pretrained=True) , and the 2027 sample P3 asks what still trains after freezing and swapping the head. u10-l09 taught the mechanics (freezing, replacing the head, truncating, hooks) on small stand-in models. This lesson does the same with torchvision's real models and adds what the stand-ins could not show: loading weights, choosing what to unfreeze, and saving CPU time. torchvision models and their weights torchvision.models builds the standard architectures. The weights argument chooses the starting parameters: Call What you get --- --- resnet18(weights=None) random initialization; nothing downloaded resnet18(weights="DEFAULT") the best ImageNet weights torchvision has for this architecture resnet18(weights=ResNet18 Weights.IMAGENET1K V1) one specific set of weights, named explicitly resnet50(pretrained=True) the old spelling (2026 starter code): still works but warns; means IMAGENET1K V1 With weights, the first call downloads a file from download.pytorch.org (45 MB for ResNet-18, 98 MB for ResNet-50) into ~/.cache/torch/hub/checkpoints/ , then loads it into the model with load state dict (u10-l08). Later calls in the same Colab session reuse the file. The architecture, parameter names and counts are identical with or without weights, which is why this site uses weights=None (it does not download) and its counts still match the contest's. The weights object also carries two useful things. ResNet18 Weights.DEFAULT.transforms() is the preprocessing the weights were trained with (resize to 256, center crop to 224, scale to $[0, 1]$, normalize with ImageNet's mean and standard deviation; lesson 8), and .meta["categories"] lists the 1000 ImageNet class names. Feed a pretrained model images prepared any other way and its accuracy drops. Feature extraction: freeze, replace fc , train the head The standard recipe for a torchvision ResNet, with the u10-l09 rules (freeze first, then replace, so the new layer trains): Using a frozen pretrained network as a fixed feature maker and training only a new head is called feature extraction . The count to remember: a new head on a ResNet has $\text{in\ features} \cdot C + C$ trainable parameters, with in features 512 for ResNet-18/34 and 2048 for ResNet-50. The check below cuts a ResNet with nn.Sequential( list(m.children())[:6]) . m.children() yields a model's top-level modules in order (the ones named children() named in u10-l09), so the slice [:6] is conv1 through layer2 , and unpacks that list into separate arguments for nn.Sequential . Fine-tuning: unfreeze the last stage With more data, or images unlike ImageNet's (X-rays, satellite tiles), also train the last stage. Fine-tuning usually unfreezes from the top down ( layer4 first), because deep features are the most specific to the original task while early edge and color detectors transfer to almost anything (lesson 5). Give the pretrained part a smaller learning rate than the new head, with parameter groups (u11): a list of dicts, each with its own "lr" : A truncated backbone (2026 P8.4) P8.4 wanted ResNet-50 "up to the output from model.layer3[4] " as a frozen backbone for 5 classes. The stage table from lesson 6 gives the channels without running anything: layer3 blocks output 1024 channels at 14 by 14 for a 224 input. So the head is global average pooling, flatten, Linear(1024, 5) : $1024 \cdot 5 + 5 = 5{,}125$ trainable parameters. nn.Sequential( list(m.children())[:6]) is a shorter way to cut a model after its sixth child ( layer2 here); unpacks the list into separate arguments. It works only when the children run in order with nothing else in forward : for a ResNet it would break if you kept fc , because the flatten before fc happens inside forward , not in a child module. Saving CPU time in the exam With a frozen backbone, every epoch recomputes the same backbone outputs. Compute them once instead: put the backbone in eval mode, run all images through it under torch.no grad() , store the pooled features (a tensor of shape (N, 512) for ResNet-18), and train the linear head on those for as many epochs as you like. Training a linear layer on stored features takes seconds on a CPU. Apply the same backbone to the test images at prediction time. 1. Different preprocessing than the weights expect (lesson 8): forgetting to scale to $[0, 1]$ or to normalize. 2. Leaving batch norm in training mode while predicting: call model.eval() before inference. 3. Replacing the head before freezing everything: the new head is frozen too, and nothing trains.

An image task in Part 2 goes wrong long before the model if the data is in the wrong layout, the wrong dtype or the wrong range: the network either crashes or trains on nonsense without complaint. This lesson covers the conversions from files to (N, C, H, W) float tensors, normalization, and data augmentation (u11) for images with torchvision.transforms.v2 , including which transforms belong in training only. From pixels to tensors Image files decode (with PIL, the Python imaging library, or NumPy) to arrays of shape (H, W, C) , channels-last , with dtype uint8 and values 0 to 255. PyTorch layers want channels-first (C, H, W) floats, usually scaled to $[0, 1]$. Three steps, in order: 1. move the channel axis to the front: permute(2, 0, 1) ; 2. convert to float: .float() ; 3. scale: / 255 . A grayscale image (H, W) needs a channel axis added: unsqueeze(0) gives (1, H, W) . A stacked dataset like MNIST, (N, 28, 28) , becomes (N, 1, 28, 28) with unsqueeze(1) . To display a tensor with matplotlib, go back to channels-last: img.permute(1, 2, 0) . reshape(3, H, W) on a (H, W, 3) array gives the right shape and wrong content: it refills the new shape in memory order, mixing the colors of neighboring pixels. Moving an axis takes permute (or np.transpose ). transforms.v2 torchvision's transforms are callable objects; v2.Compose([t1, t2, ...]) chains them. With from torchvision.transforms import v2 : Transform Does --- --- v2.ToImage() PIL image or (H, W, C) array to a (C, H, W) uint8 tensor v2.ToDtype(torch.float32, scale=True) uint8 0..255 to float 0..1 v2.Normalize(mean, std) per channel $c$: $(x c - \text{mean} c)/\text{std} c$ v2.Resize(256) shorter side to 256, aspect ratio kept v2.CenterCrop(224) the central 224 by 224 Image normalization subtracts each channel's mean and divides by its standard deviation, so every input channel has roughly mean 0 and variance 1, which suits the initialization of the first layer. Pretrained ImageNet models expect ImageNet's statistics, mean=[0.485, 0.456, 0.406] and std=[0.229, 0.224, 0.225] (red, green, blue, on the $[0, 1]$ scale); for a model trained from scratch, compute your own from the training images with x.mean(dim=(0, 2, 3)) and x.std(dim=(0, 2, 3)) over a batch (N, C, H, W) . v2.ToDtype(torch.float32) converts the type but keeps values 0 to 255. Normalizing those with ImageNet's statistics gives inputs around 1000 instead of around 0. Write scale=True . Augmentation The standard random image transforms, each producing a new random version every time it is called: - v2.RandomHorizontalFlip(p=0.5) : mirror left-right with probability $p$. To mirror a tensor always, img.flip(-1) reverses its last axis (the width); img.flip(-2) mirrors top to bottom. - v2.RandomResizedCrop(size, scale=(0.08, 1.0), ratio=(3/4, 4/3)) : pick a random rectangle covering a fraction of the image's area in scale , with aspect ratio in ratio , and resize it to size . The standard ImageNet training transform. - v2.RandomCrop(32, padding=4) : pad by 4 and cut a random 32 by 32 window, a small random shift (the standard for 32 by 32 datasets). - v2.ColorJitter(brightness=0.2, contrast=0.2) , v2.RandomRotation(10) : lighting changes and small rotations. - Noise: x + 0.05 torch.randn like(x) on a float image, then clamp(0, 1) . An augmentation must keep the label true. A mirrored cat is still a cat, but a mirrored "b" is a "d", a rotated "6" can become a "9", and a vertically flipped street scene never occurs in test data. Choose transforms that produce images the model could really meet. Augment only the training data . Validation and test images get the fixed, deterministic version, otherwise your scores are noisy and do not describe real inputs: Apply the training transform per image, inside the Dataset's getitem (u10-l07), so every image in every epoch gets its own random draw. Round 1 Part 2 ends with an open-ended problem: you pick and train any model, and a grader scores its predictions on a test set you never see. The 2027 sample of this kind (SP5, "Learning an unknown function") is the model for this whole unit. The boxes run on a practice dataset built the same way (the same three files, sizes, $x$ range and noise level) but with a different function, so their numbers are not the official ones. Two facts shape everything: a submission that raises an error gets the worst possible score, and nobody can check your model on the hidden data before the grader does. So the work follows a fixed loop: look at the data, build a baseline, measure on validation data, improve one change at a time, and only then package. This lesson is the loop; lessons 2 to 5 fill in the steps. The task SP5 says: $y = f(x) + \text{noise}$, where $f$ is an unknown function of one number $x$. Noise is the random part of $y$ that no function of $x$ can predict. You get: - train.json : one JSON object {"x": [...], "y": [...]} with 8000 points, - val input.json ( {"x": [...]} ) and val answer.json ( {"y": [...]} ): a validation set of 400 points with answers, - a hidden test file {"x": [...]} that only the grader sees. You write predict(test path) , which returns a Python list of predictions. The score is the mean squared error (MSE) on the hidden test, turned into a normalized score between 0 and 1: Any error (a crash, a wrong return type, a timeout of 30 seconds per call) counts as MSE 10000, which gives score 0. Lesson 4 covers the four files you upload. Step 1: load the data and look at it The box opens the three practice files in a folder named fun data , which sits in the box's working folder (the site copies it there before each run), so the code opens them by relative path. Path (from the standard module pathlib , lesson 4) builds file paths: DATA / "train.json" means the file train.json inside the folder DATA . To run the boxes in Colab, download train.json, val input.json and val answer.json and upload them into a Colab folder named fun data (Files panel, u00-l02). The script that made them is make fun data.py; look at the plot before you read it. The official SP5 files are on the organizers' Hugging Face page (folder Approx fun ), and the statement is with the other 2027 sample problems on contest.usaaio.org. Before reading on, write one line describing $f$ from the plot. These are the questions to answer every time: - Range. Which $x$ values does the training data cover? Does the validation data cover the same range? Here both cover $[-1, 2]$. - Shape. Is the curve smooth? Does it trend up or down? Does it repeat? Lesson 2 builds models from what you see here. - Noise. How thick is the band of points around the curve? That thickness sets the best MSE any model can reach. - Oddities. Outliers, gaps in $x$, duplicated points. Step 2: a baseline A baseline is the simplest reasonable predictor. For a regression scored by MSE it is "predict the training mean $\bar y$ for every $x$". The mean is the best constant: the derivative of $\sum i (y i - c)^2$ in $c$ is $-2\sum i (y i - c)$, which is zero exactly at $c = \bar y$. On the training data, the MSE of this baseline is exactly the variance of $y$; on validation it comes out close to it. For a classification task the baseline is "predict the most common class". A baseline does three jobs: 1. It is the bar. A model that does not beat 0.300 on validation has learned nothing. 2. It tests the whole path from files to a submission while the model is still trivial. Bugs in loading, saving and returning show up now, when they are easy to find. 3. It is a real submission. The arithmetic above says that if the hidden test looks like the validation data, the baseline already has a normalized score of 0.9975, while an error scores 0. Point 3 also shows how this score behaves. Improving the MSE from 0.0102 to 0.0100 (two of the models in lesson 2) changes the score by $0.0002/120 \approx 0.000002$. In SP5 the score depends far more on never failing and never making wild predictions than on the last digits of the MSE. Lesson 2 shows where wild predictions come from. Step 3: a validation estimate you trust You choose models by their validation score, so you need to know how precise that score is. The validation MSE is an average of 400 squared errors, so it has a standard error of about $s/\sqrt{n}$, where $s$ is the standard deviation of the squared errors and $n = 400$. Two models whose validation MSEs differ by less than about one standard error are a tie as far as this data can tell. The cubic (0.290) is less than one standard error better than the mean (0.300), so as far as this data can tell they tie. Degree 5 (0.123) beats both by more than 10 standard errors, so that gain is real. When validation is too small to separate the models you care about, make it bigger: hold out part of train.json yourself, or use k-fold cross-validation (u06-l08). The given validation set has one advantage over your own split: the organizers built it, so it is the best guess you have at what the test looks like. Check its $x$ range against the training range, as in step 1. Everything you fit (the model, a scaler, the choice of features) must be fit on training data only while you are comparing models. If validation data leaks into any of these, the validation score comes out too good, and you choose worse models. This is data leakage (u06-l02). Step 4: change one thing at a time, and write it down Each experiment changes one thing: the model, one hyperparameter, or one feature. If you change two things and the score moves, you do not know which one moved it. Record every run in a results log , one row per experiment. The log tells you what to try next, and lesson 5 turns it into the report. Step 5: choose, then freeze Pick the model with the best validation score. If the top models tie within the noise, prefer the simpler one, or the one that behaves better outside the training range (lesson 2). Some people then refit the chosen settings on training plus validation data, which gives the model more data but leaves you no untouched check; if you do it, say so in the report. Then stop changing the model, package it (lesson 4) and run the self-check before you upload. 1. Load, print shapes and ranges, plot. 2. Baseline, packaged and submitted. Now you have a score that is not zero. 3. A validation estimate with its standard error. 4. One change at a time, each one logged. 5. Choose by validation, package, self-check, upload, write the report.

entries.t: Picking a model for the data
entries.x: Part 2 gives you 75 minutes for all its problems, so in the open-ended one you cannot try every model. You need a short list to try first for each kind of data, and a way to choose when several candidates score the same on validation. This lesson gives the short list, then runs it on the practice data from lesson 1, which is built like SP5's. On that data the in-range scores tie, and the choice comes down to what each model predicts outside the training range. What to try first data try first then --- --- --- tabular (rows of numeric and categorical columns) gradient boosting or a random forest (u08-l03) logistic or linear regression with standardization and one-hot encoding, as a check one input number $x$ (a 1D function) plot it; kNN regression or a polynomial for a smooth curve Fourier features if it repeats (below) small images or 1D signals a small convolutional network in PyTorch (u12), kept small for the CPU (lesson 3) summary features (max, mean, position of the peak) fed to a tree model short texts word counts with logistic regression pretrained text models are Round 2 material (u17) Tree ensembles are the tabular default because they need no scaling, pick up interactions between features by themselves, and work well with default settings. For any data, keep the baseline from lesson 1 in the table. The candidates on validation KNeighborsRegressor predicts the mean $y$ of the $k$ nearest training points (u08-l01). scikit-learn wants inputs of shape (n, d) , so one feature becomes x[:, None] , shape (n, 1) . Read the table the way u06-l03 taught: - Polynomials of degree 1 to 5 underfit: training and validation MSE are both high. The validation error drops sharply from degree 5 (0.123) to degree 7 (0.019) and degree 9 (0.0101); degree 12 gets 0.0100. - kNN with $k = 1$ overfits: training MSE 0 (each point is its own nearest neighbor), validation 0.0196. With $k = 1000$ each prediction averages over an eighth of the data and blurs the curve (0.0261). $k = 100$ gives 0.0101. - GradientBoostingRegressor() with default settings gets 0.0102 on validation (measured; it appears again below). The noise floor The best models all stop near 0.0100. That is the noise floor : even the true $f$ would have an MSE equal to the noise variance on new points, because the noise cannot be predicted. Here the noise has a standard deviation of about 0.10, so the floor is about $0.10^2 = 0.010$. Once several models reach the floor, more tuning cannot lower the in-range MSE by more than the noise in your estimate (lesson 1: about 0.0008). Spend the remaining time on what else can go wrong. A repeating curve: Fourier features Look at the plot from lesson 1 again. The curve repeats: its peaks are about 1.25 apart (near $x = 0.2$ and $x = 1.45$), a little over two full waves between $-1$ and $2$. A periodic function with period $P$ satisfies $f(x + P) = f(x)$ for every $x$. A model that is periodic by construction is linear regression on Fourier features : for a period $P$ and a number of harmonics $K$, the columns which is $2K + 1$ columns. Each column repeats with period $P$ (harmonic $k$ repeats $k$ times per period), so every weighted sum of them does too. The weights come from least squares, as in any linear regression (u07-l01). np.linalg.lstsq(A, y, rcond=None) returns the least-squares weights as its first output. Three things to read off: 1. With $P = 1.25$ the validation MSE is 0.0100 for every $K$: on the noise floor with 3 weights. Extra harmonics add nothing. 2. The weights: 0.301 on the constant, 0.661 on the sine and 0.452 on the cosine. A sine and a cosine of the same period add up to one shifted sine: $a\sin\theta + b\cos\theta = R\sin(\theta + \varphi)$ with $R = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ (expand $\sin(\theta + \varphi)$ to check). So the fit is a wave of amplitude $\sqrt{0.661^2 + 0.452^2} \approx 0.80$ around the level 0.30. That is your description of $f$, now measured, and it is why the features include both a sine and a cosine: together they can fit a wave of any phase. 3. The period was not guessed. The scan over $P$ has one sharp dip, at $P = 1.25$; a period off by 5% already has validation MSE above 0.026. Hyperparameters such as $P$ and $K$ are chosen on validation like any others. This $f$ is a single sine, so scanning with $K = 1$ works. If the wave has more shape (sharper peaks, flat stretches), scan with a few harmonics, such as $K = 4$. With too few, the missing harmonics pull the best period away from the true one: on one of the u13-p02 datasets the $K = 1$ scan finds $P = 1.266$ where the true period is $1.30$, and with that period the MSE outside the training range is 0.058 instead of 0.009, even with $K = 4$ in the final fit. Outside the training range Predicting at an $x$ inside the training range is interpolation ; predicting outside it is extrapolation . The SP5 statement does not say which $x$ values the hidden test contains. It does use 120 as the normalizer, while the baseline's MSE on data like this is well under 1 (0.30 on the practice data). That suggests (it proves nothing) that the organizers expect some submissions to have very large errors, and the usual source of very large errors is extrapolation. So before choosing, look at what each model does beyond the data. What each model does past the edge of the data: - kNN regression : every query beyond the edge has the same $k$ nearest neighbors (the $k$ points closest to the edge), so the prediction is a constant: their mean $y$ (here $-0.418$ for all $x 2$). - Trees, random forests, gradient boosting : each tree is constant beyond its last split, so a sum or average of trees is constant too. - Polynomials : they grow like their highest-power term. The degree 12 fit predicts 48 at $x = 2.5$ and 1,799 at $x = 3$. - Linear regression : continues its straight line. ReLU networks compute piecewise linear functions (u11-l01), so far enough out they also continue a straight line. - Fourier features : repeat the fitted period forever. Right if $f$ really repeats, wrong if the repetition was a coincidence of the training range. Now the score. Suppose part of the hidden test were in $[2, 3]$ and the wave really continued there. A constant prediction is off by about the size of the wave (here the constant sits near the bottom of it), so the squared errors there average about 1.0 and the score drops by less than 0.009. The degree 12 polynomial is off by up to 1,800, its squared errors pass $10^6$, and its score is 0. A flat guess costs little; an explosion costs everything. np.clip(pred, y.min(), y.max()) keeps every prediction inside the range of the training labels, here $[-0.79, 1.39]$. If the true values outside the training range stay in that band (an assumption, but a mild one), no squared error can exceed $(0.79 + 1.39)^2 \approx 4.8$, and the score stays above $(120 - 4.8)/120 \approx 0.96$ whatever the test contains. Clipping costs nothing in range, because good in-range predictions are already inside the band. The exam angle: choosing in SP5 In range, kNN with $k = 100$ (0.0101), the degree 12 polynomial (0.0100), gradient boosting (0.0102) and the Fourier model (0.0100) are all within about one standard error (0.0008) of the noise floor, so validation cannot rank them. So decide with the other facts you have: 1. The Fourier model matches the structure you saw in the plot, and the period scan confirmed that structure with a sharp dip at $P = 1.25$. 2. It is bounded: it can never explode. 3. It is tiny (3 numbers to save) and fast to evaluate. If the plot had shown no repeating pattern, a bounded model such as kNN or boosting, with clipping, would be the safe default, and a high-degree polynomial would be the one to avoid. Either way, write the reasoning and the alternatives into the report (lesson 5), so whoever reads problem5.md sees what you chose and why. Practice: u13-p02 gives you periodic data whose hidden test reaches past both ends of the training range, with a period you have to find. Do it after lesson 4, which covers the submission format.

entries.t: Training on CPU within time limits
entries.x: Two clocks run during the open-ended problem. The first is yours: Part 2 gives 75 minutes for all its problems, and training happens inside that time on Colab's CPU (no GPU in Round 1). A model that takes 10 minutes to train lets you try three ideas; one that takes 10 seconds lets you try fifty. The second is the grader's: in SP5 each predict call may take at most 30 seconds on the grader's CPU, and the statement does not say how many test points there are. This lesson is how to measure time, predict it before you run, keep training short, and get the same result every run. Measuring time time.perf counter() returns a clock reading in seconds, made for measuring short intervals. Read it before and after, and subtract: In Colab, a cell whose first line is %%time prints how long the whole cell took (a cell command like %%writefile , so it must be the first line). Times vary from run to run, and the first call of anything can include one-time costs such as loading a library, so time a second run before trusting a number. Predict the cost before you run Time a small version, then scale it by how the cost grows with the sizes involved: work cost grows like --- --- brute-force kNN prediction (training points) $\times$ (test points) least squares with $p$ columns (polynomial, Fourier features) $n p^2$ to fit, $n p$ to predict gradient boosting with $T$ trees about $T \times n$ to fit, $T \times$ (test points) to predict a neural network epochs $\times\ n \times$ (parameters) to train So if kNN prediction on 2000 test points takes 0.25 s, 20,000 points take about 2.5 s. The box measures this, and also shows the other cost of brute force: memory. The distance array has one entry per (query, training point) pair, 8 bytes each. np.argpartition(dist, k, axis=1) returns, for each row, the column indices arranged so that the first $k$ of them belong to the $k$ smallest values (in no particular order). That is cheaper than a full sort. Without the chunks, 100,000 test points would need a 6.4 GB array, enough to crash a Colab session. With chunks, memory stays at 128 MB per chunk and time grows in proportion to the number of queries. scikit-learn's KNeighborsRegressor already works in pieces and uses search trees, so it avoids this problem. Write predict so that its time and memory grow in proportion to the number of test points, with no array of shape (test points, training points) built in one piece. Then time it on a fake test file 10 to 100 times bigger than the validation set. Aim well under the limit, since the grader's CPU may be slower than yours. Small models first At the noise floor (lesson 2) a bigger model cannot score better, so start with the smallest model that might work, and grow it only when validation says it is underfitting. Explore on a sample: tune on 2000 points, then confirm the winner on all of them. For neural networks on CPU: two hidden layers of 32 to 64 units, full-batch or large mini-batches when the data is small, Adam with learning rate around 0.01 to 0.001. Early stopping Early stopping (u06-l04) keeps the parameters from the epoch with the lowest validation loss. It also saves time: stop when the validation loss has not improved for a set number of epochs, called the patience (u11-l08). The box trains a small network on 2000 of the practice training points from lesson 1, full batch, and stops after 30 epochs without improvement. The network reaches the noise floor too (val MSE 0.0104), in well under a second of training. Two details matter: - copy.deepcopy(model.state dict()) . A state dict holds the model's live tensors, not copies, so best state = model.state dict() would keep changing as training goes on, and you would "restore" the last epoch. Deep copy it (or copy each tensor with .clone() ). - torch.set num threads(1) tells PyTorch to use one CPU thread. For models this small, more threads often do not make training faster (measure it), and the problems on this site run PyTorch with one thread so that timings stay steady. In Colab, os.cpu count() shows how many cores you have. Fixed seeds Set every seed at the top of the training notebook: - NumPy: rng = np.random.default rng(0) , and draw everything from rng . - scikit-learn: random state=0 in every model and split that has the argument. - PyTorch: torch.manual seed(0) before building the model (initial weights) and before training (shuffling, dropout). Seeds make a rerun of the notebook produce the same model, the same files and the same numbers in your report. They also make comparisons fair: if two runs differ in one setting and in nothing else, the setting caused the difference. Measure how much the seed alone moves the score; a "gain" smaller than that is luck. The same seed gives the identical score (the first and last rows); other seeds move it by less than 0.0001. A random forest draws a bootstrap sample for each tree, so its result depends on the seed. A change that moves validation MSE by less than this spread is not a real improvement. - Time a small run with time.perf counter() , then scale by how the cost grows. - Keep each training run to a minute or two; explore on a sample. - Write predict in chunks and time it on a test file much bigger than validation. - Early stopping with a deep-copied best state. - Seeds for NumPy, scikit-learn and PyTorch at the top of the notebook. Practice: u13-p04 asks for a small PyTorch model on 1D signals with a 60-second training budget, saved as a checkpoint. Do it after lesson 4.

In an open-ended problem the grader never runs your notebooks. It gets a ZIP file, unpacks it on its own machine, imports submission.py from it and calls the prediction function. If one file is missing or one path points at your Colab folder, the score is 0 however good the model is. You get the official "Guideline: Submitting Trained Models for Open-Ended Problems" during the exam (u00-l04 introduced it); this lesson follows it step by step on SP5, with the Fourier model from lesson 2, and ends with a self-check you can run on your own ZIP. The guideline, step by step The provided materials are three starter notebooks (Training, Inference, Write md) and a Self-check notebook. The roadmap, in the guideline's order: 1. Training notebook. Build and train the model, validate if you want. Then save and download every file inference will use: "the preprocessing parameters, trained model and learned weights". 2. Inference notebook. Complete submission.py , the file the grader calls; it may load any of the files from step 1. Then create and download a ZIP containing submission.py and every training output that inference uses. 3. Self-check notebook. Run it on the ZIP from step 2. It checks whether your submission will work on the grader's side. Never edit it. 4. Write md notebook (if the problem asks): document your approach. Lesson 5. 5. Upload the training notebook, the inference notebook, the ZIP, and the .md file. The guideline says the grader's script is "very similar to Self-check.ipynb": it extracts the package, imports submission.py , calls the required prediction function with the path to the hidden test data (which you cannot access or guess), and scores the output. It "may include additional features, such as anti-cheating measures". SP5 adds its own rules: predict(test path) returns a Python list, each call has 30 seconds on CPU, the inference notebook must not retrain, and any error scores as MSE 10000. Each Colab notebook runs in its own runtime, so the inference notebook cannot see files that the training notebook wrote. That is why step 1 says download: you then upload those files into the inference notebook's Files panel (u00-l02). Files in a runtime also disappear when the session ends, so download each artifact as soon as it is final. Artifacts: what goes in the ZIP An artifact is a file the training notebook produces that predict needs. The ZIP holds submission.py plus every artifact the training notebook produced (SP5's wording). Check the other direction too: every file predict opens must be one of them, and nothing predict uses may live only in your notebook's memory. your model artifacts format (cheat sheet) --- --- --- a few numbers: weights, period, clip bounds, scaler means one dict .json NumPy arrays (a kNN model's stored training points, big weight matrices) the arrays .npy / .npz a fitted scikit-learn model or pipeline the object .joblib a PyTorch model a checkpoint: model config plus model state dict .pt The save and load calls are in u00-l04's table, for example joblib.dump(model, "model.joblib") and joblib.load(...) . Plain pickle works the same way on a file opened in binary mode: with open("scaler.pkl", "wb") as f: pickle.dump(obj, f) to save, and pickle.load(f) on a file opened with "rb" to load. For a kNN model the training points are the model, so they are an artifact. For every other model, leave the training data out: predict must not retrain, and reading the training file is what retraining would look like. JSON can store only plain Python values (dicts, lists, strings, numbers, True / False , None ). json.dump fails on a NumPy array, a np.float32 or a np.int64 ( TypeError: Object of type float32 is not JSON serializable , measured). Convert first: arr.tolist() for arrays, float(v) and int(v) for single values. For PyTorch, u10-l08 covers the checkpoint: rebuild the model with Net( ckpt["model config"]) , then load state dict , eval() , and predict under torch.no grad() . The class itself is code, so it must be in the ZIP too. The simplest place is inside submission.py . If you follow the cheat sheet and keep it in its own file such as cnn model.py , put that file in the ZIP, and let the self-check confirm that from cnn model import SmallCNN works on the grader's side. Writing submission.py Line by line: - Path( file ) : file is the path of this module's own file (u00-l04). .resolve() makes it a full path from the root of the disk, and .parent drops the file name, leaving its folder. HERE / "model.json" is the artifact next to submission.py , wherever the grader unzipped it. A bare open("model.json") would look in the grader's current folder instead, which is not that folder in general. - The artifact is loaded inside predict . Loading it once at import (at the top level of the file) also works on the real grader and saves a little time per call. On this site's practice problems, though, your file is imported once before train has written any artifacts, so load them inside predict there. - Besides its own artifact, predict reads only test path . It handles any number of points, including 0, because every step is array arithmetic on the whole input. - .tolist() turns the float64 array into a list of Python floats. list(arr) would give a list of NumPy scalars, and returning the array itself is not a list at all. - model["clip"] unpacks the two-element list into the a min and a max arguments of np.clip (u01-l03). The whole round trip, with a self-check The box runs both notebooks and then a check of your own, which goes beyond the official one: it unzips into a fresh folder, imports from there while running in another folder, and calls predict on the validation set, on 100,000 points far outside the training range, and on an empty file. Now break it on purpose. In the submission.py text, change open(HERE / "model.json", ...) to open("model.json", ...) and run again: predict fails with FileNotFoundError , because the check runs from a different folder. Change it back, then delete "model.json" from the list of files to zip: the same error, for a different reason. Each of these would have scored 0. z.write(name) stores the file under the name you give it, so z.write("submission.py") puts it at the top level of the ZIP. If you zip a file by a longer path such as z.write("out/model.json") , it is stored as out/model.json , and HERE / "model.json" will not find it. Pass arcname="model.json" to store it under the short name, and always print namelist() before uploading. What breaks a submission - Opening artifacts by a relative path ( open("model.json") ) or by a Colab path ( /content/model.json ). - An artifact saved but not put in the ZIP, or stored inside a folder in the ZIP. - Using a name that exists only in your notebook (a variable model , an import done in another cell): NameError on the grader. - Returning a NumPy array, a tensor, or a list of NumPy scalars instead of a list of Python floats. - Pickling an object of a class you defined in a notebook cell. Pickle (and joblib) saves an object's class by module and name; for a class MyScaler defined in a notebook cell that is main .MyScaler , so loading it anywhere else fails with AttributeError: Can't get attribute 'MyScaler' on (measured). Save the numbers inside it as JSON instead, or define the class in a .py file that both notebooks import and that goes in the ZIP. scikit-learn's own classes are safe: their module is importable everywhere. - torch.save(model, ...) (the whole object): torch.load refuses it by default (u10-l08). Save a checkpoint with the state dict . - Forgetting model.eval() , so dropout stays on and predictions are noisy. - Training, or reading the training file, inside predict . Practice The problems on this site turn this format into one importable file. You write train(train path, val path, out dir) , which plays the training notebook and saves its artifacts into out dir , and predict(test path) , which plays submission.py . The grader zips your file with the artifacts, deletes the training data, unzips everything in a fresh folder, imports it from there and calls predict from yet another folder. Start with u13-p03 (a tabular classification scored by macro F1, saved with joblib), then u13-p02 (extrapolation, lesson 2) and u13-p04 (a PyTorch checkpoint, lesson 3). For the real thing, run the whole guideline in Colab on the official SP5 files (lesson 1 links them), with the self-check above.

SP5 asks for a fourth file, problem5.md , that explains "approach, alternatives, abandoned ideas". The sample does not say how the report is graded. A reasonable assumption is that a person reads it to see that the work is yours, that your choices had reasons, and that the numbers match your notebooks. It is the cheapest part of the problem to get right: if you kept the results log from lesson 1, the report is mostly a copy of it with one reason per decision. Plan five minutes for it at the end, and write the headings as soon as you start. What goes in it Three required parts, plus one that the extrapolation question makes worth adding: 1. Approach : the final model, its features and hyperparameters, how each setting was chosen, the validation score with its standard error, and the artifacts in the ZIP. 2. Alternatives tried : a table from the results log: model, setting, validation score. 3. Abandoned ideas : things you tried or started and dropped, each with the reason (scored worse, tied but riskier, too slow, could not get it working in time). 4. Risks and checks : what you could not verify (such as the hidden test's $x$ range), what you did about it, and what your self-check covered. A full report for SP5, in Markdown (u00-l03), with the numbers from the practice data of lessons 1 to 4: Every number in it came from a box in lessons 1 to 4. That is the standard: numbers from your log or a notebook output, never from memory. Sentences that do work and sentences that do not weak better --- --- "I used an advanced model to accurately learn the function." "Linear regression on Fourier features, P = 1.25, K = 1: validation MSE 0.0100." "kNN didn't work." "kNN, k = 100: validation MSE 0.0101, a tie; not chosen because it predicts a constant past x = 2." "The model generalizes well." "Validation MSE 0.0100 ± 0.0007, at the noise floor (residual SD 0.10)." "I tried many things." The alternatives table. "The test set will be in [-1, 2]." "The test range is not given; predictions are periodic and clipped, so they stay bounded anywhere." The rules behind the right column: name the model and the settings, give the number, give the reason for each decision, and say what you do not know instead of guessing it. Keep it to about a page. Long text is not more convincing, and every extra claim is one more thing that can disagree with your notebooks. Generating it from the log The provided "Write md" starter notebook is where the guideline says to produce the file ("Generate the required Markdown explanation of the approach"); follow its cells. If you write the file yourself, build the text in Python from your log, so the table cannot disagree with your results, and save it with Path("problem5.md").write text(text, encoding="utf-8") (or put the text in a %%writefile problem5.md cell). The box also checks that the required headings are there. - Final model, settings, and how each setting was chosen. - Validation score with its standard error, and the baseline for comparison. - The alternatives table, generated from the log. - Each abandoned idea with its reason. - What you could not check, and what you did about it. - Every number matches a notebook output.

Part 1 is 20 problems in 60 minutes, closed book, with no calculator. Each problem is worth 7.5 points: a right answer earns 7.5, a wrong answer earns 0, and a blank earns 1.5. So the maximum is 150, and a paper left entirely blank still scores 30. Pace 60 minutes for 20 problems is 3 minutes each on average. The problems are not equally hard, so do not spend 3 minutes on each in order. Use two passes: 1. First pass (about 35 minutes). Answer everything you can do quickly and are sure of. If a problem will clearly take more than about 4 minutes, flag it and move on. 2. Second pass (the rest). Go back to flagged problems, easiest first. 3. Last 3 minutes. Decide what to do with every problem still open, using the rule below. Never leave the decision to the clock. When to guess and when to leave a blank The expected value of a choice is the average number of points it earns if you made the same choice many times. A blank always earns 1.5. A guess earns 7.5 with some probability $p$ and 0 otherwise, so its expected value is $7.5p$. Guessing beats a blank when Rule: answer whenever you are more than 20% sure. Otherwise leave it blank. What that means for multiple choice with five options: Choices you can rule out Left Chance of a random guess Expected points Blank earns --- --- --- --- --- 0 5 20% 1.50 1.5 1 4 25% 1.88 1.5 2 3 33% 2.50 1.5 3 2 50% 3.75 1.5 A pure guess among five ties with a blank. As soon as you can eliminate one choice for a real reason, guess. For the integer answers (000 to 999), a random guess almost never works: its expected value is about $7.5/1000$, close to 0. Only write a number if you actually computed it or are confident in your estimate. "Pretty sure but not certain" is usually well above 20%. Fear of losing points makes people leave blanks they should have answered. Answer it. Habits that save points - Read the last line first. Know what is being asked (recall or precision? the number of parameters that train, or all of them?) before reading the setup. - Check units and form. Three digits with leading zeros: 27 is entered as 027 . "Compute $1000b$" means multiply before you round or truncate, exactly as stated. - For "what does this code print?" problems , write the shapes and values of each line on scratch paper. Most mistakes are an axis or a shape. - Use the choices. If you computed something that is not among the choices, you made an error; the distractors are usually the results of common errors, so check which mistake each one represents. - Watch float rounding in "what does this print" problems. int() truncates toward zero, and most decimals are not exact in binary: 0.29 100 is 28.999999999999996 , so int(0.29 100) prints 28, not 29. Values like 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75 are exact; 0.1, 0.29 and 1.8 are not. If a problem says "compute 1000x", work it exactly by hand. - Do not change an answer on the second pass unless you found a specific mistake. The official samples Three of the six official Part 1 samples sit in the units that teach them: recall (WildWatch) and test-set reuse in ML fundamentals, and the minimum-norm reconstruction in linear algebra. The other three are here.

Part 2 is 75 minutes of coding in Google Colab on a CPU. Each problem states exactly what to write, which imports are allowed, which functions are banned, and the time limits. A grader imports your .py file, calls your function or class on hidden tests, and checks every rule. Correct numbers are not enough: a banned function, a wrong file name or a modified input can cost the whole problem. Before you write any code (about 2 minutes per problem) 1. Read the restrictions first. Allowed imports, banned functions (for example np.mean , np.linalg , @ , loops), and whether helper functions are allowed. Write the banned list at the top of your notebook as a comment so you see it while coding. 2. Copy the exact signature. Function name, argument names, return order ( return Z, means, standard deviations, covariance ), attribute names ( self.weights , self.bias ), and output dtypes ( torch.int32 ). 3. Note the shapes. Input shapes, output shapes, and whether a 1D output must be (n,) and not (n, 1) . 4. Note the file names. They must match exactly, including problem1 submission.py vs submission.py . While coding - Start from the example in the statement. Make it pass first. It catches most shape and indexing mistakes. - Never modify an input. Use X - mu , not X -= mu . Graders check this. - Then test edge cases the constraints allow: $n = 2$, $d = 1$, a constant column, zeros, a length-1 segment, the largest sizes (for the time limit). - Time it. Wrap a call on the largest allowed input with %time . Colab's CPU is slower than a laptop, so leave a margin. - Use help() . It shows a function's arguments inside Colab, for example help(np.where) . Every model in this unit and the next reads a batch of sequences. Round 2 problems start there too: the 2025 CLIP problem had you tokenize captions with a BERT tokenizer, pad a batch by hand inside a collate function, and build an int64 attention mask; the 2026 linear-attention problem fed sequences of 500 sensor readings to a transformer. This lesson fixes the shapes and vocabulary the rest of the unit uses: tokens, vocabularies, padding, and the masks that keep padding from leaking into the answer. Sequences as tensors A sequence is an ordered list $x 0, x 1, \dots, x {T-1}$; $T$ is the sequence length . Order matters: "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" hold the same words. This unit uses three letters for shapes: Letter Meaning --- --- B batch size, the number of sequences processed together (u10 to u12 wrote it N ) T sequence length, the number of positions d features per position (called d model inside a transformer) Text arrives as integer ids of shape (B, T) . A time series, or text after an embedding layer, is a float tensor of shape (B, T, d) : one vector of length d per position. Tokens and vocabularies A token is the unit of text a model reads: a character, a word, or a piece of a word, stored as an integer id. A tokenizer turns text into a list of token ids and back. The vocabulary is the fixed list of tokens it knows; its size $V$ sets the number of rows of the embedding table and the number of outputs of a language model. Three choices: - Character level. $V$ is small (the characters in the data), every string can be encoded, but sequences are long: a 1000-character paragraph is 1000 tokens. - Word level. Sequences are short, but $V$ grows past hundreds of thousands, and a word never seen in training is out of vocabulary : it becomes a single unknown token [UNK] and its meaning is lost. - Subword level (what real models use). Frequent words are one token; rare words are split into pieces, so nothing is out of vocabulary and $V$ stays moderate. GPT-2's tokenizer has $V = 50{,}257$ and BERT's has $V = 30{,}522$. A character tokenizer is two dictionaries: Byte-pair encoding Byte-pair encoding (BPE), used by GPT models, builds a subword vocabulary from data. Start with single characters. Count every adjacent pair of tokens in the corpus (weighted by how often each word occurs), merge the most frequent pair into one new token, and repeat until the vocabulary reaches the target size. Each merge adds one token to the vocabulary and shortens the corpus by the number of times the pair occurred. BERT's WordPiece is similar but chooses merges by a likelihood score; it marks a piece that continues a word with , so a split looks like play , ing . Special tokens Tokenizers reserve ids for special tokens that are not text. BERT's vocabulary has [PAD] = 0 (filler, below), [UNK] = 100, [CLS] = 101 (put at the start; its output vector summarizes the whole input for classification), [SEP] = 102 (put at the end, and between two sentences) and [MASK] = 103 (used in pretraining, u16-l02). So every BERT-tokenized caption in the 2025 problem started with 101 and ended with 102. GPT-2 has one special token, = 50256, which separates documents. Padding a batch Sentences have different lengths, but a tensor is a rectangle. The fix is padding : append a pad id to each shorter sequence until all have the length of the longest one in the batch. A tokenizer usually also does truncation : sequences longer than a max length are cut. The attention mask records which positions are real: shape (B, T) , 1 for a real token and 0 for padding (the Hugging Face convention). torch.nn.utils.rnn.pad sequence pads a list of 1D tensors. Pass batch first=True , or you get shape (T, B) . The mask comes from the lengths by broadcasting a row of positions against a column of lengths: A collate function is what a DataLoader (u10-l07) calls to turn a list of samples into one batch; for text it is exactly the cell above. Write it as def collate(batch): ... returning (ids, mask) and pass DataLoader(ds, batch size=16, collate fn=collate) . Using the mask Padding is filler, so every step that combines positions must skip it. 1. Embeddings. nn.Embedding(V, d, padding idx=0) (u11-l10) maps the pad id to a zero vector that never trains. That does not make padding harmless: the layers after it mix positions. 2. Pooling. To get one vector per sequence from h of shape (B, T, d) , average only the real positions. This is masked mean pooling : multiply by the mask, sum over T , divide by the number of real tokens. 3. Loss. Positions that are padding get no loss (u16-l02 does this with ignore index ). 4. Attention. In the next lessons each position takes a weighted average over all positions. The mask removes padding positions from every average (u15-l03). Masks do not agree on what True means. A Hugging Face attention mask uses 1 = real token. F.scaled dot product attention takes a boolean attn mask where True = may attend. nn.MultiheadAttention takes a key padding mask where True = ignore . Converting between them is one == 0 or ~ ; getting it backward silently attends only to padding. Read the convention in the problem statement before writing the first line. Right or left padding. Encoders pad on the right. When a decoder generates text for a batch of prompts, the new token is appended at the last position, so prompts are padded on the left to make the last position of every row a real token (u16-l04). Exam angle - Write the shape of every tensor in a comment: ids (B, T) long, mask (B, T) , features (B, T, d) . - torch.tensor(list of ints) gives int64 , which nn.Embedding needs. torch.Tensor(list of ints) gives float32 and fails. - Pooling, loss and attention each need the mask. A model that ignores it still runs and gives slightly wrong numbers, the hardest kind of bug to see.

Before attention, sequences were read by recurrent neural networks (RNNs): one step per position, carrying a memory vector forward. You need them for three reasons. Round 2 can ask for their parameter counts and output shapes, or let you use nn.LSTM or nn.GRU as a quick baseline on a time series. The reasons they were replaced are the design goals of the transformer. And the linear attention of lesson 6 (the 2026 Round 2 problem) turns out to be an RNN in disguise. The plain RNN An RNN keeps a hidden state $h t \in \mathbb{R}^H$, a summary of the sequence up to position $t$. Starting from $h {-1} = 0$, each step reads one input $x t \in \mathbb{R}^I$ and updates the state: The same $W {ih}$ (shape $H \times I$), $W {hh}$ ($H \times H$) and biases are used at every step, the time version of weight sharing. So the parameter count does not depend on $T$: PyTorch stores two bias vectors ( bias ih l0 and bias hh l0 ) even though one would do, so the $2H$ is what nn.RNN reports. nn.RNN(10, 20) has $200 + 400 + 40 = 640$ parameters. The outputs are every state, shape (B, T, H) , and the last state. The loop is three lines; nn.RNN computes the same thing: h n has shape (num layers num directions, B, H) even with batch first=True ; only the input and out follow batch first . For a classifier, the last layer's final state is h n[-1] , shape (B, H) . With padded batches, out[:, -1] is the state after the padding, not after the last real token; use the lengths to pick the right position (or nn.utils.rnn.pack padded sequence ). num layers=2 stacks two RNNs: the second reads the first one's states, so its input size is $H$, not $I$. bidirectional=True runs a second RNN from right to left and concatenates the two states at each position, so out has last axis $2H$ and the parameter count doubles. A bidirectional RNN can only be used when the whole sequence is known in advance, never to generate text left to right. Why gradients vanish Training unrolls the loop into a $T$-layer network with shared weights and runs backpropagation through it, which is called backpropagation through time . The gradient that reaches an early state is a product of one Jacobian per step. Write $a t$ for the argument of $\tanh$, so $h t = \tanh(a t)$ and $\partial h t / \partial h {t-1} = \operatorname{diag}(1 - h t^2)\, W {hh}$. Then Each factor has $\tanh' \le 1$ times the same matrix. If those factors shrink vectors, the product decays geometrically: a factor of size 0.9 per step leaves $0.9^{100} \approx 2.7 \times 10^{-5}$ after 100 steps. That is the vanishing gradient problem, and the model cannot learn that a token 100 steps back matters. If the factors stretch vectors, the product blows up instead (exploding gradient problem); gradient clipping fixes that one, but nothing simple fixes vanishing. LSTM and GRU The LSTM (long short-term memory) adds a second state, the cell state $c t$, and three gates : vectors in $(0, 1)$ made by a sigmoid that scale other vectors entry by entry. With $\sigma$ the sigmoid, $\odot$ entrywise product, and every gate computed from $x t$ and $h {t-1}$ by its own affine map, The forget gate $f t$ decides how much of the old cell to keep, the input gate $i t$ how much of the candidate $g t$ to write, the output gate $o t$ how much of the cell to show. The cell update adds to the old cell instead of passing it through $\tanh$ and a matrix, so $\partial c t / \partial c {t-1} = \operatorname{diag}(f t)$: with forget gates near 1 the gradient survives. With $f = 0.99$ at every step, $0.99^{100} \approx 0.37$ of the gradient reaches 100 steps back, compared with $2.7 \times 10^{-5}$ above. There are four affine maps (i, f, g, o), each the size of a plain RNN's, so nn.LSTM has $4\,(H I + H^2 + 2H)$ parameters per layer. It returns out, (h n, c n) . The GRU (gated recurrent unit) has no separate cell. An update gate $z t$ mixes old and new, $h t = (1 - z t) \odot n t + z t \odot h {t-1}$, where the candidate $n t$ uses a reset gate $r t$ to decide how much of $h {t-1}$ to read. Three affine maps: $3\,(H I + H^2 + 2H)$ parameters, and it returns out, h n like nn.RNN . Why attention replaced them RNN self-attention (lesson 3) --- --- --- steps that must run one after another $T$ 1 (all positions at once) path between positions 0 and $T-1$ $T - 1$ steps 1 step memory of the past one vector of length $H$ every earlier position, directly work per layer $O(T H^2)$ $O(T^2 d)$ 1. No parallelism over time. $h t$ needs $h {t-1}$, so a GPU cannot compute the $T$ steps at once. Attention computes every position with a few large matrix products. 2. A bottleneck. Everything about the past must squeeze through one vector of length $H$. 3. Long paths. Information from position 0 reaches position $T - 1$ through $T - 1$ multiplications, which is why gradients vanish. Attention connects every pair of positions directly. The price is the $T^2$: attention compares every pair. Lesson 6 shows how linear attention gets back to $O(T)$ work, and its causal form is again a recurrence, with a matrix as the hidden state. Exam angle - Parameter counts: RNN 1, GRU 3, LSTM 4 copies of $H I + H^2 + 2H$; a second layer has input size $H$ (or $2H$ if bidirectional). - Shapes: out is (B, T, num directions H) with batch first=True ; h n is (num layers num directions, B, H) always. - "Why transformers": parallel over positions, direct paths, no fixed-size bottleneck; cost $O(T^2)$.

Attention is the one operation a transformer adds to the layers you already know. The official syllabus says contestants "must have a thorough understanding of transformers", and both Round 2 papers so far built attention from scratch: 2025 Problem 2 (multi-head attention and its variants, each written as your own module) and 2026 Problem 1 (complexity of attention, then linear attention). This lesson derives scaled dot-product attention, explains the $\sqrt{d k}$, and builds the masks. The practice problem bans F.scaled dot product attention , so you write it yourself. A soft lookup A Python dict lookup compares a query with every key and returns the value of the one key that matches. Attention does the same thing softly. Each position has three vectors: - a query $q$: what this position is looking for; - a key $k$: what this position offers to be matched against; - a value $v$: what this position hands over when it is matched. For one query $q$ and keys $k 0, \dots, k {n-1}$ (all of length $d k$) with values $v 0, \dots, v {n-1}$ (length $d v$), the attention scores are dot products, the attention weights are their softmax, and the output is the weighted average of the values: The weights are positive and sum to 1, so $o$ is a blend of the values, mostly of those whose keys point the same way as $q$. $d k = 4$, so $\sqrt{d k} = 2$. Take $q = (1, 0, 1, 0)$, keys $k 0 = (2, 0, 0, 0)$, $k 1 = (0, 0, 2, 2)$, $k 2 = (0, 2, 0, 0)$ and values $v 0 = (1, 0)$, $v 1 = (0, 1)$, $v 2 = (1, 1)$. Dot products $2, 2, 0$; scores $1, 1, 0$. Softmax: $e^1 / (2e + 1) = 0.422$ twice and $1/(2e+1) = 0.155$. Output: $0.422\,(1, 0) + 0.422\,(0, 1) + 0.155\,(1, 1) = (0.578, 0.578)$. Stack the queries as rows of $Q$ (shape $n q \times d k$), the keys as rows of $K$ ($n k \times d k$) and the values as rows of $V$ ($n k \times d v$). Every query at once: where softmax acts on each row. The weight matrix $A$ is $n q \times n k$ with rows summing to 1, and the output is $n q \times d v$. This is scaled dot-product attention . Why divide by the square root of d k Suppose the entries of $q$ and $k$ are independent, with mean 0 and variance 1, which is roughly what a well-initialized layer produces. Each term $q i k i$ has mean 0 and variance $E[q i^2]\,E[k i^2] = 1$, and the $d k$ terms are independent, so their variances add: Without the scale, scores have standard deviation $\sqrt{d k}$: 8 for $d k = 64$. Softmax of numbers that far apart is nearly one-hot. That is bad for training: the softmax derivative is $\partial a i / \partial s j = a i(\delta {ij} - a j)$, which is close to 0 for every $i, j$ when one $a$ is near 1 and the rest near 0, so almost no gradient reaches the queries and keys (saturation again). Dividing by $\sqrt{d k}$ keeps the scores at variance 1 whatever the head size. Self-attention and cross-attention In self-attention the queries, keys and values all come from the same sequence $X$ (shape $T \times d {\text{model}}$) through three learned linear layers: $Q = X W Q^\top$, $K = X W K^\top$, $V = X W V^\top$ in PyTorch's nn.Linear layout. Each position then reads from every position, itself included. In cross-attention the queries come from one sequence and the keys and values from another: a translation decoder's positions (queries) read the encoder's outputs (keys and values), so $n q \ne n k$ is normal (u16-l02). The function below also takes an optional boolean mask (True = this query may attend to this key); the Masks section explains it. In code, batch axes go in front: q is (B, n q, d k) , k is (B, n k, d k) , v is (B, n k, d v) . Swap the last two axes of k with k.transpose(-2, -1) ; .T would reverse every axis of a 3D tensor. The softmax runs over the keys, dim=-1 . Masks A mask removes some (query, key) pairs before the softmax. Set those scores to $-\infty$: then $e^{-\infty} = 0$, so their weights are exactly 0 and the remaining weights still sum to 1. Padding mask. Keys at padding positions (lesson 1) must get no weight. A (B, n k) mask with True at real tokens becomes mask[:, None, :] , shape (B, 1, n k) , which broadcasts over every query row of the (B, n q, n k) scores. Causal mask. A model that predicts the next token must not look ahead: position $i$ may attend to $j \le i$ only. The allowed pairs form the lower triangle, diagonal included: torch.tril keeps the lower triangle and torch.triu(..., diagonal=1) the part strictly above the diagonal; use whichever matches your masked fill . Three bugs to recognize: 1. Masking after the softmax. weights mask zeroes the right entries, but the rows no longer sum to 1, so every output shrinks toward 0. 2. Filling with 0 instead of $-\infty$. A score of 0 still gets weight $e^0 / \sum$, so masked positions leak in. 3. Off by one. torch.triu(..., diagonal=0) also blocks the diagonal. Then position 0 has no allowed key at all, its row is all $-\infty$, and softmax returns nan ($0/0$). Attention ignores order Shuffle the rows of $X$ and self-attention's outputs come out shuffled the same way, with the same values: nothing in $QK^\top$ knows which position is which. Self-attention is permutation equivariant : it treats the sequence as a set. "Dog bites man" and "man bites dog" get the same vectors, just in a different order. Lesson 5 adds position information to fix this. Cost For $n$ queries and $n$ keys, $QK^\top$ takes $n^2 d k$ multiply-adds and $AV$ takes $n^2 d v$, so time is $O(n^2 d)$, and the score matrix needs $n^2$ numbers of memory per head per sequence. At $n = 4096$ in float32 that is $4096^2 \cdot 4$ bytes $= 64$ MiB for one head of one sequence. The $n^2$ is what lesson 6 removes. Exam angle - Scale by $\sqrt{d k}$, the length of one query or key vector (the head size), not $d {\text{model}}$. - k.transpose(-2, -1) , softmax(dim=-1) , mask with masked fill(..., float("-inf")) before the softmax. - Sanity checks that catch most bugs: weights w.sum(-1) all 1; with a causal mask, changing a later token leaves earlier outputs unchanged; compare with F.scaled dot product attention on a small case when it is not banned (it takes is causal=True for the causal mask, or a boolean attn mask with True = may attend). Practice problem: u15-p01 Scaled dot-product attention with a mask (write it with the built-in banned, as Round 2 does).

Real transformers never run one attention; they run several side by side. The 2025 Round 2 Problem 2 was entirely about this: the weight shapes of multi-head attention , a module written without loops, then two variants that shrink memory (grouped-query and latent attention) and the size of the KV cache for each. The 2026 Problem 1 added a trap: its head size $d$ was not $d {\text{model}} / H$. This lesson builds the module with explicit shapes, counts its parameters, and works out the cache sizes. Several heads One attention gives each position one weighted average. Often a position needs several things at once, such as the previous word and the subject of the sentence. Multi-head attention runs $H$ attentions, called attention heads , in parallel, each with its own projections into a smaller space of size $d k$ (queries, keys) and $d v$ (values): The heads are concatenated side by side, $T \times H d v$, and an output projection $W O$ (shape $d {\text{model}} \times H d v$) maps back to $d {\text{model}}$. The usual choice $d k = d v = d {\text{model}} / H$ makes $H$ heads cost about the same as one head of full width. Shapes in code Nobody stores $H$ separate matrices. Stack every head's $W Q^{(h)}$ into one nn.Linear(d model, H d k) . Its output for each token is $H$ blocks of length $d k$, head 0 first. Two moves turn that into a batch of heads: 1. view(B, T, H, d k) splits each token's features into its $H$ blocks; 2. transpose(1, 2) gives (B, H, T, d k) , so the attention of lesson 3, written for (..., T, d k) , runs once per (batch, head) pair. Afterward, undo it: transpose(1, 2) back to (B, T, H, d v) , then reshape(B, T, H d v) ( view fails here because the transpose made the tensor non-contiguous), then $W O$. self.q(x).view(B, H, T, d k) has the right shape and is wrong. Memory holds token 0's $H d k$ features, then token 1's, and so on; reading that as (H, T, d k) makes "head 0" consist of token 0's first block, token 0's second block, ..., so features of different tokens get treated as different positions. Split the last axis first ( view(B, T, H, d k) ), then move heads forward with transpose . Counting parameters With biases, and writing $d = d {\text{model}}$: When $H d k = H d v = d$ this is $4d^2 + 4d$: nn.MultiheadAttention(512, 8) has $4 \cdot 512^2 + 4 \cdot 512 = 1{,}050{,}624$, and the number of heads does not matter. When the problem says not to assume $H d = d {\text{model}}$ (2026 P1), use the general form. The KV cache A language model generates one token at a time: run the model on the prompt, sample the next token, append it, run again. That is autoregressive generation . Under a causal mask, the keys and values of earlier positions never change when a token is appended, so recomputing them every step is waste. The KV cache stores every layer's keys and values; each new token computes only its own $q, k, v$, appends $k$ and $v$ to the cache, and attends over the cache. The cache holds keys and values (factor 2) for every layer, position, key/value head and head coordinate: With 32 layers, 32 heads of size 128, $T = 4096$ and 16-bit numbers (2 bytes), one sequence needs $2 \cdot 32 \cdot 4096 \cdot 32 \cdot 128 \cdot 2 = 2^{31}$ bytes, 2 GiB. Multiply by the batch size and the cache soon rivals the weights in memory, which is why the variants below exist. Multi-query and grouped-query attention Multi-query attention (MQA) keeps $H$ query heads but only one key head and one value head, shared by all of them: the cache shrinks by a factor of $H$. Grouped-query attention (GQA) sits in between: $G$ key/value heads, $G$ dividing $H$, and query head $h$ uses key/value head $\lfloor h / (H/G) \rfloor$, so consecutive groups of $H/G$ query heads share one. $G = H$ is ordinary MHA and $G = 1$ is MQA. Llama 2 70B, for example, has 64 query heads and 8 key/value heads. Only $W K$ and $W V$ shrink, to nn.Linear(d model, G d k) . In the forward pass, expand the $G$ heads to $H$ before attention with repeat interleave , which repeats each head $H/G$ times in a row: heads $0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1$ for $H = 8$, $G = 2$. ( repeat would give $0, 1, 0, 1, \dots$, a different assignment.) The cache stores the $G$ heads before expansion, so it is $H/G$ times smaller than MHA's. Multi-head latent attention Multi-head latent attention (MLA, from DeepSeek-V2) caches a compressed vector instead of keys and values. Each token's input $x t$ is projected down to a latent $c t = W {DKV}\, x t$ of small size $r$, and every head's key and value are projected back up from it: $k t^{(h)} = W {UK}^{(h)} c t$, $v t^{(h)} = W {UV}^{(h)} c t$. Only $c t$ goes in the cache: $r$ numbers per token per layer instead of $2 H d {\text{head}}$. The up-projections need not be applied at inference. A score is $q^{(h)\top} k t^{(h)} = q^{(h)\top} W {UK}^{(h)} c t = \big(W {UK}^{(h)\top} q^{(h)}\big)^\top c t$, so $W {UK}^{(h)}$ can be folded into the query projection and attention runs directly on the cached latents; in the same way $W {UV}^{(h)}$ folds into $W O$. The 2025 problem asked for exactly these folded matrices. DeepSeek-V2 caches 576 numbers per token per layer, where full MHA with its 128 heads of size 128 would cache $2 \cdot 128 \cdot 128 = 32{,}768$. Rotary position encodings (lesson 5) rotate queries and keys by a position-dependent matrix between $W {UK}$ and the dot product, so $W {UK}$ can no longer be folded into the query. DeepSeek-V2 therefore adds a small extra key part (64 numbers) that carries the rotation and is cached alongside the 512-number latent: $512 + 64 = 576$. per token, per layer cache size (numbers) --- --- MHA $2 H d {\text{head}}$ GQA with $G$ groups $2 G d {\text{head}}$ MQA $2 d {\text{head}}$ MLA $r$ (plus any position part) Exam angle - Shapes: (B, T, H d) - view(B, T, H, d) - transpose(1, 2) - (B, H, T, d) , and back with transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, H d) . - Parameters: $4d^2 + 4d$ only when $H d k = H d v = d$; otherwise count each projection. - Cache: $2 \times$ layers $\times$ tokens $\times$ KV heads $\times$ head size $\times$ bytes. Read whether the problem counts per token, per layer, or in total. Practice problem: u15-p02 Multi-head self-attention from scratch (head size not tied to d model , padding and causal masks, a parameter-count test).

Lesson 3 showed that self-attention is permutation equivariant: shuffle the tokens and the outputs shuffle with them, so without help a transformer cannot tell "dog bites man" from "man bites dog". A positional encoding puts position information back. The 2026 Round 2 Problem 1 asked you to add a learned relative encoding to the attention scores, count its parameters and initialize it; most current language models use the rotary encoding at the end of this lesson. There are four main designs, and each is a few lines of tensor code. Learned absolute positions The simplest fix: a second embedding table indexed by position, added to the token embeddings. This is a learned positional embedding , used by BERT (512 positions) and GPT-2 (1024). It costs max len d parameters and has no vector at all for position max len , so the model cannot run on longer inputs. Sinusoidal encoding The original transformer used fixed vectors instead. For position $p$ and pair index $i = 0, \dots, d/2 - 1$: Pair 0 turns fastest ($\omega 0 = 1$, wavelength $2\pi$ positions); the last pair turns slowest (wavelength close to $10000 \cdot 2\pi$). For $d = 4$: $\omega 0 = 1$, $\omega 1 = 10000^{-1/2} = 0.01$, and position 1 gets $(\sin 1, \cos 1, \sin 0.01, \cos 0.01) = (0.841, 0.540, 0.010, 1.000)$. The vector is added to the token embeddings, like the learned version, but has no parameters and exists for every $p$. Why sines and cosines? Each pair $(\sin p\omega i, \cos p\omega i)$ is a point on a circle at angle $p\omega i$. Moving $k$ positions rotates it by the angle $k\omega i$, and a rotation is a fixed linear map: The matrix depends on the offset $k$ and not on $p$, so "the token 3 places back" is the same linear function of the encoding at every position, which a linear layer can learn. The table is fixed, so store it with register buffer (buffer, u10-l03): it moves with .to(device) and never trains. Relative positions in the scores For many tasks, what matters is how far apart two tokens are, not where they sit: in a sensor signal a spike two steps before another means the same at step 10 and at step 400. A relative positional encoding puts the offset $j - i$ into the score between query $i$ and key $j$. The 2026 problem used this form (from Shaw et al., 2018): with one learned vector $r \delta \in \mathbb{R}^d$ per offset $\delta$. For positions $0, \dots, T-1$ the offset $j - i$ ranges over $-(T-1), \dots, T-1$: that is $2T - 1$ vectors, $(2T - 1)\,d$ parameters per table. To use them, build the matrix of offsets, shift it to start at 0, and look the vectors up: The (T, T, d) tensor R is the cost: memory grows like $T^2 d$. Cheaper relatives add one learned number per offset instead of a vector: T5 adds a scalar bias $b {j-i}$ per head to each score (sharing one value among far offsets), and ALiBi adds $-m\, i - j $ with a fixed slope $m$ per head, a penalty that grows with distance and needs no parameters. Because a bias depends only on the offset, both still work on sequences longer than those seen in training, where a learned absolute table cannot (extrapolation). Rotary position embedding (RoPE) RoPE makes the score depend on $j - i$ without adding anything. Split a query or key vector $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ into pairs $(x {2i}, x {2i+1})$ and rotate pair $i$ of the vector at position $m$ by the angle $m\theta i$, with $\theta i = 10000^{-2i/d}$ as before: Write $R m$ for the $d \times d$ block-diagonal matrix of these rotations, so the rotated query is $R m q$ and the rotated key at position $n$ is $R n k$. Rotations satisfy $R(\alpha)^\top = R(-\alpha)$ and $R(\alpha)R(\beta) = R(\alpha + \beta)$, block by block, so The score depends on the positions only through the signed offset $n - m$. (In complex numbers: pair $i$ is $z = x {2i} + \mathrm{i}\,x {2i+1}$, the rotation multiplies it by $e^{\mathrm{i} m\theta i}$, and the score is the real part of $z q \bar z k\, e^{\mathrm{i}(m - n)\theta i}$.) RoPE has no parameters, is applied to $q$ and $k$ in every layer after the projections (never to $v$), and keeps every vector's length. The paper pairs neighbors $(x 0, x 1), (x 2, x 3), \dots$ as above. Hugging Face's Llama code pairs $x i$ with $x {i + d/2}$ (the "rotate half" layout). Both give the relative property; they are different functions, so a model must use the same one for queries and keys and the one its pretrained weights were trained with. Swapping layouts, or rotating $q$ but not $k$, runs without error and breaks the model. Comparison method parameters where it enters longer inputs than training --- --- --- --- learned absolute max len d added to the input no sinusoidal none (buffer) added to the input defined, often weak relative vectors $r {j-i}$ $(2T-1)\,d$ inside every score only up to the trained offsets T5 bias, ALiBi few or none added to every score yes RoPE none rotates $q$ and $k$ partly, with tricks Exam angle - Sinusoidal: exponent $2i/d$ (pair index times 2), sine on even columns, cosine on odd. - Offsets $j - i$ run from $-(T-1)$ to $T-1$: $2T - 1$ values; index with offset + T - 1 . - RoPE: same rotation for $q$ and $k$, none for $v$; check with the test in the cell above (equal scores at equal offsets). Practice problems: u15-p03 Sinusoidal positional encoding as a buffer and u15-p04 Rotary position embedding (RoPE) .

The 2026 Round 2 opened with a 90-point problem titled "Linear Attention Is All You Need" (official PDF). It asked for the cost of attention, a rewrite of attention through a feature map, the cost of that rewrite, why the exponential cannot be written exactly that way, an explicit feature map from a truncated Taylor series, and then a module built on the feature map $1 + \mathrm{ELU}$. This lesson derives every one of those steps. They follow from one fact: matrix products can be grouped either way. The cost of softmax attention Take $Q, K, V \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times d}$ (one head, $d k = d v = d$). Computing $\operatorname{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d})\,V$ takes three steps: 1. $QK^\top$: $T^2$ dot products of length $d$, so $T^2 d$ multiply-adds; 2. softmax of each of the $T$ rows of length $T$: $O(T^2)$; 3. the $T \times T$ weights times $V$: $T^2 d$. Total time $O(T^2 d)$, and the $T \times T$ matrix takes $O(T^2)$ memory. Doubling the sequence length quadruples both. Attention through a feature map Write the unnormalized weight as a similarity, $\operatorname{sim}(q, k) = \exp(q^\top k / \sqrt{d})$. Then output $i$ (as a row vector) is Now suppose the similarity were a dot product of features: $\operatorname{sim}(q, k) = \phi(q)^\top \phi(k)$ for some feature map $\phi: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^\ell$. The factor $\phi(q i)^\top$ does not depend on $j$, so it moves out of both sums: $S$ and $z$ are the same for every query, so they are computed once. Stack the features as rows, $\phi(Q), \phi(K) \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times \ell}$. Then $S = \phi(K)^\top V$ and $z = \phi(K)^\top \mathbf{1}$, and Softmax attention computes $\big(\phi(Q)\phi(K)^\top\big)V$ in effect: a $T \times T$ matrix first. Linear attention computes $\phi(Q)\big(\phi(K)^\top V\big)$: an $\ell \times d$ matrix first. Matrix multiplication is associative, so the two are equal, but the costs differ: step multiply-adds --- --- $\phi(K)^\top V$ $T \ell d$ $\phi(Q)\, S$ $T \ell d$ denominators $T \ell$ (twice) Time $O(T \ell d)$, linear in $T$, and extra memory $O(\ell d)$ beyond the inputs, which does not grow with $T$ at all. It pays when $T$ is larger than $\ell$. This is the kernel trick (u08-l04) run backward: an SVM uses a kernel to avoid computing $\phi$; here computing $\phi$ avoids the $T \times T$ matrix. Why the exponential needs infinitely many features Expand $\exp$ in its Taylor series with $x = q^\top k / \sqrt{d}$: $\exp(x) = \sum {r \ge 0} x^r / r!$. Each power is itself a dot product: the dot product of two vectors of length $d^r$ that list every product of $r$ coordinates. So $\exp(q^\top k/\sqrt{d})$ is a dot product of feature vectors containing the products of every degree $r = 0, 1, 2, \dots$, each scaled by $1/\sqrt{r!\, d^{r/2}}$: infinitely many features, so $\ell = \infty$. Stopping at any degree drops the higher terms, which are not zero for general $q$ and $k$; the box below shows that no other finite feature map can be exact either. If $\exp(q^\top k / \sqrt d) = \phi(q)^\top \phi(k)$ with $\phi$ into $\mathbb{R}^\ell$, then for any $n$ queries and $n$ keys the $n \times n$ matrix $M {ij} = \exp(q i^\top k j/\sqrt d)$ equals $\phi(Q)\phi(K)^\top$, whose rank is at most $\ell$. Take $q i = a i e 1$ and $k j = \sqrt{d}\, b j e 1$ for distinct numbers $a 1 < \dots < a n$ and $b 1 < \dots < b n$: then $M {ij} = e^{a i b j}$, and this matrix is invertible for every $n$ (the kernel $e^{ab}$ is strictly totally positive, so its determinant is positive). Rank $n$ for every $n$ needs $\ell \ge n$ for every $n$. A finite feature map from the Taylor series Keep three terms: $\exp(x) \approx 1 + x + x^2/2$. Each term is a dot product: where $\operatorname{vec}(qq^\top)$ lists all $d^2$ products $q a q b$, because $\sum {a,b} q a q b k a k b = (q^\top k)^2$. Concatenate: The products $q a q b$ and $q b q a$ are equal, so you can keep each unordered pair once (multiplying the $a \ne b$ entries by $\sqrt 2$) and get $\ell = 1 + d + d(d+1)/2$. Either way $\ell$ grows like $d^2$: for $d = 64$ it is 4161 (or 2145), so this feature map beats softmax only for sequences longer than that. A useful fact: $1 + x + x^2/2 = \tfrac12\big((x+1)^2 + 1\big) 0$ for every $x$, so the weights stay positive. Positive feature maps: 1 + ELU The weights $\phi(q i)^\top\phi(k j)$ play the role of softmax numerators, so they should be nonnegative, and the denominator must stay away from 0 or the division blows up. Katharopoulos et al. (2020) used $\phi$ is $x + 1$ for $x \ge 0$ and $e^x$ for $x < 0$: always positive, smooth, and cheap. It does not approximate $\exp(q^\top k/\sqrt d)$; it defines a different similarity that trains well, at cost $O(T d^2)$. In PyTorch it is F.elu(x) + 1 or nn.ELU()(x) + 1 . Causal linear attention is an RNN With a causal mask, query $i$ sums only over $j \le i$: These are prefix sums, so $S i = S {i-1} + \phi(k i)\, v i^\top$ and $z i = z {i-1} + \phi(k i)$. That is a recurrent network (lesson 2) whose hidden state is the $\ell \times d$ matrix $S i$ and the vector $z i$. Generating a token costs $O(\ell d)$ and the state never grows, while softmax attention's KV cache (lesson 4) grows by one key and one value per token. For training, compute all prefix sums at once: form the $T$ outer products $\phi(k j) v j^\top$ as a (B, T, ℓ, d) tensor and take cumsum over the time axis.
