Memory is $O(T \ell d)$, still linear in $T$. A loop over $t$ that keeps only the current $S$ uses $O(\ell d)$ memory, at the price of $T$ sequential steps. Here masking by multiplying is correct, unlike lesson 3: these weights are not exponentiated scores, so zeroing $W {ij}$ for $j i$ and then dividing by the row sum is exactly the causal formula. Two bugs to recognize: using the exclusive prefix sum $S {i-1}$ (each token cannot see itself, and token 0 divides $0/0$), and dividing by the full $z = \sum {\text{all } j} \phi(k j)$ instead of $z i$ (the denominator then counts future keys). Relative positions inside linear attention The 2026 problem then asked how a relative positional encoding fits this framework. The rule: the $O(T)$ trick needs every weight to factor as (something of $i$)$^\top$(something of $j$), so that the $j$-part can be summed in advance. A term like $q i^\top r {j-i}$ couples $i$ and $j$ through the offset and does not factor; computing it for every pair brings back the $T^2$. Options that keep linear cost: - Rotate the features. Apply RoPE (lesson 5) to $\phi(q i)$ and $\phi(k j)$ in the numerator only: $(R i \phi(q i))^\top (R j \phi(k j)) = \phi(q i)^\top R {j-i}\, \phi(k j)$ depends on the offset, and each factor depends on one position, so prefix sums still work. The denominator stays unrotated so it stays positive (the RoFormer paper does this). - Limit the offsets. If $r \delta = 0$ for $ \delta w$, the extra term touches only $T(2w+1)$ pairs: cost $O(T w d)$. Exam angle - Softmax attention: time $O(T^2 d)$, memory $O(T^2)$. Linear attention: time $O(T \ell d)$, memory $O(\ell d)$ beyond the inputs (or $O(T\ell d)$ with cumsum ). - Second-order Taylor features: $\ell = 1 + d + d^2$ (or $1 + d + d(d+1)/2$ without duplicates); $1 + \mathrm{ELU}$: $\ell = d$. - Causal form: inclusive prefix sums of $\phi(k j) v j^\top$ and $\phi(k j)$; check against a masked $T \times T$ reference on a small input. Practice problems, one three-part chain adapted from the 2026 problem: u15-p05 (feature maps), u15-p06 (attention in linear time, no $T \times T$ matrix allowed) and u15-p07 (causal attention with prefix sums, and the one-step recurrence).

A transformer is one block repeated: attention, then a small MLP, each wrapped in a residual connection and a layer norm. The 2026 Round 2 Problem 1 ended with "build an encoder-only transformer from scratch" with nn.TransformerEncoder banned, and Round 2 items ask for parameter counts of such blocks with every bias and layer norm included. This lesson assembles the block from the parts of u15 and u11, explains the two places the layer norm can go, and counts a whole GPT-2. The block Let $x$ be the input, shape (B, T, d) with $d = d {\text{model}}$. The transformer block used by almost every current model is - Multi-head attention (u15-l04) is the only step that mixes positions. With a causal mask the block is a decoder block; without one, an encoder block. - The position-wise MLP applies the same two-layer network to every position separately: nn.Linear(d, d ff) , GELU, nn.Linear(d ff, d) , usually with $d {\text{ff}} = 4d$. It is where most of the parameters are. - The two residual connections mean each sublayer only adds an update to $x$. The running sum that flows from block to block, $x$ plus every update so far, is often called the residual stream . - Layer norm (u11-l09) normalizes each token's $d$ features, so every sublayer sees inputs of a steady size. - Dropout, when used, is applied to each sublayer's output just before it is added to the stream. Every step keeps the shape (B, T, d) , so blocks stack: a model is an embedding, $L$ blocks, a final layer norm, and an output layer. Pre-norm and post-norm The original 2017 transformer put the layer norm after the addition, $h = \operatorname{LN}(x + \operatorname{MHA}(x))$. That is post-norm . The form above, with the norm inside the branch, is pre-norm (GPT-2 and most later models). The difference is the path from the output back to the input. In pre-norm, $y = x + (\text{update} 1) + (\text{update} 2)$, and stacking $L$ blocks gives $x L = x 0 + \sum l (\text{updates of block } l)$: an identity path runs from the last block to the first, so $\partial x L / \partial x 0 = I + (\text{other terms})$ and gradients reach early layers directly. In post-norm every path passes through $L$ layer norms, each of which rescales. In practice post-norm needs a careful learning-rate warmup and becomes hard to train as $L$ grows, while pre-norm is far less sensitive to the warmup and the learning rate. Pre-norm models need one extra layer norm after the last block, because the stream itself is never normalized. Code nn.TransformerEncoderLayer builds this block, and a Round 2 problem will ban it, so know what is inside. The cell writes the pre-norm forward pass by hand with the layer's own submodules and checks it against the layer: The practice problem asks for the same block with your own attention module (u15-p02) in place of self attn . Counting parameters With biases everywhere and $d {\text{ff}} = 4d$: part parameters --- --- attention: $W Q, W K, W V, W O$ with biases $4d^2 + 4d$ MLP: Linear(d, 4d) and Linear(4d, d) $(4d^2 + 4d) + (4d^2 + d) = 8d^2 + 5d$ two layer norms ($\gamma$ and $\beta$ each) $4d$ block $12d^2 + 13d$ The MLP holds two thirds of the weights. For general $d {\text{ff}}$ the MLP is $2 d\, d {\text{ff}} + d {\text{ff}} + d$. For $d = 768$ the block has $12 \cdot 768^2 + 13 \cdot 768 = 7{,}087{,}872$ parameters, exactly one layer of BERT-base or GPT-2 small. A whole GPT-2 GPT-2 small has a vocabulary of $V = 50{,}257$ tokens, 1024 learned positions, $d = 768$, $L = 12$ blocks and a final layer norm. Its output layer maps $d$ to $V$ logits, and it reuses the token embedding matrix as that layer's weight, so it adds no parameters. Sharing one matrix between the input embedding and the output layer is weight tying . In code it is one assignment, lm head.weight = tok.weight : nn.Linear(d, V, bias=False).weight and nn.Embedding(V, d).weight both have shape (V, d) . That is the "124M" in its name. Almost a third of it is the embedding table. A useful rule: the blocks hold about $12 L d^2$ parameters. Exam angle - Pre-norm: x = x + attn(ln1(x)); x = x + mlp(ln2(x)) , plus a final layer norm. Post-norm: x = ln1(x + attn(x)); x = ln2(x + mlp(x)) . - Block parameters $12d^2 + 13d$ when $d {\text{ff}} = 4d$; otherwise $4d^2 + 4d + 2d\,d {\text{ff}} + d {\text{ff}} + d + 4d$. Read whether the output layer is tied. - A list of blocks must be an nn.ModuleList ; [Block()] L repeats one block (shared weights). Practice problem: u16-p01 A pre-norm transformer block from scratch .

The same block from lesson 1 builds three kinds of model, and they differ in only two things: which attention mask they use and what they are trained to predict. Round 2 relies on knowing which is which. The 2025 CLIP problem took BERT's output at the [CLS] position as a sentence vector, the 2026 problem built an encoder-only classifier, and the IOAI syllabus lists BERT-style encoders, language modeling and encoder-decoder models by name. This lesson gives the three families, their training objectives in code, and the masks each one needs. Three families encoder-only decoder-only encoder-decoder --- --- --- --- examples BERT, RoBERTa GPT-2, Llama original transformer, T5, BART self-attention mask padding only (bidirectional) causal + padding encoder: padding; decoder: causal + padding extra sublayer none none cross-attention in every decoder block trained to fill in masked tokens predict the next token produce an output sequence from an input sequence used for classification, tagging, embeddings generating text translation, summarization An encoder-only model lets every position see every other position, so each output vector describes its token in the context of the whole input. A decoder-only model uses the causal mask, so it can generate one token at a time. An encoder-decoder model reads the input with an encoder, then generates the output with a decoder whose blocks also attend to the encoder's outputs. BERT: masked language modeling You cannot train a bidirectional model to predict the next token: it would see the answer. BERT (bidirectional encoder representations from transformers) is trained by masked language modeling (MLM) instead: hide some input tokens and predict them from both sides. 1. Choose 15% of the positions at random, never special tokens or padding. 2. Of the chosen positions, replace 80% by [MASK] , 10% by a random token, and leave 10% unchanged. 3. The loss is cross-entropy at the chosen positions only. Why not always [MASK] ? That token never appears when the model is later fine-tuned on real text, so the model would learn that only [MASK] positions need a good prediction. Random and unchanged tokens force it to build a useful vector for every token. The original BERT also had a next sentence prediction task (does sentence B follow sentence A, predicted from [CLS] ); RoBERTa (BERT retrained on more data without this task) did better. "Loss at the chosen positions only" is written with a label of $-100$ everywhere else: nn.CrossEntropyLoss (and F.cross entropy ) skip targets equal to ignore index , which defaults to $-100$, and average over the rest. The shares come out close to 15%, 80% and 10%. (A random replacement occasionally draws the original token, which then also counts as unchanged.) For classification, BERT puts [CLS] first (u15-l01); after fine-tuning, its output vector feeds a linear head. Masked mean pooling over the real tokens is the common alternative. GPT: next-token prediction A GPT (generative pretrained transformer) is decoder-only and trained by next-token prediction : at every position, predict the token that comes next. With the causal mask, one forward pass on a sequence of length $T$ makes $T$ predictions at once, each using only earlier tokens. In code the targets are the inputs shifted by one: reshape(-1, V) stacks all $B(T-1)$ positions as rows, because F.cross entropy wants logits (N, V) and targets (N,) . Feeding the true earlier tokens during training, instead of the model's own guesses, is called teacher forcing . Lesson 4 covers the loss in detail and how to generate. Encoder-decoders and T5 The decoder of an encoder-decoder has three sublayers per block: causal self-attention over the output so far, cross-attention (u15-l03) whose queries come from the decoder and whose keys and values are the encoder's final outputs, and the MLP. Cross-attention uses the encoder's padding mask and no causal mask: the whole input is known. Counting with three layer norms and $d {\text{ff}} = 4d$: per decoder block. Training is teacher forcing on (input, output) pairs: the decoder reads the true output shifted right, starting from a start token. T5 (text-to-text transfer transformer) casts every task as text in, text out ("translate English to German: ...", "summarize: ..."). Its pretraining objective is span corruption : drop random spans of the input (15% of tokens, spans of about 3 tokens), put a sentinel token in place of each span, and train the decoder to output each sentinel followed by the tokens it replaced: The target is short (only the dropped spans), which makes pretraining cheap. Exam angle - Encoder: bidirectional, MLM with 15% chosen and 80/10/10, labels $-100$ elsewhere. Decoder: causal, next token, targets ids[:, 1:] . Encoder-decoder: cross-attention, T5 span corruption with sentinels. - F.cross entropy wants (N, V) and (N,) : reshape (B, T, V) first. ignore index=-100 is the default. - Decoder block of an encoder-decoder: $16d^2 + 19d$ parameters ($d {\text{ff}} = 4d$, with biases and three layer norms).

A vision transformer (ViT) runs the encoder of lessons 1 and 2 on an image by cutting the image into square patches and treating each patch as a token. The 2025 Round 2 CLIP problem used the pretrained google/vit-base-patch16-224 as its image encoder, and the IOAI syllabus lists "patching" under data processing. You should be able to patchify an image with reshape and permute , show that the patch embedding is a convolution, and count a ViT's tokens and parameters. From an image to tokens Take an image of shape (C, H, W) (channels first, u12-l08) and a patch size $P$ that divides $H$ and $W$. A patch is one $P \times P$ square across all channels. There are patches, each with $C P^2$ numbers. ViT-B/16 on a $224 \times 224$ RGB image uses $P = 16$: $N = 14 \cdot 14 = 196$ patches of $3 \cdot 256 = 768$ numbers. Patchify with two reshapes and a permute. Split each spatial axis into (patch index, offset within the patch), move the two patch indices to the front, then flatten: The order inside each patch vector is channel, then row, then column: exactly the order in which a convolution weight of shape (d, C, P, P) flattens. That matters in the next step. The patch embedding is a convolution Each patch vector is mapped to $d$ numbers by one shared linear layer, the patch embedding $E \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times CP^2}$ with bias $b$. Compare with nn.Conv2d(C, d, kernel size=P, stride=P) : with stride equal to the kernel size, the windows tile the image without overlap, one window per patch, and output channel $o$ at patch $(r, s)$ is a dot product of the flattened kernel K[o] with that patch's vector. So the convolution equals the linear layer with $E$ = K.reshape(d, -1) , and in code a ViT's patch embedding is usually a Conv2d followed by flatten(2).transpose(1, 2) : The rest of the model 1. Class token. A learned vector cls of shape (1, 1, d) is prepended to the patch tokens, giving $N + 1$ tokens. Like BERT's [CLS] (lesson 2), its final vector summarizes the image. Many newer models drop it and average the patch tokens instead. 2. Positions. A learned position embedding of shape (1, N + 1, d) is added (learned positional embedding, u15-l05). Without it the model would see a bag of patches. 3. Encoder. $L$ pre-norm blocks with no mask: every patch attends to every patch. 4. Head. A final layer norm, then nn.Linear(d, num classes) on the class token's output. Counting ViT-B/16 ($d = 768$, 12 blocks, $d {\text{ff}} = 3072$, 1000 classes): part parameters --- --- patch embedding Conv2d(3, 768, 16, stride=16) $3 \cdot 16^2 \cdot 768 + 768 = 590{,}592$ class token $768$ position embedding, $197$ tokens $197 \cdot 768 = 151{,}296$ 12 blocks, $12d^2 + 13d$ each $85{,}054{,}464$ final layer norm $1{,}536$ head Linear(768, 1000) $769{,}000$ total $86{,}567{,}656$ At a different resolution the patch count changes: $384 \times 384$ with $P = 16$ gives $24^2 = 576$ patches, 577 tokens. The weights still apply, except the position table, which is resized to the new grid by 2D interpolation when a model is fine-tuned at the higher resolution. ViT versus CNN A CNN builds two assumptions into its architecture: each output looks only at a small neighborhood (local connectivity), and the same kernel is used everywhere (translation equivariance). Such built-in assumptions are called an inductive bias . A ViT has much less: after the patch embedding, any patch can attend to any other from the first layer, and it must learn from data that nearby patches matter. The consequences: - Data. Trained only on ImageNet's 1.3 million images, the original ViT did worse than a ResNet of similar size; pretrained on 14 to 300 million images it did better. With strong augmentation, regularization and knowledge distillation (the DeiT recipe), a ViT trains well on ImageNet alone. - Cost. Attention costs $O(N^2 d)$ with $N = HW / P^2$. Halving $P$ makes $N$ four times larger and the attention cost sixteen times larger, so patch size is the main speed knob. - Global context. One attention layer relates opposite corners of the image; a CNN needs many layers to grow its receptive field that far. For small images and small datasets (a Round 2 task with a few thousand training images and no pretrained weights, like 2026 Problem 4), a small CNN is usually the stronger first try. Exam angle - $N = HW/P^2$ patches, $CP^2$ numbers each, plus 1 class token. - Patchify: reshape(B, C, H//P, P, W//P, P).permute(0, 2, 4, 1, 3, 5).reshape(B, N, C P P) ; patch embedding = Conv2d(C, d, P, stride=P) then flatten(2).transpose(1, 2) . - Parameters: patch embedding $CP^2 d + d$, class token $d$, positions $(N + 1)d$, then the blocks. Practice problem: u16-p02 Patchify and the patch embedding .

A language model assigns a probability to the next token given the tokens so far. Training it is the cross-entropy of lesson 2; using it means decoding : turning those probabilities into actual text, one token at a time. The IOAI syllabus lists language modeling as a core topic, and Round 2 items can ask you to apply a temperature, top-k or top-p to a small distribution by hand. This lesson covers the loss and its usual summary, perplexity, then each decoding rule with worked numbers and code. The loss and perplexity For a sequence $x 0, \dots, x {T-1}$ a causal model outputs, at each position $t$, a distribution $p \theta(\cdot \mid x {\le t})$ over the vocabulary of size $V$. The training loss is the average negative log-likelihood of the true next tokens: averaged over the batch too. It is reported as perplexity , $e^{\mathcal{L}}$ (with natural logs). A model that spreads its probability evenly over $k$ tokens at every step has $\mathcal{L} = \log k$ and perplexity $k$, so perplexity reads as "how many tokens the model is choosing between". Two checks follow: - At initialization, logits near 0 give the uniform distribution, so the first loss should be close to $\log V$: $\log 50{,}257 = 10.82$ for GPT-2's vocabulary. A much larger first loss means a bug (often logits that are too large). - A character model's loss is often quoted in bits per character , $\mathcal{L} / \ln 2$. Generating text Generation is a loop: run the model on the tokens so far, take the logits at the last position, pick a token, append it, repeat until an end token or a length limit. With a KV cache (u15-l04) each step only processes the new token. The decoding rule is the "pick a token" step. Greedy decoding takes the argmax. It is deterministic, and it tends to repeat itself: once it is in a loop, the most likely continuation is often the loop again. Picking the best token at each step also need not give the most likely sequence. Beam search keeps the $b$ best partial sequences by total log-probability at every step; it is standard for translation, where there is one right answer, and less used for open-ended text. Sampling draws the next token at random from the model's distribution, torch.multinomial(probs, 1, generator=g) . Three knobs reshape the distribution first, in this order (the order Hugging Face uses). Temperature Divide the logits by a temperature $\tau 0$ before the softmax: $p i = \operatorname{softmax}(z / \tau) i$. For logits $z = (2, 1, 0)$: $\tau$ probabilities --- --- 0.5 $(0.867, 0.117, 0.016)$ 1 $(0.665, 0.245, 0.090)$ 2 $(0.506, 0.307, 0.186)$ $\tau 1$ flattens it. Top-k Top-k sampling keeps the $k$ tokens with the largest logits, sets the rest to $-\infty$, and renormalizes with the softmax. It cuts off the long tail of unlikely tokens, each tiny but many in total. With $k = 2$ on the logits above at $\tau = 1$: keep $(2, 1)$ and get $(0.731, 0.269, 0)$. Top-p (nucleus) A fixed $k$ is too many when the model is sure and too few when it is not. Top-p sampling (nucleus sampling) keeps the smallest set of most likely tokens whose total probability reaches $p$: 1. sort the probabilities in decreasing order; 2. keep tokens until the running total is at least $p$, including the token that crosses $p$; 3. renormalize the kept probabilities. Probabilities $(0.5, 0.2, 0.15, 0.1, 0.05)$, already sorted. Running totals: $0.5, 0.7, 0.85, \dots$. The total first reaches 0.8 at the third token, so keep three and renormalize by 0.85: $(0.588, 0.235, 0.176, 0, 0)$. In code, the rule "keep the token that crosses $p$" is easiest with the exclusive running total (the total of the tokens before each one): remove a token when that total is already at least $p$. The first token always survives, because its exclusive total is 0. z < kth keeps every token tied with the $k$-th largest, so a tie can keep more than $k$ tokens; problem statements usually say what to do. Apply temperature before top-p: a higher temperature flattens the distribution, so the nucleus holds more tokens. Swapping the two gives a different distribution. A decoding loop A real model is not needed to see the behavior. Below, the "model" is a fixed random table of next-token logits (a bigram model: the next token depends only on the current one). Greedy decoding falls into a cycle; sampling with a temperature and top-p wanders. Exam angle - Perplexity $= e^{\text{mean NLL}}$; uniform over $V$ gives $V$; first loss of a fresh model $\approx \log V$. - Order: temperature, then top-k, then top-p, then sample. Top-p keeps the token that crosses $p$; renormalize after filtering. - Seed with a torch.Generator passed to torch.multinomial(..., generator=g) so results are reproducible without touching the global seed. Practice problems: u16-p03 Top-k and top-p sampling and u16-p05 Train a tiny character-level language model .

Almost nobody trains a transformer from random weights for a real task. A model is first pretrained on a huge unlabeled corpus with a self-supervised objective (lesson 2), then adapted to the task with a much smaller labeled set. The IOAI syllabus lists "fine-tuning (full and parameter-efficient)", and the 2025 Round 2 CLIP problem froze pretrained ViT and BERT encoders and trained only small projection layers. This lesson compares the ways to adapt a model, then builds LoRA , the most common parameter-efficient method, and counts its parameters. Three ways to adapt a pretrained model 1. Linear probe. Freeze the whole pretrained model and train only a new head on its features (u10-l09). Cheap and hard to overfit, but the features cannot change. 2. Full fine-tuning. Train every parameter, starting from the pretrained values, with a small learning rate (for BERT typically $2 \times 10^{-5}$ to $5 \times 10^{-5}$, for a few epochs). Usually the most accurate. On a small dataset it can overfit, and pushed too far the model loses what it knew before ( catastrophic forgetting ). 3. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). Keep the pretrained weights frozen and train a small number of new parameters inserted into the model. Options include adapters (small bottleneck MLPs added inside each block), prompt tuning (learned vectors prepended to the input sequence), and LoRA below. Why bother with the third? Memory. Training with Adam keeps, for every trained parameter, the parameter, its gradient, and Adam's two running averages (Adam, u11-l07): 16 bytes per parameter in float32. Full fine-tuning of a 7-billion-parameter model therefore needs about $7 \times 10^9 \cdot 16 = 112$ GB before counting activations. With PEFT the frozen weights need no gradients or optimizer state, and a single copy of the base model can serve many tasks, each with its own small set of extra weights. LoRA LoRA (low-rank adaptation) freezes a weight matrix $W \in \mathbb{R}^{d {\text{out}} \times d {\text{in}}}$ and learns an update of rank at most $r$: - Parameters. $r(d {\text{in}} + d {\text{out}})$ per adapted matrix instead of $d {\text{in}} d {\text{out}}$. For a $4096 \times 4096$ projection with $r = 8$: $8 \cdot 8192 = 65{,}536$ instead of $16{,}777{,}216$, about 0.4%. Applied to $W Q$ and $W V$ in each of 32 layers, that is $32 \cdot 2 \cdot 65{,}536 = 4{,}194{,}304$ trained parameters for a 7-billion-parameter model. - Initialization. $A$ starts random and $B$ starts at zero, so $BA = 0$ and the adapted model starts exactly equal to the pretrained one. Both cannot start at zero: the gradients are $\partial L/\partial B = \tfrac{\alpha}{r}\, g\,(Ax)^\top$ and $\partial L/\partial A = \tfrac{\alpha}{r}\, B^\top g\, x^\top$ (with $g = \partial L/\partial h$), and if $A = B = 0$ both vanish forever. With $B = 0$ and $A$ random, the first step moves only $B$; after that both train. - Scale. The factor $\alpha/r$ (with $\alpha$ a constant such as 16) keeps the size of the update roughly the same when you change $r$, so the learning rate does not need retuning. - Compute order. Multiply $x$ by $A$ first: $B(Ax)$ costs $r(d {\text{in}} + d {\text{out}})$ per token, while forming $BA$ would cost $d {\text{in}} d {\text{out}} r$. - Merging. After training, replace $W$ by $W + \tfrac{\alpha}{r} BA$. The model is then an ordinary model with no extra inference cost. The LoRA paper's finding is that the change fine-tuning makes to a weight matrix is close to low rank, so small $r$ (4 to 16) loses little accuracy. The printout shows that the first step changed B but not A : $A$'s gradient contains the factor $B = 0$. The frozen base.weight and base.bias never change. A frozen parameter has requires grad=False , so its .grad stays None , and PyTorch's optimizers skip parameters whose gradient is None , even if you passed them in. Passing only the trainable ones, as above, is still the clean habit: it makes the count of optimized parameters obvious and avoids surprises if something later sets a gradient. Libraries Hugging Face's peft library wraps this pattern. It is not needed in a from-scratch Round 2 problem, but the IOAI environment ships it: target modules names the nn.Linear submodules to adapt ( "query" , "value" in BERT; "q proj" , "v proj" in Llama). QLoRA goes one step further and stores the frozen base weights in 4 bits, so a large model fits on one GPU while A and B train in higher precision. Exam angle - LoRA parameters: $r(d {\text{in}} + d {\text{out}})$ per matrix, times matrices per layer, times layers. Biases of the base layer stay frozen. - $B = 0$, $A$ random; output unchanged at the start; first step updates only $B$. - Full fine-tuning with Adam in float32: 16 bytes per parameter (weight, gradient, two moments). Practice problem: u16-p04 A LoRA linear layer .

The Hugging Face transformers library holds the pretrained models used in practice: BERT, GPT-2, ViT, T5 and thousands more. Round 2 has gone both ways on it. The 2025 CLIP problem loaded bert-base-uncased and google/vit-base-patch16-224 from it; the 2026 shape-classification problem banned every pretrained model, from torchvision or Hugging Face, on pain of 0 points. The IOAI contest machines ship transformers , datasets and peft with no internet for new downloads. So you need the API in your fingers, and you need to know how to work offline. Every cell below builds tiny models from configurations, so nothing is downloaded. Loading pretrained models The Auto classes read a model's configuration and pick the right class: from pretrained downloads the files once into a cache (by default ~/.cache/huggingface/hub ) and reads them from there afterward. Offline, set the environment variable HF HUB OFFLINE=1 or pass local files only=True : the call then uses the cache or fails at once instead of trying the network. You can also pass a folder path: model.save pretrained("ckpt") writes the weights and config, and AutoModel.from pretrained("ckpt") reads them back. A pipeline bundles tokenizer, model and post-processing for quick use, pipeline("sentiment-analysis")("great movie") , but hides the tensors, so in a from-scratch problem you will call the pieces yourself. The classification model above gets a fresh, randomly initialized head; the library warns that some weights are "newly initialized". That is expected: the head must be trained. Tokenizers A tokenizer call returns a dict of tensors. For BERT: input ids , token type ids (which sentence each token belongs to, for sentence pairs) and the attention mask of u15-l01. The arguments to remember are padding=True (pad to the longest in the batch), truncation=True with max length , and return tensors="pt" . Here is a BERT WordPiece tokenizer built from a 14-word vocabulary: [CLS] and [SEP] are added automatically, the text is lowercased (this is an "uncased" vocabulary), "playing" becomes play + ing , and an unknown word becomes [UNK] . Models and their outputs A model's forward pass takes the tokenizer's dict ( model( enc) ) and returns an output object whose fields you read by name. For BertModel : last hidden state , shape (B, T, d) , one vector per token; and pooler output , shape (B, d) , the [CLS] vector passed through one more linear layer and $\tanh$. output hidden states=True also returns every layer's output. Model classes with a head ( ...ForSequenceClassification , ...ForMaskedLM , ...LMHeadModel ) return logits , and if you pass labels they also return the loss . The embedding count has four parts: tokens $Vd$, positions $Pd$, the two token types $2d$, and the embedding layer norm $2d$. Each layer is the $12d^2 + 13d$ of lesson 1, and the pooler adds $d^2 + d$. Language models and generation GPT2LMHeadModel returns next-token logits of shape (B, T, V) . Pass labels=input ids and it computes the next-token loss itself, shifting by one inside (so do not shift first). generate runs the decoding loop of lesson 4 with a KV cache: do sample=False is greedy; do sample=True with temperature , top k , top p samples. It draws from PyTorch's global random generator, so seed with torch.manual seed . Exam angle - Read the restrictions first: "no pretrained models" means no from pretrained with downloaded weights, from Hugging Face or torchvision. Building an architecture from a config with random weights is a different thing; check whether the problem allows even that. - Shapes: last hidden state (B, T, d) , [CLS] vector last hidden state[:, 0] , pooler output (B, d) , LM logits (B, T, V) . - labels are shifted inside causal LM classes; label -100 marks positions without loss, as in lesson 2. - model.eval() and torch.no grad() for inference; requires grad (False) on model.bert (or model.base model ) for a linear probe.

The IOAI syllabus lists text classification (giving each text one label: spam or not, topic, sentiment) as a practice topic, and national selection contests often open with one, such as sorting news articles by topic. Two tools cover most of it. Word counts with a linear model train in seconds on a CPU and are the baseline to beat. A fine-tuned pretrained encoder (u16-l02) is usually more accurate, but needs a GPU and a rule that allows pretrained weights. This lesson builds both. Bag of words In text work a document is one text example and a corpus is a collection of them. The bag of words representation describes a document by how often each vocabulary word occurs in it, ignoring order. Stacking these count vectors gives the document-term matrix , of shape (number of documents, vocabulary size $V$). Most entries are 0, so scikit-learn stores it as a sparse matrix : only the nonzero entries and their positions. Three defaults to know: text is lowercased; the vocabulary is sorted alphabetically; and the default token pattern keeps only tokens of two or more letters or digits, so "a" and "I" disappear. Some pipelines also drop stop words , very common words like "the" and "of" ( stop words="english" ). TF-IDF Raw counts let common words dominate: "the" says little about the topic but is the largest entry above. TF-IDF reweights each count: - term frequency $\text{tf}(t, d)$: the count of word $t$ in document $d$; - document frequency $\text{df}(t)$: the number of documents containing $t$; - inverse document frequency , in scikit-learn's default form, for $n$ documents: The weight is $\text{tf}(t, d) \cdot \text{idf}(t)$, and then each document's row is divided by its L2 norm, so long and short documents are comparable. A word in every document gets the smallest idf, exactly 1; a word in one document gets the largest. (The $1 +$ terms act as if one extra document contained every word, which avoids dividing by 0.) In "the dog sat" the three words have the same df, hence the same weight $1/\sqrt{3} = 0.577$. n-grams and a linear classifier Order matters for meaning: "not good" and "good" share a word. An n-gram is a run of $n$ consecutive tokens; ngram range=(1, 2) adds every bigram (pair) as an extra column. The classifier on top is usually logistic regression (u07-l04) or a linear SVM: both handle tens of thousands of sparse columns quickly. Fit the vectorizer on the training texts only and call transform on the test texts; refitting on the test set changes the vocabulary and leaks test statistics (data leakage, u06-l02). A pipeline does this for you: With unigrams alone, "not" pushes "not good" and "not bad" in the same direction, so a linear model cannot get both right; bigrams give each phrase its own weight. Useful arguments: min df=2 drops words seen in only one document (often typos), max features caps $V$, sublinear tf=True uses $1 + \ln(\text{tf})$ so a word repeated ten times does not count ten times as much, and analyzer="char wb", ngram range=(2, 5) counts character n-grams, which handles misspellings and languages without spaces. Fine-tuning a pretrained encoder Word counts miss synonyms and context. A pretrained encoder such as BERT reads the whole text and gives each token a context-dependent vector. For classification, a linear head on the [CLS] vector is trained together with all the encoder's weights: fine-tuning (u16-l05). The recipe that usually works: learning rate $2 \times 10^{-5}$ to $5 \times 10^{-5}$ with AdamW, 2 to 4 epochs, batch size 16 or 32, max length 128 to 256, a short warmup. The tokenizer and model calls are the ones of u16-l06; passing labels makes the model return the cross-entropy loss. Validate after each epoch and keep the best checkpoint: with a few thousand examples the encoder can overfit by epoch 3. Which to use. Start with TF-IDF and logistic regression: a minute of work, a real baseline, and often within a few points of the best when keywords decide the label. Use sentence embeddings with a linear model (u17-l03) when meaning matters but you cannot fine-tune. Fine-tune an encoder when you have a GPU, pretrained weights are allowed, and the labels depend on context. Prompt a language model (u17-l04) when you have almost no labeled data. Exam angle - CountVectorizer and TfidfVectorizer : fit transform on train, transform on test; shapes (n docs, V); one-letter words are dropped by default. - TF-IDF by hand: count, df, $\ln\frac{1+n}{1+\text{df}} + 1$, multiply, L2-normalize each row. - Bigrams fix negation for linear models. - Fine-tuning: small learning rate, few epochs, model( enc, labels=y).loss . Practice problems: u17-p01 TF-IDF from scratch and u17-p04 A text classifier on a CPU budget .

A sequence-to-sequence task maps an input sequence to an output sequence of a different length: translation, summarization, turning a question into an answer, or audio into text (Whisper, u17-l05). The IOAI syllabus lists sequence-to-sequence tasks and conditional generation (here: generating text token by token given an input) as practice topics. You know the parts from u16: encoder-decoders, teacher forcing and decoding. This lesson puts them together the way a task uses them: the training batch, a greedy decoding loop you can write by hand, and the metrics that score the output. Two ways to build one - Encoder-decoder (T5, BART, Marian translation models, Whisper): the encoder reads the whole input once; the decoder generates the output while cross-attending to the encoder's vectors (u16-l02). - Decoder-only with a prompt : put the input in the prompt ("Translate to French: ... French:") and let a language model continue it (u17-l04). Encoder-decoders are the usual choice when you fine-tune on (input, output) pairs; T5 casts every task as text in, text out, with a task prefix such as "summarize: " . Training batch Each example is a (source, target) pair. Tokenize both. The target ids become labels , with padding set to $-100$ so the loss skips it (ignore index). The decoder reads the labels shifted right by one, starting with the decoder start token (pad, id 0, for T5): this is teacher forcing. Pass labels and the Hugging Face model builds the shifted input and the loss itself: The shifted input replaces $-100$ by the pad id, and the logits have shape (B, T out, V) : batch size $B$ (u10 to u12 wrote it $N$), one row per target position, one score per vocabulary token. The loss, 12.4, is far above the $\ln 12 = 2.5$ of a uniform guess because this untrained T5 starts with large logits (standard deviation about 6.7), so the "initial loss near $\ln V$" check does not apply to every architecture. Greedy decoding by hand At inference there is no target. Encode the input once, start the decoder with the start token, and repeat: run the decoder on the tokens so far, take the logits at the last position, append the most likely token. A batch needs one more piece: a row that has produced the end token is finished, and from then on emits padding while the others continue. Stop when every row is finished or a length limit is reached. The untrained model repeats one token per row, but the loop matches generate exactly. Real implementations also keep a KV cache (u15-l04) so each step costs one position instead of the whole prefix. Beam search (u16-l04) keeps the few best partial outputs by total log-probability; num beams=4 is a common setting for translation and summarization, usually with a length penalty so short outputs are not favored. Scoring the output Generated text rarely matches the reference word for word, so metrics count overlapping n-grams (u17-l01): - BLEU (translation): for $n = 1$ to $4$, the clipped precision : candidate n-grams that occur in the reference, each counted at most as often as in the reference; then the geometric mean of the four, times a brevity penalty $e^{1 - r/c}$ when the candidate length $c$ is below the reference length $r$. Without clipping, "the the the" would score perfect precision. - ROUGE (summarization): ROUGE-1 and ROUGE-2 count overlapping unigrams and bigrams and report recall, precision or $F 1$; ROUGE-L uses the longest common subsequence. - Exact match for short answers, and accuracy or macro F1 when the output is a label. The reordered sentence has every word right but no matching 4-gram, so this sentence-level BLEU is 0 while ROUGE-1 is perfect. Corpus BLEU (the sacrebleu package) adds counts over all sentences before taking the ratios, so one sentence cannot zero the score. The library calls Exam angle - Labels: target ids with padding set to $-100$; decoder input: start token plus labels shifted right. - Greedy loop: encode once; last-position argmax; append with [:, None] ; done = nxt == eos ; finished rows emit padding. - BLEU: clipped n-gram precision, geometric mean over $n = 1..4$, brevity penalty. ROUGE: overlap counts, recall-oriented. Practice problem: u17-p05 Greedy decoding for a seq2seq model .

Many tasks reduce to "which texts are close in meaning": search, removing near-duplicates, labeling a text by its nearest labeled neighbors, clustering, and finding passages to give a language model. The tool is a sentence embedding : one fixed-length vector per text, trained so that texts with similar meaning have a high cosine similarity (u03-l01). The IOAI syllabus lists pretrained text encoders and text embeddings, and the IOAI 2026 contest machines shipped the sentence-transformers library. This lesson covers where the vectors come from and how to search with them. Where the vectors come from An encoder such as BERT gives one vector per token, last hidden state of shape (B, T, d) (u16-l06). Two ways to get one vector per text: take the [CLS] vector, or average the token vectors over the real tokens only (masked mean pooling, u15-l01). Either way, a plain pretrained BERT gives poor similarities, because masked language modeling never asked its vectors to be comparable. Sentence-embedding models (Sentence-BERT and its successors) are BERT-style encoders fine-tuned with a contrastive loss (u19-l03) on pairs of texts that mean the same thing, which pulls paraphrases together and pushes unrelated texts apart. encode runs the encoder, pools and, with normalize embeddings=True , scales every vector to unit length. Cosine search Retrieval means finding the documents in a corpus most relevant to a query. With unit-length rows, the matrix product of queries and documents gives every cosine similarity at once; then keep the top $k$ per row. Two ways to measure a retrieval system on queries with known answers: recall@k , the fraction of queries whose correct document is among the top $k$, and the mean reciprocal rank (MRR), the average of $1/\text{rank}$ of the correct document. The cell below uses TF-IDF vectors (u17-l01) as the embeddings. Their rows are already unit length, so Q @ E.T is the cosine matrix. "forgot password" ranks the reset question first: the only shared word is "password", and "forgot" and "forgotten" are different tokens. This is lexical retrieval , matching by shared words (TF-IDF, or its refinement BM25). Dense retrieval with sentence embeddings matches meaning instead and would place "forgotten login password" first. Lexical search is still useful for rare names and codes that an embedding blurs; combining both scores is common. Normalization details Normalize along the embedding axis (one vector per row: axis=1 , keepdims=True ), or use F.normalize(E, dim=1) in PyTorch, which also leaves an all-zero row at zero instead of dividing by 0. For unit vectors, $\lVert q - e \rVert^2 = 2 - 2\cos(q, e)$, so ranking by smallest Euclidean distance gives exactly the cosine ranking: For a few million documents the full matrix product is still fine on a GPU, done in chunks of queries. Beyond that, approximate nearest-neighbor libraries such as FAISS index the vectors so a search does not touch every document. Uses beyond search - Classification with few labels : embed the texts with a frozen encoder and train logistic regression on the vectors (a linear probe, u16-l05), or predict the majority label of the $k$ nearest labeled texts. - Clustering and deduplication : k-means on normalized embeddings; pairs with cosine above a threshold such as 0.9 are near-duplicates. - Retrieval-augmented generation : retrieve the top passages for a question and put them into a language model's prompt (u17-l04), so it answers from the given text. Exam angle - One vector per text: [CLS] or masked mean pooling; sentence-embedding models are trained contrastively. - Cosine matrix: normalize rows ( axis=1, keepdims=True or F.normalize(dim=1) ), then Q @ E.T , then topk(k, dim=1) . - recall@k and MRR from the rank of the correct document; for unit vectors, distance and cosine give the same ranking. Practice problem: u17-p02 Cosine top-k retrieval .

Large language models show up in two roles at IOAI. They are a tool you are given: in 2026 the contest platform included an official LLM (Gemma 3, at most 1,000 output tokens per query), and every other LLM, copilot or API was banned unless a task allowed it; in 2025 the allowed model was GPT-4o-mini with at most 4,000 tokens per query. And they are a component a task can ask you to use, through the syllabus line "pretrained language models: open-source and closed-source (API-based)". USAAIO Round 1 allows no AI at all; plan the same for Round 2 unless told otherwise. This lesson covers the kinds of model, how to prompt them, how to turn their output into labels you can trust, and how to use a capped contest assistant well. Open-weight and API models An open-weight model has published weights (Llama, Gemma, Qwen, Mistral): you download it once, run it on your own GPU, read its logits, and fine-tune it (LoRA, u16-l05). Nothing leaves your machine and it works offline, which is how contest environments provide models. The cost is GPU memory: weights alone take 2 bytes per parameter in bfloat16, so a 7-billion-parameter model needs 14 GB before any computation. An API model (GPT, Claude, Gemini) runs on the provider's servers. You send text over the internet and pay per token; you cannot see or change the weights, and many APIs return only text, not logits. They are usually the strongest models, but they need a network and a key, so an offline contest cannot use them unless the organizers route one in. Chat format and prompts Chat models are trained on conversations: a list of messages, each with a role ( system , user , assistant ) and content. The system message comes first and holds instructions for the whole conversation. The tokenizer's chat template turns the list into the exact token sequence the model was trained on, with its special tokens. Always use the template; hand-written role markers that differ from training degrade the answers. A real tokenizer loaded with from pretrained carries its own template; add generation prompt=True ends the text with the assistant's header so the model writes the reply. Prompting habits that work: - Zero-shot prompting : an instruction alone. State the task, the allowed outputs and the exact format ("Answer with one word: positive or negative"). - Few-shot prompting : add a few worked input-output examples before the real input. The model copies the pattern without any weight change; this is in-context learning . Pick examples that cover every label. - Put the instructions before long inputs, and mark where the input starts and ends (for example with triple quotes). - Use greedy decoding ( do sample=False , or temperature 0 in an API) when you need the same answer every run. - Everything, prompt plus output, must fit in the model's context window , counted in tokens, not words. Labels you can trust Free text must be parsed, and a model sometimes answers "Negative." or "It is mostly positive". Two fixes. Constrain the output and map anything unexpected to a fallback. Or, with an open-weight model, skip generation: compute the log-probability of each allowed label as a continuation of the prompt and pick the largest. Every input then gets a valid label, and the scores can be calibrated or thresholded like any classifier's. With logits of shape (1, T, V) , position $t$ predicts token $t + 1$: The untrained model's numbers mean nothing, but the mechanics are those of a real one: the manual sum matches the library's loss. Note the length effect: a two-token label pays for two probabilities. Measure any prompt like a model: label a sample by hand (a few hundred), compute accuracy or macro F1, and compare prompts on that sample, not on impressions. Using a capped contest assistant With 1,000 output tokens per query, ask for one function or one fix at a time, not a whole notebook. Give it what it cannot know: the exact error message, the shapes, the library and its version. Treat the answer as a draft. Language models produce hallucinations , fluent but false statements such as a function argument that does not exist, so run every suggestion on a tiny input before relying on it. Good uses: recalling an API ("arguments of torch.optim.lr scheduler.OneCycleLR "), explaining an error, writing boilerplate (a Dataset class, a plotting cell). Poor uses: choosing your model or your validation scheme, which is where the points are. Exam angle - Weights in bfloat16: 2 bytes per parameter; open-weight models run offline and expose logits, API models do not. - Messages with roles; apply chat template(..., add generation prompt=True) ; greedy decoding for reproducible labels. - Score fixed labels by log-probability: log softmax , shift by one, gather ; totals favor short labels. - Verify every assistant answer on a tiny input.

entries.t: Audio: spectrograms and pretrained audio models
entries.x: Audio entered the IOAI syllabus in 2026 at practice level: pretrained audio encoders (HuBERT) and audio models (Qwen-Audio, Whisper, Voxtral). Practice level means knowing what each model takes in, what it returns, and how to get audio into that form; the IOAI 2026 contest machines shipped torchaudio for it. This lesson builds the standard input, the log-mel spectrogram, in NumPy, and then shows the model interfaces. Waveforms and sampling A microphone records air pressure over time as a waveform : a 1-D array of amplitudes, usually floats in $[-1, 1]$. The sampling rate is the number of samples per second: 16,000 Hz for speech models, 44,100 Hz for music. A clip of $n$ samples lasts $n / \text{sr}$ seconds. The highest frequency a sampled signal can hold is the Nyquist frequency , $\text{sr}/2$; a higher tone is aliased , appearing as a false lower frequency. Two practical rules. Feed a model the rate it was trained on: resampling converts rates, for example scipy.signal.resample poly(wave, 160, 441) from 44.1 kHz to 16 kHz; audio at the wrong rate plays too fast or too slow to the model, and nothing raises an error. And make it mono: torchaudio.load returns (channels, samples), so average the channels. Spectrograms Speech and music change over time, so a single Fourier transform (u21-l02) of the whole clip is not enough. The short-time Fourier transform cuts the waveform into overlapping frames of n fft samples every hop samples, multiplies each by a window function (the Hann window tapers the ends to 0, which reduces leakage between frequency bins), and takes the FFT of each frame. The squared magnitude is the power spectrogram : shape (frames, n fft // 2 + 1 ), where bin $k$ is the frequency $k \cdot \text{sr}/\text{n\ fft}$. Without padding there are $1 + \lfloor (n - \text{n\ fft})/\text{hop} \rfloor$ frames. The window length is a trade-off: longer frames separate frequencies more finely (bins every $\text{sr}/\text{n\ fft}$ Hz) but blur when things happen. Libraries differ in conventions, so check shapes before comparing: scipy.signal.stft returns (f, t, Z) with Z of shape (bins, frames), pads the edges unless you pass boundary=None, padded=False , and scales by the window's sum; torch.stft pads by n fft // 2 on each side by default ( center=True ), giving $1 + \lfloor n/\text{hop} \rfloor$ frames. Mel spectrograms We hear pitch roughly logarithmically: 100 Hz to 200 Hz sounds like the same step as 1,000 Hz to 2,000 Hz. The mel scale $m = 2595 \log {10}(1 + f/700)$ models this. A mel filterbank is a set of n mels triangular filters whose centers are equally spaced in mels: narrow at low frequencies, wide at high ones. Multiplying the power spectrogram by the filterbank gives mel energies, and their logarithm is the log-mel spectrogram , the input of most speech models. The log matters because loudness spans many orders of magnitude. Whisper uses these frame settings at 16 kHz: n fft = 400 , hop = 160 (100 frames per second), 80 mel bins (128 in large-v3). Its filterbank uses the Slaney variant of the mel scale (linear below 1 kHz) and scales each triangle to unit area, so its filters differ slightly from the cell above. It then raises every value to at least 8 below the clip's maximum and rescales, so its features span at most 2. Libraries differ in small ways (natural log or decibels, filter normalization), so use one pipeline for training and test. Classic alternatives: MFCC s, a cosine transform of the log-mel energies. A baseline for audio classification (speaker, emotion, keyword): treat the log-mel spectrogram as a one-channel image and train a small 2-D CNN (u12), or pool each mel bin's mean and standard deviation over time and fit logistic regression. SpecAugment , masking random bands of frames and of mel bins, is the standard augmentation. Pretrained audio models Model Input Output --- --- --- HuBERT (encoder) raw 16 kHz waveform, (B, samples) one vector per 20 ms frame, (B, frames, 768) for the base size Whisper (encoder-decoder) log-mel, (B, 80, 3000) : always 30 s, padded text tokens: a transcription, or a translation to English Qwen-Audio, Voxtral ( audio-language models ) audio plus a text prompt text: answers, transcripts, summaries HuBERT is self-supervised, like BERT on audio: its convolutional front end turns every 320 samples (20 ms) into a frame, a transformer contextualizes the frames, and pretraining predicts cluster ids of masked frames. Mean-pool its frames and train a linear head for clip-level labels, or fine-tune it. The original Whisper models were trained on 680,000 hours of transcribed audio (large-v3 on more); its encoder turns the 3,000 mel frames into 1,500 vectors and its decoder generates text (u17-l02). Audio-language models put a Whisper-style audio encoder in front of a text language model and are prompted like a chat model (u17-l04). The library calls (they download weights, so they are not run here): Exam angle - Duration $n/\text{sr}$; Nyquist $\text{sr}/2$; resample to the model's rate; mono. - Frames: $1 + \lfloor (n - \text{n\ fft})/\text{hop} \rfloor$ without padding; window, rfft along each frame, squared magnitude; bin $k$ at $k\,\text{sr}/\text{n\ fft}$ Hz. - Mel: triangles equally spaced in mels; log10(max(P @ M.T, 1e-10)) . - HuBERT: waveform in, 50 frames per second out. Whisper: (80, 3000) log-mel in, text out. Practice problem: u17-p03 A log-mel spectrogram from scratch .

Every model so far in this course was trained to predict a label. A generative model learns the distribution of the data itself, so it can produce new examples that look like the training set: new images, new molecules, new sounds. This unit builds the four families on the official syllabus (autoencoders, VAEs, GANs, diffusion models). The autoencoder comes first because the other three reuse its parts: the VAE is a probabilistic autoencoder, and a diffusion model is a stack of denoising autoencoders. Round 2 in 2026 spent a 50-point problem on the diffusion loss, and it assumed this vocabulary. Encoder, bottleneck, decoder An autoencoder is a network trained to output its own input. It has two halves: - an encoder $f \phi$ that maps an input $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ to a short vector $z = f \phi(x) \in \mathbb{R}^k$, - a decoder $g \theta$ that maps $z$ back to a reconstruction $\hat{x} = g \theta(z) \in \mathbb{R}^d$. Here $\phi$ and $\theta$ are the weights of the two networks. The vector $z$ is the latent vector (also called the code), and the set of all possible codes is the latent space . "Latent" means hidden: nobody labels $z$, the network invents it. If $k \ge d$ the network could learn the identity map and nothing would be gained. The point is the bottleneck : with $k < d$ (an undercomplete autoencoder ) the encoder must squeeze $x$ into fewer numbers, so it has to keep what matters most for rebuilding $x$ and drop the rest. For 28 by 28 grayscale digits, $d = 784$ and a typical $k$ is 2 to 32. A standard fully connected autoencoder for digits ($B$ is the batch size, written $N$ in u10): The decoder usually mirrors the encoder. For images in $[0, 1]$ you may end the decoder with nn.Sigmoid() so outputs stay in range. Convolutional autoencoders use Conv2d layers with stride 2 going down and ConvTranspose2d going back up (a "transposed convolution": a layer with learned weights whose stride enlarges the image, for example 7 by 7 to 14 by 14 at stride 2; plain nn.Upsample followed by a Conv2d also works). The reconstruction loss and its reduction Training minimizes a reconstruction loss that measures how far $\hat{x}$ is from $x$. The usual choice is squared error, summed over the $d$ coordinates and averaged over the $B$ examples in the batch: For pixel values in $[0, 1]$, binary cross-entropy per pixel is also common (u05-l07 showed that squared error is the negative log-likelihood under Gaussian noise and BCE is the one under a Bernoulli model). The reduction matters. F.mse loss(x hat, x) averages over all $B \cdot d$ numbers, so it is the formula above divided by $d$. For a plain autoencoder that only rescales the gradient (Adam barely notices). In the next lesson the reconstruction term is added to a second term, and then a factor of 784 changes which term wins. Build the habit now: sum over the data dimensions, average over the batch. A linear autoencoder learns PCA If both halves are linear ($z = W 1 x$, $\hat{x} = W 2 z$, centered data) and the loss is squared error, the best possible reconstruction is the projection onto the top $k$ principal components (u08-l07). The weights need not be orthonormal, but the span of $W 2$'s columns is the PCA subspace, and the minimum loss is the sum of the discarded eigenvalues of the covariance matrix. The nonlinear version (ReLU layers) can fit curved surfaces that PCA cannot. The cell below trains a linear autoencoder on 8-dimensional points that lie near a plane and compares it with PCA. After 200 steps the autoencoder (0.0164) is close to the PCA optimum (0.0144), which no linear autoencoder with $k = 2$ can beat. Two uses, and one thing it cannot do Denoising autoencoder. Corrupt the input, for example $\tilde{x} = x + \sigma\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon \sim N(0, I)$, and train $g(f(\tilde{x}))$ to match the clean $x$. Now the identity map is useless even without a bottleneck, so the network must learn what clean data looks like. In code the only change is the input: x noisy = x + 0.1 torch.randn like(x) , and the loss still compares with x . Diffusion models (lesson 4) are built from exactly this task, repeated at many noise levels. Anomaly detection. Train on normal data only. At test time, an input unlike the training data reconstructs badly, so the per-example error ((x hat - x) 2).sum(dim=1) is a score: flag the inputs whose score is above a threshold chosen on validation data. What it cannot do: generate. Decoding a random $z$ usually gives garbage. Training only asks the decoder to work on the codes of training examples, and those codes can sit anywhere: in odd clusters, with large empty gaps, at any scale. Nothing tells you which region of the latent space is "inside the data". A generative model needs a known distribution $p(z)$ that you can sample from and a decoder that works on samples from it. That is the variational autoencoder in the next lesson. Expect a parameter count for an encoder-decoder pair (count each Linear as $\text{in} \cdot \text{out} + \text{out}$), a reduction question (mean over all elements is the per-example sum divided by $d$), and the PCA link (the minimum linear-autoencoder loss is the sum of the discarded eigenvalues).

The variational autoencoder (VAE) fixes the problem the last lesson ended on: it trains the decoder on codes drawn from a known distribution, so sampling $z \sim N(0, I)$ and decoding gives new data. Its loss is derived from maximum likelihood with one inequality, and the same steps (a Gaussian KL in closed form, a bound on $\log p(x)$) are the core of the diffusion derivation in lesson 4. Round 2 grades such derivations line by line, so this lesson does them in full. A latent variable model A latent variable model explains each data point $x$ by an unobserved latent variable $z$: 1. draw $z$ from a fixed prior $p(z) = N(0, I k)$, the standard normal in $k$ dimensions; 2. draw $x$ from the decoder's distribution $p \theta(x \mid z)$. A common choice is $N(g \theta(z), \sigma^2 I d)$: the decoder network $g \theta$ gives the mean, and $\sigma$ is a fixed number. Maximum likelihood (u05-l07) would maximize $\sum i \log p \theta(x i)$ (in this unit $\log$ is the natural log, as in ML code), where the marginal likelihood (also called the evidence) is For a neural network $g \theta$ this integral has no closed form, and estimating it by averaging $p \theta(x \mid z)$ over random $z$ fails in high dimension: almost no random $z$ decodes to anything near a given $x$. The posterior $p \theta(z \mid x) = p \theta(x \mid z)p(z)/p \theta(x)$ would tell us which $z$ matter, but it needs $p \theta(x)$ too. The VAE's answer: train an encoder to guess the posterior. The approximate posterior $q \phi(z \mid x)$ is a diagonal Gaussian , a normal distribution whose covariance matrix is diagonal (independent coordinates): The encoder outputs $2k$ numbers per input: the mean $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^k$ and the log-variance $\log \sigma^2 \in \mathbb{R}^k$ (called logvar in code). Outputting the log lets the last layer be a plain Linear : any real number gives a positive variance $\sigma^2 = e^{\text{logvar}}$, and $\sigma = e^{\text{logvar}/2}$. The evidence lower bound (ELBO) For continuous distributions the KL divergence of u05-l08 becomes an expectation, $D {\mathrm{KL}}(q \,\ \, p) = \mathbb{E} {z \sim q}\big[\log \frac{q(z)}{p(z)}\big]$, with the same properties: never negative, zero only when $q = p$. Fix one $x$ and write $q = q \phi(z \mid x)$. Since $\log p \theta(x)$ does not depend on $z$, it equals its own average under $q$. Then use Bayes' rule in the form $p \theta(x) = p \theta(x, z)/p \theta(z \mid x)$, where $p \theta(x, z) = p \theta(x \mid z)\,p(z)$ is the joint density of the two steps above, and multiply and divide by $q$: The KL term is at least 0, so the first term is a lower bound on the log-evidence: the evidence lower bound (ELBO). Splitting $p \theta(x, z) = p \theta(x \mid z)\,p(z)$ inside the log gives the form you train with: The first term rewards decoding the code back to $x$ (reconstruction). The second keeps each $q \phi(z \mid x)$ close to the prior, so the codes of all training points fill the region that $N(0, I)$ samples from. Maximizing the ELBO over $\theta$ and $\phi$ together pushes $\log p \theta(x)$ up and shrinks the gap, which is exactly the KL from $q$ to the true posterior. The VAE loss is the negative ELBO. Jensen's inequality : for a concave function $f$ (such as $\log$) and a random variable $Y$, $f(\mathbb{E}[Y]) \ge \mathbb{E}[f(Y)]$. A chord of a concave curve lies below the curve. Take $Y = p \theta(x, z)/q(z \mid x)$ with $z \sim q$. Then $\mathbb{E} q[Y] = \int q \cdot \frac{p \theta(x, z)}{q}\, dz = \int p \theta(x, z)\, dz = p \theta(x)$, so This route is shorter but hides the size of the gap; the KL route above shows it. The KL term in closed form Start in one dimension with $q = N(\mu 1, \sigma 1^2)$ and $p = N(\mu 2, \sigma 2^2)$. From the normal density (u05-l05), Take the expectation under $z \sim q$. Two facts do all the work: $\mathbb{E}[(z - \mu 1)^2] = \sigma 1^2$, and, writing $z - \mu 2 = (z - \mu 1) + (\mu 1 - \mu 2)$, $\mathbb{E}[(z - \mu 2)^2] = \sigma 1^2 + (\mu 1 - \mu 2)^2$ (the cross term has mean 0). So For diagonal Gaussians the coordinates are independent, the log-density is a sum over coordinates, and the KL is the sum of the one-dimensional KLs. With $p = N(0, I)$ ($\mu 2 = 0$, $\sigma 2 = 1$) and $\log\frac{1}{\sigma} = -\frac12 \log\sigma^2$: Each term is 0 exactly when $\mu j = 0$ and $\sigma j = 1$. Code usually writes it as -0.5 torch.sum(1 + logvar - mu 2 - logvar.exp()) , the same thing with the sign moved outside. The cell checks the formula against torch.distributions and against a Monte Carlo average of $\log q - \log p$. The reconstruction term With the Gaussian decoder $p \theta(x \mid z) = N(g \theta(z), \sigma^2 I d)$, and the last term is a constant. The expectation over $z \sim q$ is estimated with one sample per example (training averages over many steps anyway). With $\sigma^2 = \frac12$ the weight is 1, and the loss per example is averaged over the batch. A Bernoulli decoder replaces the squared error by binary cross-entropy summed over pixels. If you write F.mse loss(x hat, x) (a mean over all $B \cdot d$ numbers) next to a KL summed over $k$, the reconstruction weight drops by a factor of $d$ (784 for digits). The KL then wins: the encoder outputs $\mu \approx 0$, $\sigma \approx 1$ for every input, $z$ carries no information about $x$, and the decoder outputs one blurry average. This failure is called posterior collapse . A weight $\beta$ on the KL term (a $\beta$-VAE) is a deliberate version of the same dial. The reparameterization trick The loss contains $\mathbb{E} {z \sim q \phi}[\,\cdot\,]$, and we need its gradient with respect to the encoder weights $\phi$. If the code draws z from $N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ with a sampling routine, autograd sees a fresh constant: it has no record of how z depends on mu and logvar , and no gradient reaches the encoder. The reparameterization trick moves the randomness into an input that does not depend on $\phi$: where $\odot$ is elementwise multiplication. This $z$ has exactly the distribution $q \phi(z \mid x)$. Now the expectation is over $\varepsilon$, whose distribution is fixed, so the gradient can move inside it: One sample of $\varepsilon$ gives an unbiased gradient estimate that backpropagation computes: $\partial z j/\partial \mu j = 1$ and $\partial z j / \partial \sigma j = \varepsilon j$, and through $\sigma = e^{\text{logvar}/2}$, $\partial z j / \partial\,\text{logvar} j = \varepsilon j \sigma j / 2$. Check the first coordinate by hand: $z = 1 + 1.541 = 2.541$, so $\partial L/\partial \mu = 2z = 5.082$ and $\partial L/\partial\,\text{logvar} = 2z \cdot \varepsilon \cdot \sigma/2 = 2.541 \cdot 1.541 = 3.916$. In torch.distributions , rsample() is the reparameterized draw and keeps the graph; sample() does not. The whole model To generate, skip the encoder: x new = model.dec(torch.randn(16, k)) . VAE samples are often blurry, because the Gaussian decoder's mean is an average over the images that fit a code. GANs (next lesson) and diffusion models (lesson 4) give sharper samples. Know three lines cold: the ELBO identity ($\log p = \text{ELBO} + \text{KL to the true posterior}$), the Gaussian KL formula with its $-\frac12$, and the reparameterized sample mu + exp(0.5 logvar) randn like(mu) . Typical errors: a KL with the wrong sign, exp(logvar) used as the standard deviation, and mismatched reductions.

A generative adversarial network (GAN) trains a generator without ever writing down a likelihood: a second network, the discriminator, learns to tell real data from generated data, and the generator learns to fool it. The IOAI syllabus lists GANs as a practice topic, and a Round 2 problem can ask for the losses in code, the optimal discriminator, or why a training run failed. All three come from one formula. Two networks and one game - The generator $G \theta$ maps noise $z \sim p(z)$ (usually $N(0, I)$) to a fake sample $G \theta(z)$. Its outputs have some distribution $p g$. - The discriminator $D \psi$ maps a sample $x$ to $D \psi(x) \in (0, 1)$, its probability that $x$ is real. In code $D$ outputs a logit $a$ and $D = \sigma(a)$. The discriminator is a binary classifier with label 1 for real and 0 for fake. Its binary cross-entropy loss, negated, is the value function $D$ maximizes $V$ (classify well) and $G$ minimizes it (make $D$ wrong on fakes). This is a minimax game : $\min G \max D V(D, G)$. Training alternates one gradient step on $D$ with one on $G$. The optimal discriminator Fix $G$. Write both expectations as integrals over $x$ (the second one over the fakes, whose density is $p g$): $D$ can choose its value at each $x$ separately, so maximize the bracket pointwise. For $a, b 0$ the function $y \mapsto a\log y + b\log(1 - y)$ on $(0, 1)$ has derivative $\frac{a}{y} - \frac{b}{1 - y}$, which is zero at $y = \frac{a}{a + b}$ (and the function is concave, so this is the maximum). Hence Where real data is three times as dense as fakes, $D^ = 0.75$. Where $p g = p \text{data}$, $D^ = \frac12$: the best discriminator can only guess. Put $D^ $ back into $V$. With the average $m = \frac12(p \text{data} + p g)$, each fraction is $\frac{p}{2m}$, and $\log\frac{p}{2m} = \log\frac{p}{m} - \log 2$. So each expectation is a KL divergence to $m$, minus $\log 2$: where the Jensen-Shannon divergence is $\mathrm{JSD}(p\,\ \,q) = \frac12 D {\mathrm{KL}}(p\,\ \,m) + \frac12 D {\mathrm{KL}}(q\,\ \,m)$, a symmetric cousin of the KL divergence that is 0 only when $p = q$. So against a perfect discriminator the generator minimizes the JSD, the global minimum is $p g = p \text{data}$, and there $V = -\log 4 \approx -1.386$ and $D = \frac12$ everywhere. The non-saturating generator loss Early in training the fakes are bad, $D$ rejects them easily, and $D(G(z)) = \sigma(a)$ is near 0. The generator's term $\log(1 - \sigma(a))$ then has derivative $-\sigma(a) \approx 0$ with respect to the logit $a$: the loss is flat exactly when $G$ most needs to improve. This is the saturation of the sigmoid. The fix is the non-saturating loss : the generator maximizes $\log D(G(z))$ instead, that is, it minimizes whose derivative with respect to $a$ is $-(1 - \sigma(a)) \approx -1$ when $D$ rejects the fake. It has the same fixed point ($D$ fooled) and strong gradients at the start. In code it is binary cross-entropy with the fakes labeled 1 . At logit $-5$ (a fake that $D$ gives probability 0.007) the saturating gradient is $-0.0067$ and the non-saturating one $-0.9933$. The last line is the numerical reason to work with logits: torch.log(torch.sigmoid(-200)) is $-\infty$ because the sigmoid underflows to 0, while F.logsigmoid and F.binary cross entropy with logits use the log-sum-exp form and return $-200$ and $200$ exactly. The training loop Three details carry the marks. fake.detach() in the discriminator step stops loss d.backward() from computing gradients for $G$ (and keeps fake 's graph alive for step 2). The generator step re-runs D(fake) on the updated discriminator. Each network has its own optimizer, so opt g.step() only moves $G$, even though loss g.backward() also fills $D$'s .grad (which opt d.zero grad() clears next time). DCGAN, the standard convolutional GAN, uses Adam with lr=2e-4, betas=(0.5, 0.999) . Failure modes The cell trains a GAN on one-dimensional data from $N(3, 0.5^2)$. The generator is linear, $G(z) = az + b$, so it could match the data exactly with $a = 0.5$, $b = 3$. The mean is right, but $a \approx 0$: every $z$ maps to about 2.97, and the small discriminator is fooled on average (0.50) by a spike in the middle of the real bell. This is mode collapse in its simplest form: the generator covers a small part of the data distribution (here one point; with images, a few similar faces) because that is enough to fool the current discriminator. When $D$ catches on, $G$ can jump to another spot, and the two chase each other instead of converging. The usual failure modes: 1. Mode collapse : low diversity, many $z$ giving the same output. 2. Non-convergence : the losses oscillate; a falling generator loss does not mean better samples, because each loss only measures one network against the current other. 3. Discriminator too strong : $D(G(z)) \to 0$ everywhere, and with the saturating loss the generator gets almost no gradient. Common fixes are the non-saturating loss, Adam with $\beta 1 = 0.5$, label smoothing on the real labels (targets 0.9 instead of 1), and different loss functions such as the Wasserstein GAN. Diffusion models (next lesson) avoid the game entirely, which is a large part of why they replaced GANs for image generation. Know $D^ = \frac{p \text{data}}{p \text{data} + p g}$ and its derivation, the value $-\log 4$ at the optimum, why the non-saturating loss exists, and which tensors get detach() in the discriminator step. Losses on logits use binary cross entropy with logits , never log(sigmoid(...)) .

Diffusion models generate images by starting from pure noise and removing it a little at a time. They power Stable Diffusion and most current image and audio generators, and Round 2 in 2026 gave them a 50-point derivation problem: the closed form of the noising process, the KL between two Gaussians, the posterior of one denoising step, the noise-prediction loss, and how a network takes the time step as input. This lesson derives each of those in the order that problem asked for them. Everything is in one dimension, as in the contest; for images every pixel follows the same formulas. The forward process Pick numbers $0 < \alpha t < 1$ for $t = 1, \dots, T$ and write $\beta t = 1 - \alpha t$. The forward process turns a data point $x 0$ into noise in $T$ small steps: Each step shrinks the signal a little and adds a little fresh noise, so $x t \mid x {t-1} \sim N(\sqrt{\alpha t}\,x {t-1}, \beta t)$. The sequence $x 0, x 1, \dots, x T$ is a Markov chain : given $x {t-1}$, the next value does not depend on anything earlier. The list $\beta 1, \dots, \beta T$ is the noise schedule . The original DDPM paper (denoising diffusion probabilistic models, Ho et al. 2020) uses $T = 1000$ and $\beta t$ rising linearly from $10^{-4}$ to $0.02$. Define The closed form for $x t$ given $x 0$ One fact about normals does the work: if $\varepsilon, \varepsilon'$ are independent $N(0, 1)$, then $a\varepsilon + b\varepsilon' \sim N(0, a^2 + b^2)$. (The sum of independent normals is normal, and variances of independent terms add.) Two steps. Substitute $x 1 = \sqrt{\alpha 1}x 0 + \sqrt{1 - \alpha 1}\,\varepsilon 1$ into the step for $x 2$: So $x 2 = A 2 x 0 + B 2\bar\varepsilon 2$ with $A 2 = \sqrt{\bar\alpha 2}$, $B 2 = \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha 2}$ and $\bar\varepsilon 2 \sim N(0, 1)$. Any $t$, by induction. Suppose $x {t-1} = \sqrt{\bar\alpha {t-1}}\,x 0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha {t-1}}\,\bar\varepsilon {t-1}$ with $\bar\varepsilon {t-1}$ independent of $\varepsilon t$ (it is built from $\varepsilon 1, \dots, \varepsilon {t-1}$ only). Then and the noise variance is $\alpha t - \bar\alpha t + 1 - \alpha t = 1 - \bar\alpha t$. Hence for every $t \ge 1$ This is why diffusion training is cheap: you can jump to any $t$ in one line, without running the chain. The limit. If every $\alpha t \le a$ for some $a < 1$, then $\bar\alpha t \le a^t \to 0$. So the mean $\sqrt{\bar\alpha t}\,x 0 \to 0$ and the variance $1 - \bar\alpha t \to 1$: $x T$ is approximately $N(0, 1)$ whatever $x 0$ was. That is the distribution generation starts from. The DDPM schedule in code, with the zero-based indexing every implementation uses: Halfway through ($t = 500$) only 28% of the signal's scale is left, and at $t = 1000$ it is 0.6%. The reverse process and what it must match To generate, run the chain backwards: sample $x T \sim N(0, 1)$, then draw $x {t-1}$ from the reverse process $p \theta(x {t-1} \mid x t) = N\big(\mu \theta(x t, t), \sigma t^2\big)$, where a network computes the mean and $\sigma t^2$ is a fixed number. Training treats $x 1, \dots, x T$ as latent variables, exactly as the VAE treated $z$ (lesson 2). The ELBO for this chain splits into one term per step, and the step-$t$ term is Here $q(x {t-1} \mid x t, x 0)$ is the true distribution of the previous step when you know both the noisy point and the clean one. We need it in closed form, and then the KL. The KL between two normals (lesson 2, now with general variances): for $q = N(\mu q, \sigma q^2)$ and $p = N(\mu p, \sigma p^2)$, When the two variances are equal, only $\frac{(\mu q - \mu p)^2}{2\sigma p^2}$ is left: matching the distributions means matching the means. The posterior of one step By Bayes' rule, and because the chain is Markov ($x t$ depends on $x 0$ only through $x {t-1}$), Here $\propto$ means "equal up to a factor that does not depend on $x {t-1}$": Bayes' rule, with every term also conditioned on $x 0$, divides by $q(x t \mid x 0)$, a constant once $x t$ and $x 0$ are fixed. Both factors are normal densities in $y = x {t-1}$: $q(x t \mid y) \propto \exp\big(-\frac{(x t - \sqrt{\alpha t}\,y)^2}{2\beta t}\big)$ and, by the closed form, $q(y \mid x 0) \propto \exp\big(-\frac{(y - \sqrt{\bar\alpha {t-1}}\,x 0)^2}{2(1 - \bar\alpha {t-1})}\big)$. Multiply and expand. The exponent is $-\frac12(P y^2 - 2 L y) + \text{const}$ with (The simplification of $P$ uses $\alpha t - \alpha t\bar\alpha {t-1} + 1 - \alpha t = 1 - \bar\alpha t$.) A density proportional to $\exp\big(-\frac12(Py^2 - 2Ly)\big)$ is the normal with variance $1/P$ and mean $L/P$, by completing the square: $-\frac12(Py^2 - 2Ly) = -\frac{P}{2}\big(y - \frac{L}{P}\big)^2 + \frac{L^2}{2P}$. Therefore $q(x {t-1} \mid x t, x 0) = N(\tilde\mu t, \tilde\beta t)$ with The cell checks both by simulation: generate many pairs $(x {t-1}, x t)$ from one $x 0$, keep the pairs whose $x t$ is near 0.5, and look at their $x {t-1}$. Predicting the noise The network cannot see $x 0$ at generation time, so rewrite $\tilde\mu t$ without it. From the closed form, $x 0 = \big(x t - \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha t}\,\bar\varepsilon t\big)/\sqrt{\bar\alpha t}$. Substitute, and use $\sqrt{\bar\alpha {t-1}}/\sqrt{\bar\alpha t} = 1/\sqrt{\alpha t}$. The coefficient of $x t$ becomes $\frac{\alpha t(1 - \bar\alpha {t-1}) + \beta t}{\sqrt{\alpha t}\,(1 - \bar\alpha t)} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha t}}$, and Everything here is known at time $t$ except the noise $\bar\varepsilon t$. So let the network output a noise estimate $\varepsilon \theta(x t, t)$ and define the model's mean in the same form, $\mu \theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha t}}\big(x t - \frac{\beta t}{\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha t}}\varepsilon \theta(x t, t)\big)$. With $\sigma t^2 = \tilde\beta t$ the variances match, and the KL is the squared mean difference: (The last step substitutes $\tilde\beta t$; it needs $t \ge 2$, since $\tilde\beta 1 = 0$. DDPM handles the first step with a separate decoder term.) DDPM found that dropping the weight works better, which gives the simple loss used in practice: A diffusion model is a denoising autoencoder trained at every noise level at once, with the noise itself as the target. Giving the network the time step The same network must denoise at every $t$, and the right amount of denoising depends on $t$, so $t$ is an input. Its output has the input's shape, $(B, C, L 0, \dots, L {M-1})$ for data with $M$ spatial axes ($(B, C, H, W)$ for images), so image models use a U-Net : a convolutional encoder that downsamples, a decoder that upsamples back to full size, and skip connections joining matching resolutions. The time step goes in through a time embedding : 1. Map the integer $t$ to a vector of $D$ sinusoids ($D$ even; transformers encode token positions the same way, u15-l05): $e {2i}(t) = \sin(t/10000^{2i/D})$, $e {2i+1}(t) = \cos(t/10000^{2i/D})$ for $i < D/2$. Nearby steps get similar vectors, and every frequency is present. 2. Pass it through a small MLP to get a learned vector $h(t)$. 3. In every residual block, project $h(t)$ with a Linear layer to $C$ numbers (the block's channel count), reshape to $(B, C, 1, \dots, 1)$ and add it to the feature map, which broadcasts it over all positions. A variant predicts a scale and a shift per channel instead. Simpler options (append $t/T$ as an extra input channel) work for toy problems; the embedding is the standard answer. Keep the indices straight: $\bar\alpha t$ is a product up to and including $t$, the posterior uses $\bar\alpha {t-1}$, and in code alpha bars[i] is $\bar\alpha {i+1}$. The noise coefficient is $\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha t}$, not $\sqrt{\beta t}$ (that is the one-step coefficient). For a derivation, state the Gaussian facts you use (sum of independent normals, the KL formula, completing the square).

Lesson 4 trained a noise predictor $\varepsilon \theta(x t, t)$. This lesson turns it into samples: the DDPM sampler that runs all $T$ steps, the DDIM sampler that skips most of them, and classifier-free guidance, the trick that makes text-to-image models follow the prompt. Expect a Round 2 part that asks you to code one sampling step or to explain what the guidance scale does. DDPM sampling Generation runs the reverse process from lesson 4. Start with $x T \sim N(0, I)$ and for $t = T, T-1, \dots, 1$ set The first part is the model's mean $\mu \theta$ (the noise-prediction form of $\tilde\mu t$). The noise $\sigma t z$ makes each step a random draw from $p \theta(x {t-1} \mid x t)$; drawing each variable from its conditional distribution in order like this is called ancestral sampling .
