DDPM uses $\sigma t^2 = \tilde\beta t$ or $\sigma t^2 = \beta t$; both work. The last step adds no noise, because $x 0$ is the output. Note the if i 0 guard: alpha bars[i - 1] at i = 0 would be alpha bars[-1] , the last entry, without any error. The cost is the problem: 1000 network evaluations per batch of images. DDIM: fewer, deterministic steps At any step the network's noise estimate also gives an estimate of the clean data, by solving the closed form for $x 0$: DDIM (denoising diffusion implicit models) jumps from step $t$ to any earlier step $s < t$ by putting $\hat{x} 0$ and the same noise estimate back into the closed form at level $s$: This version adds no fresh noise (DDIM's $\eta = 0$ setting), so the same starting $x T$ always gives the same output. It uses the network trained with the DDPM loss, unchanged, and works with 20 to 50 steps instead of 1000. For images, implementations usually clamp $\hat{x} 0$ to the data range $[-1, 1]$ before the jump. The cell checks both samplers on a case where the perfect noise predictor has a formula: one-dimensional data from $N(3, 0.5^2)$. Then $x t$ given $x 0$ is Gaussian and the best prediction of the noise from $x t$ is a linear function of $x t$ (see the note below the cell). If the samplers are right, both outputs should have mean 3 and standard deviation 0.5. DDPM gives mean 3.004 and standard deviation 0.494. DDIM with 50 steps gives 2.993 and 0.476, a small error from the large jumps; with 200 steps it gives 0.497. With $x 0 \sim N(m, s^2)$ and $x t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha t}x 0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha t}\,\varepsilon$, the pair $(\varepsilon, x t)$ is jointly normal with $\mathrm{Cov}(\varepsilon, x t) = \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha t}$ and $\mathrm{Var}(x t) = \bar\alpha t s^2 + 1 - \bar\alpha t$. For jointly normal variables the best prediction under squared error is the linear regression of one on the other, $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon \mid x t] = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}}{\mathrm{Var}}\,(x t - \sqrt{\bar\alpha t}\,m)$. A trained network approximates this function; for real data it has no formula. Conditioning and classifier-free guidance For conditional generation (a class label, or a text prompt), give the network the condition as an extra input: $\varepsilon \theta(x t, t, c)$. Train it exactly as before, on (image, condition) pairs. In practice the samples then follow $c$ only loosely. Classifier-free guidance (CFG) strengthens the condition with one network: 1. During training, replace $c$ by a special null condition $\varnothing$ (an extra "no label" class, or an empty prompt) with probability around 10 to 20%. The network learns both the conditional prediction $\varepsilon \theta(x t, t, c)$ and the unconditional one $\varepsilon \theta(x t, t, \varnothing)$. 2. At each sampling step, run both and extrapolate from the unconditional prediction toward the conditional one: then use $\tilde\varepsilon$ in the DDPM or DDIM update. The guidance scale $w$ sets the strength: $w = 0$ ignores the condition, $w = 1$ is the plain conditional model, and $w 1$ exaggerates whatever separates "with $c$" from "without $c$". Stable Diffusion's default is 7.5. Larger $w$ follows the prompt more closely but gives less varied, more saturated images: a trade between fidelity and diversity. Some papers write the same rule as $(1 + w')\varepsilon c - w'\varepsilon \varnothing$, so $w' = w - 1$; read which convention a problem uses. Guidance doubles the network calls. Implementations put both in one batch: Latent diffusion and Stable Diffusion Running a U-Net 50 times on a 512 by 512 by 3 image is expensive. Latent diffusion first trains an autoencoder (a VAE, lesson 2) that compresses the image to a small latent, for example 64 by 64 by 4, and runs the whole diffusion process on latents; the decoder turns the final latent into an image. Stable Diffusion is latent diffusion conditioned on text: a frozen text encoder turns the prompt into vectors, and the U-Net reads them through cross-attention layers (attention whose queries come from the image features and whose keys and values come from the text; u15-l03, u16-l02). Sampling uses DDIM-style samplers and classifier-free guidance. With the diffusers library: One DDPM step: the mean uses $\beta t/\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha t}$ and divides by $\sqrt{\alpha t}$; no noise on the last step. DDIM: compute $\hat{x} 0$, then re-noise it to the earlier level with the same $\varepsilon \theta$. CFG: $\varepsilon \varnothing + w(\varepsilon c - \varepsilon \varnothing)$, with the null condition learned by dropping $c$ during training.

The IOAI syllabus lists object detection (YOLO, SSD, DETR) at practice level: you should know what each model outputs, how predictions are matched and scored, and be able to write the box arithmetic yourself. That arithmetic (box formats, IoU, non-maximum suppression, mean average precision) is also exactly what a Round 2 part can ask you to implement with the library versions banned. This lesson builds it from zero. Boxes Object detection means finding every object in an image and giving each one a class and a bounding box , the smallest axis-aligned rectangle around it. Three formats are common, all in pixels with $y$ pointing down: - xyxy : $(x 1, y 1, x 2, y 2)$, the top-left and bottom-right corners (torchvision's format); - xywh : $(x 1, y 1, w, h)$, the top-left corner, width and height (COCO's annotation format); - cxcywh : $(c x, c y, w, h)$, the center and the size (YOLO and DETR predict this, often divided by the image size so it lies in $[0, 1]$). Converting is one line each way, and mixing formats up is the most common detection bug: a box (10, 10, 4, 4) is a 4 by 4 square in xywh but an empty box in xyxy . Intersection over union The IoU (intersection over union, also called the Jaccard index) of two boxes is the area of their overlap divided by the area of their union: In xyxy , the intersection is itself a box with corners $(\max(x 1^A, x 1^B), \max(y 1^A, y 1^B))$ and $(\min(x 2^A, x 2^B), \min(y 2^A, y 2^B))$; its width and height are clamped at 0 when the boxes do not overlap. IoU is 1 for identical boxes and 0 for disjoint ones. For $n$ boxes against $m$ boxes, broadcasting gives the whole $(n, m)$ matrix at once: Non-maximum suppression A detector proposes many overlapping boxes for the same object, each with a confidence score . Non-maximum suppression (NMS) keeps one per object, greedily: 1. Sort the boxes by score, highest first. 2. Keep the top box. Remove every remaining box whose IoU with it exceeds a threshold (typically 0.5). 3. Repeat with the highest remaining box until none are left. NMS is applied per class (a cat box should not suppress an overlapping dog box). torchvision has torchvision.ops.nms(boxes, scores, iou threshold) , which returns the kept indices in decreasing score order, and batched nms(boxes, scores, classes, iou threshold) for the per-class version. Problem u19-p01 has you write both IoU and NMS with these banned. How detectors predict boxes - YOLO (you only look once) splits the image into an $S \times S$ grid. Each cell predicts a few boxes (offsets of the center within the cell and a width and height, usually relative to preset anchor boxes ), an objectness score and class probabilities, all in one forward pass of a CNN. NMS cleans up the output. - SSD (single shot detector) does the same from feature maps at several resolutions: coarse maps (large receptive fields) handle big objects and fine maps small ones. - DETR (detection transformer) replaces anchors and NMS with set prediction : a CNN backbone and a transformer encoder-decoder produce a fixed number of object slots (for example 100), each a box and a class, with a "no object" class for empty slots. Training matches slots to ground-truth objects one-to-one with the Hungarian algorithm (the assignment of minimum total cost, using class probability, L1 box distance and an IoU-based term), then applies the box losses to the matched pairs and a classification loss to every slot, with the unmatched slots trained toward "no object". Duplicates are penalized by the matching itself, so no NMS is needed. Training a YOLO-style model combines three losses: a box regression loss on cells that contain an object, a binary cross-entropy objectness loss everywhere, and a classification loss. Mean average precision A predicted box is a true positive if its IoU with a ground-truth box of the same class is at least a threshold (0.5 is usual) and that ground-truth box has not already been matched by a higher-scoring prediction; otherwise it is a false positive. Unmatched ground-truth boxes are false negatives. To score one class, sort its predictions by confidence and walk down the list, recording precision and recall after each one. The average precision (AP) is the area under this precision-recall curve (average precision, u06-l06). The mAP is the mean of AP over classes. "mAP@0.5" uses the IoU threshold 0.5; the COCO metric averages mAP over thresholds $0.5, 0.55, \dots, 0.95$, which rewards tight boxes. Three ground-truth objects. Four predictions sorted by score: TP, FP, TP, TP. After each: precision $1, \frac12, \frac23, \frac34$; recall $\frac13, \frac13, \frac23, 1$. Recall rises at predictions 1, 3 and 4, by $\frac13$ each, so with the simple sum $\sum (\Delta \text{recall}) \cdot \text{precision}$ the AP is $\frac13(1 + \frac23 + \frac34) = 0.806$. (The VOC and COCO tools first make precision non-increasing from the right: each precision is replaced by the largest precision at the same or a higher recall. Here that raises the $\frac23$ at prediction 3 to $\frac34$, so their AP is $\frac13(1 + \frac34 + \frac34) = 0.833$. The items in this unit use the simple sum.) Exam angle - State the box format in a comment next to every tensor of boxes. Convert once, at the input. - IoU: maximum of the top-left corners, minimum of the bottom-right, clamp(min=0) , then intersection over union. - NMS: sort, keep, suppress by IoU, repeat; per class. - API recall (when allowed): torchvision.ops.box iou(a, b) , nms(boxes, scores, iou threshold) , batched nms(boxes, scores, idxs, iou threshold) , box convert(boxes, in fmt="cxcywh", out fmt="xyxy") . - mAP is computed per class, at a stated IoU threshold, from score-sorted predictions. Practice problem: u19-p01 IoU and NMS from scratch .

The IOAI syllabus lists image segmentation with U-Net at practice level, and the USAAIO syllabus names UNet under computer vision. U-Nets also do the denoising inside diffusion models (u18-l04). This lesson covers what a segmentation model outputs, how a U-Net keeps the input's resolution, the loss and metrics, and the Dice loss, which problem u19-p02 asks you to write. Labels for every pixel Semantic segmentation gives every pixel a class: road, car, sky, or background and tumor. Instance segmentation also separates objects of the same class (car 1, car 2), usually by predicting a mask inside each detected box. Panoptic segmentation does both for the whole image. This lesson is about semantic segmentation. A model for $K$ classes outputs logits of shape (B, K, H, W) for a batch of $B$ images (u10 to u12 wrote the batch size $N$): a score per class at every pixel. The target is a mask of shape (B, H, W) holding class ids. F.cross entropy accepts these shapes directly, because it treats dimension 1 as the class axis and averages over every other position: For a single foreground class use one logit channel, shape (B, 1, H, W) , and BCEWithLogitsLoss against a float mask of the same shape. The U-Net A classification CNN shrinks the image to a vector. A segmentation network must give back a full-size map, so it needs a way back up. The U-Net (U-Net) is an encoder-decoder with one extra idea: - The encoder (contracting path) repeats: two 3 by 3 convolutions with ReLU, then a 2 by 2 max pool that halves $H$ and $W$. Channels usually double at each level. Deep levels see a large area (receptive field) but have lost the exact positions. - The decoder (expanding path) repeats: a transposed convolution nn.ConvTranspose2d(c, c // 2, kernel size=2, stride=2) that doubles $H$ and $W$ (each input pixel becomes a learned 2 by 2 patch), then concatenation with the encoder's feature map of the same size, then two 3 by 3 convolutions. - The concatenations are the skip connections : they hand the decoder the fine detail the encoder had before pooling, so boundaries come out sharp. Without them the decoder must guess edges from a 16 times coarser map (after the four poolings of the original U-Net). - A final 1x1 convolution maps the channels to $K$ logits per pixel. The skips concatenate along the channel axis ( torch.cat([up, skip], dim=1) ), so the decoder block after them takes twice the channels of the upsampled map. The original U-Net used unpadded convolutions and cropped the skips; the common modern form uses padding=1 so every size matches, which requires $H$ and $W$ divisible by $2^{\text{depth}}$. Each pooling halves the size and each transposed convolution doubles it back, so the logits have the input's $64 \times 64$ resolution. At initialization the loss is close to $\ln 4 = 1.386$, the loss of a uniform guess over 4 classes, which is a quick sanity check for any classifier. Dice loss In medical images the foreground (a tumor) may be 1% of the pixels. Cross-entropy averages over pixels, so predicting background everywhere already scores well. The Dice coefficient of a predicted mask $A$ and a true mask $B$ measures overlap relative to their sizes: It is 1 for a perfect mask and 0 for no overlap, whatever the size of the object, and it relates to IoU by $\text{Dice} = 2\,\text{IoU}/(1 + \text{IoU})$ (since $ A + B = A \cup B + A \cap B $, divide the numerator and the denominator of Dice by $ A \cup B $). To train with it, replace the hard masks with probabilities $p i$ (softmax over classes) and one-hot targets $g i \in \{0, 1\}$, summed over all pixels $i$: This soft Dice loss is differentiable. The smoothing constant $\epsilon$ (often 1) keeps a class that is absent from both the target and the prediction at Dice 1 instead of $0/0$. Averaging over classes gives small classes the same weight as large ones, like macro averaging. In practice loss = cross entropy + dice is a common, stable combination. Metrics Pixel accuracy has the same flaw as accuracy on imbalanced data. Report the mean IoU (mIoU): for each class, IoU between the predicted and true masks of that class over the whole dataset, then the mean over classes. Exam angle - Shapes: logits (B, K, H, W) , target (B, H, W) long, argmax(dim=1) for the mask, softmax(dim=1) for probabilities. - U-Net: conv block, pool, ..., ConvTranspose2d(c, c // 2, 2, stride=2) , cat([up, skip], dim=1) , conv block, 1x1 head. Count channels after every concatenation. - Dice: soft probabilities, sums over pixels, $\epsilon$ in numerator and denominator, mean over classes, 1 - dice . Practice problem: u19-p02 The soft Dice loss .

Labels are expensive and images are cheap. Self-supervised learning (self-supervised learning, u06-l01) trains an encoder on unlabeled images with a task made from the images themselves; the encoder's features then make a small labeled set go much further. The IOAI syllabus lists it under computer vision, the 2026 Round 2 Problem 4 gave 200 labeled and 800 unlabeled images, and CLIP (next lesson) uses the same loss with text as the second view. This lesson derives the contrastive loss of SimCLR, computes it, and describes masked autoencoders. The contrastive idea Contrastive learning pulls together the representations of two views of the same image and pushes apart those of different images. A view is a random augmentation of an image: a random crop resized to full size, a horizontal flip, color jitter, grayscale, blur. Two views of one image form a positive pair ; views of different images are negatives . If the encoder maps both views of a cat photo close together and far from every other photo, it must have captured what stays the same under cropping and recoloring: the content. SimCLR (a simple framework for contrastive learning) does this with: 1. a batch of $N$ images, each augmented twice, giving $2N$ views; 2. an encoder $f$ (a ResNet) giving representations $h = f(x)$; 3. a small MLP projection head $g$ giving $z = g(h)$, the vectors the loss sees; 4. the NT-Xent loss on the $z$'s. After training, $g$ is thrown away and $h$ is used downstream, usually evaluated with a linear probe. The head absorbs the invariances the loss forces (such as ignoring color), which would otherwise be removed from $h$ too. Deriving NT-Xent Normalize every $z$ to unit length, so the dot product $s {ij} = z i^\top z j$ is the cosine similarity. Number the views so that $i$ and $i + N$ are the two views of image $i$. For anchor $i$ with positive partner $p(i)$, ask the model to pick the partner out of all the other $2N - 1$ views, as a classification with a softmax over similarities divided by a temperature $\tau$: The NT-Xent loss (normalized temperature-scaled cross-entropy) is the mean of $\ell i$ over all $2N$ anchors. The sum excludes $k = i$ (a view is trivially most similar to itself). So $\ell i$ is exactly cross-entropy loss for a $(2N-1)$-way problem whose logits are the scaled similarities and whose correct class is the partner. That gives the implementation: build the $2N \times 2N$ similarity matrix, set the diagonal to $-\infty$, and call F.cross entropy with targets $p(i)$. What the pieces do: - Each anchor has $2N - 2$ negatives, so larger batches give a harder task and better features; SimCLR used batches of thousands. - A small $\tau$ (0.1 to 0.5) sharpens the softmax so the hardest negatives (the most similar wrong views) dominate the gradient. Since cosines lie in $[-1, 1]$, the logits lie in $[-1/\tau, 1/\tau]$. - If the embeddings carry no information, all similarities are equal and the loss is $\ln(2N - 1)$, a useful reference value. Unrelated views score a little above $\ln 15 = 2.71$, the value for exactly equal similarities (here 2.89: random vectors in 16 dimensions are not exactly orthogonal, and uneven similarities raise the loss); views that agree score far lower. The last line checks the worked example below. $N = 2$, $\tau = 0.5$, unit vectors $z 0 = (1, 0)$, $z 1 = (0, 1)$ (view a of images 0 and 1) and $z 2 = (0.8, 0.6)$, $z 3 = (0.6, 0.8)$ (view b). Anchor 0's partner is $z 2$. Similarities: $s {01} = 0$, $s {02} = 0.8$, $s {03} = 0.6$; divided by $\tau$: $0, 1.6, 1.2$. Then $\ell 0 = -\log \frac{e^{1.6}}{e^{0} + e^{1.6} + e^{1.2}} = -\log \frac{4.953}{9.273} = 0.627$. Masked autoencoders A masked autoencoder (MAE) is the image version of masked language modeling. Cut the image into patches as a vision transformer does, hide a random 75% of them, run the encoder on the visible 25% only, and let a light decoder (which receives the encoded visible patches plus a learned mask token at each hidden position) reconstruct the pixels of the hidden patches. The loss is the mean squared error on the masked patches only. Because the encoder sees a quarter of the tokens, pretraining is several times cheaper than running it on the full image. Afterward the decoder is dropped and the encoder is fine-tuned or probed. Random masking in a batch of $B$ images with $L$ patches each is one line: keep = torch.rand(B, L).argsort(dim=1)[:, :L // 4] gives each image its own random set of kept patch indices (sorting uniform noise gives a random permutation per row). Other methods drop the negatives: BYOL and DINO train a student network to match a slowly updated teacher (an exponential moving average of the student's weights) on a different view, and avoid the trivial constant solution through that asymmetry. Exam angle - NT-Xent: concatenate the views, F.normalize(z, dim=1) , z @ z.T / tau , diagonal to -inf (not 0), targets cat([arange(N, 2N), arange(N)]) , F.cross entropy . - Reference values: $\ln(2N - 1)$ for random embeddings; the loss falls as views align. - Pretraining with a projection head, evaluation with a linear probe on $h$. - MAE: mask most patches, encode the visible ones only, MSE on the masked ones. Practice problem: u19-p03 The NT-Xent loss .

The third problem of the 2025 Round 2 (100 points, 20 parts) built CLIP from a pretrained ViT and a pretrained BERT: preprocess images and captions, write a collate function, add projection layers and a learnable temperature, freeze the encoders, write the symmetric contrastive loss, train, and then answer questions about cosine similarity in high dimensions and the limits of the temperature. The IOAI syllabus lists vision-text encoders (CLIP) at practice level. This lesson covers all of those ideas; the contrastive loss is the one from u19-l03 with captions as the second view. Two encoders, one space CLIP (contrastive language-image pretraining) learns from image-caption pairs scraped from the web. It has - an image encoder (a vision transformer or ResNet) whose class token output (or pooled features) summarizes the image; - a text encoder (a transformer, BERT-like in the 2025 problem) whose first-token or end-of-text output summarizes the caption; - two linear projections mapping both summaries into one shared $d$-dimensional embedding space (the encoders' widths differ, so this step is needed even to compare them); - a learnable temperature $\tau$. Both embeddings are normalized to unit length, so their dot product is the cosine similarity. For a batch of $N$ pairs, stack the image embeddings as rows of $I$ and the text embeddings as rows of $T$ (both $N \times d$). The similarity matrix of logits is The correct pairs are on the diagonal. The symmetric loss Each row of $S$ is an $N$-way classification "which caption belongs to image $i$?" with answer $i$; each column is "which image belongs to caption $j$?" with answer $j$. CLIP averages the two cross-entropies: In code the labels are torch.arange(N) for both directions, and the second direction is the transpose: F.cross entropy(S.T, labels) . Unlike NT-Xent, the negatives of an image are only the other captions, not the other images. Why learn $\log \tau$. $\tau$ must stay positive. Storing $\log\tau$ as the parameter and using $\tau = e^{\log\tau}$ makes every value of the parameter legal, and a gradient step changes $\tau$ by a factor rather than by an amount, which suits a scale that may need to move from 1 to 0.01. (The official CLIP stores $\log(1/\tau)$, starts it at $\log(1/0.07)$, and multiplies instead of dividing.) The limits of $\tau$. As $\tau \to 0^+$, $\operatorname{softmax}(z/\tau)$ tends to 1 at the largest $z i$ and 0 elsewhere (a hard argmax). As $\tau \to \infty$ every $z i/\tau \to 0$ and the softmax tends to the uniform $1/N$. Training settles in between: small enough to separate the right caption from close wrong ones, large enough to keep gradients for all of them. Matched pairs give a loss near 0. Random pairs give more than $\ln N$: at $\tau = 0.07$ even the small random cosines (about $\pm 0.14$ in 32 dimensions) become logits of size about 2, so the softmax is confidently wrong. The last line shows why cosine similarity works in high dimensions: two random directions in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ have cosine with mean 0 and standard deviation about $1/\sqrt d$ (0.044 for $d = 512$). By Chebyshev's inequality, $P( \cos \epsilon) \le 1/(\epsilon^2 d)$, so unrelated images and captions are almost orthogonal and only genuinely related pairs get a large similarity. Zero-shot classification A trained CLIP classifies images into classes it was never trained on as labels. Write a prompt per class, such as "a photo of a dog.", embed the prompts with the text encoder, normalize, and pick for each image the class whose prompt embedding has the largest cosine with the image embedding: This is zero-shot classification : no labeled training image of any class was used. Averaging the embeddings of several templates per class ("a photo of a {c}.", "a blurry photo of a {c}.") is called prompt ensembling and usually adds a few points of accuracy. Normalize before comparing: raw dot products favor whichever embedding happens to be long. Training CLIP on a budget The 2025 problem froze both pretrained encoders and trained only the two projections and $\log\tau$. That is a linear probe on both sides: cheap (only the small layers get gradients, so the encoders can run under torch.no grad() or even be precomputed once) and stable on a few thousand pairs. Unfreezing the encoders needs far more data and a small learning rate. The Hugging Face API, for reference (needs a download; not runnable offline): Exam angle - Normalize both sides, logits = img @ txt.T / log tau.exp() , labels = torch.arange(N) , average F.cross entropy(logits, labels) and F.cross entropy(logits.T, labels) . - log tau is an nn.Parameter ; include it in the optimizer. - Zero-shot: prompts, normalize, cosine, argmax over classes. - Derivation parts: limits of the temperature, near-orthogonality ($\operatorname{std} \approx 1/\sqrt d$, Chebyshev), why the projection is needed. Practice problem: u19-p04 CLIP loss and zero-shot prediction .

The 2026 Round 2 Problem 4 (40 points) gave 1,000 training images of one colored shape each (circle, triangle or rectangle, at random positions, sizes, rotations and colors), of which only the first 200 had labels, and scored a CNN by macro F1 on 300 test images. All pretrained models were banned, and so was labeling images by eye: unlabeled data could be ignored or labeled by code only. The official rationale named pseudo-labeling, clustering and validation design as the skills tested. This lesson covers those methods. The setting Semi-supervised learning trains on a small labeled set $\{(x i, y i)\}$ plus a larger unlabeled set $\{u j\}$ from the same distribution. It helps when the classes form separate clumps in a good feature space: the unlabeled points show where the clumps and the gaps are, and the decision boundary should run through the gaps. Always start with the supervised baseline (labeled data only, with strong data augmentation), since every method below must beat it on validation. Pseudo-labeling Pseudo-labeling (self-training) uses the model's own confident predictions as labels: 1. Train on the labeled set. 2. Predict the unlabeled set. Keep the examples whose top probability is at least a confidence threshold (0.9 to 0.95 is typical) and give each its predicted class as a pseudo-label . 3. Retrain on labeled plus pseudo-labeled data. Repeat a few rounds, possibly lowering the threshold. Two failure modes. Confirmation bias : a wrong pseudo-label is trained on, which makes the model more confident in the same mistake. Class imbalance : one class is often easier, so it dominates the confident predictions and the model drifts toward it. Remedies: a high threshold, class-balanced selection (keep at most the same number of the most confident examples per class), and re-predicting all pseudo-labels from scratch each round instead of keeping old ones. Consistency regularization The second idea needs no labels at all: a good classifier should give the same answer for two augmentations of the same image. Consistency regularization adds a loss on unlabeled data that penalizes disagreement between predictions on two perturbed versions, such as the squared difference of their softmax outputs (the Π-model) or the disagreement with a mean teacher , a copy of the model whose weights are an exponential moving average of the student's. FixMatch combines both ideas in one step per unlabeled batch: - predict on a weak augmentation (flip and small shift) without gradients; if the top probability is at least $\tau$ (0.95), take its class as the pseudo-label; - compute cross-entropy of the prediction on a strong augmentation (large crops, color changes, cutout) against that pseudo-label, only for the confident examples; - total loss $L = L {\text{sup}} + \lambda L {\text{unsup}}$, with $L {\text{unsup}}$ averaged over the whole unlabeled batch (unconfident examples contribute 0). The model here is untrained, which shows the two dangers in miniature. At a strict threshold nothing passes yet (early in training that is normal, and it is why FixMatch works: unconfident examples do no harm). At a loose threshold almost every pseudo-label is the same class: training on them would push the model further toward class 1. Clustering, then labeling When the classes are visually distinct, as simple shapes are, unsupervised structure goes a long way: 1. Compute features for all 1,000 images: a self-supervised encoder (u19-l03), a CNN trained on the 200 labels, or hand-made features (an outline's corner count, the ratio of the area to the bounding box area). 2. Cluster with k-means into a few more clusters than classes. 3. Give each cluster the majority label of the labeled images inside it, and use those labels for the unlabeled members. This is labeling by code, which the 2026 rules allow; labeling by looking at the images is not. Combine it with the other methods: the cluster labels can seed a first round of pseudo-labels. Validation with few labels With 200 labels, a validation set of 40 gives a noisy macro F1 (one image is 2.5% of accuracy). Use stratified k-fold cross-validation on the labeled set to compare methods, and never validate on pseudo-labels, which are the model's own opinion. Fix the split before trying methods, so every method is judged on the same images, and keep a results log for the report, which was a required part of the submission. Exam angle - Read the rules: no pretrained weights (also no torchvision.models architectures with random weights if the rule says "all pretrained models"; build your own CNN), no manual labels, predictions from code. - Baseline first: a small CNN on the labeled images with augmentation. Then pseudo-labels or FixMatch, class-balanced, with a high threshold. - Code: with torch.no grad(): probs = model(weak).softmax(1) , conf, pseudo = probs.max(1) , mask = conf = tau , (F.cross entropy(model(strong), pseudo, reduction="none") mask).mean() . - Validate on held-out true labels only. Practice problems: u19-p05 Choosing pseudo-labels (threshold plus a per-class cap) and u19-p06 Shapes from 60 labels (open-ended: macro F1 on a CPU budget, with 1,140 unlabeled images).

The IOAI 2027 syllabus adds a new section, "Basics of reinforcement learning", and names the Sutton and Barto textbook ( Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction , 2nd edition, written S&B below) as the reference. This unit follows the sections it lists. Reinforcement learning (RL) differs from everything before it in one way: nobody gives the correct output. A learner acts, sees a number that says how well things went, and must work out which of its earlier choices deserve the credit. This lesson sets up the vocabulary (S&B 3.1 to 3.3) and the one quantity everything later estimates, the discounted return. The agent-environment loop The learner is the agent ; everything it interacts with is the environment . Time runs in discrete time steps $t = 0, 1, 2, \dots$ At each step: 1. the agent observes the state $S t$, a description of the situation (a board position, a robot's joint angles, a cell of a grid); 2. it picks an action $A t$ from the allowed set; 3. the environment answers with a reward $R {t+1}$, a real number, and the next state $S {t+1}$. The reward is indexed $t + 1$ because it arrives together with the next state. The sequence $S 0, A 0, R 1, S 1, A 1, R 2, S 2, \dots$ is a trajectory . In an episodic task the interaction breaks into episodes that end in a terminal state (a game is won or lost, the robot falls), after which the environment resets. A continuing task never ends (a thermostat, a trading agent). The agent's goal is to collect as much reward as possible in the long run. Rewards say what to achieve, never how : a chess agent gets $+1$ for a win, not points for capturing pieces, or it would learn to capture pieces and lose. Markov decision processes A Markov decision process (MDP) is the formal model of the environment. It has a set of states, a set of actions, and dynamics the probability of each next state and reward given the current state and action. The Markov property is the assumption hidden in this notation: the next state and reward depend only on the current state and action, not on the earlier history. (A Markov chain is the same idea without actions.) If the state leaves out something that matters (a single frame of a ball, which shows position but not velocity), the property fails, and the usual fix is to put more into the state (stack the last few frames). The agent's behavior is a policy $\pi$: for each state, a distribution over actions, $\pi(a \mid s)$. A deterministic policy puts all probability on one action, written $\pi(s)$; a stochastic policy spreads it. The reset and step methods copy the interface of Gymnasium , the standard RL environment library. Its real signatures carry two more fields: The difference between terminated and truncated matters from lesson 4 on: after a true terminal state there is no future reward, while a time limit only stops the recording. Returns and discounting The agent maximizes the expected return $G t$, a function of the rewards after time $t$. The simplest choice is their sum. With a discount factor $0 \le \gamma \le 1$, A reward $k$ steps in the future counts $\gamma^k$ times as much as an immediate one. Two reasons for $\gamma < 1$: 1. Continuing tasks need it. If every reward is at most $R \text{max}$ in size, the geometric series gives $ G t \le R \text{max}/(1 - \gamma)$, a finite number. With $\gamma = 1$ an endless task could have an infinite return. A constant reward of 1 forever is worth $\frac{1}{1 - \gamma}$: 10 at $\gamma = 0.9$, 100 at $\gamma = 0.99$. That number, $\frac{1}{1-\gamma}$, is a rough horizon : how many steps ahead the agent effectively cares about. 2. Sooner is better. With $\gamma < 1$ the same reward reached in fewer steps has a larger return, so the agent prefers short paths even when every path eventually gets there. $\gamma = 0$ makes the agent greedy for the next reward only; $\gamma$ near 1 makes it far-sighted. Episodic tasks may use $\gamma = 1$ when every episode is guaranteed to end. The recursion. Factor $\gamma$ out of every term after the first: This one line is the root of the Bellman equations in the next lesson. It also gives the fast way to compute all returns of an episode: start at the end ($G = 0$ after the terminal step) and go backwards, as the cell does. For the episode above, with rewards $-1, -1, -1, +10$ and $\gamma = 0.9$: $G 3 = 10$, $G 2 = -1 + 0.9 \cdot 10 = 8$, $G 1 = -1 + 0.9 \cdot 8 = 6.2$, $G 0 = -1 + 0.9\cdot 6.2 = 4.58$. A maze with reward 0 per step, $+1$ at the exit and $\gamma = 1$ gives every exiting policy the same return 1, so nothing favors short routes. Either discount ($\gamma < 1$) or charge $-1$ per step. Rewards that are easy to collect without doing the task (points for touching the ball in a soccer game) get collected instead of doing the task. Know the index convention ($R {t+1}$ follows $A t$), compute a discounted return by hand from the end backwards, and use $\frac{1}{1-\gamma}$ for constant rewards. Code returns with a reversed loop: G = r + gamma G .

Almost every RL method estimates a value function: how good it is to be in a state, or to take an action in a state, when you follow some policy afterwards. The Bellman equations say how the value of a state relates to the values of the states after it. They are the target that dynamic programming (lesson 3), TD learning (lesson 4), Q-learning (lesson 5) and DQN (lesson 6) all aim at, and a Bellman backup by hand is a natural contest item. This lesson covers S&B 3.5 and 3.6. State values and action values Fix a policy $\pi$. The state-value function of $\pi$ is the expected return from state $s$ when the agent follows $\pi$: The action-value function fixes the first action too, then follows $\pi$: The expectation $\mathbb{E} \pi$ averages over the policy's random choices and the environment's random transitions. A terminal state has value 0, since no reward follows it. The two functions are linked in both directions: The first averages over the policy's first action. The second takes one step of the dynamics and uses the recursion $G t = R {t+1} + \gamma G {t+1}$ from lesson 1: the return is the next reward plus $\gamma$ times the return from wherever you land, whose expectation is $v \pi(s')$. The Bellman expectation equation Substituting the second relation into the first gives an equation that involves $v \pi$ alone, the Bellman expectation equation : Read it as a backup : the value of $s$ is computed from the values of its possible successors, one step ahead. The version for action values is $q \pi(s, a) = \sum {s', r} p(s', r \mid s, a)\big[r + \gamma \sum {a'} \pi(a' \mid s') q \pi(s', a')\big]$. In state $s$ the policy picks each of two actions with probability $\frac12$, and $\gamma = 0.9$. Action 1 gives reward 1 and always leads to a state worth 4. Action 2 gives reward 0 and leads to a state worth 10 or one worth 2, each with probability $\frac12$. Then $q \pi(s, 1) = 1 + 0.9\cdot 4 = 4.6$, $q \pi(s, 2) = 0 + 0.9\cdot(0.5\cdot 10 + 0.5\cdot 2) = 5.4$, and $v \pi(s) = 0.5\cdot 4.6 + 0.5\cdot 5.4 = 5.0$. Solving it as a linear system For a finite MDP the Bellman expectation equation is a system of linear equations, one per state. Collect the policy's one-step quantities: the matrix $P \pi$ with $P \pi[s, s'] = \sum a \pi(a \mid s)\, p(s' \mid s, a)$ and the vector $r \pi[s] = \sum a \pi(a \mid s)\, r(s, a)$, where $r(s, a)$ is the expected reward. Then $v \pi = r \pi + \gamma P \pi v \pi$, so For $\gamma < 1$ the matrix $I - \gamma P \pi$ is always invertible (each row of $\gamma P \pi$ sums to $\gamma < 1$). In code, store the MDP as two arrays: P[s, a, s2] for transition probabilities and R[s, a] for expected rewards. P @ V multiplies the last axis of P (shape (3, 2, 3) ) with V (shape (3,) ), giving the expected next value for every pair $(s, a)$, shape (3, 2) . Check state 2 by hand: it is absorbing with rewards 0 and 0.5, so under the uniform policy it earns 0.25 per step forever: $v = 0.25/(1 - 0.9) = 2.5$. Solving costs about $ S ^3$ operations, fine for 100 states and hopeless for a million. Lesson 3 replaces it with iteration, and later lessons replace the known $p$ with samples. Optimal values and the Bellman optimality equation One policy is at least as good as another if its value is at least as large in every state. There is always a policy that is at least as good as every other, an optimal policy $\pi $, and all optimal policies share the optimal value functions An optimal agent takes the best action, so the average over $\pi$ becomes a maximum. This gives the Bellman optimality equations : In the backup example above, the optimal backup is $\max(4.6, 5.4) = 5.4$ (if the successor values were optimal values). Two consequences carry the rest of the unit: 1. Acting greedily on $q $ is optimal. A greedy policy picks $\arg\max a q(s, a)$. Any policy greedy with respect to $q $ is optimal. With $v $ you can also act optimally, but choosing the action needs the dynamics $p$ to look one step ahead; with $q $ the lookahead is already done. That is why model-free control (Q-learning) learns $q$, not $v$. 2. The max makes the system nonlinear. There is no matrix formula for $v $. It is found by iteration (value iteration, next lesson) or by learning from experience. A Bellman backup by hand: for each action, reward plus $\gamma$ times the expected next value; then average over the policy ($v \pi$) or take the max ($v $). In code, Q = R + gamma P @ V , then (pi Q).sum(1) or Q.max(1) . Terminal states have value 0.

When the dynamics $p(s', r \mid s, a)$ are known, the Bellman equations can be solved by repeating backups until nothing changes. This is dynamic programming (DP) in the RL sense: computing value functions from a full model of the MDP. Real agents rarely have the model, but every learning method in the rest of the unit is DP with the model replaced by samples, so the algorithms here are the templates. This lesson covers S&B 4.1 and 4.2, plus value iteration (S&B 4.4), and runs them on a small gridworld. Iterative policy evaluation Lesson 2 solved $v \pi = r \pi + \gamma P \pi v \pi$ with a linear solve. Iterative policy evaluation instead starts from any guess $V 0$ (zeros) and applies the Bellman expectation backup to every state, over and over: One pass over all states is a sweep . Stop when the largest change in a sweep is below a small threshold $\theta$. Why it converges, for $\gamma < 1$: if two guesses differ by at most $\delta$ in every state, one backup makes them differ by at most $\gamma\delta$, because each backup is an average of rewards plus $\gamma$ times successor values. A map that shrinks distances by a fixed factor like this is a contraction , and it has exactly one fixed point, $v \pi$. After $k$ sweeps the error is at most $\gamma^k$ times the starting error. (With $\gamma = 1$ it still converges when every episode is sure to end.) There are two ways to store the sweep: with two arrays (compute all of $V {k+1}$ from $V k$), or in place , overwriting $V(s)$ immediately so that later states in the same sweep already use the new values. Both converge to $v \pi$; in place usually needs fewer sweeps. With NumPy, the two-array version is one line. A gridworld The cell builds a gridworld : a 4 by 4 grid, states 0 to 15 in row-major order, with state 15 (bottom right) terminal. The four actions move up, right, down or left; a move into the wall leaves the agent in place. Every step costs $-1$, so the value of a state is minus the expected number of steps to reach the corner. It evaluates the uniform random policy with $\gamma = 1$. A random walk from the far corner needs about 59 steps on average. The terminal state is stored as an absorbing state with reward 0, so its value stays 0 and backups through it add nothing. Policy improvement Given $v \pi$, look one step ahead and act greedily: The policy improvement theorem says $\pi'$ is at least as good as $\pi$ in every state. Sketch: in each state, $\pi'$'s first action has $q \pi(s, \pi'(s)) \ge v \pi(s)$, because a maximum is at least an average. Taking $\pi'$ for one step and then following $\pi$ is therefore no worse than $\pi$; applying the same argument at every later step shows that following $\pi'$ throughout is no worse either. If the greedy policy equals the old one, $v \pi$ satisfies the Bellman optimality equation, so $\pi$ is already optimal. In the cell, one improvement step from the random policy already gives an optimal policy: its values are minus the Manhattan distance to the corner ($-6$ from the far corner). That is luck of this small problem. In general you alternate the two steps, policy iteration : Each policy is strictly better until one repeats, and a finite MDP has finitely many deterministic policies, so policy iteration stops at an optimal policy after finitely many rounds (usually very few). Value iteration Policy iteration runs a full evaluation (hundreds of sweeps above) between improvements. Value iteration cuts evaluation to a single sweep and folds the improvement into it: apply the Bellman optimality backup directly, It is also a $\gamma$-contraction, now with fixed point $v $. When it has converged, read off a greedy policy with one more lookahead. Seven sweeps: the correct values spread outward from the goal one cell per sweep (6 sweeps reach the far corner), and the seventh sweep confirms nothing changed. Many states have ties: from the top-left corner, right and down are equally good. argmax returns the first maximal index, so this greedy policy always prefers "right" (action 1) over "down" (action 2). For DP that is harmless, since any greedy choice is optimal. When an agent is still learning, always taking the first tied action is a bias, and lesson 5 breaks ties at random. Know the two backups (average over $\pi$ for evaluation, max over actions for value iteration), the stopping rule, the contraction bound ($\gamma^k$ times the initial error), and that terminal states are absorbing with value 0. Policy iteration alternates full evaluation with greedy improvement; value iteration does one optimality backup per sweep.

Dynamic programming needs the dynamics $p(s', r \mid s, a)$. A robot, a game played against people, or a recommender system does not come with them. Model-free methods learn value functions from experience alone: episodes the agent actually plays. This lesson covers the two basic ways to do it (S&B 5.1 and 5.2 for Monte Carlo, 6.1 for TD). Temporal-difference learning, the second, is the core of Q-learning and DQN. Monte Carlo prediction The goal is prediction : estimate $v \pi$ for a fixed policy $\pi$. By definition $v \pi(s) = \mathbb{E} \pi[G t \mid S t = s]$, an expectation, so Monte Carlo estimation applies: play many episodes with $\pi$, compute the return after each visit to $s$, and average. - First-visit MC averages the return after the first visit to $s$ in each episode. - Every-visit MC averages the returns after every visit. Both converge to $v \pi(s)$ as the number of visits grows (first-visit by the law of large numbers directly, since its samples are iid). Returns are computed backwards at the end of the episode, $G = R {t+1} + \gamma G$, exactly as in lesson 1. Keeping every return to average is wasteful. The incremental mean updates in place: after the $n$-th sample $x n$, $\bar{x} n = \bar{x} {n-1} + \frac{1}{n}(x n - \bar{x} {n-1})$. Replacing $\frac1n$ by a constant step size $\alpha$ gives the update used in practice, which weights recent episodes more, useful when the policy (and so the target) keeps changing. The same idea estimates action values $q \pi(s, a)$ (S&B 5.2): average the returns after each visit to the pair $(s, a)$. The catch is coverage. A deterministic policy only ever tries one action per state, so the other pairs get no samples; the agent must keep exploring, for example by starting episodes at random state-action pairs ( exploring starts ) or by acting randomly some of the time (lesson 5). Monte Carlo has two properties worth remembering. Its target $G t$ is an unbiased sample of $v \pi(S t)$. But a return adds up many random rewards and transitions, so its variance can be large, and nothing can be updated until the episode ends. It does not work at all for continuing tasks. Temporal-difference learning TD learning replaces the full return by one real reward plus the current estimate of what follows, using $G t = R {t+1} + \gamma G {t+1}$ with $v \pi(S {t+1})$ in place of $G {t+1}$. The TD(0) update, applied right after each step $(S t, R {t+1}, S {t+1})$, is The bracket is the TD error $\delta t = R {t+1} + \gamma V(S {t+1}) - V(S t)$: how much better or worse the step went than predicted. Updating an estimate from another estimate is called bootstrapping . DP bootstraps too (its backups use $V k$), but it averages over all successors with the model; TD uses the one successor that actually happened. Terminal states. If $S {t+1}$ is terminal, there is no future: the target is just $R {t+1}$. With a table that stores a 0 for terminal states and never updates them, the formula handles this by itself. But if terminal entries can be nonzero (a value table initialized optimistically, or a neural network that outputs something for every input), you must cut the bootstrap explicitly: With Gymnasium, done here means terminated . A truncated episode (time limit) did not reach a terminal state, so its last step should still bootstrap. Comparing the two on a random walk States 0 to 6 lie in a row; 0 and 6 are terminal. Each episode starts in state 3 and steps left or right at random. Entering state 6 gives reward 1, everything else 0, and $\gamma = 1$. Then $v(s)$ is the probability of finishing on the right, which is $s/6$. The cell runs constant-$\alpha$ every-visit MC and TD(0), both with $\alpha = 0.05$ and values started at 0.5, and reports the root mean squared error over states 1 to 5, averaged over 50 runs. After 100 episodes TD's error (0.036) is about a third of MC's (0.124). TD's targets are biased, because they use the current, wrong estimates, but each target contains only one random step, so its variance is small, and the bias shrinks as the estimates improve. MC's targets are unbiased but noisy. Neither always wins; on problems like this TD usually learns faster, and it can learn during an episode and in continuing tasks. Monte Carlo TD(0) --- --- --- target $G t$ (full return) $R {t+1} + \gamma V(S {t+1})$ bias of target none yes, from $V(S {t+1})$ variance of target high low updates at the end of the episode after every step continuing tasks no yes A TD update by hand: compute $\delta = r + \gamma V(s') - V(s)$, then add $\alpha\delta$. If $s'$ is terminal, drop the $\gamma V(s')$ term whatever the table says. MC needs whole episodes and is unbiased; TD bootstraps, has lower variance and learns online.

Prediction (lesson 4) evaluates a fixed policy. Control finds a good policy. The model-free recipe is the policy iteration loop of lesson 3 with samples: estimate action values from experience, act (mostly) greedily on them, repeat. Q-learning is the version that the IOAI syllabus names (S&B 6.5), and DQN in the next lesson is Q-learning with a neural network. This lesson also covers SARSA, its on-policy twin, because the difference between the two is a standard exam question. Exploration and epsilon-greedy To improve without a model, the agent learns $Q(s, a)$ (lesson 2: acting greedily on $q$ needs no lookahead). But an agent that always takes the action it currently thinks is best never tries the others, and if its first estimates are wrong it may never find out. This is the trade-off between exploration (trying actions to learn about them) and exploitation (taking the best-known action to collect reward). The standard compromise is the epsilon-greedy policy with a small $\varepsilon$ (often 0.1): - with probability $\varepsilon$, pick an action uniformly at random from all $ \mathcal{A} $ actions; - otherwise pick a greedy action, $\arg\max a Q(s, a)$. So the greedy action has probability $1 - \varepsilon + \frac{\varepsilon}{ \mathcal{A} }$ (the random draw can pick it too) and every other action $\frac{\varepsilon}{ \mathcal{A} }$. With 4 actions and $\varepsilon = 0.2$: 0.85 and 0.05. Ties. At the start every $Q$ is 0, so every action is tied. np.argmax returns the first maximal index, so a greedy agent would always pick action 0 in unexplored states, a systematic bias that can stall learning. Break ties at random among the maximal actions: With ties broken this way, $k$ tied greedy actions share the $1 - \varepsilon$ equally: each has probability $\frac{1 - \varepsilon}{k} + \frac{\varepsilon}{ \mathcal{A} }$. SARSA and Q-learning Both update $Q(S t, A t)$ after each step with a TD error, like TD(0) in lesson 4. They differ in the target. SARSA uses the action the agent actually takes next. After observing $S t, A t, R {t+1}, S {t+1}$, it chooses $A {t+1}$ with its $\varepsilon$-greedy policy (the name lists these five quantities) and updates Q-learning uses the best next action, whatever the agent does next: At a terminal $S {t+1}$ both targets are just $R {t+1}$, as in lesson 4. The Q-learning target is a sample of the Bellman optimality equation for $q $ (lesson 2), so Q-learning estimates $q $ directly, as long as every state-action pair keeps being tried and the step sizes shrink appropriately. The SARSA target is a sample of the Bellman expectation equation for the policy being followed, so SARSA estimates $q$ of its own $\varepsilon$-greedy policy. This is the distinction between on-policy and off-policy learning. The behavior policy is the one that chooses actions and generates the data; the target policy is the one whose values are being learned. SARSA is on-policy: both are the $\varepsilon$-greedy policy. Q-learning is off-policy: it behaves $\varepsilon$-greedily but learns about the greedy policy. Off-policy learning is what lets DQN learn from old experience stored in a buffer. The cliff walk A 4 by 12 grid. The agent starts bottom left and must reach bottom right. The ten cells between them on the bottom row are a cliff: stepping in costs $-100$ and sends the agent back to the start. Every other step costs $-1$, and $\gamma = 1$. The shortest route runs along the cliff edge (13 steps, return $-13$). The cell trains both methods for 500 episodes with $\alpha = 0.5$ and $\varepsilon = 0.1$, then draws each one's greedy route ( ) next to the cliff ( C ). Q-learning finds the optimal 13-step route along the edge. SARSA learns a 17-step route along the top. Yet while training, SARSA's episodes earn more ($-26.2$ against $-61.8$ on average over the last 100). The reason is the targets. Q-learning values the edge as if it will act greedily from then on, but it actually explores 10% of the time, and a random "down" next to the cliff costs 100. SARSA's values include its own exploration, so it learns that cells next to the cliff are dangerous for an agent that sometimes slips , and keeps away. If $\varepsilon$ is lowered to 0 over time, both end up with the optimal route. Q-learning target: $r + \gamma \max a Q(s', a)$, off-policy, learns $q $. SARSA target: $r + \gamma Q(s', a')$ with the action actually taken next, on-policy. Epsilon-greedy explores over all actions, so the greedy action has probability $1 - \varepsilon + \varepsilon/ \mathcal{A} $. Break ties at random, and never bootstrap from a terminal state.

A Q-table needs one entry per state-action pair. Atari games have more screen images than atoms in the universe, so DQN (Mnih et al., "Human-level control through deep reinforcement learning", 2015) replaced the table by a convolutional network and learned 49 games from pixels. This lesson covers value-function approximation (S&B 9.1 to 9.3, 11.1) and the two tricks that made DQN train: experience replay and a target network. The code is where Round 2 style problems bite: gather , done masks and detach . Approximating values with parameters Replace the table by a function $\hat{v}(s, \mathbf{w})$ with weights $\mathbf{w}$ (a linear model of state features, or a neural network). Changing $\mathbf{w}$ changes the values of many states at once, which is the point: similar states share what was learned, so the agent can generalize to states it has never seen. The price is that the values can no longer all be exact. S&B's prediction objective says which errors matter, weighting states by how often they occur, $\mu(s)$: Stochastic gradient descent on one visited state would step along $[v \pi(S t) - \hat{v}(S t, \mathbf{w})]\nabla\hat{v}(S t, \mathbf{w})$. We do not know $v \pi(S t)$, so substitute a target: the return $G t$ (Monte Carlo, a true gradient method) or the TD target $R {t+1} + \gamma\hat{v}(S {t+1}, \mathbf{w})$. The TD version is The target depends on $\mathbf{w}$ too, but the update ignores that and differentiates only the prediction. This makes it a semi-gradient method : it is not the gradient of any fixed loss. In code, "treat the target as a constant" means computing it without gradient tracking ( torch.no grad() or .detach() ). Semi-gradient TD works well on-policy with linear features. S&B 11.1 shows that function approximation , bootstrapping and off-policy learning together, the deadly triad , can make the weights diverge. Q-learning with a neural network has all three. DQN's two tricks are what keep it stable in practice. DQN The network $Q(s, \cdot\,; \theta)$ takes a state and outputs one value per action, shape (B, n actions) for a batch of $B$ states (the batch size, written $N$ in u10). Acting is $\varepsilon$-greedy on these outputs, with $\varepsilon$ decayed from 1 to a small value over training (to 0.1 over the first million frames in the paper). Learning minimizes the squared TD error of Q-learning: where $d = 1$ if $s'$ is terminal. 1. Experience replay. Every transition $(s, a, r, s', d)$ goes into a replay buffer (the last million in the paper). Each update trains on a random mini-batch from the buffer. Consecutive frames of a game are nearly identical, and random sampling breaks those correlations; each transition is also reused many times. Learning from old transitions, generated by older policies, is fine because Q-learning is off-policy. 2. Target network. $\theta^-$ is a copy of $\theta$ that is updated only every $C$ steps (10,000 in the paper). Without it the target $y$ moves with every gradient step, and the network chases its own changing output. The paper also clipped rewards to $[-1, 1]$ and the TD error's gradient to $[-1, 1]$, which is the same as using the Huber loss ( F.smooth l1 loss ) instead of squared error. The loss in PyTorch gather(1, idx) picks, in each row $i$, the column idx[i, 0] ; idx must have shape (B, 1) and dtype long, which is why a is unsqueezed and the result squeezed back. Every update ends with opt.zero grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step() , and every $C$ steps target net.load state dict(q net.state dict()) . The last line shows the most common silent bug: forget the squeeze(1) and (B, 1) - (B,) broadcasts to (B, B) , so the loss averages 25 wrong differences without any error. A replay buffer needs nothing more than a deque: The DQN target is $r + \gamma(1 - d)\max {a'}Q \text{target}(s', a')$, computed without gradients. Check shapes: gather needs a (B, 1) long index; squeeze before subtracting. The target network is copied, never trained by the loss. Replay is allowed because Q-learning is off-policy.

Every method so far learned values and derived the policy from them (greedy or $\varepsilon$-greedy). Policy gradient methods learn the policy directly: a network outputs action probabilities, and its weights move in the direction that raises the expected return. REINFORCE is the simplest one and the third algorithm the IOAI syllabus names (S&B 13.1, 13.3). The derivation rests on one identity, the log-derivative trick, which is worth knowing by heart. Parameterized policies Write the policy as $\pi(a \mid s,  oldsymbol	heta)$ with weights $ oldsymbol	heta$. For discrete actions the standard choice is a softmax policy : a network (or linear model) computes one score $h(s, a,  oldsymbol	heta)$ per action, called the action preferences , and the softmax of the preferences, exactly a classifier's logits. Advantages over acting greedily on values (S&B 13.1): the policy can stay stochastic where that is best (in a game of rock-paper-scissors, or when the state hides information); small weight changes change the action probabilities smoothly, while a greedy policy can flip abruptly; continuous actions are easy (output the mean and standard deviation of a normal distribution); and sometimes the policy is simply a simpler function to learn than the values. The log-derivative trick The objective is the expected return from the start, $J( oldsymbol	heta) = \mathbb{E} {	au \sim \pi { oldsymbol	heta}}[G 0]$, where $	au$ is a whole trajectory. The difficulty: $ oldsymbol	heta$ changes the distribution we average over, and we cannot differentiate through sampling (the VAE of u18-l02 had the same problem and reparameterized; here actions are discrete, so we use another route). For any distribution $p { oldsymbol	heta}(x)$ and function $f(x)$ that does not depend on $ oldsymbol	heta$, use $
abla p = p\,
abla\log p$: The gradient is again an expectation, so samples estimate it. For a trajectory, $p { oldsymbol	heta}(	au) = p(S 0)\prod t \pi(A t \mid S t,  oldsymbol	heta)\, p(S {t+1}, R {t+1} \mid S t, A t)$. In the log the product becomes a sum, and the dynamics terms do not depend on $ oldsymbol	heta$, so their gradient is 0: the gradient needs no model . A reward earned before time $t$ cannot depend on the action at $t$, and one can show its term has expectation 0. Dropping those terms leaves the reward-to-go $G t$ in place of $G 0$, which has lower variance. That is REINFORCE (Monte Carlo policy gradient, S&B 13.3): after each episode, for every step $t$, (S&B keeps the $\gamma^t$ factor; most code drops it.) For a softmax over preferences that are the weights themselves (one logit per action), $
abla { oldsymbol	heta}\log\pi(a) = \mathbf{e} a -  oldsymbol\pi$: the one-hot vector of the action taken minus the probability vector, the cross-entropy gradient of u04-l09 ($ oldsymbol\pi - \mathbf{e} a$ with respect to the logits) with the sign flipped. A good return pushes up the action taken and pushes down the others in proportion to their probabilities. Baselines Any function $b(s)$ of the state alone can be subtracted from the return: This changes nothing in expectation, because the expected score $
abla\log\pi$ is zero: But it can cut the variance a lot. If every return is positive, plain REINFORCE raises the probability of every action it samples and relies on the good ones being raised more; with $b \approx$ the average return, below-average actions are pushed down. A common baseline is a learned state-value estimate $\hat{v}(s, \mathbf{w})$, trained by regression on the returns; then $G t - \hat{v}(S t)$ estimates the advantage , how much better the action was than usual. Using a learned TD estimate in place of $G t$ as well leads to actor-critic methods (S&B 13.5, beyond the syllabus). The cell estimates the policy gradient of a 3-armed bandit (one action per episode, mean rewards 1, 2, 3) at the uniform policy, with $b = 0$ and with $b = 2$, then trains with a running-average baseline. Both estimates agree (about $- rac13, 0, + rac13$, the exact gradient), but the baseline cuts the variance from 3.58 to 0.90. After 300 episodes the policy picks the best arm 97% of the time. REINFORCE in PyTorch Autograd computes $
abla\log\pi$ if you write a loss whose gradient is the update. Optimizers minimize , so put a minus sign in front: The returns and the baseline are constants for the policy's update: they come from the environment and from another network, so detach the baseline (and train it separately, for example with F.mse loss(baseline(states).squeeze(1), G) ). Many implementations also standardize the advantages, (adv - adv.mean()) / (adv.std() + 1e-8) , which acts like a baseline and a step-size control at once. Derive $
abla\mathbb{E}[f] = \mathbb{E}[f\,
abla\log p]$ in one line, and show a baseline is unbiased because $\mathbb{E}[
abla\log\pi] = 0$. For a softmax over logits, $
abla\log\pi(a) = \mathbf{e} a -  oldsymbol\pi$. In code: loss $= -\sum t \log\pi(A t \mid S t)(G t - b t)$, with $G t$ computed backwards and the baseline detached.

The first problem of the 2025 Round 2 was worth 100 of its 300 points: build a physics-informed neural network for the heat equation, train it, and compare it with the exact solution. The parts mixed a short proof, autograd practice with second derivatives, Dataset and DataLoader code, a training loop and a test-grid plot. This lesson gives you every piece: what the equation and its conditions mean, how to put them in a loss, and how torch.autograd.grad computes the derivatives the loss needs. The heat equation A partial differential equation (PDE) is an equation between an unknown function of several variables and its partial derivatives. The heat equation in one space dimension describes the temperature $u(t, x)$ of a thin rod at time $t$ and position $x$: Here $u t = \partial u / \partial t$, $u {xx} = \partial^2 u / \partial x^2$, and $\alpha 0$ is the diffusivity (how fast heat spreads). The equation says a point warms up when it is colder than the average of its neighbors ($u {xx} 0$ there) and cools when it is hotter. Many functions satisfy the PDE, so two more conditions pin down one solution: - an initial condition (IC) fixes the temperature at $t = 0$, here $u(0, x) = \sin(\pi x)$; - a boundary condition (BC) fixes it at the ends for all $t$, here $u(t, 0) = u(t, 1) = 0$ (both ends held at temperature 0). With these, the solution is $u(t, x) = e^{-\alpha \pi^2 t} \sin(\pi x)$. Check it by differentiating: $u t = -\alpha\pi^2 e^{-\alpha\pi^2 t}\sin(\pi x)$ and $u {xx} = -\pi^2 e^{-\alpha\pi^2 t} \sin(\pi x)$, so $u t = \alpha u {xx}$; at $t = 0$ the exponential is 1; and $\sin 0 = \sin \pi = 0$. A formula like this is an analytic solution . Most PDEs have none, which is why numerical and neural methods exist, but this one lets you measure your network's error exactly. Putting the physics in the loss A PINN is an ordinary multilayer perceptron $u \theta(t, x)$: input a pair $(t, x)$, output one number. Nothing in the architecture knows about heat. The physics enters only through the loss, which has three terms: and $L = L {\text{PDE}} + L {\text{IC}} + L {\text{BC}}$. The quantity inside $L {\text{PDE}}$ is the PDE residual : how far the network is from satisfying the equation at that point. The points $(t i, x i)$ where it is measured are collocation points , usually sampled uniformly from the domain. They need no labels: the PDE is the label. Only the IC and BC points need target values, and those come from the problem statement, not from data. Each term alone is not enough. $u = 0$ has zero PDE residual and zero BC error; only $L {\text{IC}}$ rules it out. That is also why the 2025 problem used all IC and BC points in every step while it sampled mini-batches of collocation points: the conditions are few (about 300 points) and they are what makes the solution unique, so every update should see all of them. Derivatives of the network with autograd The loss needs $u t$ and $u {xx}$ of the network with respect to its inputs. Autograd gives them. Put the inputs in a tensor tx of shape (N, 2) with columns $(t, x)$, and mark it with requires grad (True) so that PyTorch records how u depends on it. Three details: 1. grad outputs . autograd.grad differentiates a scalar. u has shape (N, 1) , so you pass a weight per output and it differentiates $\sum i w i u i$. With all weights 1, row $i$ of the result is $\partial u i / \partial (t i, x i)$, because $u i$ depends only on row $i$ of tx . (This trick is only valid because the rows do not interact. Batch norm across rows would break it.) 2. [0] . It returns a tuple, one gradient per input tensor. 3. create graph=True . It records the derivative computation itself, so you can differentiate again (for $u {xx}$) and so that loss.backward() can reach the network's parameters through $u t$ and $u {xx}$. Without it the first derivative is a constant tensor with no history: the second autograd.grad raises an error, and a loss built from it trains nothing. Columns are kept 2D with slices: du[:, 0:1] is $u t$, shape (N, 1) , while du[:, 0] would be shape (N,) and broadcast wrongly against (N, 1) tensors. A complete PINN The network uses tanh, not ReLU. A ReLU network is piecewise linear in its inputs, so its second derivative is 0 almost everywhere: $u {xx}$ would be identically 0 and the PDE term could never be satisfied except by $u t = 0$. Smooth activations (tanh, softplus, sine) have useful second derivatives. At step 0 the IC term dominates (the network starts near 0, and $\sin(\pi x)$ is not). After a few hundred Adam steps all three terms are small and the test error against the analytic solution is about $10^{-4}$. Training longer, or with more collocation points, lowers it further. Variations you may meet - Inverse problems. Make $\alpha$ a learnable nn.Parameter and add a data term $\frac{1}{M}\sum (u \theta(t m, x m) - u m)^2$ on measured temperatures. Training then fits both the field and the physical constant (lesson u21-l02 is about such inverse problems). - Loss weights. $L = L {\text{PDE}} + \lambda (L {\text{IC}} + L {\text{BC}})$ with $\lambda$ around 1 to 100 helps when the conditions are learned too slowly. - Hard constraints. Writing $u \theta(t, x) = x(1 - x)\, N \theta(t, x)$ satisfies the BC exactly for any network $N \theta$, so $L {\text{BC}}$ disappears. Exam angle - Input (N, 2) with an agreed column order, tx.clone().requires grad (True) , then autograd.grad(u, tx, torch.ones like(u), create graph=True)[0] , then 2D column slices. - Use smooth activations. If u xx is all zeros, check for ReLU. - Evaluate on a grid: torch.meshgrid(..., indexing="ij") , flatten and stack to (N, 2) ; the 101 by 101 grid has 10201 rows. - Training on a GPU: move the model and every tensor to the device (lesson u21-l04). Evaluating or plotting needs .detach().cpu() first. - Expect proof parts: verifying an analytic solution, as above, earns points with three lines of calculus. Practice problem: u21-p01 The heat-equation PINN loss (write the three loss terms; the grader checks them against functions with known derivatives).

Two of the five 2026 Round 2 problems (120 of 300 points) handed you measurements produced by a physical or mathematical law and asked for the law's hidden numbers. Problem 2 gave a vector field on a grid and asked where its source was and how its strength fell off with distance. Problem 5 gave groups of points drawn from four kinds of curves and asked for all eleven curve parameters. Both were open-ended: your score was placed between a weak baseline (for Problem 2, a CNN that regresses the answers directly) and the best submission. This lesson is about the methods that beat such baselines: writing the forward model, fitting it, and checking that the answer is well defined. Forward and inverse problems A forward problem computes data from known parameters: given a source position and a profile, compute the field. An inverse problem goes the other way: given noisy data, recover the parameters. Forward problems are usually easy and unique. Inverse problems can be ill-posed: several parameter values may explain the data equally well, and small noise may move the answer a lot. There are three ways to attack one: 1. Fit each sample. Write the forward model $y = g(x; \theta)$ and choose $\theta$ to minimize the squared misfit $\sum i (y i - g(x i; \theta))^2$. This is least squares when $g$ is linear in $\theta$ and nonlinear least squares otherwise. scipy.optimize.curve fit does the nonlinear case. 2. Learn the inverse map. Train a network on (data, parameters) pairs from the training set to output $\theta$ directly. This is amortized inference : the cost of fitting is paid once, in training, and each prediction is one forward pass. The 2026 baselines were of this kind. 3. Combine them. Use physics or a network for a good first guess, then refine each sample with a fit. In practice this wins most often. Fitting needs a good start Nonlinear least squares is solved iteratively from a starting guess p0 , and the loss surface can have many local minima. Periodic models are the classic trap: a sine with the wrong frequency matches some wiggles, and small changes of the frequency make the fit worse before it gets better. A starting frequency from the Fourier transform of the data avoids this. The fast Fourier transform ( np.fft.rfft ) writes evenly spaced samples as a sum of sines and cosines; the frequency whose coefficient has the largest magnitude is the dominant one. For $n$ samples with spacing $\Delta x$, coefficient $k$ belongs to the frequency $k/(n\,\Delta x)$ cycles per unit of $x$ (this is what np.fft.rfftfreq(n, d=dx) returns), and a sine $\sin(c 1 x + c 2)$ needs the angular frequency $c 1 = 2\pi k/(n\,\Delta x)$. The naive start stops in a local minimum with a fit RMSE of about 1, ten times the noise level. The FFT start recovers $(1.5, 3, 0.5, 1)$, and its fit RMSE of 0.097 matches the noise standard deviation 0.1, which is the most any fit can do. That comparison is your check: a fit whose residual RMSE is well above the noise level has not found the right minimum. curve fit(f, x, y, p0=...) calls f(x, params) , so the parameters come after x in the signature. It returns popt (the fitted parameters) and pcov (their estimated covariance; np.sqrt(np.diag(pcov)) gives standard errors). maxfev caps the number of function evaluations, and bounds=(lower, upper) keeps parameters in a physical range. Identifiability A parameter is identifiable when different values of it give different data. Three ways it fails: - Products and sums. In $y = a\,b\,x$ only the product $ab$ matters. A test: the Jacobian of the predictions with respect to the parameters has rank below the number of parameters, so some direction of parameter change leaves every prediction unchanged. - Symmetries. $c 0 \sin(c 1 x + c 2) = (-c 0)\sin(c 1 x + c 2 + \pi)$, and $c 2$ only matters modulo $2\pi$. A fit can return either form. If the score is an RMSE on the parameters themselves, as in 2026 Problem 5, you must report the same form as the training labels: inspect them, then map every fit to that canonical form (for example $c 0 0$ and $c 2 \in [0, 2\pi)$). - Weak data. $a 0 e^{a 1 x} + a 2$ with $a 1 x$ small everywhere is almost $a 0 + a 2 + a 0 a 1 x$, a straight line: $a 0$ and $a 2$ are nearly impossible to separate. The fit is unstable, and a prior guess (such as the training mean of $a 0$) may score better than the fit. Units and scaling Fitting and training both behave better when every number is of order 1. - Scale the targets. If one parameter is in the hundreds and another is about 0.01, a network trained with plain mean squared error on the raw targets spends all its effort on the large one. Standardize each target column with the training mean and standard deviation, train on the standardized values, and undo the scaling at prediction time. - Use logs for positive scale parameters. A diffusivity or a decay length that ranges over a factor of 100 is better predicted as its logarithm, and a learnable one is safer as nn.Parameter holding $\log\alpha$, used as log alpha.exp() , which can never become negative. - Know the units of the metric. The official Problem 2 metric multiplied the location error by a large constant and the profile error by a small one, so the source position decided most of the score. Read the metric before you decide where to spend time. A physics shortcut: where all the lines meet A central field is $\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}) = f(\lVert \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r} s\rVert)\,(\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r} s)/\lVert \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r} s\rVert$: at every point it points along the line through the source $\mathbf{r} s$, whatever the profile $f$ is. So each measured vector $\mathbf{F} i$ at point $\mathbf{p} i$ defines a line, and the source is the point closest to all of them. With unit direction $\mathbf{u} i$, the matrix $P i = I - \mathbf{u} i\mathbf{u} i^\top$ projects onto the line's normal, so $\lVert P i(\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{p} i)\rVert$ is the distance from a point $\mathbf{c}$ to line $i$. Minimizing the weighted sum of squared distances $\sum i w i \lVert P i(\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{p} i)\rVert^2$ is linear least squares. Its gradient in $\mathbf{c}$ is $2\sum i w i P i^\top P i(\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{p} i)$, and $P i^\top P i = P i$ (a projector is symmetric, and projecting twice changes nothing), so setting the gradient to zero gives a 2 by 2 system: Weights $w i = \lVert\mathbf{F} i\rVert^2$ trust strong vectors more, since noise changes their direction least. Once $\mathbf{c}$ is known, the profile is the signed radial component $f i = \mathbf{F} i \cdot (\mathbf{p} i - \mathbf{c}) / \lVert \mathbf{p} i - \mathbf{c} \rVert$, averaged over points at each distance. No training, no labels, and the source comes out within 0.02 in each coordinate, with the profile within about 0.007 at the three radii. A CNN trained to regress the source (the official baseline, trained on 10,000 examples) has to discover this geometry from data, while the physics route gets it from one sample with no training at all. The same habit pays everywhere: before training anything, ask what structure the forward model forces on the data. Exam angle - Write the forward model first, generate data with known parameters, and check your inverse method recovers them. That doubles as a validation set when the given one is small. - For fits: a sensible p0 (FFT for frequencies, data range for amplitudes, the training mean for everything else), bounds , and a residual check against the noise level. - Map answers to the canonical form of the labels before computing any parameter RMSE. - Mixtures (2026 Problem 5): the official baseline clustered the points with k-means and fitted every model to every cluster. Assigning points by the residual of the current fits and refitting, repeated a few times, is the same alternating idea as k-means, with curves as the "centers". - The report should say why the method works (the geometry, the symmetry you removed), not only what it scored. Practice problems: u21-p02 Find the source of a central field (adapted-2026-R2-P2) and u21-p03 Parameters of a damped oscillation .

The last part of the 2026 Round 2 Problem 1 (20 points) asked for an encoder-only transformer, built from your own linear-attention module, trained on the FordA dataset: 500-sample recordings from an automotive sensor, in two classes, scored by macro F1 on a hidden test set, with the points scaled between random guessing (about 0.5) and the best submission. The IOAI syllabus also lists time series under feature engineering and data processing. This lesson covers how sequences of numbers go into a 1-D CNN or a transformer, the metric, and the habits that get a submission accepted. Shapes A time series is a sequence of measurements in time order. A univariate series has one number per time step, so a dataset is an array of shape (N, L) : $N$ series of length $L$. A multivariate series has $C$ numbers per step (several sensors), shape (N, C, L) or (N, L, C) . - 1-D CNN. nn.Conv1d expects channels-first input (B, C, L) . A univariate batch needs a channel axis: x.unsqueeze(1) turns (B, L) into (B, 1, L) . Each 1D convolution slides a kernel along time, so a pattern is detected wherever it occurs (translation equivariance, as in u12-l01). - Transformer. Attention expects tokens (B, T, d) . Either each time step is a token ( nn.Linear(1, d) applied to x.unsqueeze(-1) ), or a patch embedding cuts the series into non-overlapping windows of $P$ steps and maps each to a $d$-vector: nn.Conv1d(1, d, kernel size=P, stride=P) gives (B, d, L/P) , then .transpose(1, 2) gives (B, L/P, d) . With $L = 500$ and $P = 10$, the 500 tokens become 50, and the attention score matrix shrinks from $500^2$ to $50^2$ entries per head (the same idea as ViT patches, u16-l03). Both end with pooling over time to get one vector per series: the mean ( h.mean(dim=-1) for a CNN's (B, C, L) ) or the max ( h.amax(dim=-1) ), then a linear head. Max pooling answers "did the pattern occur anywhere?", which suits detecting a short event; mean pooling suits properties spread over the whole series. A transformer can also use a class token. Normalize each series Recordings often differ in offset and gain for reasons unrelated to the label (a sensor's calibration, the loudness of an engine). Per-series z-normalization removes both: subtract each series' own mean and divide by its own standard deviation, The FordA series are already distributed this way (every row of the 2026 training file has mean 0 and standard deviation 1). This is different from standardization of features, which uses one mean per column computed on the training set; here every row uses its own statistics, so there is nothing to fit and nothing to leak. Augmentation for series, applied to training batches only: a random circular shift torch.roll(x, s, dims=-1) (when the event's position does not matter), multiplying by a random gain, adding small noise.
