Flipping the time axis or the sign is only allowed when it cannot change the label; check that with the physics of the problem, not by assumption. A small 1-D CNN The model has about 2,600 parameters and trains in a second on a CPU. For FordA-sized data (a few thousand series of length 500) a CNN of this kind, a few layers wider, is a strong baseline, and it is the thing to build first even when the problem asks for a transformer: it tells you what score is reachable. A small transformer The 2026 problem required a transformer encoder (u16-l01) built from your own attention (the linear attention with relative positions of u15-l06), and banned extra positional encodings at the input. The pipeline: z-normalize, embed each step or patch to $d$ (32 to 64 is plenty), a few encoder blocks (attention, MLP, residuals, layer normalization), masked mean pooling or mean pooling over tokens, linear head to 2 logits, cross-entropy loss. Patching keeps the sequence short enough to train fast. Expect the transformer to need more epochs, a learning rate schedule with warmup, and more care than the CNN to reach the same score on a few thousand examples: it has less inductive bias about locality. Macro F1 The F1 score of one class is $2TP/(2TP + FP + FN)$, with that class as the positive one. Macro F1 is the plain mean of the per-class F1 scores (macro average, u06-l05). For two classes, compute F1 with class 1 as positive and again with class 0 as positive, then average. It punishes ignoring a class. On a test set with 90 examples of class 0 and 10 of class 1, always predicting 0 gets 90% accuracy but class 1 has $F1 = 0$, so macro F1 is about 0.47, below random guessing on balanced data. Two consequences: - With class imbalance, train with class weights ( F.cross entropy(logits, y, weight=w) with $w c \propto 1/n c$) or a balanced sampler, and choose the decision threshold on the validation set to maximize macro F1 rather than using 0.5. - sklearn.metrics.f1 score(y true, y pred, average="macro") computes it. Check which labels the metric expects: the 2026 FordA training file uses FordA's original labels $-1$ and $1$, so in a CSV written with 0 and 1 every 0 is an invalid label and counts as wrong. Submitting predictions The 2026 problems were graded from a CSV that had to have the format of a sample file: the same columns, one valid label per row (missing or invalid labels count as wrong). Build it with pandas from the sample file, not from scratch, so the ids and their order come from the file: Take the column names from the file, not from the problem text: in 2026 the PDF named the columns test sample id and label , while the released sample file has sample id and predicted label . Then reload your file and check its shape, its column names, its unique labels and its first rows. That costs a minute and protects all 20 points. Exam angle - Shapes: (B, L) to (B, 1, L) for Conv1d ; (B, d, T) to (B, T, d) for attention, with transpose(1, 2) . - Normalize each series; augment with shifts and gains if the label allows it. - Build a CNN baseline first, then the required architecture; keep the better validation model with early stopping. - Macro F1, class weights, threshold on validation, labels in the sample file's format. - The official part required training and testing on an L4 GPU: lesson u21-l04 covers moving the code there. Practice problem: u21-p04 Find the burst: time-series classification by macro F1 (train a classifier to a macro-F1 target within a CPU time budget).

entries.t: Training on a GPU in Colab
entries.x: Round 2 gives you Google Colab with an NVIDIA L4 GPU, and some parts require it: in 2026 the FordA part said a notebook that does not run on the L4 gets 0 for that part. Round 1 never used a GPU, so this lesson covers what changes: devices, batch sizes, mixed precision, feeding data fast enough, and saving checkpoints because a Colab session can disconnect. Lesson u21-l05 turns to the exam itself. Devices A GPU (graphics processing unit) runs thousands of simple arithmetic operations in parallel, which is what matrix products and convolutions are made of. In Colab choose Runtime, Change runtime type, L4 GPU; the notebook restarts with an empty runtime. PyTorch calls the GPU "cuda" (CUDA is NVIDIA's GPU programming system). Rules that prevent most errors: - Every tensor in one operation must be on the same device; otherwise PyTorch raises "Expected all tensors to be on the same device". The usual culprits are a batch, a mask or a constant made with torch.zeros(...) inside forward . Create those with device=x.device , or register them as a buffer so model.to moves them. - module.to(device) moves the module in place (and returns it). tensor.to(device) returns a new tensor and leaves the old one where it was, so xb.to(device) without assigning the result does nothing. - Build the optimizer after model.to(device) , so it holds the moved parameters. - NumPy and matplotlib only see CPU memory: pred.detach().cpu().numpy() . Save checkpoints from anywhere and load them with map location (map location, u10-l08). nvidia-smi in a cell ( !nvidia-smi ) shows the GPU, its memory use and the processes using it. The L4 has 24 GB of memory. Batch size and memory The GPU is fastest when each operation is large, so batches of 128 to 1024 small examples often take the same time per step as batches of 32. Bigger batches mean fewer steps per epoch; raise the learning rate somewhat when you raise the batch size, and check on validation. If you see "CUDA out of memory", halve the batch size, free stale tensors ( del them, then torch.cuda.empty cache() ), or restart the runtime. Training memory is roughly the parameters, their gradients and the optimizer state, plus the activations saved for the backward pass. In float32 with Adam that is $4 + 4 + 8 = 16$ bytes per parameter before activations; the activations grow with the batch size. Mixed precision float32 uses 4 bytes per number. Mixed precision runs most matrix products in a 2-byte format, which modern GPUs process several times faster, while keeping the weights and the sensitive steps (reductions, softmax, losses) in float32. torch.autocast does the bookkeeping: Two 2-byte formats exist. float16 has more precision but a small range: its smallest normal positive number is about $6 \times 10^{-5}$, below that precision drops, and values under about $3 \times 10^{-8}$ round to 0 (underflow), so tiny gradients vanish. It needs torch.amp.GradScaler , which multiplies the loss by a large factor before backward and divides the gradients by it before the step. bfloat16 keeps float32's range with less precision, so it needs no scaler. The L4 supports bfloat16: use it. Autocast also works on the CPU, which lets you see what it does: Feeding the GPU A fast GPU waits if the data arrives slowly. In order of effect: 1. Small datasets: put everything on the GPU once. The 2026 FordA training file (the UCR release) has 3,601 series of length 500: 7.2 MB in float32. Move X and y to the device before training and index them with a random permutation; no DataLoader needed. 2. Larger datasets: DataLoader workers. DataLoader(ds, batch size=256, shuffle=True, num workers=2, pin memory=True) prepares batches in 2 background processes (Colab has few CPU cores, so 2 is the usual choice) and pin memory speeds up the copy; then xb.to(device, non blocking=True) lets that copy overlap with the GPU's work. 3. Do augmentation on the GPU in batched tensor code instead of per-example Python. GPU calls are asynchronous: Python continues while the GPU works. To time GPU code, call torch.cuda.synchronize() before reading the clock. Checkpoints A Colab session can disconnect, and its files vanish with the runtime. Save a checkpoint (checkpoint, u00-l04) every epoch, to Google Drive for long runs: The optimizer state matters: Adam's moment estimates are part of where training is. Keep a separate copy of the best model by validation score; that is the one you submit. Seed everything ( torch.manual seed , NumPy's generator, a seeded torch.Generator for shuffling) so a rerun reproduces your numbers. Exam angle - device once at the top; .to(device) for the model (before the optimizer) and for every batch, mask and constant. - bfloat16 autocast around the forward pass and loss; backward and step outside. - Small data lives on the GPU; otherwise num workers=2, pin memory=True . - Checkpoint model, optimizer and epoch every epoch; keep the best validation model separately. Practice problem: u21-p05 Resumable training (checkpoint and resume so that an interrupted run ends exactly where an uninterrupted one does).

Round 2 is graded part by part, and many points are lost to things that have nothing to do with modeling: a part never reached, a derivation the grader cannot follow, a CSV with a missing row, a notebook that does not run on the GPU. This lesson covers the format, what is not published, how to order a paper, how open-ended work is scored, and how to end a day with files that count. What is known about the format From the 2025 and 2026 papers and the 2027 contest page on usaaio.org: - Setting. Invitation only, from Round 1 results; in person and proctored, with the software setup of every round (contest platform, Lateran AI, OBS recording). 2026 had two competition days at Harvard and MIT; 2025 was held at MIT. - 2027. "March or April 2027", all syllabus topics, and Round 1's format "except that some problems may require contestants to use GPUs" (an L4 in Google Colab). - Points. About 300. 2026: Day 1 had Problem 1 (90 points, 14 parts on linear attention, ending in a GPU training part) and Problem 2 (70, open-ended); Day 2 had Problem 3 (50, diffusion derivations), Problems 4 (40) and 5 (50), both open-ended. 2025: three problems of 100 points in parts of 5 or 10. - Two kinds of problem. A non-open-ended problem is a chain of fixed parts with definite answers: derivations, shape and count questions, modules built from scratch with named built-ins banned, a training part. An open-ended problem is scored by a metric on a hidden test set. - Files. One notebook per problem, named like Attn LastName FirstName SchoolName.ipynb , with each part's number in a bold heading cell such as Part 1.3.4 . Open-ended problems add a prediction CSV in the exact format of the sample submission and a .docx report. Not published (as of late 2026): the length of each session, the breaks, whether notes, documentation or any AI assistant are allowed, and the cutoffs for medals and camp. Plan for Round 1's rules (no AI, no documents beyond any the organizers hand out) and for long days. Read the whole paper first Spend the first 10 to 15 minutes reading every problem of the day. In a text cell at the top of each notebook, write one line per part: number, points, kind, the minutes you expect, and which earlier parts it uses. Copy the rules into the same cell, because breaking one can cost a whole part or problem: - banned modules (2026 Problem 1: nn.MultiheadAttention , nn.TransformerEncoder , Hugging Face models); - banned pretrained models (2026 Problem 4: any pretrained model means 0 for the problem); - GPU requirements (2026 Problem 1: a training part that does not run properly on the L4 gets 0); - no labeling by eye; file names; the CSV format. Bank the easy parts Parts are worth similar points but cost very different time: a 5-point derivation can take 5 minutes, a 20-point training part an hour. 1. Short parts first, in order. Later parts reuse earlier code, so doing parts in order means a later part never waits on one you skipped. 2. Test every module on a tiny input. Check the shape, then compare values with something computed another way (a slow loop version, a hand-worked case). A wrong module costs every later part that uses it. 3. Simple and correct first. If a part asks for an efficient version, a correct slow one in its own cell is the fallback. 4. Cap the time per part. At twice your estimate, note where you are, move on, and come back at the end. Write derivations a grader can follow Several 2026 parts said "A complete derivation is required." Write it in a Markdown cell with LaTeX (u00-l03): state the goal, define any symbol the problem did not, write one step per line with its reason, and end with the result in the asked form. For example, to show that binary cross-entropy $L(z) = -\left[y \log \sigma(z) + (1-y)\log(1 - \sigma(z))\right]$ on a logit $z$ has $\frac{dL}{dz} = \sigma(z) - y$: A skipped step is where a grader stops giving credit. When a result can be checked in a few lines (here, autograd at a few values of $z$), do it in a code cell below: it catches sign and factor errors. How open-ended parts are scored Each open-ended part is scored on the hidden test between a baseline and the best result, with a floor at 0: The same formula works for an error (lower is better), because the numerator and denominator both change sign. In 2026, $X {\text{best}}$ was the best contestant in Problems 1, 4 and 5, and in Problem 2 the better of the best contestant and a jury model, so there even the top student could fall short of full marks. (IOAI uses the larger of the best submission and 0.9 times the organizers' solution.) Three consequences: 1. Any valid file above the baseline scores. Submit one from a simple model early, then improve it. 2. Invalid rows are expensive. Missing or invalid predictions count as wrong; in 2026 Problem 2 a missing source coordinate set that sample's location error to 10, 200 times the 0.05 of the good model below (and the official metric then multiplied the location error by 1000). 3. The scale is steep. With a baseline of 0.50 and a best of 0.95, each 0.01 of macro F1 is $1/45$ of the points, so choose models by a validation estimate you trust (u13-l01). Ten missing rows out of 500 cost 14% of the points. Check the file you upload by reading it back and comparing it with the sample submission: The report The 2026 open-ended problems asked for a .docx report on the model you submitted, the models you tried and dropped, and your reasoning. Use the structure of u13-l05. Write the headings when you start the problem and keep a results log in a text cell (setting, validation score, one line of why); the report is then ten minutes of editing, and its numbers must match the notebook. Google Docs exports .docx with File, Download, Microsoft Word. GPU habits on the L4 The mechanics are in u21-l04. The exam habits: - Switch to the L4 at the start of a problem that needs it: the switch restarts the runtime and clears every variable. Run !nvidia-smi once. - Develop on a few batches, then start the long run in its own cell with a checkpoint every epoch. Download the best weights and the CSV as soon as they exist. - A notebook runs one code cell at a time, but you can edit text cells meanwhile: write derivations and the report during training. - Before the end, prove the notebook runs top to bottom on the L4 (Runtime, Restart session and run all). If full training is too long to repeat, do it with one or two epochs, and keep the real run's cells and printed output. A time plan Session lengths are not published, so here is the shape of a plan for a day like 2026 Day 1 (one non-open-ended and one open-ended problem), written for 6 hours as an example (IOAI contests are six hours); scale it to the real length. Time Work --- --- 0:00 to 0:15 Read both problems; planning cell with parts, points, minutes, rules 0:15 to 0:45 Open-ended: load data, simple baseline, valid CSV checked against the sample; report headings 0:45 to 2:45 Non-open-ended short parts in order, each tested; start the GPU training part when you reach it 2:45 to 4:45 Remaining parts while training runs; then improve the open-ended model, one logged change at a time 4:45 to 5:30 Freeze: final predictions, run-all on the L4, CSV check, report 5:30 to 6:00 Buffer for file names, uploads and surprises Stop starting new ideas with about 15% of the session left. A finished, valid submission beats a better model still training. Exam angle - Read every problem first; plan parts by points, minutes and dependencies; copy the rules. - Short parts first, in order, each module tested on a tiny input; derivations one step per line with a reason. - Open-ended: a valid file early, checked against the sample submission; report from the results log; run-all on the L4 before the end.

The IOAI 2027 syllabus lists "basic Linux terminal commands" as a practice topic and names ten of them: ls , cd , rm , mkdir , chmod , sudo , nvidia-smi , htop , ps and grep . At IOAI 2026 the contestants' laptops ran Ubuntu (a Linux system) and training ran on GPU machines reached through JupyterLab (a notebook interface in the browser, which also has a terminal; u22-l03). National camps and selection tests often hand out a login to a Linux GPU server. This lesson covers those ten commands and the four ideas behind them: paths, permissions, processes and pipes. The shell A terminal is a text window for typing commands. The shell is the program inside it that reads each line and runs it; Ubuntu's default shell is bash . A command is a program name followed by arguments separated by spaces. Arguments that start with - are options (also called flags): they change what the program does. Short options can be combined, so ls -l -a is the same as ls -la . Most commands print a summary with --help , and man ls opens the manual for ls (press q to leave it). Three keys save time: Tab completes a file or command name, the up arrow brings back earlier commands, and Ctrl-C stops the command that is running. In a Jupyter or Colab cell, a line that starts with ! goes to the shell, as in !nvidia-smi (u21-l04). Each ! line runs in a new shell that exits afterward, so !cd data changes nothing for the next cell. Use %cd data to change the notebook's folder. Paths: where you are Files live in a tree of directories (folders) that starts at the root directory , written / . A path names a file or directory. An absolute path starts at the root, like /tmp/ioai/train.py . A relative path starts from the working directory , the directory the shell is in right now. Three short names help: ~ is your home directory ( /home/ followed by your user name), . is the working directory and .. is its parent. cd with no argument takes you home. In the blocks below, a line starting with $ is what you type (without the $ ), and the lines under it are what the shell prints. Text after is a comment. Two helpers appear first: echo text prints the text, and file (explained under redirection below) puts that output into a file instead of the screen; cat file prints a file's contents. ls -l gives the long listing: type and permissions, number of links, owner , group , size in bytes, date modified and name. ls -a also shows hidden files , those whose names start with a dot (such as .gitignore or .ssh ), including . and .. themselves. ls -lh prints sizes in a readable form, such as 4.0K , 1.3M or 2.4G . Copy, move and delete cp a b copies a file, mv a b moves or renames it, and rm a deletes it. rm does not use a trash folder: a deleted file is gone. rm refuses a directory; rm -r removes a directory and everything inside it. rm -rf adds "force": no questions and no errors for missing files, so read the path twice before you press Enter. Permissions, chmod and sudo Every file has an owner and a group, and three sets of file permissions : for the owner (user), for members of the group, and for everyone else (others). Each set holds read r , write w and execute x . In ls -l , the first character is the type ( - for a file, d for a directory, l for a link, a shortcut to another file) and the next nine are the three sets. For a directory, x means you may enter it. chmod changes permissions. In the numeric form, each digit is a sum: read 4, write 2, execute 1. So 7 = 4 + 2 + 1 is rwx , 5 = 4 + 1 is r-x , 6 is rw- and 4 is r-- , and the three digits are owner, group, others. The letter form adds ( + ) or removes ( - ) rights for u , g , o or a (user, group, others, all): chmod o-r file stops others from reading. The common values: 755 ( rwxr-xr-x ) for scripts and directories, 644 ( rw-r--r-- ) for ordinary files, 600 ( rw------- ) for private files such as SSH keys (u22-l03). A script needs x before you can run it as ./run.sh ; without it the shell answers "Permission denied". The root user is the administrator account, allowed to change any file. sudo runs one command as root after asking for your password, and only works if the machine's administrator allows your account to use it. System folders such as /etc belong to root, so touch /etc/test (which creates an empty file) fails with "Permission denied", while sudo apt install htop ( apt is Ubuntu's program installer) installs a program for everyone. On a contest machine you usually have no sudo , and IOAI 2026 did not allow installing packages during the contest. Use sudo only when you know why the command needs it. Processes: ps, htop, kill and nvidia-smi A running program is a process , and the system gives each one a number, its PID (process ID). A command followed by & runs in the background, so the shell is free for the next command. ps lists the processes of this terminal; ps aux lists every process on the machine with its owner, CPU and memory use, so ps aux grep python finds a training run. kill PID asks a process to stop, and kill -9 PID forces it. In the output below, the grep sleep line is the search itself: grep 's own command line contains the word it looks for. htop is a live, full-screen version of ps : bars for each CPU core and for memory at the top, then processes sorted by CPU use. F6 changes the sort column, F9 sends a kill signal to the selected process, and q quits. If htop is not installed, top shows the same table more plainly. nvidia-smi does the same for NVIDIA GPUs: the GPU model, memory used and total, utilization, and the processes using each GPU. Run it before training on a shared machine to see whether the GPU is free, and while training to see how much memory your batch takes. For a short, script-friendly answer, ask for named fields. Here it is on a desktop with one consumer GPU that another job was already filling: MiB means mebibytes: 1 MiB is $2^{20}$ bytes, so 16376 MiB is about $17.2 \times 10^9$ bytes. watch -n 1 nvidia-smi reruns the full table every second (Ctrl-C to stop). The IOAI 2026 training machines split each NVIDIA H200 into several Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) slices, with an 18 GB memory limit, so the "memory used" number is the one to watch. grep, pipes and redirection grep pattern file prints the lines of file that contain pattern . The useful options: -n adds line numbers, -i ignores case, -v prints the lines that do not match, -c prints only the number of matching lines, and -r searches every file under a directory. The pattern matches anywhere inside a line, not only whole words. A pipe sends one command's output into the next command as its input. Redirection writes a command's output into a file (replacing what was there), and appends to it. head -n 5 and tail -n 5 keep the first or last 5 lines, tail -f log.txt keeps printing a log as it grows (Ctrl-C to stop), and wc -l counts lines. Here the working directory holds a training log, log.txt , and a two-line settings file, data/config.yaml . Exam angle - Paths: absolute from / , relative from pwd ; .. is the parent, ~ is home, cd - goes back. - ls -la for hidden files and permissions; mkdir -p ; rm -r for directories, with no undo. - chmod digits: read 4, write 2, execute 1, in the order owner, group, others. 755, 644 and 600 cover most cases. - ps aux grep name , then kill PID ; htop and nvidia-smi to watch CPU, memory and GPU. - grep -n -i -v -c -r ; chains commands, overwrites a file, appends.

The IOAI 2027 syllabus lists "basic Git" as a practice topic and names seven commands: add , commit , push , reset , diff , status and restore . Git is how code moves between a laptop, a GPU server and GitHub (where IOAI publishes its past tasks), and it is how you get back the version of a training script that worked yesterday. This lesson builds one small repository command by command; every output shown is what Git printed. Repositories and commits Version control keeps the history of a project's files, and Git is the standard tool for it. A repository (repo) is a project folder whose history Git tracks; the history lives in a hidden .git folder inside it. A commit is a saved snapshot of the tracked files, with a message, an author, a date and an ID called the commit hash (40 hexadecimal characters; Git usually shows the first 7). Git keeps three versions of each file: 1. the working tree : the files on disk that you edit; 2. the staging area (also called the index): the snapshot you are preparing for the next commit; 3. the last commit, which Git calls HEAD . Commits form a chain, and a branch is a name that points at the newest commit of one such chain; main is the usual name of the first. HEAD is the newest commit of the branch you are on. git add copies a file from the working tree into the staging area, and git commit turns the staging area into a new commit. A file that Git has never been told to track is untracked . On a new machine, first tell Git who you are with git config --global user.name "Your Name" and git config --global user.email you@example.com ; every commit records them. Seeing changes: status and diff git status says which files differ, and where. git status --short prints two columns before each name: the left one compares the staging area with HEAD, the right one compares the working tree with the staging area. M means modified, A added (new in the staging area), and ?? untracked. git diff shows the difference between the working tree and the staging area, that is, what you have not staged yet. git diff --staged shows the difference between the staging area and HEAD, which is what the next commit will contain. Lines starting with - are removed and lines starting with + are added. git add stages the file as it is at that moment. Edit it again afterward, and the file is in two states at once: (The two diffs are shortened to their last three lines.) git commit -am "message" stages every modified tracked file and commits in one step, but it never adds untracked files. Undoing: restore and reset git restore file throws away your unstaged edits: it copies the staged version of the file over the working copy. The edit is gone for good, since Git never saw it. git restore --staged file does the opposite job: it unstages the file (copies HEAD's version into the staging area) and leaves your working copy alone. git reset moves the current branch to another commit. HEAD~1 means the commit before HEAD, HEAD~2 the one before that. Its three modes differ in what happens to the changes of the commits you remove: command history staging area working tree --- --- --- --- git reset --soft HEAD~1 last commit removed keeps its changes (staged) unchanged git reset HEAD~1 (mixed, the default) last commit removed reset keeps the changes (unstaged) git reset --hard HEAD~1 last commit removed reset reset: the commit's changes and all uncommitted changes to tracked files are lost Untracked files are never touched by reset , even with --hard . git reset --hard HEAD (no ~1 ) removes no commit; it only throws away every uncommitted change to tracked files. Only reset commits that you have not pushed: removing a commit that others already have makes their history and yours disagree. Keeping data and checkpoints out: .gitignore A file named .gitignore lists names and patterns that Git should treat as invisible, one per line: data/ matches a folder, .pt every file ending in .pt . Datasets and model weights do not belong in a repository: they are large, and GitHub rejects very large files. .gitignore only hides untracked files. A file you already committed stays tracked; git rm --cached file stops tracking it and keeps it on disk. Remotes: clone, push and pull A remote is another copy of the repository, usually on GitHub; the default name for it is origin . git clone URL copies a repository with its whole history and sets up origin . git push sends your new commits to the remote, and git pull fetches the remote's new commits and merges them into yours (a merge joins two lines of history, adding a merge commit if both sides changed something). GitHub does not accept your account password for git push : use a personal access token, or an SSH key (u22-l03). When someone else (or you, from another machine) pushed first, your push is rejected until you pull. In this run a second copy of the repository had pushed a new README.md while this copy made a commit of its own; the remote was a folder on the same machine, which behaves like a GitHub URL: git push --force would make the push succeed by deleting the other person's commits from the remote. Pull instead. Exam angle - Three places: working tree, staging area, HEAD. add moves work into the staging area, commit records the staging area. - git diff : working tree vs staging area. git diff --staged : staging area vs HEAD. Short status MM : changed in both. - git restore file discards unstaged edits (no undo); git restore --staged file unstages. - reset --soft keeps changes staged, the default keeps them unstaged, --hard discards them; untracked files survive all three. - Rejected push: git pull , then git push . Keep data and weights out with .gitignore .

The IOAI 2027 syllabus lists two practice topics for this lesson: "Jupyter Notebook / JupyterLab" and "work on remote servers (via SSH)". At IOAI 2026 the contest laptops had no GPU: contestants trained models in JupyterLab running on GPU machines, and VS Code on the laptop had no GPU access. Training camps and national selection rounds often give each student an account on a shared GPU server instead, reached with SSH. Both setups have the same shape: a weak machine in front of you and a strong one somewhere else. Logging in with SSH A server is a computer that other computers connect to over the network; a remote server is one you reach that way rather than by sitting at it. SSH (secure shell) opens an encrypted connection to a server and gives you a shell on it. You run ssh on your laptop with a user name and a host (the server's name or address): A port is a numbered entry point on a machine; each network service listens on its own (SSH on 22 unless the administrator chose another). The first time you connect, ssh shows the server's fingerprint and asks whether to trust it (a fingerprint is a short code that identifies the server's key); answer yes once and it remembers the server. Every command you type after logging in runs on the server: nvidia-smi shows the server's GPUs, and ls lists the server's files. Keys instead of passwords An SSH key pair is two files made together. The private key stays on your laptop and must never be shared. The public key can be given to anyone; a server that has your public key in its list of authorized keys lets in whoever holds the matching private key, with no password. Send the .pub file to the server's administrator, or run ssh-copy-id ana@gpu01.example.org once with your password. The private key must stay at permission 600 (u22-l01): if others can read it, ssh refuses to use it. chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id ed25519 fixes it. To stop typing the full address, put an alias in the SSH config file ~/.ssh/config : Now ssh gpu is enough, and the alias works in scp and rsync too. Copying files scp copies files over SSH. Its arguments are source then destination, and a remote path is written host:path . Run it on your laptop: Runs that survive a lost connection A program started in a plain SSH session is stopped when that session ends: if your laptop sleeps or the Wi-Fi drops, the shell on the server receives a hangup signal (a message the system sends to a program, here meaning "the terminal is gone") and passes it to the programs it started. Two fixes: - tmux keeps shells running on the server after you disconnect. tmux new -s train opens a session named train ; start the run inside it; press Ctrl-b, then d, to detach. Later, from a new SSH login, tmux ls lists sessions and tmux attach -t train brings it back. - nohup starts one command that ignores the hangup signal. Redirect its output to a log file and add & to free the shell: 2 &1 sends error messages (standard error) into the same file as normal output (standard output). Add -u to python3 so each print reaches the file at once: otherwise Python holds output back in a buffer when it writes to a file, and tail -f shows nothing for a long time. In an interactive shell nohup also writes the line nohup: ignoring input at the top of the log. On a server with several GPUs, pick one with an environment variable , a named setting that a program inherits from the shell. CUDA VISIBLE DEVICES=1 python3 train.py lets PyTorch see only GPU 1 (which it then calls cuda:0 ). Check nvidia-smi first so you do not start on a GPU someone else is using. Jupyter on a remote machine JupyterLab is the browser interface for Jupyter notebooks (u00-l02 covered Colab, which is built on Jupyter), with tabs, a file browser and a terminal; the older interface is called Jupyter Notebook. The code in a notebook runs in a kernel , a Python process on the machine that serves the notebook. In a contest like IOAI 2026 the organizers run JupyterLab on the GPU machines and you open it in the laptop's browser. On your own server you start it yourself and reach it through an SSH tunnel: -L 8888:localhost:8888 is port forwarding : connections to port 8888 on the laptop travel through the SSH connection and come out at localhost:8888 as seen from the server, which is where Jupyter listens. -N means "run no remote command, only forward". Habits that matter on a GPU machine: - The kernel keeps every variable in memory, including tensors on the GPU. When nvidia-smi shows your memory still in use after a crash, delete the big tensors or restart the kernel. - Cells can run in any order, so a notebook can work only because of a cell you later deleted. Before you submit, use Kernel, Restart Kernel and Run All Cells, and check that it finishes. - %%time as the first line of a cell prints how long the cell took. Time one epoch before you start fifty. - Save checkpoints and predictions to files as soon as they exist. A restarted kernel keeps files and loses variables. - JupyterLab's terminal (File, New, Terminal) is a shell on the GPU machine: nvidia-smi , ls , grep and git all work there. Write code that runs on either machine, and check what one training run will need: Each float32 number takes 4 bytes, and a MiB is $2^{20}$ bytes. Training with Adam stores four numbers per parameter (the weight, its gradient and Adam's two running averages, u11-l07), so 16 bytes per parameter, plus the activations of the batch, which grow with the batch size. Exam angle - ssh user@host , -p for another port; keys from ssh-keygen , private key at 600, public key on the server; aliases in ~/.ssh/config . - scp source destination , with host:path for the remote side; rsync -av to resend only changes. - Long runs inside tmux or with nohup python3 -u ... log 2 &1 & ; tail -f log to watch. - Jupyter through a tunnel: ssh -N -L 8888:localhost:8888 host , then http://localhost:8888 . - Restart Kernel and Run All before submitting; 16 bytes per parameter for float32 training with Adam.

Most IOAI tasks are scored like a Kaggle competition: you train on labeled data, submit predictions for data whose labels you never see, and a hidden part of those labels decides the final ranking. The 2026 at-home round ran on Kaggle itself, many national olympiads hold their rounds there, and the IOAI contest system follows the same plan under its own names. The skill this lesson teaches is reading a leaderboard correctly: how a raw score becomes contest points, how much of a score difference is noise, and why tuning to the visible score can lower the hidden one. How a Kaggle competition works Kaggle is a website that hosts data-science competitions. A competition page gives a training set with labels, a test set without labels, the metric, and a sample submission that shows the file format (u21-l05). You upload a CSV of predictions for the test set. In a code competition you submit a notebook instead, and Kaggle runs it on its own machines within a time limit to produce the CSV. The host splits the test rows into two parts, and you are not told which row is in which: - The public leaderboard ranks everyone by their score on the first part. You see it during the contest, after every submission. - The private leaderboard ranks everyone by their score on the other part. It is revealed only when the contest ends, and it is the final result. Most competitions also cap the number of submissions per day, and before the end you mark a small number of your submissions as final; the private leaderboard scores those. Two command-line calls from Kaggle's own tool, if it is installed: Write a message with every submission saying what changed: it is your results log (u13-l01) when you choose the final ones. The IOAI version: Scoreboard A and Scoreboard B The IOAI 2026 rules (sections 2.5 and 2.6 and the technical appendix) give each task three datasets, unless the task says otherwise: - training data , with labels, for fitting your model; - validation data , without labels. Every submission is scored on it, and you see your score, the baseline's score and the highest score any other contestant has reached so far (anonymous). These results are Scoreboard A . - test data , without labels and unused during the contest. After the end, your final solution is scored on it. These results are Scoreboard B , and the official ranking and medals use Scoreboard B only. So Scoreboard A plays the part of Kaggle's public leaderboard and Scoreboard B the private one. Apart from that one anonymous best score, you see no other contestant's score or rank during the contest. Two limits applied to every task unless its statement said otherwise: at most 60 submissions, and at most 20 minutes of runtime for the notebook. Submissions may be queued while earlier ones are still being scored. From raw score to points Each IOAI task is scored on a 0 to 100 scale. The raw score of a submission (accuracy, F1 or whatever the task names) is turned into points with an IOAI normalized score : Here Min Score is the score of the task's baseline solution, SC Solution is the score of a nearly optimal solution written by the Scientific Committee (the organizers' task authors), and Max Submission is the best raw score any contestant reached. So the best contestant gets 100 only when their score is at least 90% of the organizers' solution; otherwise even the winner gets less. The rules do not say what a score below the baseline gets; this unit clips it to 0 (and the best contestant cannot go above 100, since Max Score is at least Max Submission). Scores are computed in double precision without rounding and shown with 4 decimals. (USAAIO Round 2 uses the same shape of formula, with the best result at the top, u21-l05.) Here $0.9 \times 0.96 = 0.864$ is above the best contestant's 0.85, so Max Score is 0.864 and the best contestant gets 91.4634. Every 0.01 of accuracy is worth about 6 points on this task. How noisy is a leaderboard score? A score measured on a few hundred rows is an estimate. If a model is right on each row with probability $p$, its accuracy on $n$ rows has standard error (u05-l09) With $p = 0.85$ and $n = 500$ public rows that is 0.016, so two submissions 0.01 apart on the public board are not reliably different. Your own cross-validation on 8,000 training rows has a standard error of 0.004, four times smaller, because it uses 16 times as many rows. A rule of thumb: treat differences smaller than about two standard errors as ties. Overfitting the public leaderboard Choosing among many submissions by their public score picks the one with the luckiest public rows. That is overfitting the leaderboard : the public score of the chosen submission is too high, and its private score is ordinary. The more submissions you compare this way, the larger the gap. When the private leaderboard is revealed and many teams drop, the change in ranking is called a shake-up . The simulation below runs 2,000 contests. In each, 30 submissions have true accuracies spread evenly from 0.84 to 0.86; each is scored on 8,000 rows of cross-validation, 500 public rows and 2,000 private rows. Picking by public score shows 0.884 on the public board, 0.024 above the best true accuracy, and gets 0.854 on the private board. Picking by cross-validation shows a modest public score and gets 0.8585, close to the best possible 0.86. The same holds for IOAI's Scoreboard A: 60 submissions are enough to tune a model to the validation rows. How to use the visible score: 1. Choose models and hyperparameters by your own validation on the training data (u06-l08). Use the visible score as one more check, not as the target. 2. When your validation and the visible score disagree by more than the noise, look for a bug or a difference between the training and test data before you trust either. 3. Spend submissions on real changes, not on small tweaks to one number. 4. For the final choice, take the submission that is good on both, and if two are allowed, make the second one a different kind of model. Working within the limits - Submit early. A valid file from a simple model that beats the baseline already scores points; then improve it (u21-l05). - Time the whole notebook. A 20-minute limit covers loading data and models and running inference, not only training. Time each part, then keep a margin of a few minutes for a slower machine or a busy queue. - Make it reproducible. Fix every seed so the notebook gives the same file twice, and save the weights it uses. Exam angle - Public leaderboard (Scoreboard A) during the contest; private leaderboard (Scoreboard B) decides the result. - Points $= 100\,(\text{raw} - \text{Min})/(\text{Max} - \text{Min})$, Max $= \max(0.9\,\text{SC}, \text{best submission})$, clipped to 0 to 100. - SE of an accuracy: $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$; differences under two SE are ties. - Choosing the best of many by the public score overestimates it; choose by your own validation. Practice problem: u22-p01 IOAI normalized scores .
A Colab (Jupyter) command that, as the first line of a cell, saves the rest of the cell into a file instead of running it.
A layer that applies the same small set of weights at every position of a sequence: nn.Conv1d(1, 1, 3, padding=1) gives y i = w0 x (i-1) + w1 x i + w2 x (i+1) + bias.
A convolution with kernel size 1: it mixes channels at each pixel without looking at neighbors (C in C out weights). Also called a pointwise convolution.
A normal value lies within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations of the mean with probability about 0.683, 0.954 and 0.997.
A path that starts at the root directory, such as /tmp/ioai/train.py.
The fraction of predictions that equal the true labels: (pred == y).mean().
In RL, the choice A t the agent makes at time t, from the set of allowed actions.
The per-action scores h(s, a, theta) whose softmax gives a softmax policy's probabilities.
q pi(s, a) = E pi[G t S t = s, A t = a], the expected return after taking a in s and then following pi.
The output a = phi(z) of a layer after its activation function; the input to the next layer.
The fixed nonlinear function a neural network applies to every entry after a linear step, such as ReLU, sigmoid or tanh.
An inequality constraint that holds with equality at the solution.
An optimizer that scales each parameter's step using running averages of its past gradients; torch.optim.Adam(params, lr=1e-3) is a common default.
Adam with decoupled weight decay: shrink the weights by lr lambda directly, then take the Adam step with the loss gradient alone. torch.optim.AdamW(params, lr, weight decay=0.01).
A small bottleneck MLP inserted into each transformer block and trained while the rest stays frozen.
Pooling that fixes the output size and chooses the windows to fit: nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d((h, w)) returns (N, C, h, w) for any input size.
q(s, a) - v(s): how much better action a is than the policy's average in s; G t - v hat(S t) estimates it.
A linear function plus a constant, x - W x + b. Composing affine functions gives another affine function.
In RL, the learner and decision maker: it observes states, picks actions and receives rewards.
Bottom-up hierarchical clustering: start with one cluster per point and repeatedly merge the two closest clusters.
A second name for the same thing: import numpy as np makes np an alias for numpy, and b = a makes b another name for a's object.
A frequency above the Nyquist frequency showing up as a false lower frequency after sampling.
Attention with linear biases: add -m i - j to each score, with a fixed slope m per head. No parameters; works on longer sequences than seen in training.
alpha-bar t = alpha 1 ... alpha t; then x t x 0 ~ N(sqrt(alpha-bar t) x 0, 1 - alpha-bar t).
Training a network to map data directly to parameters, so the cost of fitting is paid once in training instead of once per sample.
A solution written as an explicit formula, such as exp(-alpha pi^2 t) sin(pi x) for the heat equation with a sine initial condition.
Sampling a chain by drawing each variable from its conditional given the previous one; DDPM sampling draws x {t-1} from p(x {t-1} x t) for t = T .. 1.
A preset box shape at each grid position; YOLO and SSD predict offsets and scales relative to anchors.
Flagging inputs unlike the training data, for example by a high autoencoder reconstruction error.
A model you can only query over the internet through a provider's interface, paying per token; its weights are not available (closed-source).
A tractable distribution q(z x), in a VAE a diagonal Gaussian from the encoder, trained to be close to the true posterior p(z x).
A value passed to a function in a call.
A NumPy grid of numbers (an ndarray) in which every entry has the same type. Arithmetic on an array acts on every entry.
A file the training notebook produces that inference needs, such as learned weights, preprocessing parameters or a config. It goes in the submission ZIP next to submission.py.
An operation where each query takes a weighted average of values, with weights given by a softmax of query-key scores.
One of the H parallel attentions in multi-head attention, with its own query, key and value projections of size d k (usually d model / H).
A (B, T) tensor marking real tokens (1) and padding (0), in the Hugging Face convention. Pooling, loss and attention use it to skip padding.
The numbers q . k j / sqrt(d k) before the softmax, one per (query, key) pair; masks set some of them to -inf.
softmax of the attention scores over the keys: nonnegative, each query's row sums to 1.
A variable stored on an object, set and read as self.name or obj.name.
Area under the ROC curve: the fraction of (positive, negative) pairs in which the positive has the higher score, ties counting one half.
An audio encoder whose outputs feed a text language model, so audio plus a text prompt go in and text comes out (Qwen-Audio, Voxtral).
A network trained to reproduce its input: an encoder maps x to a short code z and a decoder maps z back to a reconstruction x hat.
PyTorch's automatic differentiation: it records operations on tensors with requires grad=True and computes gradients when backward() is called.
Producing a sequence one token at a time, each new token predicted from all earlier ones and then appended to the input.
Pooling that keeps the mean of each window: nn.AvgPool2d(k). Its gradient is shared equally over the window.
A one-number summary of the precision-recall curve, roughly the area under it.
One panel of a matplotlib figure, with its own methods such as ax.hist and ax.set title. plt.subplots(1, 2) returns a figure and two axes.
One direction of an array, numbered from 0. For shape (n, d), axis 0 runs down the rows and axis 1 across the columns.
The part of a network that turns the input into a feature vector; in transfer learning it is reused (often frozen) and a new head is put on top.
Computing the gradient of the loss with the chain rule, from the output back to the parameters, multiplying local derivatives along paths and adding over paths.
Backpropagation on an RNN unrolled over its T steps; the gradient to early steps is a product of one Jacobian per step, so it can vanish or explode.
Updating a state's (or state-action pair's) value from the values of the states one step after it.
Representing a document by how often each vocabulary word occurs in it, ignoring word order.
Bootstrap aggregating: train one model per bootstrap sample and combine them by vote or average; reduces variance.
The simplest reasonable predictor, such as the training mean (regression) or the most common class (classification). Every real model must beat its validation score.
A function b(s) subtracted from the return in a policy gradient; it keeps the estimate unbiased and can cut its variance.
The standard shell on Ubuntu and most Linux systems.
ResNet-18/34's residual block: 3x3 conv, batch norm, ReLU, 3x3 conv, batch norm, add the shortcut, ReLU.
An independent set of vectors that spans a subspace; its size is the dimension.

nn.BatchNorm1d/2d: normalize each feature (channel) with the batch's mean and biased variance, then gamma x hat + beta. Training mode uses batch statistics and updates running averages; eval mode uses the running averages.
Many matrix products at once: (B, n, k) @ (B, k, m) gives (B, n, m), one product per leading index.
P(H E) = P(E H) P(H) / P(E): posterior = likelihood times prior, divided by the probability of the evidence.
nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss(): binary cross-entropy with the sigmoid built in. Takes logits and float 0/1 targets of the same shape.
Decoding that keeps the b most likely partial sequences (by total log-probability) at every step.
The policy that actually chooses the actions and so generates the data.
v pi(s) = sum a pi(a s) sum {s', r} p(s', r s, a) [r + gamma v pi(s')]: a state's value from its successors' values.
q (s, a) = sum {s', r} p(s', r s, a) [r + gamma max a' q (s', a')] (and v with a max over the first action).
A 0/1 variable equal to 1 with probability p; mean p, variance p (1 - p).
Bidirectional encoder representations from transformers: an encoder-only model pretrained by masked language modeling; [CLS] output used for classification.
A 2-byte float format with float32's exponent range and about 3 significant digits; needs no gradient scaling.
Error from a model being too simple: how far its average prediction, over many possible training sets, is from the truth.
In Adam, dividing the running averages m and v by 1 - beta^t, because they start at 0 and are too small for the first steps.
The constant parameter b added to a model's output, such as b in w size + b.
As capacity grows, bias falls and variance rises; the best model balances the two.
Two RNNs, one reading left to right and one right to left, with their states concatenated at each position (last axis 2H). Needs the whole sequence in advance.
-[t ln q + (1 - t) ln(1 - q)] with q = sigmoid(z); its gradient with respect to the logit z is q - t. nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss takes z.
The entropy of a coin with P(heads) = p: -p log p - (1 - p) log(1 - p).
Turning a numeric feature into ranges (bins), such as Small, Medium, Large.
C(n, k) = n! / (k! (n - k)!), read 'n choose k': the number of ways to choose k items out of n, ignoring order.
Bin(n, p): the number of successes in n independent Bernoulli(p) trials; P(k) = C(n, k) p^k (1 - p)^(n - k), mean np, variance np(1 - p).
The unit of information for base-2 logs; 1 bit = ln 2 = 0.693 nats.
A character-level language model's loss in bits: mean NLL / ln 2.
A translation metric: the geometric mean of clipped 1- to 4-gram precisions of the output against the reference, times a brevity penalty for short outputs.
An array of True and False used as an index: x[mask] keeps the entries where the mask is True, and x[mask] = v assigns only there.
Building an ensemble in sequence, each new small model trained to fix the errors of the ensemble so far; reduces bias.
Estimating a statistic's standard error by recomputing it on many resamples of size n drawn with replacement from the data.
n examples drawn with replacement from a dataset of size n; it contains about 63.2% of the distinct examples.
In RL, updating an estimate from other current estimates (as TD and DP do) instead of from complete returns.
In DBSCAN, a point that is not core but lies within eps of a core point; it joins that cluster.
A layer narrower than the input (k < d) that forces an autoencoder to keep only the most useful information.
ResNet-50's residual block: 1x1 conv from 4w down to w channels, 3x3 conv at width w, 1x1 conv back up to 4w (each with batch norm), add the shortcut, ReLU.
BC: the required values of a PDE's solution on the edge of the domain for all times, such as u(t, 0) = u(t, 1) = 0.
The smallest axis-aligned rectangle around an object; stored as xyxy (corners), xywh (corner and size) or cxcywh (center and size).
BLEU's factor exp(1 - r/c) for a candidate of length c shorter than the reference length r; 1 otherwise.
NumPy's rule for combining arrays of different shapes: line the shapes up from the right; each pair of lengths must be equal or contain a 1, and length-1 axes are stretched to match.
A tensor stored with self.register buffer(name, t): part of the model and saved in state dict, but not a parameter, so it never trains. BatchNorm's running mean is one.
BPE: build a subword vocabulary by starting from characters and repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token.
One agreed representative among parameter values that give the same function, such as c0 0 and 0 <= c2 < 2 pi for c0 sin(c1 x + c2).
How flexible a model family is: how many different shapes of function it can fit.
A fine-tuned model losing abilities it had after pretraining, because training on the new task overwrote them.
One of k classes with probabilities pi 1, ..., pi k; a softmax output is one.
A pandas dtype that stores values as a fixed list of categories, as pd.cut returns. Convert with astype(str) before writing exact text.
A feature whose values are names from a fixed set, such as a city.
x . y <= x y , which keeps cosine similarity between -1 and 1.
The mask that lets position i attend only to positions j <= i: torch.tril of ones (allowed) or torch.triu(..., diagonal=1) (blocked).
Cumulative distribution function F(x) = P(X <= x); P(a < X <= b) = F(b) - F(a).
One box in a notebook: either a code cell (Python, runs and shows output) or a text cell (Markdown and math).
The LSTM's second state c t, updated by addition (c t = f c (t-1) + i g), which lets gradients survive many steps.
Data with each column's mean subtracted, so every column has mean 0: X c = X - X.mean(axis=0).
The derivative estimate (f(x + h) - f(x - h)) / (2h); its error shrinks like h^2. Use h around 1e-5.
A vector field F(r) = f( r - r s ) (r - r s)/ r - r s that points along the line through a source r s everywhere; f is the radial profile.
For large n, the mean of n iid draws is approximately normal, N(mu, sigma^2 / n), whatever the original distribution.
The center of a cluster; in k-means, the mean of the points assigned to it.
Assigning through two sets of brackets, as in df[mask]["col"] = v. The first brackets make a temporary table, so the original is not changed; use df.loc[mask, "col"] = v.
One of the grids that make up an image or feature map tensor: a color image has 3 (red, green, blue); a conv layer's output has out channels. PyTorch stores images as (N, C, H, W).
The (C, H, W) layout PyTorch uses for images; files, PIL and matplotlib use channels-last (H, W, C). Convert with permute(2, 0, 1).
det(A - lambda I), a polynomial in lambda whose roots are the eigenvalues.
The tokenizer's rule for turning a list of role-tagged messages into one token sequence with the special tokens the model was trained on.
A saved file holding a model's learned numbers (and usually the settings needed to rebuild it), so another notebook can load the trained model without retraining.
In classification, one of the k categories a sample can belong to, numbered 0 to k-1.
A blueprint for a kind of object, defining its attributes and methods.
One class being much rarer than another, which makes accuracy misleading.
A learned vector prepended to the token sequence (BERT's [CLS], ViT's cls); its final output vector is fed to the classification head.
Keeping at most the same number of the most confident pseudo-labels per class, so an easy class cannot dominate.
A supervised task whose label is one of a fixed set of categories (classes).
A model that predicts a sample's class, usually by giving one score per class and picking the highest.
Sampling with eps null + w (eps c - eps null), using one network trained with the condition sometimes replaced by a null condition.
A 4 by 12 gridworld with a cliff along the bottom edge (reward -100); the standard example separating Q-learning from SARSA.
Contrastive language-image pretraining: an image encoder and a text encoder projected into one space and trained with a symmetric contrastive loss on image-caption pairs.
In BLEU, the fraction of candidate n-grams found in the reference, where each n-gram counts at most as many times as it occurs in the reference.
A formula that gives the answer directly, with no iterating, such as w = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y.
A function that uses names from the place where it was created (a loop, a comprehension or an enclosing function). It looks those names up when it runs.
Grouping similar examples together without labels.
A competition where you submit a notebook, which the host runs within a time limit to produce the predictions.
The function a DataLoader calls (collate fn=) to turn a list of samples into one batch; for text it pads and builds the attention mask.
Points sampled from the domain where a PINN's PDE residual is evaluated; they need no labels.
All outputs Ax of a matrix A: the span of its columns.
A saved snapshot of the tracked files, with a message, an author, a date and a commit hash.
The ID of a commit: 40 hexadecimal characters computed from its contents, usually shown as the first 7.
The event 'not A', all outcomes outside A; P(not A) = 1 - P(A).
A one-expression way to build a list, dict or set: [f(x) for x in xs if condition].
A diagram of a calculation with one box per intermediate value and arrows showing which values feed which.
A function f is concave when -f is convex: chords lie on or below the graph.
For a symmetric positive definite matrix, the ratio of its largest to smallest eigenvalue. Gradient descent on a quadratic shrinks the error by about (k - 1)/(k + 1) per step at best.
Generating samples that match a given condition c, such as a class label or text prompt, from a model eps(x t, t, c).
P(A B) = P(A and B) / P(B): the probability of A once you know B happened.
A range such as estimate plus or minus 1.96 standard errors, which contains the true value for about 95% of samples.
A detector's score for one predicted box, used to sort predictions for NMS and for average precision.
The minimum top-class probability for a prediction to be used as a pseudo-label, often 0.9 to 0.95.
In pseudo-labeling, training on the model's own mistakes, which makes it more confident in them.
The table of counts of each (actual class, predicted class) pair; in scikit-learn rows are actual and columns predicted.
An unsupervised loss that penalizes different predictions for two augmentations (or noisy versions) of the same input.
A condition the solution of an optimization problem must satisfy, such as g(x) = 0 or g(x) <= 0.
The init method. It runs automatically when you create an object, to set up its attributes.
The largest number of tokens (prompt plus output) a language model can process at once.
A tensor whose entries sit in memory in row-major order. permute and .T give non-contiguous tensors, so view fails on them and reshape copies.
An array whose entries sit in memory in row-major order with no gaps. reshape of a contiguous array is a view; reshape of a transposed or strided slice usually has to copy.
An RL task that goes on forever without terminal states; it needs a discount factor below 1.
A random variable taking values in an interval, described by a density; each single value has probability 0.
A map that shrinks the distance between any two inputs by a fixed factor below 1; Bellman backups with gamma < 1 are contractions, so iteration converges.
Self-supervised learning that pulls together representations of two views of the same example and pushes apart those of different examples.
Finding a good (ideally optimal) policy, as opposed to prediction (evaluating a fixed policy).
A function whose chord between any two points lies on or above its graph; for smooth functions, one whose Hessian is positive semidefinite everywhere. Every local minimum is global.
A polygon that contains the whole segment between any two of its points; it is the intersection (AND) of the half-planes of its edges.
nn.Conv2d(in channels, out channels, k): slides out channels filters of shape (in channels, k, k) over an image. It has in out k k weights plus out biases; output height floor((H + 2p - k)/s) + 1.
A network built mainly from convolution layers (CNN for short); the standard model for images.
In DBSCAN, a point with at least min samples points (itself included) within distance eps.
A collection of documents, such as a training set of texts.
Cov(X, Y) / (sd X sd Y), between -1 and 1; plus or minus 1 exactly for a linear relation.
The matrix of correlations between features, C jk / (s j s k), with ones on the diagonal; np.corrcoef(X, rowvar=False).
x . y / ( x y ), the cosine of the angle between x and y: 1 same direction, 0 orthogonal, -1 opposite.
Cov(X, Y) = E[(X - mean X)(Y - mean Y)] = E[XY] - E[X] E[Y]; positive when X and Y tend to move together.
For a random vector, the matrix of all covariances Cov(X i, X j); symmetric, variances on the diagonal, always positive semidefinite.
A point where the gradient is zero: a minimum, a maximum or a saddle point.
Attention where queries come from one sequence and keys and values from another, as when a decoder reads an encoder's outputs.

Sliding a kernel over the input and summing kernel times input at each position, without flipping the kernel. It is what deep learning calls convolution (mathematical convolution flips the kernel first).
H(p, q) = -sum p j log q j: expected surprise under p when using probabilities q; minimized over q at q = p.
The usual loss for classifiers: the mean over samples of -log of the probability the model gave to the true class.
Estimating performance by training and validating several times on different splits of the training data.
nn.CrossEntropyLoss(): takes raw logits of shape (N, C) and class indices of shape (N,) with dtype torch.long; applies softmax itself and returns the mean of -log p(true class).
A table stored as text: one row per line, values separated by commas, usually with a header row.
The CSV rule for text containing a comma or a quote: wrap it in double quotes and double any quote inside. to csv and read csv handle it for you.
The error when tensors do not fit in GPU memory; reduce the batch size, delete unused tensors, or restart the runtime.
Problems that appear in many dimensions; for kNN, distances to the nearest and farthest points become nearly equal, so nearness says less.
Newton's method with the step multiplied by a learning rate below 1, for stability far from the minimum.
Creating extra training examples by label-preserving transformations (flips, crops, noise), applied to the training set only.
Information that will not be available at prediction time getting into training or features, which makes evaluation scores too optimistic.
A pandas table: rows, and named columns that each hold one dtype. Built with pd.DataFrame({name: list, ...}) or pd.read csv.
torch.utils.data.DataLoader(ds, batch size, shuffle): yields mini-batches of stacked samples; len(loader) is the number of batches, ceil(N / B) unless drop last=True.
A collection of examples.
A class with len (number of samples) and getitem (sample i), usually a subclass of torch.utils.data.Dataset; a DataLoader batches it.
Density-based clustering: core points have at least min samples points within eps; clusters grow through core points; other far points are noise (-1).
Deep convolutional GAN, the standard convolutional architecture and recipe (Adam with lr 2e-4, betas (0.5, 0.999)).
Denoising diffusion implicit models: a sampler that predicts x0 hat and re-noises it to an earlier level with the same eps, deterministic and with 20-50 steps.
Denoising diffusion probabilistic model (Ho et al. 2020): a diffusion model trained to predict the added noise with a plain MSE loss.
A ReLU unit whose pre-activation is negative for every input, so it outputs 0, gets zero gradient, and never recovers.
Function approximation, bootstrapping and off-policy learning together, which can make value estimates diverge.
The set of inputs where a classifier is exactly undecided; for logistic regression the hyperplane w . x + b = 0.
A decision tree of depth 1: one question and two leaves.
A model that predicts by asking a sequence of questions 'is feature j at most t?' from the root down to a leaf, which stores the prediction.
The part of a model that maps a representation back to data; in an autoencoder, z to the reconstruction x hat.
The token an encoder-decoder's decoder reads first; for T5 it is the pad id 0.
A transformer with a causal mask in every block, such as GPT; trained by next-token prediction and used to generate text.
Turning a language model's next-token distributions into text, one token at a time (greedy, beam search or sampling).
A copy of an object and everything inside it, made by copy.deepcopy.
DQN: Q-learning with a neural network Q(s, . ; theta), trained on replayed mini-batches against a periodically copied target network.
A value a parameter takes when the call leaves it out, as in def f(x, factor=2).
Removing a found eigenpair from a symmetric matrix, A - lambda v v^T, so that power iteration finds the next one.
The tree diagram of a hierarchical clustering; two branches join at the height (distance) where their clusters merged.
An autoencoder fed a corrupted input (for example x plus Gaussian noise) and trained to output the clean x.
Retrieval by cosine similarity of learned embeddings; matches meaning even without shared words.
The number of layers with weights in a network.
The number of questions on the longest root-to-leaf path of a tree.
A grouped convolution with groups = in channels: each channel is filtered by its own k x k kernel and channels never mix.
A depthwise convolution followed by a 1x1 convolution; it does the job of one ordinary convolution with far fewer parameters (MobileNet).
The (n, d) matrix X whose row i is the feature vector of example i.
The factor by which a square matrix scales volume (signed); 0 exactly when the matrix is not invertible.
A policy that puts all probability on one action in each state, written pi(s).
Detection transformer: a CNN backbone and a transformer encoder-decoder output a fixed set of box-and-class slots, trained with one-to-one Hungarian matching; no NMS.
The hardware a tensor or model lives on, such as the CPU or a GPU. In the contest it is always the CPU.
A multivariate normal with a diagonal covariance matrix, so its coordinates are independent normals.
Writing A = V Lambda V^{-1} with eigenvectors in V and eigenvalues in Lambda; then A^k = V Lambda^k V^{-1}.
2 A and B / ( A + B ) for two masks; 1 for a perfect match, 0 for no overlap; equals 2 IoU / (1 + IoU).
A mapping from keys to values, written {"cat": 0}. Looking up a missing key with d[key] raises KeyError.
A generative model that learns to reverse a gradual noising process: generation starts from pure noise and denoises step by step.
The constant alpha 0 in the heat equation; larger alpha means heat spreads and decays faster.
Spacing between a kernel's taps: with dilation d a k-tap kernel spans d(k - 1) + 1 positions but keeps k weights per axis.
Representing data with fewer features while keeping its main structure (PCA, UMAP).
The rate of change of f along a unit vector u, equal to the dot product of the gradient with u.
A folder: a named container for files and other directories.
gamma in [0, 1]: a reward k steps ahead counts gamma^k as much as an immediate one; 1/(1 - gamma) is a rough horizon.
A random variable whose possible values can be listed, such as a count or a class label.
In a GAN, the classifier D(x) in (0, 1) giving the probability that x is real; it outputs a logit in code.
The complete description of a random variable's probabilities, given by its PMF, PDF or CDF.
In text processing, one text example: a sentence, a review, an article.
df(t): the number of documents in the corpus that contain word t at least once.
The matrix of shape (number of documents, vocabulary size) whose entry (d, t) is a count or weight of word t in document d.
x . y = sum of x i y i, also written x^T y; one number. A linear model's prediction is a dot product plus a bias.
nn.Dropout(p): in training mode, sets each entry to 0 with probability p and scales the rest by 1/(1-p); in eval mode it does nothing. It has no parameters.
The data type shared by all entries of an array, such as int64, float64 or bool. Assigning a float into an int array cuts off the fraction.
In RL, computing value functions and optimal policies from a full model of the MDP by repeated Bellman backups.
In an MDP, p(s', r s, a): the probability of each next state and reward given the current state and action.
Keeping the parameters from the training step with the lowest validation loss instead of training to the end.
The truncated SVD A k is the best rank-k approximation, with A - A k F^2 = sum of the dropped sigma i^2.
The stretch factor lambda in A v = lambda v; the roots of det(A - lambda I) = 0.
A non-zero v with A v = lambda v: a direction the matrix only stretches.
np.einsum writes a product by naming each axis with a letter; letters missing after - are summed over, e.g. 'ij,jk- ik' is the matrix product.
Linear regression with both an L1 and an L2 penalty.
Evidence lower bound: E q[log p(x z)] - KL(q(z x) p(z)). It equals log p(x) minus KL(q true posterior), so it is at most log p(x).
Choosing k by plotting inertia against k and picking the bend after which more clusters reduce inertia little.
Done entry by entry: for arrays of the same shape, a + b adds matching entries.
Exponential linear unit: x for x = 0, e^x - 1 for x < 0. 1 + ELU is a positive feature map for linear attention.
A representation of each data point as a vector in a new space, such as the 2D coordinates a t-SNE or UMAP map assigns.
The length d of each embedding vector, a hyperparameter.
nn.Embedding(n, d): a learned table of n vectors of length d; index i returns row i. Equivalent to a bias-free linear layer applied to a one-hot vector. n d parameters.
The part of a model that maps an input to a representation; in an autoencoder, x to the latent vector z.
A transformer with a bidirectional encoder for the input and a causal decoder that also cross-attends to the encoder outputs (original transformer, T5, BART).
A transformer whose self-attention is bidirectional (padding mask only), such as BERT; each output vector describes its token in the context of the whole input.
A model made of many models whose predictions are combined by a vote or an average.
H(p) = -sum p j log p j, the expected surprise of a distribution; 0 when one outcome is certain, log k for uniform over k.
In RL, everything outside the agent; it answers each action with a reward and a next state.
A named setting that a program inherits from the shell, such as CUDA VISIBLE DEVICES.
One run of an episodic task, from a start state to a terminal state.
An RL task that breaks into episodes that each end in a terminal state.
One pass through the whole training set; with n examples and batch size B it has ceil(n / B) updates.
With probability eps pick a uniformly random action (from all actions), otherwise a greedy one; the greedy action then has probability 1 - eps + eps/ A .
A statistic used to estimate a population quantity, such as the sample mean for the population mean.
Any scikit-learn object that learns from data with fit; hyperparameters go in its constructor and learned values end in an underscore.
Straight-line distance: the square root of the sum of squared coordinate differences, a - b .
model.eval() sets training=False on every submodule, so dropout is off and batch norm uses its stored statistics. It does not stop gradient tracking or freeze parameters.
A set of outcomes (a subset of the sample space); it happens if the outcome lies in it.
Monte Carlo prediction that averages the returns after every visit to each state.
The fraction of outputs identical to the reference (often after lowercasing and stripping punctuation); used for short answers.
One data point, one row of a dataset (also called a sample). It has features and, in supervised learning, a label.
An error object Python raises when something goes wrong, with a type (such as KeyError) and a message.
E[X] = sum of x p(x) (or the integral of x f(x)): the probability-weighted average value. A fair die has E[X] = 3.5.
The average points per question you would get if you faced the same situation many times. For a Part 1 answer that is right with probability p, it is 7.5p.
Storing transitions in a buffer and training on random mini-batches from it, which breaks correlations and reuses data.
lambda j / sum of all eigenvalues: the fraction of the total variance carried by principal component j.
The opposite of vanishing gradients: per-layer factors above 1 multiply into huge gradients and unstable updates. Gradient clipping is the usual fix.
Taking the action that currently looks best to collect reward.
Taking actions to learn more about them, possibly giving up reward now.
Starting episodes at random state-action pairs so that every pair gets visited, for Monte Carlo estimation of q.
avg <- (1 - m) avg + m new: a running average in which old values fade out geometrically. Batch norm's running statistics and Adam's m and v are examples.
Predicting at inputs outside the range covered by the training data, where the model's form, not the data, decides the prediction.
The harmonic mean of precision and recall: 2PR / (P + R) = 2TP / (2TP + FP + FN).
n! = n (n - 1) ... 1, the number of orderings of n items; 0! = 1.
FN: an actual positive predicted negative (a miss).
FP: an actual negative predicted positive (a false alarm).
FPR = FP / (FP + TN), the fraction of actual negatives predicted positive.
The number of inputs each output of a layer sums over: in features for nn.Linear, in channels k k for a convolution.
The number of outputs of a layer that each input feeds: out features for nn.Linear.
Indexing with an array of integers. It picks those positions in order, repeats allowed, and returns a copy. X[rows, cols] pairs the two index arrays entry by entry.
One measured quantity describing each sample (age, pixel brightness). In a data table X of shape (n, d), each column is a feature.
Building new features from existing ones, such as ratios, date parts, logs or bins.
Transfer learning that keeps a pretrained backbone frozen and trains only a new head on its outputs.
Early CNN layers (small receptive field, high resolution) detect edges and colors; deeper layers (large receptive field, low resolution, many channels) detect parts and whole objects.
The output of one channel of a convolution layer: a grid saying how strongly that kernel's pattern appears at each position.
A function phi from R^d to R^l with sim(q, k) = phi(q) . phi(k); in linear attention it replaces exp(q . k / sqrt(d)).
Choosing a subset of the features to use and dropping the rest, usually the ones that carry little information about the label.
The features of one example written as a list of numbers, such as x = (80, 3).
Putting a few worked input-output examples in the prompt before the real input (in-context learning).
Read, write and execute rights for a file's owner, its group and everyone else; ls -l shows them and chmod changes them.
Training some or all of a pretrained model's parameters on a new task, usually with a small learning rate.
Monte Carlo prediction that averages, per episode, only the return after the first visit to each state.
Semi-supervised method: pseudo-label from a weak augmentation if confident, then train the strong augmentation's prediction toward it with cross-entropy.
A 2-byte float format with a small range (smallest normal number about 6e-5); small gradients underflow, so it is used with a GradScaler.
32-bit floating point (about 7 significant digits). PyTorch's default float dtype; NumPy's default is float64.
The // operator: divide, then round down toward minus infinity. -7 // 2 is -4.
Floating-point operations: multiplications and additions counted separately, so about 2 x the number of multiply-accumulates. Conventions vary; use the one a problem states.
One of the k equal parts of the data in k-fold cross-validation.
The LSTM gate f t that scales the old cell state; d c t / d c (t-1) = diag(f t).
A short string that says how to write a number as text: "%.6f" means fixed-point with six digits after the decimal point, so 2.5 becomes 2.500000.

A function attached with module.register forward hook(fn) that PyTorch calls as fn(module, inputs, output) after the module's forward; used to read intermediate shapes. Remove it with the returned handle.
Computing a model's outputs and loss from its inputs, left to right through the computational graph.
Computing the data a model produces from known parameters, such as the field of a known source.
In a diffusion model, the fixed noising chain x t = sqrt(alpha t) x {t-1} + sqrt(1 - alpha t) eps t that turns data into noise.
The columns 1, sin(2 pi k x / P), cos(2 pi k x / P) for k = 1..K: 2K + 1 columns. Linear regression on them gives a model that repeats with period P.
Writing a signal as a sum of sines and cosines; np.fft.rfft computes it for evenly spaced real samples, and np.fft.rfftfreq gives each coefficient's frequency.
A short slice of a waveform (for example 400 samples = 25 ms at 16 kHz) analyzed as a unit; consecutive frames overlap.
Setting requires grad=False on parameters so training leaves them unchanged: module.requires grad (False). A new layer added afterward still trains.
A F = square root of the sum of all squared entries; A F^2 = sum of sigma i^2.
The Hugging Face method that builds a model or tokenizer from a name (downloaded once into a cache) or a local folder; local files only=True or HF HUB OFFLINE=1 forbids the network.
Training every parameter of a pretrained model on the new task, with a small learning rate.
Training where every step uses the whole training set, so one epoch is one step.
Gradient descent that uses every training example to compute each gradient.
A layer in which every output depends on every input through its own weight: nn.Linear in PyTorch.
Representing a value function (or policy) by a parameterized function such as a linear model or neural network instead of a table.
A name in a function's def line that receives a value when the function is called.
